train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 37075/97) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. The Court ruled that the application was not admissible on 22 November 2001. The applicant appealed the decision to suspend his right to practise for one year. name: Elena Riera Blume
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The application concerned the detention of the applicants, who are presumed members of a “sect” The applicants relied on Articles 3, 5, 8 and 9 of the Convention. The case was examined by the Court of Justice of Spain. It was declared admissible on 9 March 1999 by the Chamber of Judges of the European Court of Human rights (“the Court’s” Fourth Section). The application was dismissed on 4 June 1998 by the Third Section of the Court, and was dismissed again on 6 June 1998. The Court of Judges’ decision was made by the President of the Council of Europe (‘the Council’). The applicants were Ms Elena Riera Blume, Ms Concepción Riera, Ms María Luz Casado Perez, Ms Daría Amelía Casado, and Mr Javier Bruna Reverter. The Court found that there was no basis on which such a settlement could be reached. It also decided that if there was not a friendly settlement of the case, a public hearing would be held (Rule 59 § 2). The Court also asked the applicants to submit their claims for just satisfaction under Article 41 of the Convention (Rule 60) The Court heard addresses by them and also their replies to questions from one its members. Sales Aige, Javier Bruna Reverter, were arrested in June 1984. They were part of a group known by the name of CEIS (Centro Esotérico de Investigaciones) The group was alleged to have led their followers to prostitution and other activities designed to obtain money for the organisation. A judge ordered that they be handed over to their families so that they could recover their psychological balance. In the light of information from an official at the DGSC, which was confirmed by the prosecuting authorities, there was a danger that the members of the sect would react unpredictably if they were released. The judge in question confirmed his oral instruction in a decision of 26 July 1984. The applicants were allegedly subjected to a process of ‘deprogramming’ by a psychologist and a psychiatrist at the request of Pro Juventud. On 29 and 30 June 1984, after being informed of their rights, they were questioned by C.T.R., the Assistant Director-General of Public Safety, aided by a lawyer not appointed by the applicants. The applicants lodged a criminal complaint alleging false imprisonment, offences against the exercise of personal rights, falsification of documents, usurpation of functions and misappropriation of goods. The Barcelona Audiencia Provincial acquitted the accused, holding that the acts complained of had been prompted by a philanthropic, legitimate and well-intentioned motive. The applicants lodged an appeal (recurso de amparo) with the Constitutional Court. In their appeal they alleged violations of the right to religious freedom (Article 16 of the Constitution) They also claimed the defendants' conduct was in keeping with what society and the legal order, taken as a whole, require in situations such as those of the instant case. In conclusion, the offence of false imprisonment cannot be said to have been committed since, firstly, there was no intention on the part of the defendants to deprive anybody of his or her liberty and, on the contrary, their intention, which has been fully proved, was to prevent imminent and very serious harm. Mr José Victor Riera Blume was held to have withdrawn on account of failure, through his own fault, to comply with a formal requirement. On 10 March 1997 the Constitutional Court dismissed the amparo appeal. The court added that the decisions being challenged had not infringed any of the rights relied on by the five remaining appellants, seeing that they were limited to declaring that the acts with which the defendants were charged did not amount to the offences for which they were being prosecuted. It also pointed out that, according to its case-law, the Constitution did not confer, as such, a right to secure criminal convictions of third parties.

The case originated in an application (no. 37680/97) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The application concerned the detention of the applicants, who are presumed members of a “sect’ The case was examined by the Court of Justice of the European Union in March 1999, and declared admissible on 9 March 1999. The court also ruled in favour of six of the seven applicants. The case is still pending at the European Court of Human rights in Strasbourg, France, and at the High Court of Europe in Berlin, Germany, where the case is being heard by the President of the Court. The application was brought by Ms Elena Riera Blume, Mr Javier Bruna Reverter, Ms María Luz Casado Perez and Ms Daría Amelía Casado. The applicants were seeking compensation for their deprivation of liberty and interference with their right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion. The Court found that there was no basis on which such a settlement could be reached. It declared the remainder of their application inadmissible. It decided that if there was not a friendly settlement of the case, a public hearing would be held. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 June 1999. Sales Aige, Javier Bruna Reverter, were born in 1954, 1952, 1950,. 1950, 1950, 1951 and 1957 respectively and live in Valencia (Spain). At an unknown date in 1983 the Public Safety Department (“the DGSC”) of the Generalitat (government) of Catalonia received through Pro Juventud (‘Pro Youth’), an association formed to fight against sects. Several people alleged that members of their families had been ensnared by a group known by the name of CEIS (Centro Esotérico de Investigaciones) According to the families’ complaints, those who ran the CEIS managed to bring about a complete change of personality in their followers. The applicants were taken by members of the Catalan police in official vehicles to a hotel some thirty kilometres from Barcelona. While at the hotel the applicants were allegedly subjected to a process of “deprogramming” by a psychologist and a psychiatrist at the request of Pro Juventud. On 30 June 1984 the applicants left the hotel. The applicants lodged a criminal complaint alleging false imprisonment, offences against the exercise of personal rights, falsification of documents, usurpation of functions and misappropriation of goods. The Barcelona Audiencia Provincial acquitted the accused, holding that the acts complained of had been prompted by a philanthropic, legitimate and well-intentioned motive and that there had been no intention of depriving the applicants of their liberty. ‘The detention took place with the sole aim – a very laudable and plausible one – of avoiding worse evils than those complained of by the appellants, so that there was no unlawfulness strictly and properly understood’ ‘It cannot be maintained, in order to argue the contrary, that the wishes of the persons who underwent deprogramming could only have been overridden by the members of their families after proceedings to establish incapacity, seeing that the position of those concerned called for immediate treatment, without any delay' ‘In conclusion, the offence of false imprisonment cannot be said to have been committed since, firstly, there was. no intention on the part of the defendants to deprive anybody of his or her liberty and, on the contrary. their intention, which has been fully proved, was to prevent imminent and very serious harm befalling the persons concerned’ Mr José Victor Riera Blume was held to have withdrawn on account of failure, through his own fault, to comply with a formal requirement. The court added that the decisions being challenged had not infringed any of the rights relied on by the five remaining appellants, seeing that they were limited to declaring that the acts with which the defendants were charged did not amount to the offences for which they were being prosecuted. The Constitutional Court pointed out, firstly, that there was no fundamental right to have a person convicted and, secondly, that it could not protect fundamental rights by quashing final substantive judgments whereby defendants had been acquitted. It also pointed out that, according to its case-law, the Constitution did not confer a right to secure criminal convictions of third parties.

The court added that the decisions being challenged had not infringed any of the rights relied on by the five remaining appellants, seeing that they were limited to declaring that the acts with which the defendants were charged did not amount to the offences for which they were being prosecuted. It also pointed out, according to its case-law, the Constitution did not confer a right to secure criminal convictions of third parties.

name: H.İ. Er
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 21377/04) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the criminal proceedings to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). The applicant was born in 1964 and lives in Istanbul. He served as a first lieutenant in the Turkish Armed Forces at the material time. He was arrested on suspicion of, inter alia, professional misconduct and bribery. The case was heard by the Çorlu Military Court. The case was referred to the Kırklareli Assize Court in December 2001. In December 2003, the court discontinued the proceedings against the applicant as the prosecution had become time-barred. The application was dismissed in January 2008. The applicant was found guilty as charged in relation to the offences which were not time-Barred and of which he had not already been acquitted. He was acquitted of the rest of the charges against him in August 1999. In March 2001, the Military Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the first-instance court once again.

name: Kemal Evcimen
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 21865/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was accused of membership of an illegal organisation, the DHKP-C (the Revolutionary People's Liberation Party- Front) The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the Proceedings before the Court. The case-file was sent to the Erzurum State Security Court in 1997. In 1998 the court convicted the applicant under Article 168 of the Criminal Code of membership of an illegal organisation, namely the DHKP-C. The court sentenced the applicant to twelve years and six months' imprisonment. On 29 May 2004 the applicant was conditionally released from prison. The case was closed by the Court of Cassation on 18 November 1999. The cases against the applicant and his co-accused were subsequently joined before the Erzincan State security Court. The applicant was later convicted of disseminating separatist propaganda and incitement to hatred and hostility through the medium of his newspaper.

name: Yunis Bolukoç
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35392/04) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the lack of legal assistance during detention in police custody. The application was filed by three Turkish nationals, Mr Yunis Bolukoç, Mr Ferhat Kıyak and Mr Ayhan Ateş (“the applicants”), on 9 July 2004. The applicants were represented by Mr M. Filorinali and Ms Y. Başara, lawyers practising in İstanbul. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) was represented by their Agent. The applicants were bought before the prosecutor at the ISSC, where they denied the accusations against them. The first applicant refused to make a statement to the police and stated that he was on hunger strike until his transfer to judicial authorities. The second and the third applicant took part in a reconstruction of events where they admitted, inter alia, to throwing a Molotov cocktail at a building in Istiklal on 30 March 2000. The applicants were brought before a judge at theISSC where they reiterated the statements they had made to the prosecutor. The legal representative of the second and third applicants was present at the hearing. name: Halil Kaya
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 22922/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaint concerning the lack of legal assistance to the applicant during his police custody. In convicting the applicant, the court had regard to his statements to the police and the public prosecutor, which were taken in the absence of a lawyer. The court also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicant was convicted under Article 169 of the Criminal Code. He was sentenced to three months and ten days’ imprisonment and his sentence was converted to a fine. On 7 October 2004 the applicant appealed. On 8 May 2006 the court found the applicant guilty under Article 215 of Law no. 5326 and sentenced him to twenty five days' imprisonment. This decision was upheld by the Adana Assize Court on 20 June 2007. The case file was remitted to the Court of Cassation for re-examination on 19 December 2005. In his decision, the prosecutor referred to new legislation which had entered into force on 12 October 2004. The Prosecutor drew further attention to another new amendment which had been made on 31 March 2005 to Law no, 5326 concerning misdemeanours.

The case originated in an application (no. 22922/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was taken into police custody on suspicion of aiding and abetting an illegal organisation by way of chanting slogans in favour of that organisation and by burning tyres in the streets. The same day he was interrogated by the police and the public prosecutor respectively, in the absence of a lawyer. On 3 December 2001 the State Security Court delivered its judgment. It convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to two years and six months’ imprisonment. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaint. On 11 September 2002 the applicant was sent to prison to serve his sentence. On 30 July 2003 Law no. 4963 entered into force, which amended Article 169 of the Criminal Code. On 29 August 2003 the applicant’s lawyer requested the re-opening of the proceedings. On 7 October 2004 the court held that the applicant should not be convicted under Article 169 but under Article 312. As a result, he was sentenced to three months and ten days’ imprisonment and his sentence was converted to a fine. On 19 December 2005 the Principal Public Prosecutor at the Court of Cassation decided that the case file should be remitted to the Adana Criminal Court for re-examination.

The President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the Lutz and Englert cases should be considered by the same Chamber. The Government and the Commission had until 1 July 1986 to file memorials. The applicant’s memorial - drafted in German - was lodged with the registry on 1 July. The Government's memorial was lodged on 19 November. The Court heard addresses by Mrs. Maier for the Government, by. Mr. Weitzel for the Commission and by Mr. Bergemann for the applicant, as well as their replies to its. questions. The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Commission, the government and the applicant filed a number of documents and written comments between 9 February and 22 May 1987, either at the Court's request or of their own. Martha Nölkenbockhoff, a German national, is the widow and heir of Mr. Theodor Nönkenbocks. Her husband was a senior manager in a holding company, Stumm AG, whose trading activities centred on iron, steel and fuel, including motor fuel. He was found guilty inter alia on several charges of breach of trust (Untreue), criminal bankruptcy (Bankrott) and fraud (Betrug), and given an aggregate sentence of eight years’ imprisonment. His four co-defendants were also sentenced to prison terms - two of them, for more or less identical offences and a few additional ones, to nine years, nine months and to eight years, six months. Mr. Nölkenbockhoff entered an appeal on points of law on the same day that judgment was given. The Federal Court of Justice (Bundesgerichtshof) had not given a decision by the time he died on 13 November, so that the proceedings came to an end without any decision being taken on his appeal. Three of the co-defendants, who had likewise challenged the Regional Court’s judgment, later withdrew their appeals. The appeal lodged by the fourth person convicted, Mr. M, was dismissed by the Federal Court on 7 July 1982 as being manifestly ill-founded. The applicant sought orders that the Treasury should bear the necessary costs and expenses incurred by her late husband in connection with his conviction. On 5 March 1982, the Essen Regional Court found against Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff. she requested the Regional Court to adjourn a decision on her applications until such time as the Federal Court of Justice had given judgment on the appeal brought by the co-defendant Mr. M. Its decision read as follows: “... The applications are admissible ... but ill-founded. Where proceedings are terminated by reason of a defendant’s death, his necessary costs and expenses are normally borne by the Treasury, but this does not apply where, were it not for this technical bar, the defendant would almost certainly have been convicted or his conviction almost certainly would have been upheld" The applicant appealed to the Hamm Court of Appeal against that decision on 11 March 1982. In written pleadings dated 18 March, she challenged, inter alia, the Regional Court’s finding that, had her husband not died, he “would almost certainly have been convicted”. The court caused the conviction to “become final’ posthumously, thereby prejudicing her as the defendant's widow, the court said. “The court does not consider it necessary to defer judgment until a decision has been given on the co-defendant M’’, said the court. The judge added that the reasons given for the judgment were not consistent with its assessment of the case as a whole. The Regional Court disregarded the presumption of innocence in stating that the grounds of appeal afforded no reason to suppose that the defendant would have been acquitted. It was as if it were sought to obtain a final (abschliessend) conviction of the deceased by a side wind in the form of a decision as to costs. The applicant pointed out in addition that from the outset her husband had denied having committed any offences and had indeed been acquitted on several counts. The court, however, had prejudged the Federal Court’s decision by holding that the plea alleging a breach of substantive law again provided nothing to support the hypothesis of an acquittal. Since criminal law was based on the principle of individual guilt, it was quite simply unacceptable. The Hamm Court of Appeal dismissed the action on 14 July 1982. It left open the question whether, in the event of a defendant’s death before the final conclusion (rechtskräftiger Abschluss) of criminal proceedings, a decision such as that sought by Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff could be taken, by analogy. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the charges against M and her husband were very different. The appeal was also dismissed because of the fact that the case was pending before the Federal Court of Justice. The applicant claimed that there were ‘considerable dissimilarities’ between the charges and the grounds of their appeals. Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff then applied to the Federal Constitutional Court claiming a breach of Article 1 of the Basic Law. On 30 September 1982, a bench of three judges of the Constitutional Court refused to entertain the constitutional complaint. The reasons for its decision were as follows: “The presumption of innocence, which is founded on the principle of the rule of law, precludes treating as guilty a person who has not been finally (rechtskräftig) convicted.’ ‘That does not mean, however, that in every case costs must be reimbursed where the proceedings are terminated without guilt having been established (Schuldnachweis) ... The courts’ reference to the lack of success of the appeal proceedings instituted by the co-defendant M and to the withdrawal of the appeals on points of law entered by the other defendants is clearly to be regarded merely as an additional argument, and the impugned decisions are not based on it. Nor do the grounds advanced in support of the constitutional complaint show the unreasonableness of the Regional Court’s opinion that, had the proceedings been continued, a conviction would have been more likely than an acquittal. (b) Nor was the prediction of the outcome of the proceedings arbitrary in nature. the proceedings had they been continued. That was the only relevant issue for the order as to costs. (aa) Neither the alleged defects ... in the judgment convicting the defendant nor the grounds of the Appeal on Points of Law make it possible to dismiss as untenable the conclusion reached in the contested decisions.

Mr Nölkenbockhoff entered an appeal on points of law on the same day that judgment was given. The Federal Court of Justice (Bundesgerichtshof) had not given a decision by the time he died on 13 November. Three of the co-defendants, who had likewise challenged the Regional Court’s judgment, later withdrew their appeals. The appeal lodged by the fourth person convicted, Mr. M, was dismissed by the Federal Court on 7 July 1982 as being manifestly ill-founded. The applicant sought orders that the Treasury should bear the necessary costs and expenses incurred by her late husband in connection with his conviction. The Essen Regional Court found against Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff on 5 March 1982. She had already been found guilty, in a judgment that had not become final, after lengthy court proceedings in a trial (Hauptverhandlung) lasting more than three and a half years. Three co-defendants, who were likewise sentenced to several years’ imprisonment, have withdrawn their appeals on points of law, thereby confirming the judgment against them, argues decisively in favour of the correctness (materielle Richtigkeit) of the judgment. The submissions made by the defence in its full pleadings afford no reason to suppose that the defendant would have been acquitted had the proceedings continued. The court declines to award compensation for the time spent in detention on remand. The reasons given for the judgment are not consistent with its assessment of the case as a whole. The court does not consider it necessary to defer judgment until a decision has been given on the co-defendant M’s appeal on points of law. The applicant appealed to the Hamm Court of Appeal against that decision on 11 March 1982. In written pleadings dated 18 March, she challenged, inter alia, the Regional Court's finding that, had her husband not died, he “would almost certainly have been convicted”. She claimed that that statement was erroneous and infringed the Basic Law. The Regional Court disregarded the presumption of innocence in stating that the grounds of appeal afforded no reason to suppose that the defendant would have been acquitted. It was as if it were sought to obtain a final (abschliessend) conviction of the deceased by a side wind in the form of a decision as to costs. The applicant pointed out in addition that from the outset her husband had denied having committed any offences and had indeed been acquitted on several counts. Since criminal law was based on the principle of individual guilt, it was quite simply unacceptable - and, once again, contrary to Article 6 § 2 (art. 6-2) - to judge the deceased by the conduct of three of the co-defendants. The Hamm Court of Appeal dismissed the action on 14 July 1982. It left open the question whether, in the event of a defendant’s death before the final conclusion (rechtskräftiger Abschluss) of criminal proceedings, a decision such as that sought by Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff could be taken, by analogy, under Article 467 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act (see paragraphs 24-26 below) The application was dismissed because of a lack of evidence. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that there was insufficient evidence to prove that the defendant had killed his wife. The case is still pending before the Federal Court of Justice. Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff then applied to the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) claiming a breach of the Basic Law. On 30 September 1982, a bench of three judges of the Constitutional Court refused to entertain the constitutional complaint. The reasons for its decision were as follows: “The presumption of innocence, which is founded on the principle of the rule of law, precludes treating as guilty a person who has not been finally (rechtskräftig) convicted’. The decision on the claim for compensation is based on section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act. Both provisions confer on the courts a degree of discretion. The courts’ reference to the lack of success of the appeal proceedings instituted by the co-defendant M and to the withdrawal of the appeals on points of law entered by the other defendants is clearly to be regarded merely as an additional argument, and the impugned decisions are not based on it. Nor do the grounds advanced in support of the constitutional complaint show the unreasonableness of the Regional Court’s opinion that, had the proceedings been continued, a conviction would have been more likely than an acquittal.“Eine derartige Einschätzung enthält indessen nicht die Feststellung einer Schuld, sondern lediglich die Fest stellung  einer fortbestehenden Verdachtslage”.

name: Murat Biçer
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 21316/05) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, a former military student, was born in 1981 and lives in Yalova. He was expelled from the naval academy in accordance with the Law of Military Academies (Law no. 4466) for failing his class twice. Claiming that his exam in Mathematics 1 had not been graded correctly, he demanded the reassessment of his paper in the relevant subject. On 9 January 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the application at the same time as its admissibility. Supreme Military Administrative Court held a hearing, where it dismissed the applicant's request for annulment of the expulsion order. The written opinion submitted by the principal public prosecutor to this court prior to the hearing was not communicated to the applicant. The applicant's rectification request was rejected on 12 January 2005. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the applicant had not made a good faith effort to comply with the terms of his expulsion. The court ruled that the expulsion was not a breach of the terms and conditions of his release from prison. The case was settled out of court and the applicant was allowed to return to his home country.

name: David Hood
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court, as established under former Article 19 of the Convention, by the Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland on 14 August 1998. It originated in an application (no. 27267/95) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’s”) by a British national, Mr David Hood, on 18 April 1995. After the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 on 1 November 1998 and in accordance with the provisions of Article 5 § 5 thereof, the case was referral to the Grand Chamber of the Court. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (former Rule 30). The Grand Chamber included ex officio Sir Nicolas Bratza. David Hood was a soldier with the regular forces of the British army. He went absent without leave from his unit in Germany three times. He was remanded for trial by court martial on an assault charge. He remained absent for almost two and a half years and he gave himself up to the civilian police in December 1993. The applicant, David Hood, is a British national born in 1970. He remains in the United Kingdom. He has been detained in Germany since 1993. He is serving a three-year sentence for his part in a terrorist attack on a school in the town of Wuppertal, Germany. He and his family were detained by German authorities at the time of his detention. The British government claims that he was detained for his own safety. The applicant did not return after two weeks’ leave (his fourth absence without leave) on 11 May 1994. On 27 November 1994 he was arrested at his home by the civilian police and taken by army escort to Brompton Barracks. On 4 January 1995 the applicant appeared before the unit adjutant and was given the abstract of evidence. He was told that he should read the abstract and check that it was accurate. The charge sheet, dated 25 January 1995 and signed by his commanding officer and on behalf of the convening officer, recorded two charges of absence without. leave and two of desertion contrary to the Army Act 1955. The applicant pleaded not guilty. Judge advocate found that Rule 10 of the Rules of Procedure (Army) 1972 had been followed. Given the applicant’s legal representation at the relevant time and the procedures followed, the judge advocate could not see ‘how a fairer situation could have arisen’ The applicant was convicted on the two charges of absence without leave and on one of the charges of desertion. He was sentenced to be imprisoned for eight months and to be dismissed from the service. After confirmation and promulgation of the conviction and sentence, the applicant petitioned the Army. By letter dated 13 July 1995 the applicant was informed that his petition to the Army Board had been rejected. High Court rejected the application. The court found, inter alia, that the delay report had been properly completed in a timely fashion. It noted that the expressed reason for the applicant’s continued detention was to prevent his absconding and found that “perfectly understandable” given the charges against him. The application was rejected by the Court of Appeal on Thursday. The case is still pending at the High Court in Dublin, the court said on Friday. He had been remanded for trial by court martial on an assault charge (later abandoned) He remained absent for almost two and a half years and he gave himself up to the civilian police in December 1993. The relevant detention took place in a detention centre in Germany. He was detained for more than two years. The British government appealed to the European Court of Human Rights. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 9 December 1998. The applicant, David Hood, is a British national born in 1970. He was taken by army escort to Brompton Barracks on 28 November 1994. The applicant was then remanded for trial by court martial by his commanding officer. He applied for legal aid from the military authorities. The court martial took place on 3 and 4 April 1995. The assistant prosecuting officer was the unit adjutant and the applicant, who was legally represented, pleaded not guilty. The hearing was adjourned until the applicant’s solicitor could give evidence. The applicant was convicted on the two charges of absence without leave and on one of the charges of desertion. He was sentenced to be imprisoned for eight months and to be dismissed from the service. The judge advocate found that Rule 10 of the Rules of Procedure (Army) 1972 had been followed. name: Manfred Jacubowski
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the Government of the Federal Republic of Germany. It originated in an application (no. 15088/89) against Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a German national, Mr Manfred Jacubowski, on 11 April 1989. The object of the application and of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10 ( art. 10) of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The lawyer was given leave by the President to use the German language. The Government’s memorial was received on 16 July 1993 and the applicant's memorial on 19 July. On 30 July the Deputy Secretary to the Commission informed the Registrar that the Delegate would submit his observations at the hearing. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 November 1993. The Court heard addresses by Mr Meyer-Ladewig, Mr von Mühlendahl, Mr Frowein and Mr Meilicke, and also replies to its questions. In the first case Mr Jacubowski sought to challenge his dismissal and in the second he claimed the right to reply to a press release issued by his employer. The applicant’s dismissal began on 17 July 1984. Mr Jacubowski challenged the validity of the latter dismissal, which was renewed on 12 October. A final dismissal notice, based on new grounds, was sent to him on 12 February 1985. The Cologne Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) held on 11 October 1988 that he had been validly dismissed on 28 October 1984. According to the court, the distribution of the circular and cuttings was to be regarded as a serious breach of the applicant's duty of loyalty. By sending press articles to a large number of influential professionals and endorsing in the circular their objectively unfavourable statements, MrJacubowski had knowingly run the risk of causing the employer considerable prejudice. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 43452/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, an anaesthesiologist, was working at the Kars State Hospital when criminal proceedings were instigated against him for alleged involvement in an illegal organisation. He was accused together with other suspects of, inter alia, hanging posters and banners in various places in Ankara on behalf of that organisation. On 11 September 2001 the Ankara State Security Court, on the basis of the evidence contained in the case file, convicted the applicant under Article 7 § 1 of Law no. 3713 and sentenced him to two years and six months. The applicant was acquitted of all charges on 11 May 2004. He was dismissed from the civil service on 28 February 2002. The Supreme Disciplinary Commission of the Ministry of Health decided to dismiss the applicant. This decision was subsequently upheld by the Supreme Administrative Court on 27 December 2005. According to an attestation dated 10 September 2007 the applicant is currently employed at Atasam hospital in Samsun. The applicant did not submit any court decisions in his application for a retrial. In his observations the applicant submitted that, despite his acquittal, his request for aRetrial had been rejected by the administrative court. However, he did not Submit any Court decisions.

The case was brought by a Turkish woman whose husband was killed in a car crash. name: Pierre Müller
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Twenty-five minutes after their arrival at the police station, at 3.40 p.m., they were formally arrested under section 11 (1) of the Northern Ireland law. They were then taken to the Royal Courts of Justice in London, where they were granted bail. The applicants appealed to the European Court of Human Rights for permission to stay in the UK. (Emergency Provisions) Act 1978 (“the 1978 Act’; see paragraph 16 below) They were informed that they were being arrested under this section and that this was because the arresting officer suspected them of being terrorists. (Emergency Provisions) Act 1978 (“the 1978 Act’) They were asked about their suspected involvement in intelligence gathering and courier work for the Provisional Irish Republican Army. The information underlying the suspicion against them was already known to the police when they stopped their car. No charges were brought against either applicant. The first applicant was released at 11.40 a.m. on 7 February 1986 and the second applicant five minutes later. The third applicant, Mr Samuel Hartley, resides in Waterfoot, County Antrim, Northern Ireland. On 18 August 1986 he was arrested at his home, in his parents’ presence, at 7.55 a.M. He was informed at the time of his arrest that he was being arrested as he was suspected of being a terrorist. The motive behind the kidnapping was believed to have been an attempt to force the young woman to retract an allegation of rape made the previous year. No charges were brought against him. He was released on 19 August 1986 at 2.10 p.m. after 30 hours and 15 minutes in detention. He brought no proceedings in connection with his arrest or detention. The applicant Hartley denied any involvement in the kidnap incident but he has not contradicted the Government’s assertion that he was asked about it.

name: Brian Bell
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 41534/98) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 15 November 2005, a Chamber of the Fourth Section of the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The case was decided in favour of the applicant and the Government. The applicant, Mr Brian Bell, was a soldier serving as a Private with the Grenadier Guards of the British Army, stationed in Northern Ireland. The applicant was charged with the offence of using insubordinate language to a superior. He claimed that the medical centre refused to provide a record of his examination establishing that he had not had a nose bleed on the night in question. The Government denied that Corporal G had been directed not to give evidence in support of his case. The hearing lasted approximately ten minutes. The applicant accepted that he received a version of the information pamphlet entitled “Rights of a Soldier charged with an offence under the Army Act 1955” but claimed that it was the pre-October 1997 version and thus out of date. The application was dismissed on appeal.  applicant pleaded not guilty and was sentenced to seven days' detention and seven days’ associated loss of pay. The applicant was required to stand to attention throughout the hearing and was permitted to speak only when invited to do so by the CO. An officer appointed to look after the applicant’s interests, whose identity remained unknown to the applicant and with whom he had not discussed his case, did not speak at any point during the hearing. The Government denied any such interruption. The company commander, who was present by this time, said that the applicant was a satisfactory member of his company. The CO then said that he found the applicant guilty.

A decision of 15 November 2005, a Chamber of the Fourth Section of the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant was charged with the offence of using insubordinate language to a superior contrary to section 33(1)(b) of the Army Act 1955. The applicant claimed that he then went to the medical centre and asked for a record of his examination establishing that he had not had a nose bleed on the night in question. He claimed that staff at the medical center refused to provide the record and the Government disputed this. The Government argued that it was routine for witnesses to be called into the Regimental Sergeant Major’s office so that the procedure to be followed at the hearing could be explained and they denied that Corporal G had been directed as the applicant alleged. The applicant was required to stand to attention throughout the hearing and was permitted to speak only when invited to do so by the CO. An officer appointed to look after the applicant’s interests, whose identity remained unknown to the applicant and with whom he had not discussed his case, did not speak at any point during the hearing. The CO found the applicant guilty and sentenced him to seven days’ detention and seven days' associated loss of pay. The applicant served his sentence in a locked cell in the battalion guardroom. The Government denied any such interruption. The company commander, who was present by this time, said that the applicant was a satisfactory member of his company.

eval_texts: The case stems from an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights in 1998. The applicant was a soldier serving as a Private with the Grenadier Guards of the British Army. He complained that his Commanding Officer lacked independence and impartiality. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 15 November 2005, a Chamber of the Fourth Section of the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The case continues. The applicant was charged with the offence of using insubordinate language to a superior contrary to section 33(1)(b) of the Army Act 1955. The hearing lasted approximately ten minutes. The Government argued that it was routine for witnesses to be called into the Regimental Sergeant Major’s office so that the procedure to be followed at the hearing could be explained. The applicant claimed that he then went to the medical centre and asked for a record of his examination establishing that he had not had a nose bleed on the night in question. He claimed that staff at the medical center refused to provide the record and the Government disputed this. The applicant was required to stand to attention throughout the hearing. He was permitted to speak only when invited to do so by the CO. An officer appointed to look after the applicant’s interests, whose identity remained unknown to the applicant and with whom he had not discussed his case, did not speak at any point. The CO found the applicant guilty and sentenced him to seven days’ detention and seven days' associated loss of pay. The applicant served his sentence in a locked cell in the battalion guardroom. name: Edward Szuluk
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the monitoring of his medical correspondence while he was in prison breached his right to respect for his correspondence and private life under Article 8. The application was lodged by a British national, Mr Edward Szuluk (“the applicant”), on 14 October 2005. He was sentenced by a Crown Court to a total of fourteen years’ imprisonment for conspiracy to supply Class A drugs and two offences of possession of a Class A drug with intent to supply. The Government were represented by their Agent, Ms H. Moynihan of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The applicant expressed his concerns about his medical correspondence with his external medical specialist being read. He applied to the prison governor for a direction that such correspondence should be accorded confidentiality. It was decided that the applicant’s medical correspondence would not be read provided that certain conditions were met. The prison governor subsequently reconsidered his decision after seeking advice from HM Prison Service Headquarters. On 20 February 2004 the presiding High Court judge, Mr Justice Collins, allowed the applicant's claim for judicial review. The judge concluded that there were exceptional circumstances in the applicants case. The applicant, understandably, wanted to ensure that his treatment in prison did not affect him adversely. He was concerned that his attempts to confirm that he was receiving adequate treatment in hospital might be regarded as criticism. The Court of Appeal concluded that although the procedure set out in the prison governor’s letter of 28 November 2002 amounted to an interference with the applicant's right to respect for his correspondence, the interference was justified and proportionate under Article 8 § 2 of the Convention. It considered that although it was of course possible to verify the existence, address and qualifications of the applicant’’ external medical specialist (whose bona fides was not in question), there was no way of ensuring that the latter would not be intimidated or tricked into transmitting illicit messages. The case originated in an application (no. 36936/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the monitoring of his medical correspondence while he was in prison breached his right to respect for his correspondence and private life. On 7 February 2008 the President of the Chamber decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the Application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the convention). The applicant wished to correspond confidentially with his external medical specialist to ensure that he would receive the treatment he needed. The applicant applied to the prison governor for a direction that medical correspondence should be accorded confidentiality. The prison governor agreed that the applicant’s medical correspondence would not be read provided that certain conditions were met. All outgoing and incoming mail was to be marked “medical in confidence’. The judge concluded that there were exceptional circumstances in the applicant's case and his desire to ensure that his treatment in prison did not affect him adversely. The case was heard at the High Court in February 2004 and the case was settled by the Court of Appeal in October 2006. The appeal was heard by Mr Justice Collins, who dismissed the application for judicial review. Court of Appeal ruled that the reading of the applicant’s correspondence was proportionate. Mr Justice Collins also found that the initial decision of the prison governor to enable the applicant to correspond on a confidential basis with his external medical specialist indicated that it was reasonable to permit such confidential correspondence. The Court of Appeal concluded that although it was of course possible to verify the. existence, address and qualifications of the applicants external medical. specialist, there was no way of ensuring that the latter would not be intimidated or. tricked into transmitting illicit messages. Lord Justice Sedley gave the judgment of the court. It was noted that there was. no dispute that theReading of prisoners’ correspondence was governed by law, and that it. was directed to the prevention of crime and the protection of the rights and freedoms of others. The Court of Appeal concluded that the monitoring of the applicant’s medical correspondence was a proportionate interference with his Article 8 rights. As regards correspondence with doctors, the prisoner's health was the concern and the immediate responsibility of the Prison Medical Service. It was recognised that there was an inescapable risk of abuse, for example, if the applicant's prison life or treatment was made more difficult because of what he was observed to be writing. However, the risk, having been minimised by virtue of confining surveillance to the prison medical officer, was outweighed by the above-mentioned factors. train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were represented by Mr T. Elçi, a lawyer practising in Diyarbakır. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaint concerning the applicants’ right to be brought promptly before a judge. The application was brought by 12 Turkish nationals, on 1 April 2001, in Düzova village, in Ciz. Erdal Güler was taken into custody on 27 September 2000. He was kept in custody until 11 a.m. on 1 October 2000. The applicants were then taken to the Şırnak provincial gendarmerie command. They were charged on charges of aiding and abetting the PKK contrary to Article 169 of the Criminal Code and Article 5 of Law no. 3713, and illegal possession of firearms and explosives. On 12 December 2000 the Diyarbakır State Security Court ordered the applicants’ release pending trial. In 2002 and 2003 the applicants were acquitted of the charges against them.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 62543/00) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained that they had not had a fair hearing in the judicial proceedings brought by them to halt construction of the Itoiz dam. They also complained that the Autonomous Community law in question had been enacted with a view to preventing execution of a Supreme Court judgment which had become final. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27) The case originated in an engineering project of February 1989 for the construction of a dam in Itoiz (Navarre province) which would result in the flooding of three nature reserves and a number of small villages. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits. On 1 April 2003 the Chamber decided, having regard to the circumstances of the case, to dismiss a Rule 39 request submitted by the applicants. The appeal was based on several allegations of unlawfulness which, in their opinion, had tainted the project. The case was settled by the Court of Appeal on 13 June 2003. The decision was published by the European Court of Human Rights. The Audiencia Nacional partly upheld the appeal in a judgment of 29 September 1995. The court accepted the request for precise designation of the protection zones around the nature reserves affected by the dam. In the context of the interim enforcement of its judgment, by a decision of 6 March 1996, prohibited the filling of the reservoir and displacement of the population concerned. On 17 June 1996 the parliament of the Autonomous Community of Navarre (parlamento foral de Navarra) passed Autonomous. Community Law (foral) no. 9/1996 on natural sites in Navarre. This law amended Aut autonomous Community Law no. 6/1987 of 10 April 1987, particularly with regard to the possibility of reclassifying the protection zone. The Supreme Court definitively cancelled the dam project in so far as it concerned the 500-metre protection zones around nature reserves RN 9, 10 and 11. As a result of the judgment, the size of the planned dam, and thus of the area to be flooded, was reduced, so that the village of Itoiz, where the applicants' immovable property was located, was saved from flooding. In application of the Supreme Court's judgment, by a decision of 4 September 1997, the Audiencia Nacional declared final the interim enforcement measures ordered on 6 March 1996 concerning the prohibition on filling the reservoir and other related work. The applicant association contested the authorities' argument, claiming that the Autonomous Community law of 1996 was inapplicable in the instant case. By a decision of 21 May 1998, the Constitutional Court declared the application inadmissible on account of certain errors in its presentation which could nonetheless be corrected. The Audiencia Nacional summoned the parties on 28 May 1998 so that it could hear their submissions on certain aspects of the Aut autonomous Community law whose constitutionality had been challenged. The applicant association submitted its observations on 10 June 1998. Under section 37(2) of the Judicature Act, it gave notice of the questions to the Chamber of Deputies, the Senate, the government and parliament of Navarre and the Spanish government, and invited them to file their observations. The Constitutional Court held that the impugned provisions of the Autonomous Community law of 1996 were compatible with the Constitution. It observed at the outset that enforcement of the Supreme Court's judgment of 14 July 1997 had become impossible since the entry into force of the new law. The Speaker of the Senate asked that the Senate be considered a party to the proceedings and offered its assistance. The Constitutional Court also ruled that, given the significance of the question raised by the Itoiz dam's construction, which could not simply be ignored, it was justifiable that the law specifically mentioned the aim and means of environmental protection in the peripheral protection zones around the three above-mentioned nature reserves. Constitutional Court considered that the fact that a new law had been passed amending the legal system applicable to the peripheral protection zones was not in itself incompatible with the right to execution of judicial decisions as enshrined in Article 24 of the Constitution. It found that both the Supreme Court's judgment of 14 July 1997 and the new Autonomous Community law of 1996 were intended to guarantee the existence of a peripheral protection zone around the three nature reserves affected by the dam's construction. The balance of general interests had been respected and that there was no clear lack of proportion between the conflicting interests. Consequently, the impugned provisions could not be held to be contrary to Article 24 § 1 of the constitution. Constitutional Court dismissed the application for a preliminary ruling. The judgment was published in the Official Gazette on 14 April 2000. Outlined that laws could be challenged before the Constitutional Court through the remedy provided for in Article 163 of the Constitution. Outlines that laws can be challenged through the remedies provided for by Article 163, including the right to challenge them in the Court of Appeal. The application was dismissed and the judgment published in the official gazette on 14 April 2000. The judge's decision was published in full in the Spanish edition of this article, which you can read here for free. The applicant filed a claim with the Labour Court. In a judgment dated 30 May 2002 of Labour Court no. 12 of Madrid, she was granted an entitlement to receive a survivor’s pension with a base rate of 903.29 euros per month, her Roma marriage thus being recognised as having civil effects. In our country the Roma minority (etnia gitana) has been present since time immemorial. Roma marriages are not registered in the Civil Register because they have not been regarded by the State as a feature of the ethnic culture. ... Directive 2000/43/EC implementing the principle of equal treatment between persons irrespective of racial or ethnic origin is applicable to the present case. It should be noted that the principle of equality and non-discrimination is based on the idea that equal situations should be treated equally.” A marriage solemnised solely and exclusively according to Roma rites is not covered by any of the above-mentioned cases, as even though an ethnic group is concerned, the norms or formalities of that group do not produce any legal effect. Court also said that the recognition of the civil effects of a marital relationship created by certain specific religious rites, but not one that has been solemnised according to Roma rites and customs, may entail directly or indirectly, the alleged ethnic discrimination. Court rejected the idea that the refusal of the judicial body to accept the latter mutatis mutandis may be discrimination against the Roma ethnic group. It also said the law establishes a general possibility – neutral from a racial and ethnic point of view – of marrying in the civil form, and that the legislature, not the courts, should make such a decision. Dissenting opinion was appended to judgment no. 199/2004 in which the Constitutional Court had found a violation of the right to equality. The two claimants had applied for a survivor’s pension on the basis of what they considered to be a marital relationship, albeit that it had not been registered civilly. The dissenting judge concluded as follows: “It is disproportionate for the Spanish State, which took into consideration the applicant and her Roma family by issuing them with a family record book, granting them large-family status, affording health-care assistance to her and her six children and collecting the corresponding contributions from her Roma husband for nineteen years, three months and eight days, now to refuse to recognise her.” The applicant was granted a survivor’s pension with effect from 1 January 2007, as the partner of M.D. the Roma marriage when it comes to the survivor's pension. The relevant provisions of the Spanish Constitution are as follows: Article 14 “Spaniards shall be equal before the law; they may not be discriminated against in any way on account of birth, race, sex, religion, opinion or any other condition or personal or social circumstance” Article 16 “1. Freedom of ideas, religion and worship shall be guaranteed to individuals and communities without any restrictions on its expression other than those necessary for the maintenance of public order.” The relevant provisions of the Civil Code, in its current version, read as follows: Article 44 “A man and a woman shall have the right to enter into marriage’ Article 49 “Any Spanish national is entitled to marry in Spain or abroad” Article 40 “In the religious form provided for by law, [any Spanish national] may also marry abroad in accordance with the formalities required by the law in the place where the marriage is solemnised. ” The surviving spouse of a married couple who have not been able to marry on account of the legislation currently in force can claim a survivor’s pension in the event of nullity. Law no. 40/2007 of 4 December 2007 on social security measures, amending the LGSS, reads as follows: Third transitional amendment “Exceptionally, a survivor’s pension shall be granted where the death of the insured person occurred before the entry into force of the present Act, subject to fulfilment of the following conditions”. Marriages solemnised according to the rites of those religious denominations are therefore recognised by the General Social Security Act. The recognition of the pension entitlement will take effect from 1 January 2007. The claim must be filed within a non-extendable period of twelve months following the entry of the new Act. The Council of Europe’s Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities contains the following provisions in particular. Article 1 “The protection of national minorities and of the rights and freedoms of persons belonging to those minorities forms an integral part of the international protection of human rights, and as such falls within the scope of international cooperation” Article 5 “1. The Parties undertake to promote the conditions necessary for persons. to maintain and develop their culture, and to preserve the essential elements of. their identity, namely their religion, language, traditions and cultural heritage.” The measures adopted in accordance with paragraph 2 shall not be considered to be an act of discrimination. Spain signed the Convention on the day that it was opened for signature and ratified it on 1 September 1995. It came into force in respect of Spain on 1 February 1998. The Convention was signed by all European Union members and ratified by all EU member states. It states that the EU “ shall refrain from policies or practices aimed at assimilation of persons belonging to national minorities against their will and shall protect these persons from any action aimed at such assimilation.” Spain ratified the convention on the first day it was open for signature on September 1, 1995, and signed it on September 2, 1995. Spain’s ratification of the Convention took place on September 3, 1995 and the convention came into effect on September 4, 1996.

name: Wacław Płoski
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the refusal to allow him to attend the funerals of his parents was in breach of Article 8. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. By a decision of 4 December 2001 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The case will be heard by the Chamber that would consider the case. The application for compassionate leave was made after the death of the applicant’s mother. The Wrocław-Śródmieście District Court refused the permission to grant the applicant leave considering that he “was a habitual offender whose return to the prison cannot be guaranteed” On 6 August 1994 the applicant made an application for leave to attend the funeral of his father. The application was in the following terms: “I kindly ask you to grant me a compassionate leave because my father Wacław Płoski has died. The funeral will take place on 8.08.1994 and I would like to attend it and to pay last respects to him” The Wrocław-Śródmieście District Court refused permission to grant the applicant leave on 8 August 1994. The court gave the following reasons for its decision: “The charges against the accused involve a significant danger to society. The accused Wacław Płoski is a habitual offender within the meaning of Article 60 § 2 of the Criminal Code. In the court’s view, his return to the Detention Centre cannot be guaranteed. For these reasons the above decision has been made.” On 26 May 1995 the applicant was convicted of larceny and received a prison term. He was released from prison on 27 February 1996.

name: Oleg Choumakov
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 33868/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) by a Russian national, Mr Oleg Choumakov (“the applicant”), on 7 September 2005. The Government of the Russian Federation did not exercise their right to intervene. The court found that the grounds previously invoked were still valid and that only the applicant’s detention would secure the proper conduct of the investigation. The applicant was born in 1971 and is currently detained in the Gdańsk Detention Centre. The applicant and his co‑accused were convicted and sentenced to 25 years’ imprisonment. The length of the applicant’s detention had reached the statutory time-limit of two years laid down in Article 263 § 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Kodeks postępowania karnego) The court admitted that the applicant had been detained for a rather lengthy period. However, it did not contravene the requirements of Articles 5 and 6 of the Convention as the grounds for keeping the applicant in detention remained relevant and the courts had been diligent in examining the case. The applicant lodged appeals against almost every one of the appeals. The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to 25 years' imprisonment. He lodged an appeal. The Gdańsk Court of Appeal allowed the appeal and quashed the impugned judgment. It remitted the case to the Elbląg Regional Court. The court further prolonged the applicant’s detention until 28 June 2008. The applicant remains in detention pending trial. The case was dismissed by the Gdašk Court of appeal on 15 January 2008 and the case was remitted to the regional court. It was decided that the applicant and the second co-accused had tried to contact each other illegally and to exchange information about the trial.

On 7 March 2006 his pre-trial detention was further prolonged. The court admitted that the applicant had been detained for a rather lengthy period. However, it did not contravene the requirements of Articles 5 and 6 of the Convention as the grounds for keeping the applicant in detention remained relevant. The applicant was convicted and sentenced to 25 years' imprisonment in 2007. His appeal against that decision was dismissed by the Gdańsk Court of Appeal on 15 January 2008. The judge found that the applicant and the second co-accused had made an attempt to contact each other illegally and to exchange information about the trial which justified the finding that he might interfere with the proper course of the proceedings. In addition, the court established that the co‑accuse had contacted the witnesses through other persons.

name: Hasan Aydoğan
train_texts: Six Turkish nationals, Mr Hasan Aydoğan, Ms Türkan Özen, Mr Hüseyin. İşeri, Mr Süleyman Evren, Mr Ünsal Varol and Mr. Hüeyin Öztürk were arrested and taken into custody on 22 and 23 October 1996. They were accused of taking part in armed attacks on various political party buildings and police stations and of being responsible for the death of Mr Mehmet Ünlü and causing bodily harm to two other persons. The applicants were also accused of aiding and abetting an illegal armed terrorist organisation. The application was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) Military judges were replaced by civilian judges on the bench of State Security Courts. şeri, Mr Evren, Mr Varol and Mr Öztürk were released pending trial, on various dates, in 1996 and 1997. Between 10 September 1999 and 19 October 2001 the court held eleven hearings, during which the judges dealt with procedural matters connected with the completion of the case file. The court ordered the continued detention of Mr Aydoğan and Ms Özen at the end of each hearing. On 19 October2001 the Istanbul State Security Court, after having examined the evidence in the case. file, convicted Mr Ay doğan as charged and sentenced them to death and deferred the imposition of a final sentence. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. The decision indicates that their lawyer, despite having requested the court to hold a hearing, had failed to attend it. No information was submitted by the parties as to further developments. On 24 September 2002 Mr Aydoğan’s and Ms Özen's sentences were commuted to life imprisonment. The court refused them leave to appeal since their decision in their respect was not open to appeal. The other applicants were refused permission to appeal as their case was not of a procedural or a substantive nature. The case was settled in court on 8 April 2002.

The case originated in an application (no. 41967/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Six Turkish nationals, Mr Hasan Aydoğan, Ms Türkan Özen, Mr Hüseyin İşeri, Mr Süleyman Evren, Mr Ünsal Varol and Mr Housseyin Öztürk (‘the applicants’) were accused of aiding and abetting an illegal armed terrorist organisation. The applicants were represented by Mr M. Filorinali and Ms Y. Başara, lawyers practising in Istanbul. The case against Mr Aydoğan and Ms Özen began in 1996 and 1997. The court held eleven hearings between 10 September 1999 and 19 October 2001. In October 2001 the Istanbul State Security Court, after having examined the evidence in the case file, convicted them as charged and sentenced them to death. As to the other applicants, the court decided to defer the imposition of a final sentence, pursuant to Law no. 46. The applicants’ representative complained that the prison authorities were making it difficult for him to prepare his defence, for example by not admitting him to see his client if he did not have the power of attorney on him. On 8 April 2002 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. The decision indicates that their lawyer, despite having requested the court to hold a hearing, had failed to attend it. On 24 September 2002 Mr Aydoğan’s and Ms Özen’S sentences were commuted to life imprisonment. No information was submitted by the parties as to further developments. The court refused them leave to appeal since the decision in their respect was not open to appeal. The couple were sentenced to life in prison in September 2002. The sentence was commuted on 24 September 2004. It was later extended to a maximum of 25 years.

name: Faruk Ereren
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 67522/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the length of his pre-trial detention had been excessive. On 5 September 2013 the complaint was communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The application was filed by a stateless person, Mr Faruk Ereren (“the applicant”), on 14 December 2009. He was granted legal aid and was represented by a lawyer practising in Dortmund. The German Government were represented by their Agent, Mr H.-J. Behrens, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The applicant was suspected of having ordered several terrorist attacks carried out by detonating explosives in Turkey between January 2001 and July 2005. The hearing started on 15 January 2009 and took place on 95 days. After 16 days of court hearing, the Court of Appeal quashed the arrest warrant insofar as it had been based on the suspicion that the applicant had ordered the attack which had taken place in Istanbul on 1 April 1993. There was sufficient documentary and witness evidence supporting the allegation that the. applicant, as a leading member of a terrorist organisation, was responsible for causing explosions and. committing other criminal acts. The applicant had been elected as a member of the central committee of the DHKP-C in the beginning of 1999. The applicant had neither a fixed residence nor sufficient social ties to ensure his appearance before the court. There were no milder means available to secure his presence at the trial. The Court of Appeal included a detailed account of the trial, explaining that on several occasions witnesses could not be questioned by the court because they exercised their right not to testify. In order to establish whether the applicant had committed the crimes of which he had been accused, testimony from Turkish witnesses was of paramount importance. The continuation of his detention was not disproportionate in view of the importance of the subject matter and of the considerable punishment to be expected in case of a criminal conviction. The Court of Appeal found it established that the applicant had ordered the assassination of the policemen by telephone from Germany at the end of March 1993. The court primarily based the applicant’s conviction on testimony from witness S.G. The Court of appeal found that the prolongation of the pre-trial detention was not disproportionate, having regard to the importance of the subject matter and to the seriousness of the penalty to be expected in case of a criminal conviction. On 27 September 2011 the Düsseldorf Court. of Appeal convicted the applicant of two counts of murder and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The hearing of evidence was re‑opened and the Court of. Appeal limited the charge of murder committed in April 1993, while discontinuing the proceedings. concerning the other charges. The Federal Court of Justice quashed the judgment of the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal and remitted the case to another Chamber of that court. The Federal Court considered that the assessment of the evidence by the Court. of Appeal had been erroneous as that court had wrongly assumed. that the testimony given by S.G. on the circumstances of his alleged conversation with G.G was consistent and without contradictions. The hearing was closed on 10 February 2011, but re-opened altogether three times at the request of the defence. The reading out of the applicant’s last word alone took four days. Members of the court and representatives of the parties travelled to Turkey four times in order to attend the hearing of witnesses. Düsseldorf Court of Appeal ordered the applicant’s continued detention. The detention was justified because the applicant was under strong suspicion of having committed a serious crime and because there was the risk that he might abscond. The potential contradictions in the statements made by witness S.G. had to be examined in the new main proceedings. The fact that the Federal Court of Justice had quashed the judgment did not lead to a violation of the obligation to expedite the proceedings, as there was no obvious procedural error. The contradiction in the testimony did not concern the core content of his statement, which remained unchanged. The Federal Court of Justice finally considered that the length of detention (almost six years) was not disproportionate. The Court of Appeal considered that to prolong the detention would be disproportionate. In cases involving pre-trial detention, the criminal courts were under a constitutional obligation to expedite the proceedings (Beschleunigungsgebot). This principle had to be applied even more strictly given the long duration of the applicant’s detention. In spite of several reminders, the requests for letters rogatory lodged with the Turkish authorities in April and September 2013 had not so far been disposed of. The court considered that it was not prevented from taking into account this statement by G.G. The applicant was released on that same day. The criminal proceedings were still pending before the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal in August 2014. The statements made by witness G.G. to the Turkish Authorities in 1993 could not be used because it could not been ruled out that they had been obtained by torture. The court noted that the fact that detention had already lasted almost seven years was not considered to be a relevant factor in the criminal proceedings. The case is still pending in the court of appeal. The trial is scheduled to take place in September 2014 in Istanbul, Turkey, but a date has not yet been set. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 63131/00) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that a delay in releasing him from prison had given rise to a violation of Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The application had been lodged by a Polish national, Mr Leszek Gębura (‘the applicant’), on 12 May 2000. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 17 March 2005 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. The hearing before the Court of Appeal was scheduled for 12 April 2000 at 8.45 a.m. On that day the Cracow Court of appeal upheld the decision of the Regional Court. The Tarnów Regional Court ordered the governor of the Tarnow Mościce Prison to release the applicant. The governor received these documents on 14 April 2000. According to the official release certificate, the applicant was released on 14 June 2000. The applicant submitted that he had been released on that date at 4 p.m., but in fact he was released at 4:20 p. m. His appeal was dismissed.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49398/99) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants' plots of land in İskenderun were expropriated by the General Directorate of National Roads and Highways. A committee of experts assessed the value of these lands and the determined amounts were paid to them when the expropriation took place. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning insufficient interest payable in respect of additional compensation, the delay of the authorities in payment of the additional compensation and the length of the proceedings. The ownership of the property was transferred to the National Water Board on 23 October 1996. The court ordered the administration to pay Yüksel Bozkaya TRL 80,274,368,000 plus interest at the statutory rate. The Court of Cassation upheld the above-mentioned judgments of the İskenderun First Instance Court on 11 May, 20 May and 25 May 1998 respectively. On 8 April, 13 April, 12 May and 4 June 1999 respectively, the administration paid the applicants the amounts due together with interest. The administration has since paid them all back, plus interest. It is unclear whether the case will ever be heard by a court of law.
