train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms by a Montenegrin national. The applicant alleged that his criminal conviction was based to a decisive extent on testimony given by an anonymous witness. The Government of Montenegro did not express an intention to take part in the proceedings. The application was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The applicant is currently detained in a cantonal prison in Regensdorf in Switzerland. He is suspected of having carried out the shooting of N.B. in Zurich in 2001. The applicant and his counsel were allowed to put additional questions to X. The latter refused to answer a number of questions which the defence counsel considered to be important. The applicant was convicted of manslaughter (vorsätzliche Tötung) and of several counts of drug-trafficking and sentenced to 14 years and nine months’ detention. The court considered that the testimony given by X was credible and pertinent. It noted that X had submitted in a credible and convincing way that his life was in danger in case he testified. It was further obvious that the applicant had a motive to take revenge on the witness who had contributed to his conviction. The court considered that the measures taken were both necessary and sufficient to prevent identification of the witness X. The court had taken a number of measures to compensate the restrictions imposed on the rights of the defence. The witness had not been examined by the regional prosecutor (Bezirksanwalt), but by the president of the court. It had thus been known that X had no criminal record and that there was no indication that he had any contact with the drug trafficking scene. There was also no indication X had been in any way involved in the crime. It was also known X spoke the Serbo-Croatian language. The jury court considered, however, that this information was of minor importance for the assessment of credibility. The applicant lodged a nullity appeal (Nichtigkeitsbeschwerde) with the Court of Cassation (Kassationsgericht) of the canton of Zurich. Relying on all available evidence, the jury court concluded that there was no doubt that N. B. had been shot by the applicant. By decision of 19 December 2005 the Court decided that the applicant acted with a particular degree of scrupulousness (besonders skrupellos) which would lead to the crime being characterised as murder. The jury court considered that the prosecution based its submissions mainly on testimony given by the anonymous witness. It followed that, for formal reasons, these circumstances could not be taken into account and that it had to be assumed in the applicant’s favour. Court noted that the anonymous witness had been heard in camera and that the applicant’s counsel did not have the possibility directly to question the witness. Neither the applicant nor his counsel had ever seen the witness, whose personal details remained secret. Adequate compensation could only be conceivable if at least the defence had the right directly to take part in the interrogation of the witness and was given the opportunity to assess the witness’ credibility. As this had not been the case, the court considered that the criminal court could not rely on the testimony given by theAnonymous witness for two separate reasons. The court did not call into question that the legal conditions for granting anonymity were fulfilled in the instant case and confirmed the first instance court's finding that it had been necessary to protect X against possible reprisals. The court examined whether the testimony given by the anonymous witness had to be regarded as being “decisive’ for the applicant’s conviction. modalities of the witness’ interrogation did not comply with the standards set up by the Court and were thus contrary to Article 6 § 3 (d) of the Convention. The Federal Tribunal (Kassationshof) quashed the decision of 19 December 2005 and remitted the case to the Court of Cassation. The senior public prosecutor (Oberstaatsanwalt) of Zurich lodged a nullity appeal against the decision. The tribunal confirmed that it had been necessary to protect the witness by shielding his appearance. The jury court considered that the testimony given by the witness X had been credible and that it was, furthermore, in line with the scientific conclusion that the victim had been killed by gunshot in the back of his neck on 15 October 2001. The tribunal further reviewed the other evidence examined by the jury court and concluded that this evidence, taken separately, would have been sufficient “to establish a strong suspicion of a criminal offence, or even to establish his guilt”. On 12 February 2007 the Court of Cassation rejected the applicant’s nullity appeal. On 19 April 2007 the Federal Tribunal rejected the application. of guilt.

It was further obvious that the applicant had a motive to take revenge on the witness who had contributed to his conviction and to prevent him from making further testimonies. The applicant was convicted of manslaughter (vorsätzliche Tötung) and of several counts of drug-trafficking and sentenced to fourteen years and nine months’ detention. The court considered the conditions to allow the witness’ anonymity were met. The hearing was held in one of the court’s deliberation rooms and the interrogation was transmitted via a sound link. The witness was distorted in order to prevent his being identified. The court considered that the measures taken were both necessary and sufficient to prevent identification of the witness X. The court had taken a number of measures to compensate the restrictions imposed on the rights of the defence. The witness had not been examined by the regional prosecutor (Bezirksanwalt), but by the president of the court. There was no indication that X had been in any way involved in the crime. It was further known that X spoke the Serbo-Croatian language. The jury court considered, however, that this information was of minor importance for the assessment of credibility. Conversely, the court considered the testimony given by the anonymous witness, who submitted that he had seen the applicant shooting the victim, to be credible. Neither the applicant nor his counsel had ever seen the witness, whose personal details remained secret. Adequate compensation could only be conceivable if at least the defence had the right directly to take part in the interrogation of the witness and was given the opportunity to assess the witness’ credibility. As this had not been the case, the court considered that the criminal court could not rely on the testimony given by theAnonymous witness. name: Kenan Tandoğan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 9244/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Kenan Tandoğan (“the applicant”) was represented by Mr and Mrs Kırdök, lawyers practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant was charged with attempting to undermine the constitutional order, an offence defined under Article 146 of the Criminal Code. The case brought against the applicant was joined with another case pending before the Istanbul State Security Court. The applicant was arrested in connection with the incidents in the Ümraniye Prison. He was charged with homicide, starting a riot in the prison and damage to public property. The Istanbul State Security Court ordered the applicant's release pending trial on 9 February 2001. The applicant appealed against this decision before the Üsküdar Assize Court. On 7 July 2001 at around 8.30 p.m. the applicant was released from prison. The case is apparently still pending before the Court of Cassation. It has been remitted to determine which court has jurisdiction to examine the case, which has since been declared non-jurisdiction.

The case originated in an application (no. 9244/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was charged with attempting to undermine the constitutional order, an offence defined under Article 146 of the Criminal Code. He was also accused of homicide, armed riot against prison administration and damaging prison property. The case was joined with another case pending before the Istanbul State Security Court. The judge at the Üsküdar Magistrate's Court ordered the applicant's detention on remand in absentia. The applicant was arrested in connection with the incidents in the Ümraniye Prison. He was charged with homicide, started a riot in the prison and damage to public property. His case before the Istanbul State Security Court was transferred to the Istanbul Assize Court. The Istanbul Juvenile Court held its first hearing and decided that it lacked jurisdiction to examine the case. The case was accordingly remitted before the Court of Cassation to determine which court had jurisdiction. The applicant was released from prison on 7 July 2001 at around 8.30 p.m. He now lives in Istanbul with his wife and their three children. He is married to a Turkish woman.

name: Alois Unterpertinger
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 9120/80) against the Republic of Austria, lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 1 September 1980. Both sought a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 (d) The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby Austria recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Art. 46) The Government's application referred to Article 48 ( art. 48) The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30) The hearing was held on 17 February 1986 in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg. The Government and the applicant produced documents at the hearings. The Court heard their addresses as well as their replies to its questions. The applicant was an Austrian national born in 1938, who lives in Wörgl. He complains of criminal proceedings brought against him. The hearing was adjourned until 17 February after the Commission provided the Registrar with documents which he had requested on the President’s instructions. It was heard by the President of the Chamber, Mr. Wiarda (Rule 21 § 5), and Mr. R. Macdonald, substitute judges (Rule 24 § 1). The applicant's wife and step-daughter attacked him during a quarrel. He claimed that his wife had inflicted several head wounds with a paper-knife and gashed his forehead close to his eyebrow. He admitted that he had pushed his wife at the time and had tried unsuccessfully to slap his step- daughter in the face. Miss Tappeiner admitted having called her step-father a “convict’ (Zuchthäusler) that morning, and said he had responded by slapping her in theFace. She said neither she nor her daughter had deliberately caused him any wounds to the head or face. She added that a doctor she had consulted had issued a certificate in respect of her own injury. Wörgl police sent the Kufstein District Court a report (Strafanzeige) “concerning Alois Unterpertinger and Rosi Unter PERtinger, suspected of causing actual bodily harm (Körperverletzung)’ The report indicated that the applicant’s injuries had been described as “slight’ by the doctor. The police went on to say that they had already had to intervene in several quarrels in the household. They added that the three protagonists had given conflicting accounts of the incident on 14 August. Miss Tappeiner, who had been questioned as an informant (Auskunftsperson), had clearly taken her mother's side. An X-ray at the hospital next day had shown that her right thumb was. Alois Unterpertinger accused of injuring his wife with a broken thumb. His wife claimed she tried to hit him on the head with a hairbrush, but missed and hit the stair-rail instead. Judge acquitted her of causing actual bodily harm on 28 January 1980. Innsbruck Public Prosecutor’s Department decided on 9 November 1979 to open an investigation against the applicant in respect of the two incidents. The investigation (Vorerhebungen) took place in Kufstein, Austria, between 11 September and 20 October 1979. Mrs. Unter pertinger was accused of causing grievous bodily harm, but was acquitted on 3 December 1979 after she refused to give evidence. The case was heard on 10 March 1980 by a judge of the Innsbruck Regional Court (Landesgericht), sitting alone. According to the record of the hearing, the applicant pleaded not guilty. He admitted hitting his step-daughter on the head, but not that he had injured her. He said he had not seen his wife come into contact with the stair-rail and added that he was not sufficiently agile to have been able to kick her thumb. The Regional Court then called Mrs. Unterpertinger and Miss Tappeiner. On being told by the court of their right to refuse to give evidence, they replied that they wished to avail themselves of that right. At the request of the Public Prosecutor’s Department, the documents it had mentioned in its application for leave to prosecute were read out. Mr. Unterpertinger was found guilty of causing actual bodily harm to his step-daughter. He was sentenced to six months’ imprisonment. The court found no mitigating circumstances; on the contrary, it saw the applicant’s criminal record as an aggravating circumstance. In spite of Article 152 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, his former wife and step- daughter, whose statements to the police had formed the sole basis of his conviction, had not been informed at the time of the conviction. The appeal proceedings were heard in April 1980 and Mr. Unterstertinger appealed on 9 April 1980. In the appeal proceedings, the court held that the allegations against the applicant were “sufficiently clear and specific to support a conviction“ The applicant requested that evidence should be taken from several witnesses, including two doctors, a police officer, a neighbour and his own mother, step-daughter and former wife. Mr. Unterpertinger asked the Innsbruck Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) to quash the conviction of 10 March and acquit him. Failing this, he asked it to review his sentence in the light of the degree of his guilt. The court decided to re-examine the evidence submitted to the court of first instance and to supplement it (Wiederholung und Ergänzung) by having the file on the divorce proceedings read out. Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal immediately after the hearing on 4 June 1980. The victims’ statements to the police were plausible and credible; their account of the incident was logically coherent. Except for his sister-in-law, it was unnecessary to hear the witnesses the applicant had sought to have called, since he had referred to them in connection with matters that were either of no importance or else extremely vague. The sentence imposed was consistent with the degree of his guilt (schuld) Mr. Unterpertinger was convicted on the two counts against him. He had not been acting in self-defence on 14 August 1979. The applicant served his sentence from 22 September 1980 to 22 March 1981. The full text of the Commission’s opinion and of the separate opinions contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to the present judgment. The Commission expressed the opinion that there had been no breach of paragraph 3 (d) of Article 6 (art. 6-3-d) The Court was requested by the Government, “to find that the Republic of Austria violated several provisions of the Convention in these criminal proceedings“ and to require the Republic Of Austria to pay appropriate compensation“. The Court refused to do so, finding that the facts underlying the dispute do not reveal any breach of obligations under the Convention.

The case originated in an application (no. 9120/80) against the Republic of Austria, lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 1 September 1980 by an Austrian citizen. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr. G. Wiarda, the President of the Court (Rule 21 § 3 (b)). On 27 March 1985, the. President drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of the five other members, namely Mrs. D. Bindschedler-Robert, J. Pinheiro Farinha, E. García de Enterría, B. Walsh and Sir Vincent Evans. The Government and the applicant produced documents at the hearings. The Court heard their addresses as well as their replies to its questions. The hearings were held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. There appeared before the Court: H. Türk, Legal Adviser, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Agent, M. Matzka, Federal Chancellery, Mr. H. Epp, Federal Ministry of Justice, Advisers. For the applicant Mr. F. Krall, Rechtsanwalt, Counsel, and R. R. Macdonald, substitute judges (Rule 24 § 1). The applicant's wife and step-daughter attacked him during a quarrel. He claimed his wife had inflicted several head wounds with a paper-knife and gashed his forehead close to his eyebrow. He admitted that he had pushed his wife at the time and had tried unsuccessfully to slap his step- daughter in the face. Miss Tappeiner admitted having called her step-father a ‘convict’ that morning, and said he had responded by slapping her. She said neither she nor her daughter had deliberately caused him any wounds to the head or face. A doctor she had consulted had issued a certificate in respect of her own injury. Wörgl police sent the Kufstein District Court (Bezirksgericht) a report (Strafanzeige) “concerning Alois Unterpertinger and Rosi Unter pertinger, suspected of causing actual bodily harm (Körperverletzung)’ The police went on to say that they had already had to intervene in several quarrels in the household. They added that the three protagonists had given conflicting accounts of the incident on 14 August. Miss Tappeiner, who had been questioned as an informant (Auskunftsperson), had clearly taken her mother’s side. Alois Unterpertinger was accused of injuring his wife on 9 September. He denied this, saying her hand had already been bandaged when he had come home. She had actually attempted to hit him on the head with a hairbrush, but had missed and collided with the stair-rail instead. This might have aggravated the thumb injury, but the accusation she had made against him was a complete fabrication. On 3 December 1979, Mrs. Unter pertinger appeared before a judge at Kufstein, who told her that, as the wife of the accused (Beschuldigter), she was entitled to refuse to give evidence. She replied that she nonetheless wished to do so, and gave an account of the facts in dispute, summarising what she had already told the police. The case was heard on 10 March 1980 by a judge of the Innsbruck Regional Court (Landesgericht), sitting alone. The applicant pleaded not guilty. He admitted that he had hit his step-daughter on the head, but not that she had injured her. He said he had not seen his wife come into contact with the stair-rail and added that he was not sufficiently agile to have been able to kick her thumb. Mrs. Unterpertinger and Miss Tappeiner refused to give evidence, so the court could not examine them or read out the record of their interview with the judge. At the request of the Public Prosecutor’s Department, however, the documents it had mentioned in its application for leave to prosecute were read out. Mr. Unterpertinger was found guilty of causing actual bodily harm and causing grievous bodily harm to his wife. He was sentenced to six months' imprisonment. The court found no mitigating circumstances; on the contrary, it saw the applicant’s criminal record as an aggravating circumstance. In addition, his record showed that he was quite capable of behaving in this way. In spite of Article 152 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, his former wife and step-daughter, whose statements to the police had formed the sole basis of his conviction, had not been informed at the time of the appeal. In this instance too, the applicant had acted deliberately. Mr. Unterpertinger asked the Innsbruck Court of Appeal to quash the conviction of 10 March and acquit him. Failing this, he asked it to review his sentence in the light of the degree of his guilt. The court decided to re-examine the evidence submitted to the court of first instance and to supplement it (Wiederholung und Ergänzung) by having the file on the divorce proceedings read out and hearing testimony from the wife of the applicant’s brother. She was unable to say whether the applicant's former wife had had a bandage on her. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal immediately after the hearing on 4 June 1980. Mr. Unterpertinger was convicted on two counts of attempted murder and given a sentence consistent with the degree of his guilt. The victims’ statements to the police were plausible and credible; their account of the incident was logically coherent. Except for his sister-in-law, it was unnecessary to hear the witnesses the applicant had sought to have called, since he had referred to them in connection with matters that were either of no importance or else extremely vague. As for his claim that he was not sufficiently agile to have been able to break his wife's thumb with a kick, this did not stand up to examination either. The applicant served his sentence from 22 September 1980 to 22 March 1981. The Commission declared the application admissible on 8 July 1983. In its report of 11 October 1984 the Commission expressed the opinion that there had been no breach of paragraph 3 (d) of Article 6 (art. 6-3-d) The full text of the Commission’s opinion and of the separate opinions contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to the present judgment. The Court was requested by the Government, “to hold that in the present case the provisions of the European Convention on Human Rights have not been violated“ and “ to require the Republic of Austria to pay appropriate compensation“.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Following promulgation of the Law of 27 December 1993, which abolished the jurisdiction of the Martial Law Courts, the Court of Cassation (Yargıtay) acquired jurisdiction over the case and on 4 January 1994 the case file was transmitted to it. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 37437/97) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. name: Krzysztof Wedekind
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no 26110/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was born in 1971 and lives in Tychy. He was arrested on suspicion of drug trafficking committed as part of an organised crime group on 17 January 2001. On 19 January 2001 the Katowice District Court remanded the applicant in custody, relying on the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offence. The applicant was charged with drug trafficking and membership of an organised crime group. The case was transferred to the Bielsko-Biała Regional Court. The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to five years and six months' imprisonment and to a fine. He was kept in detention pending appeal for a period of one year and one month. On 26 January 2006 the Katowice Court of Appeal heard the applicant's appeal. It reduced the sentence passed by the first-instance court to five year and left the remainder of the judgment unchanged. The judgment is final and the applicant did not lodge a cassation appeal. The appeal was rejected.

name: Steven Phillips
train_texts: The application was lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged, inter alia, that the statutory assumption made against him by the court which issued a confiscation order following his conviction for a drug offence violated his right to the presumption of innocence. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) It was declared partly admissible on 30 November 2000. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 8 February 2001 (Rule 59 § 2). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Ms H. Fieldsend, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr D. Perry, Counsel, Ms M. Dyson, Home Office, Advisers. The applicant had previous convictions, but none in respect of a drug-related offence. An inquiry was conducted into the applicant’s means, pursuant to section 2 of the Drug Trafficking Act 1994 (“the 1994 Act’ – see below) The investigation officer concluded that the applicant had benefited from drug trafficking and that the total benefit was GBP 117,838.27. On 12 July 1996 he was sentenced to nine years’ imprisonment inrespect of this offence. the Customs and Excise Management Act 1979. The applicant had no declared taxable source of income, although he was the registered owner of a house converted into four flats from which he started a bed-and-breakfast business. The applicant filed a written statement in response, in which he denied having benefited from drug trafficking. He explained that in 1990-91 he had been convicted of car theft. He claimed that he had sold the house for GBP 50,000 to X in order to clear this debt and had used the GBP 12,000 residue from the sale to purchase the newsagents premises for his parents because he owed them money too. When he was released from prison in April 1994 he began trading in telephones; this was the source of theGBP 17,000 in his building society account. He denied owning any of the cars registered in his name, claiming variously that each had been purchased and sold on behalf of a friend or stolen without insurance. In conclusion, he alleged that his only realisable assets were some GBP 200 in a building Society account and the fittings of a garage rented from the local authority. Judge found the prosecution’s allegation that the applicant still owned the house to be correct. The judge held that X's purported purchase payment of GBP 50,000 had in fact been a benefit of drug trafficking. There are real indications on the civil basis of proof that [X] was complicit in the crime of which the accused was convicted. A mobile phone at the heart of the arrangements for the haulage of the drugs was registered in the name of [X]. Just as the jury did not believe Mr Phillips, neither do I. What has happened here, in my judgment, is a device of just the sort providing a cover to explain the transfer of money which one would expect to find in concealing benefit from drugs trafficking. The judge assessed the applicant to have benefited from drug trafficking to the extent of GBP 91,400. The judge also found the purchase of a share of a business for GBP 50,000 entirely without documentation ‘unbelievable’ and ‘simply unbelievable’ The judge concluded: ‘I think family loyalty has overcome his honesty.’ He added: ’I find it. impossible, in my judgment, to see any sensible reason other than that he did not cash a cheque; that it was a simple payment. It involves my disbelieving not only the accused but also his father, but I do’ The judge allowed him three years in which to pay the confiscation order, with a period of two years’ imprisonment to be served in default of payment. In view of the difficulties inherent in realising the applicant’s share of the family business, the judge allowed the applicant to stay in prison for three years. His application to renew leave to appeal against conviction and sentence was refused on 22 January 1998 after a full hearing before the Court of Appeal. The judge is satisfied that the GBP 50,000 is a fair estimate of the likely net proceeds of a sale of that property now or in the relatively near future. Since I am satisfied as to GBP 100,000 realisable sums, that figure exceeds theGBP 91,400.

The judge found the amount to be recovered to be that figure. He said that the business was worth GBP 150,000 in 1993. The judge ruled that the application had been untruthful. The applicant appealed against the decision of the Warsaw Court of Appeal. The Supreme Court dismissed the cassation appeal on 22 May 2007. The Koszalin Regional Bar Association struck the applicant off the roll of advocates. The applicant appealed to the Minister of Justice who however dismissed his appeal on 13 May 2008. On 13 August 2008 the applicant requested the court to stay the proceedings on the ground that the Ombudsman had challenged the constitutionality of a relevant section of the amended Lustration Act. On 16 March 2010 the court resumed the proceedings at the applicant’s request. The court again stayed the proceedings. On 8 November 2010 the applicant filed a complaint with the Supreme Administrative Court under the Law of 17. The applicant's complaint was dismissed by the Supreme Administrative Court in 2010. The proceedings before the Constitutional Court appear to be pending. The applicant has submitted no further information as regards the notification. He was summoned for 17 April 2009 but has not submitted any further information. The Institute of National Remembrance notified the applicant that doubts had arisen as to the truthfulness of his lustration declaration. He has been ordered to appear in court again on 17 April 2013. The application has been dismissed on 30 November 2010 and is pending further proceedings. name: J. Peter
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 68919/10) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On the same day the President of the Section sitting in a single-judge formation declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The applicant's civil partnership had not lasted longer than a year, which would have led to statutory exclusion from the benefit even for married couples. The court pointed out that the respondent had partly acknowledged the applicant’s claim, so that the appeal concerned only the period from July 2002 until December 2004. The remaining leapfrog appeal on points of law (Sprungrevision) was dismissed on 13 December 2005 by the Federal Social Court. In its reasoning the panel explained that the complaint did not raise a pressing constitutional question as the relevant provision of the social security legislation had meanwhile been amended. However, the judge maintained that it had been in the applicant's best interest to wait for the court's ruling in the 2007 case. A new judge rapporteur had stepped in at the end of his predecessor’s term of office and his predecessor had had to finish cases of higher priority than that of the applicant. The court noted that the actual duration of the proceedings – four and a half years – was unusually long, but not excessive. Unlike the ordinary courts, the capacity and structure of a Constitutional Court were laid down in the Constitution and served further purposes beyond the administration of individual justice. Germany (dec.), no. 53126/07, §§ 19 et seq., 29 May 2012. In the event of a tie the complaint of unduedelay shall be dismissed. The decision is not subject to appeal.’’ ‘‘The complaint will be admissible 12 months at the earliest after the case has been lodged with the Federal Constitutional Court (Verzögerungsrüge)’ '‘A complaint of. undue delay shall not require a reasoned notification. ... name: Şükran Yıldız
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the length of the applicant’s detention on remand to the Government. The applicant was accused of membership of an illegal armed organisation, namely the PKK (the Kurdistan Workers’ Party) The applicant did not have the assistance of a lawyer during her interrogations and was interrogated in the absence of one by the public prosecutor and the investigating judge. She was then allowed to have access to a lawyer. The case was decided on the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Diyarbakır State Security Court concluded that the woman was a member of the PKK and accordingly sentenced her to eight years and four months’ imprisonment. The court refused to release the woman on account of the nature of the alleged offence and the state of evidence. On 10 August 2001 the Court of Cassation quashed the first-instance court's decision and the woman was released pending trial. On 7 October 2002 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court and sentenced the woman to eight years and four months in prison.

The case originated in an application (no. 4661/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the length of the applicant’s detention on remand, the right to have the lawfulness of her detention decided by a court and the right of legal assistance to the Government. The applicant was represented by Mr Beştaş, a lawyer practising in Diyarbakır. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The Diyarbakır State Security Court concluded that the woman was a member of the PKK and accordingly sentenced her to eight years and four months’ imprisonment. The Court of Cassation quashed the first-instance court's judgment. On 10 August 2001 the court released the woman pending trial. In April 2002 the court rendered its judgment and sentenced the woman to 8 years and 4 months' imprisonment. On 7 October 2002 the Court ofCassation upheld the judgment of the Diyarbak Turkish Court. The court ruled that the charges against the woman had been trumped up by the defendant's statements. The woman was released pending trial on 20 August 2001.

She was accused of being a member of the PKK and accordingly called for her to be sentenced pursuant to Article 168 § 2 of the Criminal Code. The trial commenced before the Diyarbakır State Security Court. The Diyarbakır State Security Court concluded that the woman was a member of the PKK and accordingly sentenced her to eight years and four months’ imprisonment. On 9 April 2002 the court rendered its judgment and sentenced the woman to eight-and-a-half years in prison. In convicting the woman, the court had particular regard to the police statements made by the woman. The court upheld the judgment on 7 October 2002. The woman was released from prison on 9 August 2001.

name: Franz Ladner
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 3 June 2003. On 22 September 2003 the Court decided to communicate the applicant’s complaint that the maintenance in force of Article 209 of the Criminal Code and his conviction under this provision discriminated him in the enjoyment of his private life to the Government. The applicant was found guilty under Article 209 and sentenced to three months’ imprisonment suspended on probation. On 3 December 2002 the Vienna Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant' The case was decided on the condition of payment of a penalty of 20,000 Austrian schillings. The applicant’s petition for a pardon was of no avail. The decision was served on the applicant on 4 July 2003. The conduct of the person concerned would also qualify as an offence under the newly introduced Article 207b, as in one case that person had taken advantage of the adolescent's predicament, i.e. the fact that the latter had, following a conflict with his parents, temporarily lived in that person's apartment. The Minister of Justice replied to questions put by members of Parliament concerning the granting of a pardon in cases of convictions under Article 209. In these questions the applicant's case was referred to by the file number and the date of the final decision.

He was also suspected of owning child pornographic material. A number of video-tapes were seized but the suspicion was not confirmed and the subsequent proceedings were conducted for charges under Article 209 alone. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The application was dismissed in December 2002 by the Vienna Court of Appeal. The conduct of the person concerned would also qualify as an offence under the newly introduced Article 207b, as in one case that person had taken advantage of the adolescent's predicament, i.e. the fact that the latter had, following a conflict with his parents, temporarily lived in that person's apartment. The Minister of Justice replied to questions put by members of Parliament concerning the granting of a pardon in cases of convictions under Article 209. On 14 February 2001 the Vienna Regional Criminal Court (Landesgericht für Strafsachen) ordered the applicant's detention on remand on suspicion of having committed homosexual acts with adolescents. On 24 September 2001 the Regional Court decided to discontinue the proceedings on the condition of payment of a penalty of 20,000 Austrian schillings. On 3 December 2002 the Vienna Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant' The applicant’s petition for a pardon was of no avail. The decision was served on the applicant on 4 July 2003. The conduct of the person concerned would also qualify as an offence under the newly introduced Article 207b, as in one case that person had taken advantage of the adolescent's predicament. The Minister stated, without mentioning the applicant's name, that he had denied a pardon in this case, as the conduct of that person would also be an offence. The applicant was a 17-year-old boy who had temporarily lived in his parents’ apartment after a dispute with his father. He had been convicted under Article 209 of the Criminal Code. He appealed the decision of the Constitutional Court.

name: Fatma Ormancı
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 43647/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of compensation proceedings. By a decision of 27 November 2003 the Court declared the application admissible. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 of the Rules of Court) The case was transferred to the newly composed Second Section on 1 November 2004. The Applicants were represented by Mr Dinçer Söğütlü, a lawyer practising in Ankara. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Convention institutions. The case was notified to the defendant on 28 May 1992. The Ankara Administrative Court declared itself incompetent ratione loci and sent the case file to the Gaziantep Administrative Court. The court appointed an expert to calculate the amount of pecuniary damage the applicants had sustained as a result of the death of A.O. The applicants paid an advance on the court fees. the court awarded the applicants compensation for non-pecuniary and pec uniary damage together with interest from the date of the action. The defendant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court against the decision of the court. The case was settled out of court in 1996. The case was heard by the Supreme Administrative Court of Gaziantep in 1997. The applicants were paid the amount awarded to them on 5 November 1997 and 30 April 1998. The case was allocated to the 10th Division. of the Gazianteps Administrative Court. It was decided on 10 March 1998 that the decision had been made by the first-instance court. The decision was upheld by the second-instance Court on 9 March 1998. There was no appeal against the decision of the first court. There were no appeals on the decision to award the money to the applicants. The court ruled that the money had been awarded in accordance with the law.

Five Turkish nationals filed an application against the Republic of Turkey under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained about the length of compensation proceedings. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. The Court ruled that the application was admissible on 27 November 2009. The decision was published in full on 14 October 2010. The Ankara Administrative Court declared itself incompetent ratione loci and sent the case file to the Gaziantep Administrative Court. The court also appointed an expert to calculate the amount of pecuniary damage the applicants had sustained as a result of the death of A.O. The applicants were awarded compensation for non-pecuniary and pec uniary damage together with interest from the date of the action. The defendant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court against the decision. The case was settled out of court in 1996 and the defendants were awarded a settlement of €1.5 million. The case was allocated to the 10th Division. of the Gaziantep Administrative Court. On 10 March 1998 the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the decision of the first-instance court. The applicants were paid the amount awarded to them on 5 November 1997 and 30 April 1998. The case file was received by the Supreme. Administrative Court on 28 March 1997. The public prosecutor gave his opinion on 10 November 1997. He said that the applicants should not have been awarded the amount they were awarded. The decision was upheld by the Court of Appeal on 5 March 1998. In June 1998 the case was decided and the amount was paid to the applicants.

name: Claude Mazurek
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 34406/97) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The application was examined by the Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 12 October 1999. The Court declared the application admissible and decided to invite the parties to submit their observations on the merits at a hearing. The case was heard by the European Court of Human rights (ECHR) in Strasbourg. The decision was made in accordance with Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights (“the Convention’s” Article 5). Claude Mazurek's mother died on 1 August 1990 of HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) encephalopathy, having been infected after a blood transfusion. She left two children: a son, Alain, born out of wedlock in 1936 and legitimised by his mother’s marriage in 1937, and the applicant, born in 1942. In 1991 Alain brought an action against the applicant in the Nîmes tribunal de grande instance seeking an order that his mother's estate be divided by a notary. In a judgment of 21 January 1993 the court ordered the estate to be divided. With regard to the applicant's rights, it referred to Article 760 of the Civil Code. The court ruled that Article 760 of the European Convention on Human Rights does not discriminate against children born to unmarried parents. The court also ruled that the amount of money given to the mother was not a gift, but rather part of the family’s share of the estate. The Court of Appeal said that this was in line with Article 8 of the Convention, which protects the right of parents to raise their children as long as they are not separated from each other. The judge also said that the decision to divide the money was not contrary to Article 8, but that it was an exception to the principle that children must be treated equally. The appeal was dismissed, and the court ruled in favor of dividing the money between the mother and her son. The applicant appealed on points of law to the Court of Cassation, which delivered its judgment on 25 June 1996. The court was properly entitled to hold that it was not the intention of the legislature to discriminate between children on the grounds of their birth, but to ensure minimum compliance with the marital obligations of a married parent with regard to his or her legitimate children. The applicant’s complaint of unjustified discrimination on grounds of birth between children born in wedlock and children born out of wedlock, contrary to Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention, was rejected. In respect of the complaint that the. Court of Appeal had ordered the sum transferred to the applicant's account to be returned to the estate to be. divided, the court held that in deciding that the facts of the case had not shown any intention on the part of the. deceased to bestow a gift on her son in advance of the division of her estate. The Court of. Cassation held that inheritance rights had nothing to do with respect for private and family life guaranteed by Article 8 of the European Convention.

The case originated in an application (no. 34406/97) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The application was examined by the Court following the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention on 1 November 1998. The Court declared the application admissible and invited the parties to submit their observations on the merits at a hearing. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 12 October 1999. The case was heard by the President of the Court, Mr L. Wildhaber, and the judge elected in respect of France, Mr J.-P. Costa. Claude Mazurek is a French national who was born in Avignon in 1942. His mother died on 1 August 1990 of HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) encephalopathy. She left two children: a son, Alain, born out of wedlock in 1936 and legitimised by his mother’s marriage in 1937, and the applicant. Alain brought an action against the applicant in the Nîmes tribunal de grande instance seeking an order that his mother's estate be divided by a notary. In a judgment of 21 January 1993 the court ordered the estate to be divided. With regard to the applicant's rights, it referred to Article 760 of the Civil Code. The court said that Article 760 was not intended to discriminate between the children. It was meant to protect the interests of the legitimate children of the couple. The court ruled that the money should be returned to the parents as the money was not meant to be a gift to the children, but a payment to be made to them. The case was settled by an appeals court on March 26, 2013. The Court of Appeal ruled in favor of the parents and said that they were entitled to the money as a payment for the services they had provided to their children. The decision was appealed by the father of the child, who had been left out of the decision to divide the money. The applicant appealed on points of law to the Court of Cassation, which delivered its judgment on 25 June 1996. The court was properly entitled to hold that it was not the intention of the legislature to discriminate between children on the grounds of their birth, but to ensure minimum compliance with the marital obligations of a married parent with regard to his or her legitimate children. Article 760 of the Civil Code was a provision necessary for the protection of the rights of others. It was not contrary to the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant subsequently received one quarter of the amount awarded by the Compensation Fund for Transfusion Patients and Haemophiliacs. In respect of the complaint that the. Court of Appeal had ordered the sum transferred to the applicant’s account to be returned to the estate to be divided.

The case originated in an application (no. 34406/97) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The application was examined by the Court following the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention on 1 November 1998. On 4 May 1999 the Chamber declared the application admissible and decided to invite the parties to submit their observations on the merits at a hearing. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 12 October 1999. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mrs M. Dubrocard, Deputy Director, Human Rights Division, Legal Affairs Department, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Agent, and Mr A. Ottan, Counsel. Claude Mazurek was born in 1942 and lives at La Grande-Motte. His mother died on 1 August 1990 of HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) encephalopathy. She left two children: a son, Alain, born out of wedlock in 1936 and legitimised by his mother’s marriage in 1937. Alain brought an action against the applicant in the Nîmes tribunal de grande instance seeking an order that his mother's estate be divided by a notary. In a judgment of 21 January 1993 the court ordered the estate to be divided. With regard to the applicant's rights, it referred to Article 760 of the Civil Code. The Court of Appeal ruled that Article 760 was necessary to protect the interests of legitimate children. It said that the money was not intended to be part of a gift to the child. The court said that it was part of the obligation of parents to share the benefits of their children's birth with their children. The case is still pending in the High Court of Justice of France. The decision is expected to be heard in May or June, 2014. The appeal is likely to be settled in the next few months. It is likely that the decision will be made to restore the money to the rightful owners of the child's parents' bank account. The applicant appealed on points of law to the Court of Cassation, which delivered its judgment on 25 June 1996. The court was properly entitled to hold that it was not the intention of the legislature to discriminate between children on the grounds of their birth, but to ensure minimum compliance with the marital obligations of a married parent with regard to his or her legitimate children. The applicant’s complaint of unjustified discrimination on grounds of birth between children born in wedlock and children born out of wedlock, contrary to Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention, was rejected. In respect of the complaint that the. Court of Appeal had ordered the sum transferred to the applicant's account to be returned to the estate to be divided, the Court. of. Cassation held that in deciding that the facts of the case had not shown any intention on the part of the. deceased to bestow a gift on her son in advance of the division of her estate, the court had determined an issue which it alone had jurisdiction to determine.

name: Andrzej Rybacki
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 52479/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention on remand had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3. The Court declared admissible the applicant’s complaints relating to the excessive length of his detention and the lack of unsupervised contacts with his lawyer at the investigation stage of the proceedings. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible by the Court on 9 October 2007. An appeal lodged by the applicant against the decision of 1 August 1996 was unsuccessful. On 23 December 1996 the prosecutor filed a bill of indictment against the applicant and his co-accused with the Wrocław Regional Court. The first hearing in the case was held on 21 March 1997. The court held subsequent hearings on 11 and 12 September and 18 November 1997, and 10 February and 3 March 1998. On 16 April 1998 the court heard evidence from two anonymous witnesses who answered questions which had previously been formulated in writing by. the applicant’s lawyers. On 25 March 1998 they submitted to the court a list of further questions to be put to one of those witnesses. Wrocław Regional Court requested the Supreme Court to prolong the applicant’s detention, which was about to exceed two years. The court found that apart from the reasonable suspicion that he and the two co-accused persons had committed the offence at issue, there existed an actual risk that they would obstruct the proceedings if released. The Supreme Court also recommended that the trial court should “schedule the hearings in a more rational way so as to avoid further intervals of several months in the instant case”.Subsequent hearings were held on 9 July, 16 September, 1 October and 3 November 1998. The judge found that the proceedings were lengthy because of the long intervals between the hearings. On 9 May 1996, a day after the applicant was arrested, his wife retained a lawyer to represent him. On 13 October 1998 the Supreme Court extended the applicant’s detention until 30 November 1998. The next hearing was held on 7 December 1998. On 27 October 1999 the Wrocław Court of Appeal upheld the first‑instance judgment. On 16 November 2001 that court dismissed the appeal as manifestly unsubstantiated. The applicant and his co-accused were found guilty of robbery committed by an organised criminal gang. He was sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment and a fine. The case is still ongoing. Wrocław Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 15 July 1996. The court noted that the applicant could at that time see his lawyer whenever he requested. The restrictions imposed on his contacts with his lawyer did not impair his defence rights. The only restriction imposed on the applicant concerned the possibility of having unsupervised contact with his lawyers. The fact that a prosecutor was to be present during these visits did not affect the applicant’s defence rights at that stage, the more so as the restriction was to apply only during the investigations. A defence strategy could also be discussed in accordance with the law in the presence of a person appointed by the prosecutor.

name: John Beck
train_texts: The case originated in three applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that an investigation into their sexuality and their discharge from the armed forces on the basis of their homosexuality violated their rights under Articles 3, 8 and 10. The applications were allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 of the Rules of Court) The Court decided that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 25 of the rules of court) The applicants were born in 1959, 1957 and 1967 and live in Lancashire, Tyne and Wear and Worcester. The first applicant joined the Royal Air Force (‘RAF’) in 1976. By 1993 he had reached the rank of sergeant in the Electronic Warfare Operational Support Establishment (“EWOSE”) where he was employed as a communications systems analyst. The first applicant’s service evaluations covering the period June 1990 to January 1993 all recorded his conduct as exemplary. On 10 May 1993 the first applicant informed the EWOSE security officer that he was homosexual and he made it clear that he had always been a celibate homosexual. Later that day he saw his immediate superior to whom he also admitted his homosexuality. He was suspended from his duties from 17 May 1993. The EWOSE. police investigation commenced on 20 May 1993 which included their completing a Character Defect Enquiry (“CDE”) on the first applicant. The CDE report was dated 8 June 1993, briefly described the first Applicant and his service career noting that he was currently engaged to serve until February 2006. It also outlined the detailed observations made by a number of persons to the service police, which are summarised below. The report also recorded the information received from the first. applicant’s immediate superior who had described his character and his interest in theology. The statements of two colleagues of the first applicants were also recorded in the CDE. The first applicant’s ex-wife (also in the armed forces) provided a detailed statement to the service police which was recorded in the CDE report. She described her hesitations in marrying the first applicant, their marital difficulties, their financial difficulties and their separation in 1987 and their divorce in 1988. The report concluded that no signs of homosexual tendencies were identified by the first applicants ex- wife, colleagues or friends, that the only evidence was the applicant's own admission and that the enquiry had not revealed anything to rebut his submissions that he had not had a homosexual physical relationship. It went on to record that: “[the first applicant] has been a loyal and trustworthy serviceman for 17 years and has worked hard to become a clergyman’ The first applicant is five years away from a substantial gratuity and pension, which he has now lost together with his career. His homosexual tendencies cannot be reconciled easily in the Royal Air Force and his continued retention is not consistent with good discipline or morale. This lonely and solitary individual, who has had to face up to a situation not of his own making, deserves to be treated in a compassionate and dignified manner. The Unit Commander noted: “With the current official policy on homosexuality, the simple fact is that [the first applicant] cannot be retained. This is a sad case and I am sorry for it.” The first applicant was discharged from the RAF on grounds of his homosexuality. The second applicant joined the Royal Army Medical Corps on 1 June 1978 and was indexed as a pupil nurse on 12 November 1979. In June 1981 the second applicant commenced a homosexual relationship with a civilian. Six months later he received a posting order to Germany and applied for a home posting as he wished to remain in the United Kingdom with his partner. His application was refused. He submitted that he then realised that he could not lead a double life or face separation from his. partner. Although he knew that revealing his homosexuality would lead to his discharge, he informed his nurse tutor. The latter informed the personnel officer who conducted four interviews with the first applicant. The second applicant was discharged from the army on 29 January 1982 on grounds of his homosexuality. He was required to undergo a psychiatric assessment and was advised that this was necessary in order to ascertain whether he was, in fact, homosexual. It was felt that, while his “work has as yet not deteriorated”, the “problems of his relationship” would affect his work and reliability in the near future. The third applicant joined the RAF on 10 November 1985 and commenced officer training at the RAF college. He achieved the rank of Flight Lieutenant in September 1991 and served as a second navigator at a RAF base in Scotland. Although he was not yet recommended for further promotion, he was progressing satisfactorily. The third applicant’s credit card holder, which he had previously lost, was found by an officer of the service police in the latter's internal mail. Its contents aroused suspicion that the third applicant might be homosexual. The third applicant confirmed that the cards were his and that he was homosexual. He indicated that his wife knew at the time of his statement of his homosexuality and he confirmed the statements made during his interview as to his previous homosexual relationships. He made it clear that he did not wish to provide the names of those persons with whom he had had a homosexual relationship and stated that he had not made the statement to get a discharge from service. He was suspended from his normal primary duties with immediate effect. Mr Perkins was discharged from the RAF on grounds of his homosexuality in September 1995. He was also dismissed from the Royal Navy in 1995. In 1996 he applied to the High Court for leave to take judicial review proceedings. On 3 July 1996 he was granted leave by the Court of Appeal. The High Court referred the question of the applicability of the Equal Treatment Directive to differences of treatment based on sexual orientation to the ECJ pursuant to former Article 177 of the Treaty of Rome (R. v. Secretary of State for Defence, ex parte Perkins, 13 March 1997). On 2 March 1998 the. ECJ enquired of the. High Court in the Perkins case whether it wished to maintain the Article 177 reference. After a hearing between the parties, the High. Court decided to withdraw the question. The applicants argued, inter alia, in favour of the applicability of the Equal Treatment Directive to a difference of treatment based on sexual orientation. Following a hearing before the Industrial Tribunal in August 1996, their cases together with a series of similar cases, were stayed pending the outcome of the above-described Perkins case. That stay was renewed in May 1997 and in June 1998. However, further to the High Court decision of 13 July 1998 in the Perkins case, the applicants, following legal advice, withdrew their applications before the industrial tribunal. The tribunal consequently dismissed their applications on 23 December 1998. The case was dismissed as a result.

The applicants alleged that an investigation into their sexuality and their discharge from the armed forces on the basis of their homosexuality violated their rights. The applications were allocated to the Third Section of the Court. The Court decided that no hearing on the merits was required. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. The first applicant was granted legal aid on 31 January 2000. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) and the case was transferred to the Fifth Section. The first applicant joined the Royal Air Force (“RAF”) 4 May 1976. By 1993 he had reached the rank of sergeant in the Electronic Warfare Operational Support Establishment (‘EWOSE’) where he was employed as a communications systems analyst. During his service he was awarded the Air Officer Commanding Commendation for Meritorious Service and the Long Service and Good Conduct medal. The first applicant’s service evaluations covering the period June 1990 to January 1993 all recorded his conduct as exemplary and, for the most part, his trade proficiency, supervisory ability and personal qualities were assessed at 8 out of 10. The detailed evaluations were all positive. The EWOSE. police investigation commenced on 20 May 1993 which included their completing a Character Defect Enquiry (“CDE”) on the first applicant. The CDE report was dated 8 June 1993 and outlined the detailed observations made by a number of persons to the service police, which are summarised below. The report also recorded the information received from the first. applicant’s immediate superior and his interest in theology. The statements of two colleagues of the first applicants were also recorded in the CDE. report. The first applicant had admitted his homosexuality to him two weeks before he did so to the armed forces’ authorities. He was currently engaged to serve until February 2006. The first applicant’s ex-wife (also in the armed forces) provided a detailed statement to the service police which was recorded in the CDE report. She described her hesitations in marrying the first applicant, their marital difficulties, their financial difficulties and their separation in 1987 and their divorce in 1988. The report concluded that no signs of homosexual tendencies were identified by the first applications ex-wives, colleagues or friends, that the only evidence was the first applicants own admission and that the enquiry had not revealed anything to rebut his submissions that he had not had a homosexual physical relationship. It went on to record that: “[the first applicant] has been a loyal and trustworthy serviceman for 17 years and has worked hard to become a priest’ First applicant's performance as a tradesman and supervisor has remained unaffected until his disclosure on 10 May 1993. Despite the devious and deliberate concealment of his homosexual tendencies, [the first applicant’s] honesty and character have caused him finally to admit to the truth. [The first applicant] is five years away from a substantial gratuity and pension, which he has now lost together with his career. This lonely and solitary individual, who has had to face up to a situation not of his own making, deserves to be treated in a compassionate and dignified manner. “With the current official policy on homosexuality, the simple fact is that [thefirst applicant] cannot be retained. This is a sad case and I am saddened by it” In 1993, a Board of the RAF, two of whose members thought it apt to liken the first applicant’s case to ‘a murder inquiry without a body’, recommended his administrative discharge on grounds of his homosexuality. The second applicant joined the Royal Army Medical Corps on 1 June 1978 and was indexed as a pupil nurse on 12 November 1979. In June 1981 the second applicant commenced a homosexual relationship with a civilian. Six months later he received a posting order to Germany and applied for a home posting as he wished to remain in the United Kingdom with his partner. His application was refused. He submitted that he then realised that he could not lead a double life or face separation from his partner and informed his nurse tutor. Although he knew that revealing his homosexuality would lead to his discharge, he informed his Nurse tutor. The latter informed the personnel officer who conducted four interviews with the first. applicant. The first applicant was discharged on 27 November 1993. The second applicant was discharged from the army on 29 January 1982 on grounds of his homosexuality. He had admitted to homosexual acts with civilians but there was no evidence of such activity with soldiers. The third applicant joined the RAF on 10 November 1985 and commenced officer training at the RAF college. He was commissioned as Acting Petty Officer on 27 March 1986, achieved the rank of Flight Lieutenant in September 1991 and served as a second navigator at a RAF base in Scotland. Although he was not yet recommended for further promotion, he was progressing satisfactorily in his current post and should be a contender to become a first navigator in due course. In August 1994 the third applicant’s credit card holder, which he had previously lost, was found by an officer of the service police in the latter's internal mail. The third applicant confirmed that the cards were his and that he was homosexual. He indicated that his wife knew at the time of his statement of his homosexuality and he confirmed the statements made during his interview as to his previous homosexual relationships. He made it clear that he did not wish to provide the names of those persons with whom he had had a homosexual relationship and stated that he had not made the statement to get a discharge from service. A report was prepared recommending that he be ordered to resign his commission on the grounds of unsuitability. Mr Perkins was discharged from the RAF on grounds of his homosexuality in 1995. train_texts: The application was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 19 October 2001. The applicant claims to have been insulted and beaten, in particular, hit with truncheons on the legs, and that one of the policemen sexually harassed her. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The application was dismissed on 16 December 2005. The case was brought by a Turkish national, Ms Eser Ceylan, who was born in 1975 and lives in Ankara. A forensic expert noted that there were no traces of battery on the applicant's body other than those mentioned in the report of 12 December 2000. The judge of the Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance sent a letter to the Ankara public prosecutor's office, stating that almost all of the defendants in the case had complained of ill-treatment by the security forces. On 30 January 2001 the public prosecutor decided not to prosecute the police officers who had been on duty at the relevant time. In this connection, he maintained that the complainants had taken part in a demonstration against F-type prisons. Although before intervening and making arrests the police had given the demonstrators a warning and had ordered them to disperse. The Ministry of the Interior lodged an action for compensation against the applicant and the other co-accused. The court's reasoned decision refers to evidence such as eye-witness reports, video recordings of the Security Directorate and other national television channels. On 22 January 2004 the Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance acquitted the applicant on account of lack of evidence. According to the information available in the file, the compensation proceedings were apparently still pending on the date on which the present judgment was adopted. The application was dismissed on 6 July 2001, and the case was referred to the closest assize court, against the decision of 30 January 2001.

train_texts: The case was referred to the Court in accordance with the provisions applicable prior to the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case originated in an application (no. 27644/95) against the Swiss Confederation lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicants complained that they had not had access to a “tribunal” within the meaning of Article 6 § 1. The Commission declared the application admissible on 7 April 1997. In its report of 15 April 1998 it expressed the opinion that there had been no violation of Article 1. The applicants live in the villages of Villigen, Würenlingen, Böttstein and Kleindöttingen, situated in zone 1 in the vicinity of unit II of a nuclear power plant in Beznau (Canton of Aargau). They either own or rent property. The application for an operating licence was made by a private company on 18 December 1991. The Grand Chamber decided (by sixteen votes with one abstention) not to apply Rule 39 in the present case. The applicants and the Government each filed a memorial and replied to the questions of the Court. The case will be heard by the Swiss Court of Appeal on 17 September 2015. Complaints were filed against the Beznau II nuclear power plant. The Federal Council dismissed all the objections as being unfounded. NOK was granted a limited operating licence expiring on 31 December 2004. The licence was subject to compliance with various specific conditions concerning, for instance, threshold levels for radioactive substances, tests of the safeguard system, improvements of the feedwater system, for ageing surveillance and various other continuous technical improvements. The decision was based on a safety evaluation report established by the Swiss Nuclear Safety Inspectorate (Hauptabteilung für die Sicherheit der Kernanlagen – “HSK”). The Federal Council found that no relevant deficiencies could be established. The Federal Council observed that since the Beznau II nuclear power plant had come into operation various backfittings to improve the safety of the power plant. It referred to the emergency standby system and improved power supply system (NANO), put into operation in 1992, and the filtered containment venting system. Furthermore the results of the probabilistic safety analysis showed that a nuclear accident was unlikely. The report gave the results from the point of view of nuclear safety and radiation protection, including conclusions and proposals for licence conditions to be formulated in the licensing decision. It also gave detailed reasons why it found the objections to be unfounded. The Swiss people and the majority of the cantons had expressed the wish to continue using nuclear energy. The reactor of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant was technically not comparable to a light-water reactor like that of the Beznau II power plant. The Chernobyl reactor had never undergone a safety review process as normally carried out in western countries. It was therefore not relevant in the context of the assessment of the risks of western nuclear power plants. The Federal Council also pointed out that, in accordance with the Agreement of 10 August 1982, the German authorities had been provided with the relevant documents. There would be no risk for the population of the Federal Republic of Germany. The condition of the power plant with regard to nuclear safety and radiation protection and also to its operation had been rated as good. All the safety systems installed at the Beznau II nuclear power plant for the purpose of preventing nuclear accidents were very seriously flawed compared with more modern pressurised water reactors in central Europe. The safety systems for their failure to ensure that the back-up components were physically separate and protected from fire. The standard of the emergency cooling system and residual heat removal compared to modern light water pressure reactors incentral Europe was also criticised. The unsatisfactory emergency power supply concerning certain components that were important was criticised. The lack of protection against outside influences rendered the plant much more vulnerable to a plane crash or to action by third parties. No demand had been made for an actual emergency system, such as was required for the more recent western European pressurised water reactors. Such deficiencies not only created an increased risk of accident but gave rise to concern with regard to the effectiveness of damage limitation and emergency protection in the event of serious malfunctions at the power station. The standards applied in the licensing procedure at issue were far below those applying in other central European countries – i.e. risks were accepted that would no longer be tolerated in other countries. The report further referred to the OSART mission which was conducted in 1995.
