The applicants live in the villages of Villigen, Würenlingen, Böttstein and Kleindöttingen. They either own or rent property. The Beznau II nuclear power plant consists of a dual-loop pressurised water reactor. The site is situated five kilometres from the German border. The application for an operating licence was made on 18 December 1991. The applicants and the Government each filed a memorial and replied to the questions of the Court. The Grand Chamber decided (by sixteen votes with one abstention) not to apply Rule 39 in the present case. On 28 February 2000 the applicants submitted unsolicited material relating to the supply of nuclear fuel to the Bezn Kau II nuclear plant from 1996 to 1998 by a British company. Complainants requested the Federal Council to refuse an extension of the operating licence and to order the immediate and permanent closure of the nuclear power plant. They attached an expert opinion of the Institute for Applied Ecology (Öko-Institut – Institut für angewandte Ökologie e. V.) in Darmstadt, Germany, to their objections. The Federal Council dismissed all the objections as being unfounded and granted NOK a limited operating licence expiring on 31 December 2004. The licence was subject to compliance with various specific conditions concerning, for instance, threshold levels for radioactive substances, tests of the safeguard system, improvements of the feedwater system. The Federal Council considered each of the objections in turn. The Federal Council gave detailed reasons why it found the objections to be unfounded. It concluded that on the basis of the evidence submitted no relevant deficiencies could be established. The report gave the results from the point of view of nuclear safety and radiation protection, including conclusions and proposals for licence conditions to be formulated in the licensing decision. It referred to the emergency standby system and improved power supply system (NANO), put into operation in 1992, and the filtered containment venting system. Furthermore the results of the probabilistic safety analysis carried out at the Beznau II nuclear power plant showed that a nuclear accident was unlikely. The Federal Council said that the reactor of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant was technically not comparable to a light-water reactor like that of the Beznau II power plant. Council further observed that by voting against the popular initiative of 23 September 1990 “For the Progressive Abandonment of Nuclear Energy” the Swiss people and the majority of the cantons had expressed the wish to continue using nuclear energy. The Federal Council also pointed out that, in accordance with the Agreement of 10 August 1982 between the government of the Swiss Confederation and the Federal Republic of Germany, the German authorities had been provided with the relevant documents relating to the requested operating licence. The Beznau II power plant had followed an ageing surveillance programme as a permanent task for its safety-relevant plant components. A mission of the Operational Safety Assessment Review Team (OSART) from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) was conducted at the power plant. The experts noted especially “the stringent requirements with regard to quality and safety, the professional qualities of the staff at all levels as well as the very satisfactory condition of the BeznAU II nuclear power plant”. The report criticised, for example, the safety systems for their failure to ensure that the back-up components were physically separate and protected from fire. The standard of the emergency cooling system and residual heat removal compared to modern light water pressure reactors in central Europe was also criticised. Lack of protection against outside influences rendered the plant much more vulnerable to a plane crash or to action by third parties. No demand had been made for an actual emergency system, such as was required for the more recent western European pressurised water reactors. The standards applied in the licensing procedure at issue were far below those applying in other central European countries – i.e. risks were accepted that would no longer be tolerated in other countries. The report further referred to the OSART mission which was conducted in 1995 and the criticism expressed by the experts with regard to the organisational structures and management at the Beznau II power plant.

name: Linda Grant
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained of the lack of legal recognition of her change of gender and the refusal of the Department of Social Security to pay her a retirement pension at the age of 60. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. By a decision of 19 May 2005, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine) The case was settled by the Court’s decision. Adjudication Officer issued on 31 October 1997 that she had applied ‘too early’ He stated that she was only entitled to a State pension from the age of 65, the retirement age applicable to men. Her appeal against this decision was heard by Birmingham Social Security Appeal Tribunal on 12 March 1998, which dismissed it on the basis of established case-law. In light of the judgments of 11 July 2002 given by the Grand Chamber in Christine Goodwin v. the United Kingdom, the applicant wrote to the Office of Social Security on 12 July 2002 asking for her case to be reopened. The Commissioner notified her on 14 August 2002 that leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal had been granted. By a decision of 10 April 2003, their Lordships, whilst finding the continuing failure to legislate to be a breach of Articles 8 and 12, deemed the formulation of legal norms to remedy that breach best left to the Government. The applicant was issued with a Gender Recognition Certificate on 26 April 2005. She had applied under the Gender recognition Act 2004 which had come into force on 1 July 2004. The Government refused to make any ex gratia payment of a sum representing her lost State pension. The applicant consented to a court order dismissing her appeal with no order as to costs. The Court of Appeal ruled in her favour. The case was heard at the High Court in London and the decision was returned to the Supreme Court. The Appeal Court returned a decision in favour of the applicant. The High Court ruled in the applicant’s favour and the Appeal Court ruled that the decision had been made in her behalf.

The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained of the lack of legal recognition of her change of gender and the refusal of the Department of Social Security to pay her a retirement pension at the age of 60. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine) The case was heard in May 2005 and the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The decision was made to allow the application to go ahead. The applicant applied for a State pension from the age of 65, the retirement age applicable to men. Adjudication Officer issued on 31 October 1997. He stated that she had applied “too early”, and was only entitled to a state pension from 65. Her appeal against this decision was heard by Birmingham Social Security Appeal Tribunal on 12 March 1998. At this time she claimed that she was no longer able to work due to a spinal collapse fracture of osteoporotic origin. On 1 October 1998 the applicant submitted her appeal to the Social Security Commissioner. Leave to appeal was granted but, by a decision of 1 June 2000, her appeal was dismissed following an oral hearing. In the Court of Appeal, the applicant sought, inter alia, a declaration that she is entitled to her full retirement pension. The House of Lords disapproved of attempts to seek recognition even in the clearest cases. Parliament ([2003] WLR 1174). Further, the applicant was advised by her legal representative that the prospects of persuading the Court of Appeal to depart from the Bellinger judgment were nil. If proceedings were continued, she would further risk punitive costs orders. The applicant consented to a court order dismissing her appeal with no order as to costs. The Government further refused to make any ex gratia payment of a sum representing her lost State pension. On 26 April 2005 the applicant. was issued with a Gender Recognition Certificate following her application under the Gender. Recognition Act 2004 which had come into force on 1 July 2004.

name: Kristina Sheffield
train_texts: Sheffield v. the United Kingdom and Horsham v the United UK were referred to the Court as two separate cases by the European Commission of Human Rights on 4 March 1997. The object of the requests was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the cases disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8, 12, 13 and 14 of the Convention. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them (Rule 30). On 19 March 1997 the then President of the Court, Mr R. Ryssdal, decided, under Rule 21 § 7 and in the interests of the proper administration of justice, that a single Chamber should be constituted to consider both cases. The case was heard in Strasbourg on 24 February 1998. The Court decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of a Grand Chamber. The Grand Chamber included ex officio Mr Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court, together with the other members and the four substitutes of the original Chamber. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Ms S. McCrory, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr D. Pannick QC, Mr R. Singh, Barrister-at-Law, Counsel, Mr J. Talbot, Ms C. Lloyd, Ms R. Sandby-Thomas, Advisers and Mrs G.H. Thune, Delegate. The first applicant, Miss Kristina Sheffield, is a British citizen born in 1946 and currently resident in London. At birth the applicant was registered as being of the male sex. Prior to her gender reassignment treatment she was married. She has one daughter from that marriage, which is now dissolved. She was informed by her consultant psychiatrist and her surgeon that she was required to obtain a divorce as a precondition to surgery being carried out. Following the divorce, the applicant’s former spouse applied to the court to have her contact with her daughter terminated. The applicant states that the judge granted the application on the basis that contact with a transsexual would not be allowed. The applicant's new name has been entered on her passport and driving licence. Her birth certificate and various records including social- security and police records continue to record her original name and gender. The applicant maintains that her decision to undergo gender reassignment surgery has resulted in her being subjected to discrimination at work or in relation to obtaining work. She states that she was dismissed by her employers in 1986 as a direct consequence of her gender reassigned and has found it impossible to obtain employment in the respondent State in her chosen profession. She also notes that she is obliged under the Perjury Act 1911 to disclose her former sexual identity in certain contexts under pain of criminal sanction. The second applicant, Miss Rachel Horsham, is a British citizen born in 1946. She has been living in the Netherlands since 1974 and acquired Netherlands citizenship by naturalisation in September 1993. The second applicant was registered at birth as being of the male sex. She left the United Kingdom in 1971 as she was concerned about the consequences of being identified as a transsexual. Thereafter she led her life abroad as a female and underwent gender reassignment surgery on 21 May 1992 at the Free University Hospital, Amsterdam. The British consulate issued a new passport to the applicant recording her new name and her sex as female. She states that she is forced to live in exile because of the legal situation in the United UK. Under English law, a person is entitled to adopt such first names or surname as he or she wishes. Such names are valid for purposes of identification and may be used in passports, driving licences, medical and insurance cards, etc. Under section 11(b) of the Matrimonial Causes Act 1973 any marriage where the parties are not respectively male and female is void. The criteria for determining the sex of a child at birth are not defined in the Act. The practice of the Registrar is to use exclusively the biological criteria (chromosomal, gonadal and genital) as laid down by Mr Justice Ormrod in the above-mentioned case of Corbett. The 1953 Act provides for the correction by the Registrar of clerical errors or factual errors. The official position is that an amendment may only be made if the error occurred when the birth was registered. No error is accepted to exist in the birth entry of a person who undergoes medical and surgical treatment to enable that person to assume the role of the opposite sex. A transsexual continues to be recorded for social security, national insurance and employment purposes as being of the sex recorded at birth. A male-to-female transsexual will accordingly only be entitled to a State pension at the State retirement age of 65 and not the age of 60 which is applicable to women. Ruling of the ECJ was applied by the Employment Appeal Tribunal in a decision handed down on 27 June 1997 (Chessington World of Adventures Ltd v. Reed [1997] 1 Industrial Law Reports). The majority of member States now make provision for such recognition. Only four (including the United Kingdom) do not permit a change to be made to a person’s birth certificate in one form or another to reflect the re-assigned sex of that person. To tolerate such discrimination would be tantamount to a failure to respect the dignity and freedom to which he or she is entitled and which the Court has a duty to safeguard. Miss Horsham alleged that the refusal of the respondent State to give legal recognition to her status as a woman following gender reassignment surgery gave rise to violations of Articles 3, 8, 12, 13 and 14 of the Convention. The Commission declared the application (no. 23390/94) admissible on 19 January 1996 with the exception of her complaints under Article 3 and Article 3 of Protocol No. 4 which had been declared inadmissible on 4 September 1995. The Government requested the Court to decide and declare that the facts disclose no breach of the applicants’ rights. The full text of the Commission’s opinions in the two cases and of the dissenting opinions contained in the reports is reproduced as an annex to this judgment.

According to the study carried out by Liberty, the majority of member States now make provision for such recognition. For example, out of thirty-seven countries analysed, only four do not permit a change to be made to a person’s birth certificate in one form or another to reflect the re-assigned sex of that person. The applicants in their joint memorial requested the Court to decide and declare that the facts of the case disclose a breach of their rights under Article 8 of the Convention and/or Article 14 in conjunction with Article 8, and to award them just satisfaction under Article 50. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 7505/06) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that while performing his military service he had lost the sight in his left eye as a result of the military authorities’ failure to provide him with prompt and appropriate medical assistance. On 16 December 2014 the Chamber decided, under Rule 54 § 2 (c) of the Rules of Court, to invite the parties to submit further written observations on the admissibility of the applicant’s complaint. In October 2002 he filed a claim for compensation for the damage to his eye. The court ruled that he was not entitled to compensation because he had not been treated by a doctor in the first week of his illness. He also argued that he should have been treated when he was first admitted to the hospital. He was discharged from the military in July 2002 after receiving treatment for his eye injuries for more than a year. His eyesight has since been restored. The case was settled out of court on a settlement of $2,000,000 (EUR1,500,000) with the Turkish Ministry of Health. The judge said that the case was a case of medical negligence, and that the compensation should be paid to him. The applicant asked the court to take steps to eliminate the inconsistencies by requesting and obtaining additional reports from a different set of experts. The cause of the corneal ulcer (Herpes virus? Fungal infection? Bacterial infection?) is not known. For this reason, it is not possible to decide whether the eye problem was related to his military service or whether it was idiosyncratic. The applicant should be awarded compensation either for the authorities’ negligence or if such negligence was established, according to the court’s decision. The case was heard in the Supreme Military Administrative Court in Istanbul on 5 April 2005. The hearing was adjourned until 6 April 2005, at which time it was decided to continue the case. On 18 May 2005 the Supreme Military Administrative Court, on the basis of the expert report of 6 April 2005, dismissed the applicant’s claim by a majority of four to one and held that no fault could be attributed to the military authorities in the treatment of the applicant. A medical report of 9 October 2009 issued by the Haseki Hospital deemed the applicant to be suffering from a permanent disability as a result of the loss of sight in his left eye. It was indicated that his ability to work had been reduced by 41% and that he was entitled to receive a disability pension. The applicant requested a rectification of the administrative court's decision. He claimed that his arguments had not been examined adequately by the court.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) The applicant was the owner and the editor-in-chief of a publishing house, Aram Basım ve Yayıncılık, which published a periodical, Vesta. The Istanbul public prosecutor filed an indictment with the Istanbul Assize Court, charging the applicant with disseminating propaganda in favour of a terrorist organisation. According to the indictment, certain passages of the article depicted the PKK0 as part of the Kurdish intellectual movement and hence constituted propaganda of the organisation. The court considered that the aforementioned passages and the article in its entirety constituted propaganda in favour of the PKK. It hence sentenced the applicant to ten months’ imprisonment and ordered him to pay a fine of 375 Turkish liras (TRY) Taking into account his good behaviour during the trial and his character, the court suspended the pronouncement of his conviction on condition that he did not commit another intentional offence for a period of five years, under Article 231 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (hükmün açıklanmasının geri bırakılması). On 22 October 2008 the court dismissed an objection lodged by the applicant against the above-mentioned decision.

name: Bogdan Dzierżanowski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 2983/02) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was born in 1966 and lives in Białystok, Poland. He was involved in a car accident as a result of which one person died. The application was sent to the Government on 24 August 2005. It was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Białystok District Court held a hearing on 26 November 1999. The applicant pleaded guilty and was sentenced to a suspended prison sentence on 8 June 2001. The judgment is final and the court has no power to overturn it. The trial court ordered that an expert opinion be prepared in 2000. On 10 May 2001 the next hearing was held. On the same day the applicant was found guilty and sentenced to two years in prison. The judge ordered that the expert opinion should be prepared. The expert opinion was completed in May 2001 and the applicant received a suspended sentence. The court found the applicant guilty on June 8 2001 and sentenced him to a two-year prison sentence.

name: David Gregory
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 2 December 1995. It originated in an application (no. 22299/93) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr David Gregory, a British citizen. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 and 14 of the Convention. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43) and Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 4 (b) The applicant, who is black, is a British citizen born in 1966 and currently living in Manchester, England. He was tried for robbery at Manchester Crown Court between 26 and 28 November 1991. The trial ended on the final day of the trial, at 10.46 a.m., the jury retired to consider their verdict. An hour and three quarters later a note was passed by the jury to the judge. It read: “JURY SHOWING RACIAL OVERTONES 1 MEMBER TO BE EXCUSED.” In the absence of the jury, the trial was held in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 21 October 1996. Judge showed the note to counsel for the prosecution and defence and consulted them on the appropriate response to it. defence counsel seems to recall that he did in fact ask the trial judge to discharge the jury in the circumstances, but his application was refused. Prosecution counsel recalls that defence counsel did not raise strong objections to the approach which the judge indicated he intended to pursue, namely to recall the jury and give clear directions on their duty to return a verdict on the basis of the evidence alone. The judge’s recollection is that both counsel agreed to his proposed course of action (see paragraph 11 above).The jury were recalled at 12.47 p.m. Pausing at appropriate junctures to ensure that his statement was being understood, the judge redirected the jury. The jury were unable to reach a unanimous verdict and were recalled by the judge. He told them that the time had come when he could accept a verdict of at least a majority of ten. The jury returned and delivered a ten to two majority verdict finding the applicant guilty. The applicant was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment. The appeal proceedings continued until 4.06 p.m. when the jury returned with a verdict in favour of the applicant. The Court of Appeal upheld the defendant's appeal against conviction. The judge said the trial judge had wrongly failed to make any enquiry into the note with a view to determining whether one of the members of the jury should be discharged on the grounds of racial prejudice and that this failure gave rise to the appeal. Leave to appeal was refused by the single judge on 28 February 1992. The applicant renewed his application to the full Court of Appeal. On 19 January 1993 the application was dismissed. The court continued: “Matters of this kind raise delicate issues. The jury system does require an element of give and take after proper directions from the judge. In our judgment His Honour Judge Hammond dealt with this matter sensitively, sensibly and correctly, and cannot be faulted for a conclusion that the jury should continue the deliberations which they had given their oath to undertake. We, therefore, find no ground for complaint and we dismiss this application’

name: Keith Anderson Beckles
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been denied a fair hearing since the judge at his trial misdirected the jury on the issue of the exercise by him of his right to silence during police interview. The application was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court, which declared it admissible on 28 August 2001. The Chamber decided after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The applicant and a co-defendant, M., were convicted of the robbery, false imprisonment and attempted murder of Mr Mohamed Mohamoud. M. was arrested on 13 January 1996, the applicant on 24 January and W. on 26 January. Mr Mohamoud was searched at knife-point by M. who took thirty to forty pounds in cash from him and then left to buy drugs. M. later returned with a quantity of crack cocaine which the occupants of the flat, but not Mr Mohanoud, smoked. He was prevented all this time from leaving the flat by the applicant. At some stage M.’s mood changed under the effects of the drugs and he became angry. M., together with the applicant and an unidentified woman, threw him out of the window. He fell four floors and survived, although he was left paralysed from the waist down. The applicant was interviewed by the police in September 1996 under caution. The applicant denied being in the room when Mr Mohamoud fell from the window. He stated that Mr Moh amoud had not been threatened and that “he was sitting there quite happy” The applicant declared that he had been told by W. that MrMohamoud had “gone out the window”. He had not believed this and looked out to check. He did not go to help him because he was ‘scared’ and thought he was dead. He watched the police and ambulance arrive from a neighbouring flat. When asked if he would like to offer any account of the events in question the applicant said ‘no comment’ The trial judge asked the applicant if he was prepared to testify as to what he had told his solicitor prior to the first interview during the lengthy consultation. The applicant replied that he had done so on the advice of his solicitor. The matter was not thereafter pursued by the prosecution or the trial judge. The trial judge directed the jury in his summing up to the jury to draw such inferences as seem to you to be fair and proper from the applicant’s failure to mention the points identified in his interview relating to his presence in the flat on that evening. The jury may hold that failure against them in deciding whether he is guilty. It is for each defendant ... to decide whether to answer or not. You decide what you make of the reasons given for not answering. If you thought that the reason given was a good one, then of course you could not hold it against them. But it is you who decide whether it is fair and proper to draw those adverse inferences.” At the request of the applicant’s counsel the trial judge gave the following further direction to the jury: “When dealing with the [applicant's] first [interview] when [he] failed to answer questions. I did not specifically remind you, though you have heard it any number of times, that the defendants were cautioned that they do not have to say anything” The applicant was convicted of robbery, false imprisonment and attempted murder and sentenced to a total of fifteen years’ imprisonment. The applicant and his co-accused appealed against conviction to the Court of Appeal. Lord Justice Henry stated in his judgment, with reference to section 34 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, that it could not have been the intention of Parliament to provide that the only adverse inference that could be drawn from failure to disclose facts was recent fabrication. “The purpose of the statutory provisions is to permit adverse inferences to be drawn where there has been late fabrication, to this extent, to encourage speedy disclosure of a genuine defence,” he said. Lord Justice Henry ruled that the jury could draw the adverse inference that the applicant was biding his time and seeing whether or not he would be identified. On 2 June 1998 the Court of Appeal refused to certify that that the case raised a point of public importance and refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords. The case was decided in favour of the applicant on the grounds that the trial judge should not have intervened to ask the applicant whether he wished to relate what he had said to his solicitor before the first police interview. The appeal was rejected on 9 May 1998 and the case was heard again in June 1998. The jury returned a verdict of not guilty.

He denied being in the room when Mr Mohamoud fell from the window and repeated that he had not been pushed out. The applicant was convicted of robbery, false imprisonment and attempted murder. He and his co-accused appealed against conviction to the Court of Appeal. Lord Justice Henry stated in his judgment that it could not have been the intention of Parliament to provide that the only adverse inference that could be drawn from failure to disclose facts was recent fabrication. He quoted with approval the judgment of Lord Justice Rose in the case of R. v Roble (judgment of 21 January 1997, unreported) On 7 May 1998 the Court. of Appeal in a reserved judgment and following a hearing dismissed the appeal. against the applicant. The application is still pending. The jury may make such inferences as they think proper in their task of considering their verdict. Lord Justice Henry considered that this intervention was improper and an invitation to the applicant to waive legal professional privilege. Werner, a lawyer practising in Szczecin-Mierzyn. The Polish Government (“the Government”) was represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicants are Ms Grażyna Waltoś and Ms Wanda Pawlicz, born in 1949 and 1956. The case is currently pending before the first-instance court in Koszalin. The applicants lodged a complaint under the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. In 2007 the District Court held 7 hearings and gave a judgment in the case. The judgment was quashed on 27 February 2009 and the case was remitted for re-examination. The case is being heard by the first court in the district of Koszalin, in the region of the same name as the district court where it was heard in 2007. The proceedings are being heard under the 2004 Act of the Republic of Poland.

name: Hans Salomonsson
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38978/97) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his rights under Article 6 of the Convention had been violated on account of the lack of an oral hearing before the Administrative Court of Appeal and the Supreme Administrative Court in proceedings concerning social security benefits. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. By a decision of 4 May 2000 the Court declared the application partly admissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Stockholm. The court did not hold an oral hearing nor did the applicant request one. The applicant later made a new application, which was rejected by the Office on 8 February 1995. On 5 December 1995 the applicant made yet another application for disability benefits. On 3 April 1996 the application was rejected, which again found that the applicant’s costs did not attain the required level. In a decision of 23 July 1996 the court noted that the issue in the case was whether the applicant's extra costs attained the level required for a disability allowance under the 1962 Act. In these circumstances, it gave the applicant the benefit of the doubt and granted him an allowance. The applicant requested the appellate court to hold an oral hearing in the case. It was rejected by the court on 15 May 1997. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten). He requested that the case be referred back to the Administrative Court of Appeal for re-examination or, alternatively, that the Supreme administrative court confirm the County Administrative Court’s judgment. On 26 August 1997 the applicant was refused the applicant leave to appeal. The case can be determined notwithstanding a failure to submit such written observations, the court said. The Appeals Court ruled that the applicant had met the conditions for a disability allowance but that there was no need for mineral water.

train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 29 May 1995. It originated in an application (no. 22500/93) against the French Republic lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by two French nationals. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 8 of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings. The President gave the applicants leave, as lawyers, to present their own case. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr L.-E. Pettiti, the elected judge of French nationality. The Court heard the case of a couple who wanted to give their daughter the name "Armine, Angèle" after their daughter's forenames. The case was heard in Strasbourg on 23 April 1996. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg. The Court heard addresses by Mr Martínez, Mr Guillot and Mrs Dubrocard. The applicants did not appeal against this decision and it became final and the three children moved to Switzerland clandestinely in 2009. The court ruled that the children should not be forced to return to the country they came from. They should be allowed to stay with their mother until they are older. The application was rejected on the grounds that they had not been given a chance to make their case for why they should not return to Switzerland. Cantonal Court asked the Swiss embassy in Pristina to send it a copy of the visa application the second applicant had made on 13 March 2007, in which she had allegedly mentioned the existence of her three children. In its answer the embassy informed the Cantonal Court that it could not provide a copy because in accordance with internal instructions it had been destroyed after two years. The court ruled that the domestic law indicated that the request for residence permits on the ground of family reunification for R. and L. had been submitted late. Residence permits could therefore only be issued to them if there were important family reasons as set out in Article 47 (4) of the Foreign Nationals Act. The applicants and their children appealed to the Federal Supreme Court against the Cantonal Court’s decision. They claimed expulsion of the three children would violate Article 3 of the Convention, because in their home country the children would have to be dependent on social services or be sent to an orphanage. By a decision of 18 November 2011 the Federal. Supreme Court rejected the applicants’ appeal. It ruled that the refusal of the residence permits was proportionate under domestic law as well as under Article 8 of the. Convention. The applicants requested that, pending the proceedings before it, the Swiss Government be invited to revoke the expulsion of their three children. The. applicants were informed that their request for the application of Rule 39 of the Rules of the Court had been dismissed but that their application had been granted priority. On 17 July 2012 the cantonal authorities of the Canton of Vaud issued a permanent residence permit to the second applicant. R., L. and B. were still residing in Switzerland on 18 April 2013. R. will be able to enter high school (le lycée) the following school year. B. will also be allowed to attend high school in Vaud for the next two years. A. is expected to start high school at the end of the 2013-2014 school year in Geneva. The applicants' lawyer confirmed that R. and L. will still be living in Switzerland. The application has been rejected by the Swiss authorities.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 948/12) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the refusal by the Swiss authorities to allow their three children to reside in Switzerland constituted a breach of their right to respect for family life. Pending proceedings before the Court the applicants therefore requested that Rule 39 of the Rules of Court be applied. The application was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29§1) The applicants and the Government each submitted observations on the merits (Rule 59§1). The first applicant married a Swiss national in 2000. On 26 August 2006 he got divorced. On 10 January 2007 he married the second applicant in Rahovec (Kosovo) The second applicant entered Switzerland on 6 April 2007 with a visa. On 7 June 2007 the first applicant applied for a residence permit for theSecond applicant on the ground of family reunification. The Migration Office decided on 2 June 2008 to investigate the applicants’ family situation. Both applicants, as well as first applicant’s ex-wife, were interviewed. The first applicant “had abused her naivety and her good will” and ‘had lied to her by hiding the fact that he had children, especially one born during their marriage’ The Migration Office refused the applicants’ request for family reunification with their children. It ruled that neither the first nor the second applicant had mentioned the existence of their three children when they entered Switzerland. They established that the applicants had not conducted themselves correctly with regard to the application. The applicants did not appeal against this decision and it became final on May 31, 2010. The first applicant informed the Migration Office that R., L. and B. had been living in Switzerland illegally since 15 August 2009. He explained that it had been urgent to bring them to the respondent State because L.’s chances of recovery were better in Switzerland. The three children entered Switzerland on 15 August 2009. The applicants had submitted a request for residence permits for them on the ground of family reunification. On 13 July 2010 the Migration Office informed the applicants that it intended to dismiss their request. The Migration Office established that the applicants had brought the children to Switzerland illegally despite a negative decision of 28 April 2009. It also reiterated that the children’s existence had previously been concealed from the Swiss authorities, and that the paternity of the first applicant had not been established. The request regarding R. and L., aged fifteen and 14 respectively at the time of the application, was therefore late. Conversely, the request for B., aged seven at that time, was within the set time-limit. The children were separated from their parents in 2008. The children were not reunited with their parents until 2009. They were given a chance to apply for reunification in 2010. The application was denied on the grounds that the children had been separated too long. They are now seeking reunification with their father. The case has been heard by the Swiss Court of Appeal, which has ruled in favour of the children. The appeal will be heard again in October 2014. The decision was made on the basis of the evidence presented by the children, who are still in the care of their parents. The court’s decision will be appealed to the Supreme Court of Switzerland. Cantonal Court asked the Swiss embassy in Pristina to send it a copy of the visa application the second applicant had made on 13 March 2007, in which she had allegedly mentioned the existence of her three children. In its answer the embassy informed the Cantonal Court that it could not provide a copy because in accordance with internal instructions it had been destroyed after two years. Residence permits could therefore only be issued to them if there were important family reasons as set out in Article 47 (4) of the Foreign Nationals Act. In the case of R. and L. no such important family Reasons could be identified; in particular, the positive development of L.’s recovery would not justify the permanent establishment of the children in Switzerland. The applicants and their children appealed to the Federal Supreme Court against the Cantonal Court’s decision. They argued in particular that the refusal of the residence permits for the children was in breach of Article 8 of the Convention. They claimed that expulsion of the three children would violate Article 3 of the convention, because in their home country the children would have to be dependent on social services or be sent to an orphanage. By a decision of 18 November 2011 the FederalSupreme Court rejected the applicants’ appeal. In March 2012 the applicants were informed that their request for the application of Rule 39 of the Rules of the Court had been dismissed but that their application had been granted priority. R., L. and B. were granted a permanent residence permit on 17 July 2012. Their lawyer confirmed in April 2013 that they were still living in Switzerland. R. was allowed to continue her high school education. B. was also allowed to go to high school the following year. L. was able to finish high school after her application was approved. The pair have a daughter, who was born in May 2011. The couple have a son and daughter-in-law, who were also born in 2011. They have two children, who are living in Vaud and Geneva, Switzerland. They are planning to move to France in the future.

name: Erich Kiefer
train_texts: The case concerns the duration of the proceedings instituted by the applicant and whether they were terminated within a ‘reasonable time’ The applicant is represented by Mr B. Gachnang, a lawyer practising in Lucerne in Switzerland. The Swiss Government are represented by their Agent, Mr Ph. Boillat. The case was referred to the Court by an Austrian national, Erich Kiefer (“the applicant”) on 30 December 1998 pursuant to former Article 48 § 1 (e) of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’). It originated in an application (no. 27353/95) against Switzerland. In 1983 the applicant suffered an injury and became partly disabled. On 7 November 1985 he requested pension benefits from the Swiss Invalidity Insurance. Based on ten medical reports issued between 1983 and 1987, the Compensation Office dismissed the applicant's request as he was only partly hindered in exercising his profession as a lorry driver. In 1989, various reports were filed by Austrian experts. The applicant requested the Austrian authorities to undertake a most thorough examination of his case by means of a further medical expert. on 7 February 1990 the Austrian orthopaedist Dr. L.-K. submitted another report. On 14 December 1989 the Swiss medical expert Dr. W. submitted his third report. The Invalidity Insurance Commission considered in its proposal of 19 July 1990 that the applicant had not sufficiently demonstrated his invalidity. The applicant was granted a time-limit of 30 days to reply. The Compensation Office dismissed the applicant's request for pension benefits as he had not been insured at the time concerned. On 10 May 1993 he filed an appeal against this decision which was dismissed by the Federal Appeals Commission for Old Age, Survivors and Invalidity insurance on 21 February 1993. The case was eventually settled by the Austrian pension authorities in November 1992. It was described as 'one of the most complex cases in the history of invalidity pensions' The applicant filed an administrative law appeal in 1994. The appeal was dismissed on 18 November 1994 by the Federal Insurance Court (Eidgenössisches Versicherungsgericht) The applicant applied to the Commission on 13 April 1995, complaining under Article 6 § 1 about the length of social security proceedings. The Commission declared the application admissible on 16 April 1998. In its report of 21 October 1998 (former Article 31), it expressed the unanimous opinion that there had been a violation of Article 6§ 1. The decision of 23 December 1987 refused to grant a pension on the grounds that there was no invalidity, without even dealing with the allegedly missing insurance quality.

The case was referred to the Court by an Austrian national, Erich Kiefer (“the applicant”) on 30 December 1998. It originated in an application (no. 27353/95) against Switzerland lodged by the applicant with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 13 April 1995. The applicant is represented by Mr B. Gachnang, a lawyer practising in Lucerne in Switzerland. The Swiss Government are represented by their Agent, Mr Ph. Boillat. The case concerns the duration of the proceedings instituted by the applicants and whether they were terminated within a “reasonable time” as required by Article 6§ 1 of the Convention. The applicant worked as a lorry driver in Switzerland from 1979-1984. He requested pension benefits from the Swiss Invalidity Insurance. The Compensation Office dismissed the applicant's request on 23 December 1987, as he was only partly hindered in exercising his profession. In 1989, various reports were filed by Austrian experts. On 7 February 1990 the Austrian orthopaedist Dr. L.-K. submitted another report. In December 1989 the applicant requested the Austrian authorities to undertake a most thorough examination of his case by means of a further medical expert. The case was eventually settled in 1990 by the Swiss Compensation Office. It was decided that the previous decision was contradictory in respect of the applicant’s ability to work. The Invalidity Insurance Commission considered in its proposal of 19 July 1990 that the applicant had not sufficiently demonstrated his invalidity. Dr. S., a doctor employed by the Swiss Compensation Office, submitted three reports. The applicant was granted a time-limit of 30 days to reply. On 7 April 1993 the Compensation Office dismissed the applicant's request for pension benefits as he had not been insured at the time concerned. On 10 May 1993 he filed an appeal against this decision which was dismissed by the Federal Appeals Commission for Old Age, Survivors and Invalidity insurance on 21 February 1993. The case was referred to the Austrian Court of Human Rights. The applicant filed an administrative law appeal on 5 April 1994. The appeal was dismissed on 18 November 1994 by the Federal Insurance Court (Eidgenössisches Versicherungsgericht) The applicant applied to the Commission on 13 April 1995, complaining under Article 6 § 1 about the length of social security proceedings. The Commission declared the application admissible on 16 April 1998. In its report of 21 October 1998 (former Article 31), it expressed the unanimous opinion that there had been a violation of Article 6§ 1. The applicant has been refused status as an insured person ten years after it was allegedly found missing amounts to a breach of good faith, it is arbitrary and breaches the principle of equality.

name: Dennis Sibson
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 21 February 1992. It originated in an application (no. 14327/88) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr Dennis Sibson, a British citizen, on 17 October 1988. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 11 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent him (Rule 30). The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 26 October 1992. The Court heard addresses by Mr Eadie for the Government, Mr Marxer for the Commission and Mr Bowers for the applicant. Both the Government and the applicant filed a written reply to a question put by the Court. The Registrar received, on 9 November 1992, further observations from the Government on the applicant’s claims under Article 50 (art. 50) and, on 20 January 1993, the applicant's comments on those observations. The hearing was adjourned until the end of the second week of January 1993. Until the events giving rise to the present case, the applicant was a member of the Transport and General Workers Union. He was based at its depot at Greengate, Lancashire, together with between forty and fifty other drivers. Mr Sibson was so dissatisfied with that decision that he resigned from TGWU by letter of 24 July and joined the United Road Transport Union instead. Some of his fellow drivers immediately ostracised him and others obstructed him in the performance of his work. Between July and October 1985 CNS attempted in vain to resolve the dispute. On 22 October the applicant told Mr Dear that he would rejoin the union only if he received an apology from Mr Dear. The applicant was offered a transfer to Chadderton but turned it down. Mr Sibson then lodged with the Industrial Tribunal a complaint of unfair dismissal against CNS and TGWU. Mr Dear admitted in cross-examination the absence of any evidence of constructive dismissal. The tribunal ruled in favour of the applicant and ordered Mr Dear to pay him back his lost wages. The Tribunal held that Mr Dear had breached the terms of his contract when he offered the applicant a transfer from Greengate to Chadderton. The application was dismissed on the grounds that he had ‘been ‘constructively dismissed’ for refusing to accept ‘action short of dismissal’’ Industrial Tribunal unanimously accepted the complaint of unfair dismissal. Mr Sibson was entitled to refuse to rejoin TGWU because there was no closed shop agreement in force. Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissed an appeal by CNS on points of law. Court of Appeal concluded that CNS had acted within its contractual rights in requiring the applicant to transfer to a nearby depot and that he could not be regarded as having been constructively dismissed. Lord Justice Slade stated, as regards this implied “mobility term’: “I cannot see how Mr Sibia could reasonably have objected to a term giving the contract this limited degree of flexibility when he entered the employment in 1973’ Mr Sibson applied for legal aid to appeal to the House of Lords. Legal aid was granted for the purpose of obtaining counsel’s opinion on the merits of an appeal. On 8 August counsel advised that there were no reasonable prospects of success and that leave to appeal would not be given. Further legal aid was therefore refused on 19 August. No question of unfair dismissal therefore arose. The case was dismissed without prejudice and the appeal was thrown out. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that the appeal had not been successful. The decision was overturned on 9 September 1988. The jury returned a verdict of not guilty by reason of diminished responsibility. The judge ruled that there had been no unfair dismissal.

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 21 February 1992. The Court heard addresses by Mr Eadie for the Government, Mr Marxer for the Commission and Mr Bowers for the applicant. Both the Government and the applicant filed a written reply to a question put by the Court. The applicant, who was born in 1929, was employed by Courtaulds Northern Spinning Ltd (“CNS”) from November 1973 as a textile worker. Mr Sibson was fired from his post in January 1994. He claimed to be entitled to compensation under Article 50 (art. 50) of the Convention. The applicant was a member of the Transport and General Workers Union (“TGWU“) from 1981 to 1984 he was its branch secretary. He was based at its depot at Greengate, Lancashire, together with between forty and fifty other drivers. Mr Sibson was so dissatisfied with that decision that he resigned from TGWU by letter of 24 July and joined the United Road Transport Union instead. Some of his fellow drivers immediately ostracised him and others obstructed him in the performance of his work. In 1985 the applicant told Mr Dear that he would rejoin the union only if he received an apology from Mr Dear. The applicant was offered a transfer to Chadderton but refused. He feared losing his current lorry and allowances for nights spent away from home. He could not face the aggravation from other drivers which he was sure would continue at that depot. Mr Sibson then lodged with the Industrial Tribunal a complaint of unfair dismissal against CNS and TGWU. In the grounds for his application he stated that he had “been ‘constructively dismissed’ for refusing to accept ‘action short of dismissal’“ (see paragraph 20 below) His representative in these proceedings was not legally qualified, legal aid not being available for this purpose. Industrial Tribunal unanimously accepted the complaint of unfair dismissal. Mr Sibson was entitled to refuse to rejoin TGWU because there was no closed shop agreement in force. The request that he move to Chadderton was not reasonable since it was not made for genuine operational reasons but solely to avoid a strike. Court of Appeal concluded that CNS had acted within its contractual rights in requiring the applicant to transfer to a nearby depot and that he could not be regarded as having been constructively dismissed. Lord Justice Slade stated, as regards this implied “mobility term’: “I cannot see how Mr SIBson could reasonably have objected to a term giving the contract this limited degree of flexibility’. On 15 April 1988 Mr Sibson applied for legal aid to appeal to the House of Lords. Legal aid was granted for the purpose of obtaining counsel’s opinion on the merits of an appeal. On 8 August counsel advised that there were no reasonable prospects of success and that leave to appeal would not be given. Further legal aid was therefore refused on 19 August. No question of unfair dismissal therefore arose. For confidential support call the Samaritans in the UK on 08457 90 90 90, visit a local Samaritans branch or see www.samaritans.org for details. name: Hakan Duman
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28439/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1983 and lives in Bursa. He had been previously convicted of burglary on 21 March 2001 and his prison sentence had been commuted to a fine. On 11 January 2002 at approximately 12.40 a.m. the applicant was arrested, together with a friend, and taken into custody on suspicion of having committed several burglaries. The arrest was effected on the basis of incriminating information received regarding the applicant and his friend. According to the record drafted by police officers and signed by the applicant, the latter indicated one by one the houses he had broken into. The owner of one of the guns was questioned by the police about a number of burglaries. He signed a form explaining his right to remain silent. He told the police that he had been beaten with a stick. He did not contest the charges against him. The case against him was dropped. The owner of the other gun was never charged with any crime in relation to the break-in. The owners of the two guns are still being investigated by the authorities for their role in the crime. The investigation into the burglary of the second gun is still ongoing. It is believed that the owner will be charged with a crime in the near future. The victims of the burglaries are still waiting to be identified. The applicant appealed against the trial court's judgment. He claimed that there was no evidence to demonstrate his guilt and that his statements to the police had been written in accordance with the complainants' testimonies. In part of his appeal petition the applicant submitted that he had not been in a fit condition to give a statement before the Magistrates' Court since he had been exhausted from the torture, coercion and duress. The Court of Cassation, relying on Article 318 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, dismissed the applicant's request for an oral hearing and upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. The opinion of the principal public prosecutor submitted to this court was not communicated to the applicant. The applicant was released from prison in December 2004. The first-instance court adjusted the applicant's sentence in accordance with the provisions of the new Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) The applicant was sentenced to 10 years in prison in February 2003. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 24746/94) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his son Pearse Jordan had been unjustifiably shot and killed by a police officer and that there had been no effective investigation into, or redress for, his death. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The proceedings in the present case should be conducted simultaneously with those in the cases of McKerr v. the United UK, no. 28883/95, Kelly and Others v the United. Kingdom,. no. 30054/96 and Shanaghan v the. United Kingdom. no. 37715/97 (see judgments of the same date). The applicant’s son, Pearse Jordan, aged 22, was shot and killed in Belfast by an officer of the Royal Ulster Constabulary (the RUC), later identified as Sergeant A. Treacy. The facts of the case are in dispute between the parties. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court heard addresses by Mr Weatherup and Mr Treacy, and declared the application admissible by a decision of 4 April 2000. The application was brought by the applicant's mother, Mrs Jordan, whose son Pearse was shot dead by an RUC officer in November 1992. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal, Belfast. Four civilians stopped and had an unobstructed view across the road. As Pearse Jordan reached the white line in the centre of the road, an officer about 12 feet away fired a number of shots. He staggered a little further then turned to face the police who, when they caught up with him, verbally abused him and pushed his face into the ground where he was kicked and searched. The police carried out a search of the car. The civilians heard no warning shout or challenge given by any of the officers and saw nothing in PearseJordan’s hands or anything threatening in his actions. The witnesses were subjected to hostile and threatening remarks by members of the security forces. The Independent Commission for Police Complaints (the ICPC) would supervise the RUC investigation. Sergeant A had been at a briefing at 11 a.m. the day before concerning reports of a planned distribution of kit and munitions, including weapons, explosives and mortars. A surveillance operation was to be mounted and he was in charge of the teams on the ground which were going to intervene if possible to intercept the munitions. He was carrying a Smith and Wesson 59 pistol and a MP5 Heckler and Koch. He and his teams left Woodbourne police station to wait at Andersontown police station. They heard reports there of a build up of activity at the back of two houses in Arizona street, which were under surveillance. Sergeant A thought that this was possibly the re-supply of terrorist equipment. Sergeant A said that he called out “Police. Halt.” or “Halt. Police” The driver of the Orion turned around towards him. He could not see the man’s hands which were below his waist. He feared the man was armed as he had spun round so quickly. He fired a short burst from his MP5 at the trunk of the man. The driver fell flat, toppling over. It was realised at that stage that he was seriously injured. Sergeant A quickly searched the car, while other security force personnel administered first aid to the driver. He arrived back at the station at about 5.30 to 6.00 p.m. Sergeant A said that he had a clear view of the deceased from the waist up. When the deceased turned to face him, he did not make any movements towards him. In that short space of time, he formed the opinion that the deceased was a threat to his life. The man’s actions had not been of someone about to surrender. He was certain that there were no viable alternatives to discharging his own weapon.Forensic examinations of the cars involved in the incident were carried out. Interviews were conducted with the other police officers and army personnel involved. Inspector M gave an explanation for the decision to shoot the man. The RUC concluded its inquiry in May 1993. Its report on the investigation was submitted to the Director of Public Prosecutions. The DPP’s department issued to the Chief Constable of the RUC a direction of ‘no prosecution’ in respect of the fatal shooting of Pearse Jordan. It had been concluded that the evidence was insufficient to warrant the prosecution of any person. Following that decision, the Coroner decided to hold an inquest. The inquest began on 4 January 1995 and concluded on 8 December 1995. The coroner recorded a verdict of unlawful killing. The applicant and his family were not provided with any indication as to the nature of the. RUC's findings. Defence issued certificate in which he identified information whose disclosure at the inquest he believed would be contrary to the public interest on grounds of national security. Defence made an application that the identities of certain military witnesses be withheld and that they should give their evidence from behind a screen. The Coroner sat for three and a half days, hearing evidence from 19 witnesses, including the applicant, 8 civilians, Soldiers V, W and X, 7 police officers and a pathologist. The applicant and his family were represented by a solicitor and counsel. The RUC were represented. The proceedings were adjourned on 16 January 1995, at the request of Pearse Jordan’s family, to enable the DPP, in the light of new evidence from the taxi driver, to reconsider the decision whether to bring a prosecution. The applicant’s legal representatives made an application for the Coroner to discharge himself from the Inquest on the grounds that he was not conducting the inquest fairly. The Coroner refused the application. Leave was granted to bring judicial review proceedings against the coroner on 2 June 1995. The judicial review application was heard on 9 and 10 November 1995. Lord Justice Carswell refused the applicant's claims. In doing so he had regard to the inquisitorial nature of inquest proceedings. He referred to the remarks of Griffiths J in Ex parte Peach: “A coroner's inquest is an inquisitors procedure with a very limited objective indeed” The applicant appealed against the decision of Lord Justice Carswell. The appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland on 28 June 1996. The applicant’s application for leave to appeal to the House of Lords was refused on 4 October 1996. Inquest was due to recommence on 1 December 1997. It was adjourned on 19 November 1997 by the Coroner, after consultation with the parties, pending the outcome of a judicial review application in the High Court concerning the availability of legal aid for legal representation for the family of the deceased at inquests. Final judgment was given in the case of Sharon Lavery v. the Secretary of State and the Legal Aid Department, in which a challenge concerning the unavailability of legal help for inquests was dismissed. The applicant was granted legal aid to pursue a civil action for compensation in the High Court. On 5 October 1995, the applicant served a statement of claim in the civil proceedings. On 8 October 1999, the Crown Solicitor wrote to the applicant seeking consent to a remittal of the civil action to trial. The applicant stated that the case is currently at the discovery stage but that this cannot be concluded until the inquest is terminated. On 4 April 2000 the applicant was provided with the witness statements of persons whom the Coroner has decided should be called to give evidence at the inquest. in addition to the witnesses who gave evidence in January 1995, 12 police officers and Soldier Y involved in the anti-terrorist operation.

The applicant and his family were not however provided with any indication as to the nature of the. RUC’S findings. The Coroner wrote to interested parties informing them that the inquest would begin on. 4 November 1994. The Coroner’s inquest commenced on 4 January 1995. The applicant and his family were represented by a solicitor and counsel. The RUC were represented. The Coroner sat for three and a half days, hearing evidence from 19 witnesses, including the applicant, 8 civilians, Soldiers V, W and X, 7 police officers and a pathologist. These witnesses were subject to cross-examination. Sergeant A had informed the Coroner that he would not appear. Defence issued a certificate in which he identified information whose disclosure at the inquest he believed would be contrary to the public interest on grounds of national security. The DPP decided that the evidence remained insufficient to warrant the prosecution of any person in relation to Pearse Jordan's death. On 10 March 1995, the applicant’s legal representatives made an application for the Coroner to discharge himself from the Inquest on the grounds that he was not conducting the inquest fairly. The Coroner refused the application. The applicant sought orders of certiorari to quash inter alia (a) the. Coroner's refusal to give the next of kin access to the statements of the witnesses before they gave evidence at the inquest and (b). the decision of the Cor coroner to grant anonymity to RUC witnesses. Legal aid was granted to the applicant for this purpose. The judicial review application was heard on 9 and 10 November 1995. Lord Justice Carswell refused the applicant's claims. The applicant appealed against the decision of Lord Justice Carswell. The appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland on 28 June 1996. The applicant’s application for leave to appeal to the House of Lords was refused. The inquest was due to recommence on 1 December 1997. It was adjourned on 19 November 1997 by the Coroner, after consultation with the parties, pending the outcome of a judicial review application in the High Court concerning the availability of legal aid for legal representation for the family of the deceased at inquests. On 2 February 2000, the applicant was informed that the Chief Constable would provide copies of the statements of the witnesses who were to appear at the inquest. The applicant was granted legal aid to pursue a civil action for compensation in the High Court. The case is currently at the discovery stage but that this cannot be concluded until the inquest is terminated. The applicant was provided with the witness statements of persons whom the Coroner has decided should be called to give evidence at the inquest. in addition to the witnesses who gave evidence in January 1995, 12 police officers and Soldier Y involved in the anti-terrorist operation in which Pearse Jordan died, forensic experts and three police officers involved in a RUC investigation into the shooting. The Crown Solicitor wrote to the applicant seeking consent to a remittal of the civil action to trial.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his son Pearse Jordan had been unjustifiably shot and killed by a police officer. He invoked Articles 2, 6, 13 and 14 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998. The proceedings in the present case should be conducted simultaneously with those in the cases of McKerr v. the United Kingdom, no. 28883/95, Kelly and Others v the United UK,No. 30054/96 and Shanaghan v the U.K. no. 37715/97 (see judgments of the same date). The applicant’s son, Pearse Jordan, aged 22, was shot and killed in Belfast by an officer of the Royal Ulster Constabulary (the RUC), later identified as Sergeant A. Treacy. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court heard addresses by Mr Weatherup and Mr Treacy and declared the application admissible on 4 April 2000. The facts of the case, in particular concerning what happened when PearseJordan was shot on 25 November 1992, are in dispute between the parties. The hearing was held at the Royal Courts of Justice, Belfast. The case was heard by the Honourable Court of Appeal. The jury returned a decision in favour of the applicant. Four men heard a crash behind them and turned to see a red police car pulling alongside a car (Pearse Jordan’s) and ramming it up onto the footpath. As Pearse Jordan reached the white line in the centre of the road, an officer about 12 feet away fired a number of shots. The civilians heard no warning shout or challenge given by any of the officers. The police carried out a search of the car. The four witnesses followed the ambulance which took Pearse. Jordan to hospital where they stated that they were subjected to hostile and threatening remarks by. members of the security forces. The Independent Commission for Police Complaints (the ICPC) would supervise the RUC investigation. Sergeant A was carrying a Smith and Wesson 59 pistol and a MP5 Heckler and Koch. He had been at a briefing the day before concerning reports of a planned distribution of kit and munitions, including weapons, explosives and mortars. A surveillance operation was to be mounted and he was in charge of the teams on the ground which were going to intervene if possible to intercept the munitions. A red car from the leisure centre arrived in Arizona street. Sergeant A thought that this was possibly the re-supply of terrorist equipment. He was told by radio to gather his people together – car crews with call signs 8, 9, 3 and 12. When the red Orion left Arizona street, he and his crews left the police station. Sergeant A said that he called out ‘Police. Halt’ or ‘Halt. Police’ The driver of the Orion turned around towards him. He could not see the man’s hands which were below his waist. He feared the man was armed as he had spun round so quickly. He fired a short burst from his MP5 at the trunk of the man. The driver fell flat, toppling over. It was realised at that stage that he was seriously injured. Sergeant A quickly searched the car, while other security force personnel administered first aid to the driver. He did not know that car 12 had come into contact with the Orion or the deceased. Sergeant A said he had a clear view of the deceased from the waist up. When the deceased turned to face him, he did not make any movements towards him. His arms were down and his hands out of sight. In that short space of time, he formed the opinion that the deceased was a threat to his life. The man’s actions had not been of someone about to surrender. He was certain that there were no viable alternatives to discharging his own weapon. In his statement of 6 December 1992, Sergeant H, from the car call sign 11, stated that on arrival at the scene he had instructed car 12 to be moved to facilitate the movement of a bus very close to the injured man. During the investigation, appeals were made by the police in newspapers and broadcast media for potential eyewitnesses to come forward. A number of civilians made statements to the police and subsequently gave evidence at the inquest. In May 1993, the RUC concluded its inquiry. Its report on the investigation was submitted to the Director of Public Prosecutions (the DPP) on 25 May 1993. The RUC notified the Coroner that the DPP had directed “no prosecution’ on 29 November 1993. Following that decision, the coroner decided to hold an inquest. The inquest began on 4 January 1995 and concluded on 6 March 1995. Defence issued a certificate in which he identified information whose disclosure at the inquest he believed would be contrary to the public interest on grounds of national security. Defence made an application that the identities of certain military witnesses be withheld and that they should give their evidence from behind a screen. The Coroner sat for three and a half days, hearing evidence from 19 witnesses, including the applicant, 8 civilians, Soldiers V, W and X, 7 police officers and a pathologist. The proceedings were adjourned on 16 January 1995, at the request of Pearse Jordan’s family, to enable the DPP, in the light of new evidence, to reconsider the decision whether or not to bring a prosecution. The applicant’s legal representatives made an application for the Coroner to discharge himself from the Inquest on the grounds that he was not conducting the inquest fairly. The Coroner refused the application. Leave was granted to bring judicial review proceedings against the coroner on 2 June 1995. The judicial review application was heard on 9 and 10 November 1995. By judgment of 11 December 1995, Lord Justice Carswell refused the applicant's claims. In doing so he had regard to the inquisitorial nature of inquest proceedings. The objective is limited to ascertaining the following matters: who the deceased was; how, when and where the deceased came by his death. There is a further specific limitation provided by the Coroners (Amendment) Rules 1977. These provide by rule 7 that no verdict shall be framed in such a way as to appear to determine any question of criminal liability. The applicant appealed against the decision of Lord Justice Carswell. The appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland. The applicant’s application for leave to appeal to the House of Lords was refused. The inquest was due to recommence on 1 December 1997. However, it was adjourned on 19 November 1997 by the Coroner, after consultation with the parties, pending the outcome of a judicial review application in the High Court concerning the availability of legal aid for legal representation for the family of the deceased at inquests. The Coroner informed the interested parties that he intended to resume the inquest on 1 November 1999. On 2 February 2000, the applicant was informed that the Chief Constable would provide copies of the statements of the witnesses who were to appear at the inquest. The applicant was granted legal aid to pursue a civil action for compensation in the High Court. On 5 October 1995, the applicant served a statement of claim in the civil proceedings. On 8 October 1999, the Crown Solicitor wrote to the applicant seeking consent to a remittal of the civil action to trial. The case is currently at the discovery stage but that this cannot be concluded until the inquest is terminated. The applicant did not reply to this request until a date unspecified subsequent to 27 August 1998. In addition to the witnesses who gave evidence in January 1995, 12 police officers and Soldier Y involved in the anti-terrorist operation in which Pearse Jordan died, forensic experts and three police officers involved in RUC investigation into the shooting.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18026/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Polish national, Mr Miroslaw Czaus. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 48001/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Drzewicki, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Rules of Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27) was constituted. On 27 May 1988 the court issued another interim order enjoining the applicant and his wife from carrying out any work to the house. On 24 December 1990 the applicant filed with the District Court an application for permission to carry out works on the gas supply to his apartment. In April 1993 the parties paid an advance fee towards the costs of the inspection, as ordered by the court. On 27 May 1994 the applicant’s appeal against this decision was dismissed as being inadmissible in law. As from 2 February 1995 the case file was with the Regional Court, following the applicant's appeal against an unspecified decision (procedural order) of the District court. The case file was sent to the Institute of Construction Technology in order to have the report prepared within a two-month period. Construction Technology to appoint an expert to take charge of the preparation of the report ordered by the court. On 22 November 1995 the court received the expert report and served copies on the parties. The applicant again filed with the District Court an application for permission to carry out works on the gas supply to his apartment. The proceedings were resumed on 6 October 1997. The Regional Court upheld that decision on 8 February 2000. On 30 August 2000 the court appointed G.G., the petitioner, as guardian of the estate of the late B.G. The Warsaw-Praga District Court ruled that the applicant’s sons, T.G. and E.G., were the heirs to his estate. The proceedings are still stayed and, therefore, remain pending before the District Court. The applicant's lawyer requested the President of the Civil Division of the District court to expedite the proceedings. On 23 October 2001, the lawyer of T.g. requested the court to resume the proceedings and the case was returned to the district court.
