The case involves two apartments, basements and an attic. The applicant and his wife were banned from carrying out any work to the house. The Warsaw Regional Court rejected the applicant’s appeal against the decision of 8 March 1991 as inadmissible in law. It appears that on an unspecified date in 1993 the District Court decided to carry out an inspection of the property. The parties paid an advance fee towards the costs of the inspection, as ordered by the court. The case file was returned to the district court on 27 April 1995. The District Court requested the Director of the Institute of Construction Technology (Instytut Techniki Budowlanej) to provide expert evidence. On 8 June 1995 the case file was sent to the Institute of Construction Technology in order to have the report prepared within a two-month period. On 20 March 1996 the applicant filed an application for permission to carry out works on the gas supply to his apartment. On 8 February 2000 the Regional Court upheld that decision. The applicant died at the age of ninety-six. On an unknown date in 2001 the Warsaw-Praga District Court ruled that the applicant’s sons, T.G. and E.G., were the heirs to his estate. Later, the lawyer of T. G. requested the court to resume the proceedings. It appears that the proceedings are still stayed and, therefore, remain pending before the Warsaw, Praga, District Court. name: Jerzy Pachnik

Hearings were held on 5 February 1996, 13 May 1997 and 5 January 1998 at which the court heard expert witnesses and ordered new expert opinions. On 31 July 2000 the Warsaw Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) quashed the impugned judgment in respect of the monthly allowance awarded to the applicant and remitted it to the first-instance court.

name: Jacek Gęśla
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 15915/07) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was charged with drug dealing and uttering threats while acting in an organised criminal gang. On 17 November 2008 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theapplication at the same time (Article 29 § 3). The applicant is a Polish national, born in 1970 and lives in Chełm. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant served two different prison sentences between 21 March 2005 and 21 May 2006 which had been imposed on him in another set of criminal proceedings. The criminal proceedings concerning one of the charges against the applicant are still pending before the Chełm District Court. The court stressed that the proceedings had been very complex, that they had concerned ten co-accused and that evidence had to be obtained from twenty three witnesses. The applicant lodged a complaint under section 5 of the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. It was dismissed by the Lublin Regional Court on 25 July 2007.

name: Fikret Doğan
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that his right to a fair hearing had been breached by the Ankara Martial Law Court which lacked independence and impartiality. The case was heard by the European Court of Human rights in 2000, and the case was declared inadmissible by the Court. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol no. 11). The Government and the applicant each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The applicant was arrested in 1982 and charged with membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. In a judgment of 19 July 1989 the Martial Law Court, composed of two civilian judges, two military judges and an army officer, convicted the applicant. The court acquitted the applicant of other charges. It sentenced the applicant to life imprisonment, permanently debarred him from employment in public service and placed him under judicial guardianship. In 1995 the Court of Cassation upheld the applicant’s conviction. The applicant was conditionally released pending trial.

name: Prem Singh
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 8 December 1994 by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and on 23 December 1994. It originated in an application (no. 23389/94) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 25 January 1994 by a British citizen, Mr Prem Singh. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 5 para. 4 ( art. 5-4) of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). Prem Singh was convicted at Leeds Crown Court of the murder of a 72-year-old woman in 1973. He had broken into her home, strangled her, cut her throat and had sexual intercourse with her at around the time of her death. Mr Singh received a mandatory sentence of detention ‘during Her Majesty’s pleasure’ pursuant to section 53 (1) of the Children and Young Persons Act 1933 (as amended) (see paragraph 29 below) In October 1990, having served the punitive part of his sentence (“tariff” - see paragraph 33 below), Mr Singh was released on licence. On 11 March 1991 the applicant was arrested and interviewed at Southme. Mr Singh was given a life sentence for fraud in 1973. On 21 March 1991 his life licence was revoked by the Secretary of State on its recommendation. The reason given for his recall was not the alleged offences (which were a matter for the court), but rather his failure to provide accurate information about his circumstances to his supervising probation officer. Under section 62 (4) of the Criminal Justice Act 1967 the Parole Board was empowered at this stage to take a binding decision for Mr Singh’s immediate release. On 19 December 1991 the Board decided against recommending Mr Singh's release. The case was heard by the Supreme Court and Mr Singh was awarded a new life licence. Prem Singh was held in a London prison. The criminal charges against him were dismissed because the prosecution had presented the indictment out of time. Mr Singh asked for his case to be reconsidered in the light of this development, and the Secretary of State referred it back to the Parole Board. On 30 July 1992 the Board again declined to recommend Mr Singh’s release. He was not told the reasons for this decision. The applicant then sought judicial review of the two decisions. On 20 April 1993 the Divisional Court quashed the decision of 19 December 1991 on the ground that there had been a breach of natural justice. The court held that the applicant was entitled to a fresh consideration by the Paroles Board. Parole Board considered Mr Singh’s case on 18 June 1993. He was not permitted to be present at the review and had no opportunity to give oral evidence or to question those who had made allegations against him. Board decided not to recommend release, and gave the following reasons: “There was a lack of opennessin his dealings with the Probation Service. The conduct which led to the criminal charges indicated a serious kind ofdeceptiveness’ Mr Singh applied for judicial review of this decision, but he withdrew his application on or about 7 March 1994 because he had been offered an early review of his case by the Parole Board. Prem Singh was recalled to prison in 1990 after 'serious breaches of trust' He had misled the probation service after his release in October 1990. Mr Singh applied for judicial review of the Secretary of State’s decision. On 16 March 1995 the Divisional Court quashed the decision and ordered him to reconsider it. In September 1995 Mr Singh joined a pre-release employment scheme. His provisional date for release is 18 March 1996. The court found, inter alia, that the correct test to be applied was whether Mr Singh constituted a danger to the “life or limb’ of the public. It also found that the reasoning process had been flawed because he had not properly explained how the findings he had made related to the test of dangerousness.

The case was referred to the Court on 8 December 1994 by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and on 23 December 1994. It originated in an application (no. 23389/94) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 25 January 1994 by a British citizen. On 11 March 1991 the applicant was arrested and interviewed at Southme. Mr Singh was sentenced to life in 1973 for fraud and using threatening behaviour. On 21 March 1991 his life licence was revoked by the Secretary of State on its recommendation. The Parole Board considered the applicant’s case on 27 August and 19 December 1991. It had before it a number of reports from the probation service and the police, none of which was disclosed to the applicant. The Board decided against recommending Mr Singh's immediate release. Mr Singh then sought judicial review of the two decisions of the Parole Board of 19 December 1991 and 30 July 1992. The Divisional Court quashed the Paroles Board’s decision on the ground that there had been a breach of natural justice because the Board had not disclosed to Mr Singh all the reports before it. He considered that Mr Singh’s relationship with the probation service needed to be tested in the ‘more challenging environment of an open prison’ Mr Singh applied for judicial review of the Secretary of. State’'s decision. On 16 March 1995 the Divisional Court quashed the Secretary. of State's decision and ordered him to reconsider it. His provisional date for release is 18 March 1996.

name: Lars Rey
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 17350/03) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. The first two applicants, a married couple, were born in 1935 and 1944 respectively and live in Klippan. The third applicant was a limited liability company wholly owned by the first two Applicants. The court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The case was decided on 26 September 2006. The company was declared bankrupt in September 1994. The bank paid the company the remainder of the loan on 28 June 1993. The applicants and a company named Boket Konsult AB (hereinafter ‘Boket’) claimed compensation from the bank in the amount of 37 million SEK for the damage allegedly caused by the bank's initial refusal to pay the last instalment. In February 1997, the applicants and Boket asked the court to rule on the alleged breach of contract in a partial judgment. An oral preparation was held on 7 April 1998. On 29 September 1998 the court sent a summary of the cases to the parties and, by a decision of 30 September 1998, it rejected the request for apartial judgment. Boket sued the bank for refusing to pay back 2 million SEK. The District Court found in favour of the bank in 2001. The applicants appealed to the Svea Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt) The appellate court agreed with the District Court's reasoning and upheld its judgment. On 29 November 2002, after the applicants had been granted several respites to complete their submissions, the Supreme Court refused the applicants leave to appeal. The case was finally settled in March 2003. Boket's action was struck out of the court's list on 17 January 2000. On 5 July 2000 the court delivered another summary of the cases and gave the parties the opportunity to make comments.

name: Magdalena Witek
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Ms Magdalena Witek alleged that her detention in a psychiatric hospital had been unlawful and in breach of Article 5 of the convention. She had been granted legal aid and was represented by a lawyer practising in Bielsko Biała. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was dismissed as lodged outside the prescribed time-limit. The court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. Kielce Regional Court ordered that the applicant be examined by expert psychiatrists. Psychiatric Commission on Preventive Measures submitted its opinion dated 17 August 2006 to the Kielce District Court. The applicant was subsequently admitted to the Lublin Hospital on 23 September 2006. Days after her arrival there the applicant filed an appeal against that decision. She stressed that over the previous five years her health had significantly improved and that her relations with her mother were very good. The court upheld the first-instance decision referring to the reasons given by the District Court on 23 February 2007. On 16 August 2007 the court received yet another expert opinion. The expert psychiatrists concluded that there was still a high possibility the applicant might commit another offence. Kielce District Court ordered the applicant's release from hospital. Court did not agree with the expert psychiatrists opinions of 20 July 2007, 16 August 2007 and 25 September 2007 maintaining that the applicant should be kept in a psychiatric hospital. On the prosecutor's appeal, on 16 November 2007 the Kielce Regional Court upheld the first-instance decision. The applicant was released from hospital on the same day. The court concluded that the probability of the applicant committing another similar offence was very low. It referred to the applicant’s mother's testimonies confirming that since 2002 the applicant had never behaved aggressively towards her and their relations were very good.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4789/10) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Convention, on account of the refusal by the national authorities to indicate her forename in. the civil register of births as that of the mother of her adopted child. She argued that in relation to single-parent adoptions there was a lacuna in the. Civil Code which required the court to make provision for such a situation. The court found that the Civil Code, in choosing to regulate only two-parent adoptions, intended to treat the legal relationship between the adoptive parents and the adopted child as ‘a biological relationship’ On 14 April 2008 the applicant appealed on points of law. On 15 March 2009, a new regulation entered into force entitled “Regulation on the implementation of mediation services for the adoption of minors’ (“the Regulation”) enabling a single adoptive parent to have his or her forename registered in the place of that of the biological parent. On 9 November 2010 she applied to the registry office for the registration of her fore Name. That request was granted on the same day.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4064/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Government sent a facsimile to the Court informing it that they were ready to settle the case. However, having regard to the fact that it was considering a draft of a judgment in the case at that stage, the Court decided to treat the Government's initiative as belated and to proceed with its deliberations. The Wrocław Regional Court held the first hearing on 24 September 2002. Subsequently, on seven occasions, the composition of the court changed so the proceedings had to start from the beginning. The applicant lodged a complaint about the unreasonable length of the proceedings under section 5 of the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. The court analysed the course of the impugned proceedings in the light of the criteria which the Court itself applies and concluded that the Regional Court had violated the applicant's right to the hearing without unjustified delay. The Court of Appeal upheld the judgment.

name: Charles Bernard O’Neill
train_texts: The case originated in two applications (nos. 41516/10 and 75702/13) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention. The first applicant was born in 1962 and is currently detained in HMP Glenochil in Scotland. The second applicant wasborn in 1976 and is now detained in LMP Edinburgh. The applicants’ complaints concerning the length of their criminal proceedings were communicated to the Government on 13 November 2012 and 17 December 2012 respectively. The complainer in relation to some of the offences was A.M.’s son. Following conviction, both applicants were placed on the Sexual Offenders’ Register. The applicants were detained by the police under section 14 of the Criminal Procedure (Scotland) Act 1995 and removed to Queen Street Police Office in Aberdeen. On the same day the applicants were interviewed separately by police officers for over five hours. During these interviews they were directly accused of the murder of A.M. Both applicants asked police officers if they were going to be charged with the murder, but received indications to the contrary. Following the interviews, neither applicant was arrested or charged with any offence owing to insufficient evidence. They were therefore returned to prison to continue serving their respective sentences. They both travelled to Spain without notification, thereby breaching the terms of their parole licence in contravention of the Sex Offenders Act 1997. The applicants were charged with the murder of A.M. and with concealing and disposing of her body in an attempt to pervert the course of justice. They appeared on petition at Kilmarnock Sheriff Court were they were committed for further examination and remanded in custody. On 6 June 2005 the Crown Office provisionally fixed a preliminary hearing date for 12 September 2005. That hearing date was set aside as the first applicant lodged a “devolution minute’ (see paragraphs 51-52 below) relating to a potential violation of the reasonable time guarantee contained within Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. On 14 October 2005 the Sheriff Court held that the devolution minute had been raised prematurely as no indictment had been served. On 26 April 2006 the applicants were informed that there would be “no proceedings meantime” C.M. disappeared in Spain in 2007 and returned to the UK in November 2007. The application for an extension to the time-limit on the case was granted on 20 February 2009. The applicants were granted permission to appeal, but their appeal was refused on 5 June 2009. Both applicants were served with an indictment on 10 September 2008 which contained the same charges as the 2005 petition. It also contained a number of additional charges relating to various sexual offences. The High Court found that the Crown had acted properly in investigating and reviewing the evidence between 1997 and 2008 and that new evidence had since come to light to allow the Crown to proceed against both applicants. The first applicant appealed against the decision not to dismiss the charge against him. The second applicant did not appeal the decision. The applicants’ trials for the sexual offences took place between 19 April 2010 and 13 May 2010. On 12 May 2010 the applicants were convicted on numerous counts and sentenced to periods of imprisonment ranging from eight to ten years to run concurrently. They were sentenced to life imprisonment for murder, with a tariff of thirty years for the first applicant and twenty-six year for the second applicant. Both applicants unsuccessfully sought to appeal against conviction and sentence. The Appeal Court accepted that the police had interrogated him “robustly” in 1998, but agreed with the High Court that he was not “charged” until 5 April 2005. The applicants appealed against conviction and sentence. First applicant lodged a Note of Appeal on 2 September 2010, containing numerous grounds and sub-grounds on a wide range of issues regarding all the charges. The sifting judges granted him leave to appeal against his sentence for murder, but not against his conviction. The applicants subsequently applied under section 107(8) of the Criminal Procedure (Scotland) Act 1995 (“the 1995 Act”) for leave to reinstate grounds which the judges had found to be unarguable. The main issue before the Supreme Court was whether the applicants could be said to have been “charged” on 17 September 1998 or whether the appropriate “starting point” for the purposes of Article 6 § 1 was 5 April 2005. Supreme Court observes that as the “fair trial” guarantee under Article 6 was distinct from the ‘reasonable-time’ guarantee it had to be approached separately. Court concluded that the correct “starting point” in the applicants’ proceedings was 5 April 2005 and the case was remitted to the Appeal Court. The Appeal Court dismissed the first applicant’s appeal against conviction and sentence on 27 March 2014, and the second applicant‘s appeal on 19 June 2014. The case was dismissed on the grounds that the applicants had not been given a fair trial and that the court should not have taken into account the fact that they had been subjected to questioning in September 1998.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was convicted of offences of rape and indecency with a child and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. He arrived in the UK in 1995 and claimed asylum. The asylum claim was refused but he was granted exceptional leave to remain until February 2000. On 20 May 2002 the Secretary of State for the Home Department issued the applicant with a decision to make a deportation order and on 27 May 2002 he issued an authority for detention. On 7 December 2010 the Acting President of the Section to which the case was allocated decided to apply Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, indicating to the Government that it was desirable in the interests of the parties that the applicant should not be expelled to Somalia. The applicant claimed to be a member of the Isaaq tribe, which comes from Somaliland, an autonomous region in north-west Somalia. He claimed that his parents were born in Hargeisa, but it was accepted that he was born in Mogadishu. As the applicant did not co-operate with the provision of bio-data, the Government decided that it would be preferable to remove him to Somalia. In November 2004 the applicant refused a formal request to sign such a disclaimer. In July 2006 the Government concluded an agreement with African Express Airlines which made enforced removals to Somalia possible. The first enforced removal to Somalia took place on 30 November 2006. In September 2006 the applicant was granted permission to apply for judicial review. The applicant was issued with removal directions set for 29 November 2006. He sought leave to apply for judicial review of the removal directions and the directions were cancelled pending a decision on that application. An application for interim relief in the form of an order that he be released from detention was refused. The judge reiterated the principles established by domestic case-law, most notably in the case of R v Governor of Durham Prison, ex parte Hardial Singh [1984] WLR 704. The period of detention from 3 December 2004, which was the date of the applicant’s first review following his refusal to return voluntarily, to 30 June 2006 was found to be unlawful. On 1 February 2007 the Secretary of State issued a decision refusing to revoke the deportation order. On 10 May 2007 the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal ordered reconsideration of the Immigration Judge’s decision. The rehearing took place on 18 December 2008 and, in a determination promulgated on 1 July 2009, the Tribunal dismissed the appeal. In a judgment dated 23 April 2010 the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, finding that the applicant would be at risk of ill-treatment if he were to be removed to Mogadishu. On 6 December 2010 the applicant was issued with removal directions to Somalia. The removal was to take place on 8 December 2010. On 7 December 2010 he was granted the applicant interim measures under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court to prevent his removal. In April 2006 the Home Office introduced a ‘secret’ policy creating a presumption in favour of the detention of Foreign National Prisoners pending their deportation. The policy was not disclosed until mid-2008 and was not formally published until September 2008. The case originated in an application (no. 27770/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Somali national, Mr Mustafa Abdi. The applicant was convicted of offences of rape and indecency with a child and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. On 20 May 2002 the Secretary of State for the Home Department issued the applicant with a decision to make a deportation order. On 7 December 2010 the Acting President of the Section to which the case was allocated decided to apply Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, indicating to the Government that it was desirable in the interests of the parties that the applicant should not be expelled to Somalia. The applicant had claimed to be a member of the Isaaq tribe, which comes from Somaliland, an autonomous region in north-west Somalia. He claimed that his parents were born in Hargeisa, but it was accepted that he was born in Mogadishu, in south-central Somalia. As the applicant did not co-operate with the provision of bio-data, the Government decided that it would be preferable to remove him to Somalia. In the course of the hearing, however, the immigration judge was wrongly informed that enforced removals to Somalia would be possible in the foreseeable future. In July 2006 the Government concluded an agreement with African Express Airlines which made enforced removal to Somalia possible. The applicant was issued with removal directions set for 29 November 2006. He sought leave to apply for judicial review of the removal directions and the directions were cancelled pending a decision on that application. An application for interim relief in the form of an order that he be released from detention was refused. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 19365/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the Parole Board did not provide the guarantees and procedures required by Article 5 § 4 when examining whether he should be released. The Court declared the remainder of the application admissible in a decision made on 23 September 2003. The case was heard by the Court's Fourth Section (Rule 52 of the Rules of Court) and the Government replied to the applicant's observations on just satisfaction (Rule 59 of the rules) The applicant was sentenced to mandatory life imprisonment in 1981 for the murder of an acquaintance. In June 2001 the applicant was transferred to HM Prison Manchester. He claimed that he did not receive notification of the parole decision until sometime after 13 September 2001. The applicant stated that he wanted to seek judicial review of the decision, but was unable to find a solicitor who was prepared to act on his behalf. His then solicitors gave advice that judicial review stood little prospect of success as the reports recommending a move to open conditions had been slightly ambiguous. His first Parole Board oral hearing under new arrangements was scheduled for November 2003. At the applicant's request, it was deferred until May 2004 to allow the applicant time to complete certain courses identified in the reports.

The case originated in an application (no. 34964/97) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 of the Convention on account of the national court’s decision, despite his acquittal on criminal charges, to order him to pay compensation to the victim. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 17 September 2002 (Rule 59 § 2). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr H. Harborg, Attorney-General's Office (Civil Matters), Agent, Mr F. Elgesem, Advokat, Counsel/Adviser, and (b) the applicant Mr Ivar Ringvold. The applicant was charged with the sexual abuse of a minor, G., born in December 1979. The alleged offences were said to have occurred in the applicant’s home when the child visited her father. By a judgment of 18 February 1994, the High Court, noting that the jury had answered the questions concerning criminal guilt in the negative, acquitted the applicant of the charges. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court (Høyesterett) under the rules of the 1915 Code of Civil Procedure (tvistemålsloven) against the refusal to award compensation. The High Court decided to reject G.'s compensation claim of (up to) 110,000 Norwegian kroner. G’s lawyer requested that documents produced in the context of the criminal case be submitted as evidence to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court then ordered the taking of oral evidence by the Oslo City Court (byrett). Evidence was taken between 26 and 30 June 1995, 18 and 20 October 1995, 20 November 1995 and 3 January 1996, during which time more than twenty witnesses were heard. The ruling cannot be perceived as a general procedural bar against the production of the case documents from criminal proceedings in a later case. The submission of the documents does not as such imply that the acquittal in the criminal cases is open to doubt. The statement in Sekanina case, which the lawyer for the defendant has referred to, must be read in its context. The first voting judge, Mrs Justice Gjølstad, stated on behalf of a unanimous court, inter alia: “In so far as the appeal concerns the merits, two general questions arise, namely the relationship to the acquittal in the criminal case (see Article 6 § 2 of the Convention) and the requirement of proof in such cases’ The decision on the civil compensation claim goes in a different direction from that on criminal liability, this may happen for various reasons. The presumption of innocence applies even after an acquittal. The court in such a case can rely on a finding that the defendant has in fact committed the act in relation to which he has been acquitted. Justice Gjølstad found that the evidence satisfied the standard of proof, establishing that sexual abuse had occurred. There was a basis for awarding the victim compensation under section 3-5(1)(b) of the Damage Compensation Act. The Supreme Court did not share the High Court’s view that the evidentiary value of the video recording was diminished by certain misgivings concerning the lack of synchronisation of sound and picture. Those shortcomings had been remedied before the Supreme Court. The decision was taken independently of the decision in the criminal case and that it did not undermine the acquittal. The case was brought under the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. G. found that several infringements had occurred and that, even though their extent was not possible to ascertain with precision, there had been serious violations involving a certain use of force or threats, as a result of which G. had sustained damage. G. was found to have committed a number of infringements in the course of his duties as a police officer. He was found guilty of one count of misconduct in a public office and sentenced to three years of community service. The sentence was suspended for one year and one month and he was ordered to pay a fine of £2,500. G was also ordered to serve a four-month suspended sentence and one-year community service, with the possibility of a further fine of up to £1,000.

The case originated in an application (no. 34964/97) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Norwegian Government were represented by Mr F. Elgesem, who acted as Agent until he left the Attorney-General’s Office (Civil Matters) in June 2002. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 17 September 2002 (Rule 59 § 2) The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. The applicant was charged under Articles 192 and 195 of the Criminal Code (straffeloven) with the sexual abuse of a minor. The alleged offences were said to have occurred in the applicant’s home when the child visited her father. By a judgment of 18 February 1994, the High Court, noting that the jury had answered the questions concerning criminal guilt in the negative, acquitted the applicant of the charges. Moreover, it decided to reject G.'s compensation claim. G. subsequently appealed to the Supreme Court (Høyesterett) under the rules of the 1915 Code of Civil Procedure (tvistemålsloven) against the refusal to award compensation. The Supreme Court ordered the taking of oral evidence by the Oslo City Court (byrett). Evidence was taken between 26 and 30 June 1995, 18 and 20 October 1995, 20 November 1995 and 3 January 1996, during which time more than twenty witnesses were heard. The Supreme Court authorised the documents from the criminal case to be joined to the case file in the compensation proceedings. After hearing the parties and a large number of witnesses, the Supreme Court, in a judgment of 5 June 1996, ordered the applicant to pay NOK 75,000 to G. in compensation for non-pecuniary damage, under section 3-5(1)(1) Civil compensation claims may be made in criminal proceedings by the prosecution or by the injured party. It is not a condition for the examination of civil compensation claims that the accused person should have been convicted in respect of the charge. In principle it is in principle possible to either reject or uphold a civil compensation claim, irrespective of the decision concerning criminal liability. The injured party, who does not enjoy rights as a party in the criminal case, should not forfeit his or her compensation claim as a result of an acquittal. Even assuming that the Convention provision applies to the treatment of such claims, it has not been infringed as long as no disagreement or doubt has been expressed with regard to such claims. Justice Gjølstad found that the evidence satisfied the standard of proof, establishing that sexual abuse had occurred and that, on the balance of probabilities, it was clear that the applicant was the abuser. There was a basis for awarding the victim compensation under section 3-5(1)(b) of the Damage Compensation Act. But she emphasised that this decision was taken independently of the decision in the criminal case and that it did not undermine the acquittal of the applicant. The Supreme Court did not share the High Court’s view that the evidentiary value of the video recording was diminished by certain misgivings concerning the lack of synchronisation of sound and picture. G. was found to have made several infringements. The extent was not possible to ascertain with precision. There had been serious violations involving a certain use of force or threats, as a result of which G. had sustained damage, the court found. G. was fined £500,000 and ordered to pay £100,000 in costs and costs. The judge ruled that the matter should be referred to the European Court of Human Rights, which has jurisdiction over the case. The case has been adjourned until later this year, when a decision will be made on whether to pursue a further fine of £200,000 or more. name: Michalis Michael
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18361/91) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the Turkish occupation of the northern part of Cyprus had deprived him of his home and properties. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 24 August 1999 the Court declared the application admissible and the applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). In addition, third-party comments were received from the Government of Cyprus, which had exercised its right to intervene (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 1 (b) The applicant acquired ownership of this property on 27 June 1990, when it was transferred to him by way of inheritance from his grandfather and a gift from his parents. On 9 December 1990 the applicant made one further attempt to return to his property in northern Cyprus by participating in a convoy of cars of fellow refugees intending to return home. The applicant and his fellow refugees, who had informed the Commander of the United Nations (UN) forces in Cyprus of their intentions, stopped at the check point in the ‘buffer zone’, on the main road linking Nicosia with Ayios Amvrosios and Kyrenia. There, they asked the UN officer on duty to be allowed toreturn to their homes, property and villages. The officer replied that the latter had refused their request.

name: Kamuran Alican
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 21868/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The application concerns the wounding of the first applicant, who was eleven years old at the time, and the death of the second and third applicants' sons, who were fourteen and thirteen years old respectively. The applicants were represented by Mr F. Gümüş, a lawyer practising in Diyarbakır. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented. by their Agent. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. Children were grazing their sheep in the field when they found an object with an iron head which looked like a bullet. The first applicant left the other two children to find water while they were trying to hit the iron head with pieces of metal. At that moment the bullet exploded. As a result of the explosion, the first applicant suffered partial loss of the sight of one eye and the total loss of sight in the other. The criminal investigation into the incident was launched by the Tatvan public prosecutor on 23 April 1994. On 6 May 1997 the military prosecutor gave a decision that there was no need to initiate criminal proceedings on the ground that there had been no fault or negligence attributable to anyone except the children. The first and the second applicants, and on 17 April 1995 the third applicant, brought actions for compensation against the Ministry before the Van Administrative Court. In their petitions, the applicants claimed that Kamuran Alican had been injured and Çetin Alican and Ilhami Alican died as a result of a mine which had been placed there by the gendarmerie police station. The court awarded the first applicant's claim in full. The Ministry appealed. The Supreme Administrative Court quashed the judgment of the first-instance court on the ground that the latter had failed to determine which administrative entity, that is either the Ministry of the Interior or the Ministry Of Defence, had responsibility for compensating the applicant. Explosion occurred in area where rockets are launched. origin of the grenade which caused the explosion is unknown. The rocket launcher in question is frequently used by members of the PKK terrorist organisation. Incident took place 1,500 metres from the barracks, in an area, which according to the attached map, has been declared to be a 2nd degree military security zone. It should be concluded that the damage in the present case was not caused by the activities of military forces but rather by terrorist activities. ... The plaintiff should therefore be paid his claim in full, TRL 1,000,000,.0000 for pecuniary damage... although according to. the expert reports, pec uniary damage could amount to TRL 19,237,229,0000. ... As regards non-pecuniaries damage, the plaintiff should be awarded TRL 100,000.000. In respect of Ramazan Alican the Van Administrative Court awarded the applicant TRL 366,954,3670 in respect of pecuniary damage together with legal interest running from the date of the incident, 23 April 1994. The Ministry appealed. 23 May 2002 the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. In respect of Ahmet Alican, the application was dismissed on the ground that the latter had failed to determine which administrative entity, either the Ministry of the Interior or the Ministry. of Defence, had responsibility for compensating the applicant. The appeal was dismissed and the appeal was upheld.

name: Władysław Gajewski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 27225/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the civil proceedings in his case had been unfair and that his claim had not been heard by an impartial tribunal. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wolasiewicz of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. It was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (former Article 29 § 3, now Article 29§ 1) The applicant applied to the District Court in Zamość and requested the sum of PLN 577,292 as payment for his eight years of trustee duties. The insolvency judge, in her submissions to the court (przedstawienie), asked it to grant the applicant remuneration in a lower amount, namely PLN 317,989. The applicant appealed against this decision. The Lublin Regional Court at a session held in camera dismissed the applicant's appeal on 5 January 2005. He filed a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court. On 3 March 2005 the Lublin. Regional Court rejected his cassated appeal as inadmissible in law. The liquidation procedure was terminated on 9 October 2007. The applicant asked to be paid further partial remuneration in the amount of PLN 66,945 for the period between 7 June 2003 and 6 February 2005. On 20 December 2005 the Zamość District Court held a hearing in that case. The court noted that the insolvency judge would have pre-conceived notions about the issues in the case. In reply, on 24 March 2006 the Lublin Regional Court ordered judge M.S. to withdraw from the panel. The Supreme Court dismissed his appeal confirming that a second-instance court's decision on trustee's remunerance could not be the subject of an appeal.

In reply, on 24 March 2006 the Lublin Regional Court ordered judge M.-S. to withdraw from the panel. On 27 April 2006 the Zamość District Court granted the applicant partial remuneration in the amount of PLN 22,000. In September 2005 the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal confirming that a second-instance court's decision on trustee's remuneral could not be the subject of an appeal. The court noted that the insolvency judge would have pre-conceived notions about the issues in the case. In February 2005 the applicant asked to be paid further partial Remuneration for the period between 7 June 2003 and 6 February 2005.

train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 15 December 1997. It originated in an application (no. 28090/95) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by a Spanish national. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1. The applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent her (Rule 30), Mr M. Dopico Fradrique, of the Madrid, Pamplona, Oviedo and Alcalá de Henares Bars. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr J.M. Morenilla, the elected judge of Spanish nationality. The applicant had been in dispute with a neighbour concerning a view over her property at Lumbier in the province of Navarre. On 28 July 1992 a settlement agreement was concluded between the parties before the deputy judge of first instance at Aoiz. In the agreement the neighbour undertook to block the view from his patio over the applicant’s property within six months. When that period expired without the neighbour having carried out his undertaking, the applicant applied to the Aoiz Court of First Instance for enforcement of the agreement. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 June 1998. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr J. Borrego Bor rego, Head of the Legal Service for the European Commission and Court of Human Rights, Ministry of Justice, Agent; (b) for. the Commission M. F. Martínez, Delegate. In a decision (auto) of 7 September 1993 the deputy judge of the Aoiz Court of First Instance dismissed the applicant’s application. The judge held that the agreement was void on the ground that the neighbour, who was merely a life tenant, could not carry out the works needed to block the view without the consent of the reversioner. The decision was at last served on the applicant in the person of her domestic help, since she herself was out at the time. The agreement was defective because one of the parties had no capacity to conclude such an agreement. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the defendant had not raised the nullity of the agreement within the prescribed time. The applicant lodged a reposición application and, in the alternative, an ordinary appeal against the decision of 7 September 1993 with the registry of the duty court in Madrid. The application was dated 27 November 1993 and had been signed by the applicant and her counsel at Lumbier. The first page was postmarked 30 November 1993. The Court of First Instance dismissed the application and upheld the impugned decision, on the ground that the application should have been registered at the court registry within the prescribed period of three days. The court also held that allowing an application to be lodged by post would undermine ‘judicial authenticity’ The applicant made an appeal with the Navarre Audiencia Provincial, which dismissed it in a decision (auto) of 23 December 1994. On 20 January 1995 the applicant lodged an amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court, relying on the right to protection by the courts. In a decision of 8 May 1995 the application was declared inadmissible on the following grounds: “… This Court’s case-law on the filing of applications. applies to the instant case. Applications are normally to be filed with the registry of the court applied to or with the duty judge and filing [of an application] at the headquarters of administrative bodies is, as an exception, permissible only where the litigant is not represented by a lawyer’” The relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure concerning time-limits and the filing of applications are worded as follows. Article 477 “An action to have the terms of a settlement agreement declared void may be brought on the same grounds as one for annulling contracts. Such an action must be brought in the appropriate court within fifteen days of the conclusion of the agreement, using the procedure corresponding to the amount in dispute.” Article 377 “Reposición applications must be filed within three days and must specify the provision of this Code that is alleged to have been infringed. Where these two requirements have not been satisfied, the court shall, without further consideration, make a declaration, against which no appeal shall lie, that no ruling will be made” The rules on the postal service, as enacted in Decree no. 1653/1964 of 14 May 1964 and amended by the Order of 14 August 1971, provide: Article 205 “Acceptance of applications and documents sent to administrative institutions …” The documents and applications in question shall be submitted in an open envelope. The official who accepts the item for despatch shall stamp it with the date in the upper left-hand corner of the main document, so that the name of the post office and the date of submission are clearly visible. In a judgment of 31 January 1991 (no. 20/1991, Official Gazette (Boletín oficial del Estado) of 25 February 1991) the Constitutional Court, citing its own case-law, held that the right to effective protection by the courts was infringed “where a member of the public found it impossible to lodge an application”. In two judgments of 18 November 1993 and 27 October 1994 the Constitutional Court held that applications were to be filed with the registry of the court applied to or the duty judge of the town. The Commission declared the application (no. 28090/95) admissible on 25 November 1996. In its report of 21 October 1997 (Article 31), it expressed the unanimous opinion that there had been a violation of Article 6 § 1. The full text of the Commission’s opinion is reproduced as an annex to this judgment. The Government asked the Court to hold that the dismissal of the application against the judgment of 7 September 1993 had not violated the rights guaranteed in Article 6§ 1 of the Convention.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47328/99) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purpose of the proceedings before the Court. On 27 April 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the applicant’s right to a fair trial by an independent and impartial tribunal. The opinion was not notified to the applicant. It was read out during the Court of Cassation's hearing. The opinion was written by the Chief Public Prosecutor of Turkey. The court has since rejected the request for rectification. The case was adjourned until December 27, 1998. The decision was made on the basis of the merits of the case. The application was dismissed on December 26, 1998, on the grounds that it did not meet the requirements for a case to be heard in court. The applicant was denied the right to appeal the decision. The appeal was denied and the case was settled on December 29, 1998 on a technicality. The original appeal was rejected.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56971/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the Swiss authorities’ refusal of their request for family reunification constituted a breach of their right to respect for family life as provided in Article 8 of the convention. The application was communicated to the Government of Switzerland on 18 January 2011. The case was decided by the Court of Appeal on 14 February 2012. The decision was delivered by the Chief Justice of the European Court of Justice, who upheld the decision of the original court of appeal. The first applicant lodged a request for family reunification with the second applicant, who was 15 and a half years old at the time. On 15 February 2007 the Migration Office of the Canton of Aargau refused that request. The applicant lodged an appeal against that decision with the Court of Appeal in Foreigners’ Law (Rekursgericht im Ausländerrecht) of the canton. On 2 February 2010 the Federal Administrative Court dismissed the appeal. The second applicant's mother had moved to Kuwait with her new spouse and he was now cared for exclusively by his paternal grandmother. The court considered that the applicants’ interests in respect for their family life prevailed over those of the public. On 5 July 2010 the Federal Supreme Court dismissed that appeal. It considered, in particular, that the relationship between the two applicants was not paramount. It noted that the first applicant had not applied for family reunification immediately after his arrival in Switzerland. train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 11 March 1994 and by the German Government on 29 March 1994. It originated in an application (no. 17851/91) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 13 February 1991. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings. The Registrar received the applicant's observations on 9 and 11 August 1994 and the Government's memorial on 17 August 1994. On 19 August 1994 the Commission produced various documents, as requested by the Registrar on the President's instructions. By a letter of 4 November 1994 the Agent of the Government sought leave to submit an additional memorial and requested that the hearing initially set down for 23 November be postponed. On 26 January 1995 the Chamber decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of a Grand Chamber (Rule 51). The Grand Chamber comprised as ex officio members the President and the Vice-President, Mr Bernhardt, who in this case was already sitting as national judge, together with the other members of the Chamber. Mrs Dorothea Vogt, a German national born in 1949, lives in Jever in the Land of Lower Saxony. She studied literature and languages at the University of Marburg/Lahn for six years. In November 1975 she sat the examination to become a secondary-school teacher. On 1 February 1979, before the end of her probationary period, she was appointed a permanent civil servant (Beamtin auf Lebenszeit) In an assessment report drawn up in March 1981 her capabilities and work were described as entirely satisfactory. The Court heard addresses by Mr Trechsel, Mr Becker, Mr Jäckel, Mr Damman and Mr Meyer-Ladewig. The applicant had engaged in various political activities on behalf of the DKP since the autumn of 1980. She had stood as a DKP candidate in the 1982 elections to the Parliament (Landtag) of the Land of Lower Saxony. The proceedings were stayed in order to widen the investigations to include further instances of the applicant's political activity that had come to light. Mrs Vogt was accused of also failing to comply with her duties as a civil servant in that she had been a member of the “Executive Committee“ of the Bremen/North LowerSaxony regional branch (Bezirksorganisation) since the end of 1983. By an order of 12 August 1986 the Weser-Ems regional council notified the applicant that she had been temporarily suspended from her post. “Although you knew the views of your superiors and the case-law of the disciplinary courts you have nevertheless, over a considerable period of time, deliberately violated your duty of oyalty. For a permanent civil servant that is anextraordinarily serious breach of duty.” Mrs Vogt argued that her conduct could not amount to a failure to fulfil her duties as a civil servant. She had always carried out such activity within the law and within the limits laid down in the Constitution. Her action to promote peace within the Federal Republic of Germany and in its external relations was in no way indicative of an anti-constitutional stance. In its judgment of 15 October 1987 the Disciplinary Division dismissed applications by Mrs Vogt to have the proceedings stayed and witnesses examined. It considered that active membership of a political party that pursued anti-constitutional aims was incompatible with a civil servant's duty of political loyalty. It granted her a sum equivalent to 75 per cent of her pension entitlement at that date, to be paid for a six-month period. The division found in the first place that neither ILO Convention No. 111 nor the recommendations made in the Commission of Inquiry's report of 20 February 1987 constituted a bar to the opening of disciplinary proceedings. The DKP's aims, as described in the Mannheim programme of 21 October 1978, were clearly opposed to the free democratic constitutional system of the Federal Republic of Germany. The duty of political loyalty was one of the traditional principles of the civil service and had constitutional status by virtue of Article 33 para. 5 of the Basic Law (see paragraph 25 below). This rule did not apply to measures, such as disciplinary proceedings, which initially had a different purpose and restricted the freedom to stand for election to, and to sit as a member of, parliament only as an indirect and unavoidable consequence of their implementation. The applicant had carried out her political activities despite being familiar with the case-law establishing that active membership of the DKP was incompatible with the duty ofpolitical loyalty. The Disciplinary Division finally ordered that Mrs Vogt should be paid 75 per cent of her pension allowance for a period of six months. Mrs Vogt held senior political post within the DKP and espoused anti-constitutional aims. The court held that the applicant's reference to Article 5 para. 1 of the Basic Law, which secured the right to freedom of expression, was not relevant. The same approach applied in cases where a person had already been appointed to a permanent civil service post. Even though Mrs Vogt sought above all to support both systems at the same time, she had to be considered to be opposed to the Constitution herself, even though she proclaimed her attachment to the Basic law. The European Court of Human Rights had ruled that a decision by a competent authority relating to admission to the civil service did not amount to an interference with freedom of speech. The DKP's aims were admittedly not all anti-constitutional; some of them were compatible with the Basic Law. However, civil servants could not, as a means of furthering their own political objectives, make use of a party with anti- constitutional aims and help it to come to power. It is not necessary to resolve that question here. It appears doubtful whether the. view of the Constitution espoused by the official and described above reflects accurately the principles enshrined in the Basic. Law. The former Communist Party (KPD) (BVerfGE 5, p. 85), the Federal Constitutional Court held that not only the 'tactics of conflict' employed by the former KPD but also the different phases of the process leading to attainment of its final objective of 'socialist rule' were incompatible with the free democratic constitutional system. The court also considered that the applicant's commitment to changing the DKP's policies could not exculpate her. The court added that such a breach of duty was especially serious in the case of a teacher, who was supposed to teach the children entrusted to her care the fundamental values of the Constitution. Her dismissal had therefore been justified, since a civil servant who thus persisted in breaching her duties and refusing to see reason (unbelehrbar) was no longer capable of serving the State. Parents, who because of compulsory education had to send their children to State schools, were entitled to expect the State to rely on its servants' loyalty to the Constitution, the court said. The Federal Constitutional Court said Mrs Vogt had breached her duties as a civil servant. The court said the State was under a duty to dismiss teachers who played an active role in an anti-constitutional organisation. It added that a radical change in a civil service's attitude could affect its assessment of the seriousness of professional misconduct. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint (Verfassungsbeschwerde) but the court decided on 7 August 1990 not to entertain the constitutional complaint, on the ground that it had insufficient prospects of success. It said the dismissal had therefore not amounted to a breach of the principle of proportionality as regards her constitutional rights. From 1987 to 1991 the applicant worked as a playwright and drama teacher at the North Lower Saxony regional theatre (Landesbühne) in Wilhelmshaven. From 1 February 1991 she was reinstated in her post as a teacher for the LowerSaxony education authority. The Land government had beforehand repealed the decree on the employment of extremists in the Lower Saxonies civil service (Ministerpräsidentenbeschluß - also known as the Radikalenerlaß - see paragraph 32 below) and had published regulations for dealing with “earlier cases“ (see paragraph 33 below)

Disciplinary proceedings against Mrs Vogt began on 1 February 1979 and ended on 1 March 1980. The case was heard in the Supreme Court of Germany. The Weser-Ems regional council issued an order (Verfügung) on 13 July 1982 instituting disciplinary proceedings against the applicant. She had failed to comply with the duty of loyalty to the Constitution (“duty of political loyalty’ - politische Treuepflicht) that she owed as a civil servant under section 61 (2) of the Lower Saxony Civil Service Act (Niedersächsisches Beamtengesetz - see paragraph 28 below). She had, it was said, engaged in various political activities on behalf of the DKP since the autumn of 1980 and in particular had stood as a DKP candidate in the 1982 elections to the Landtag. By an order of 12 August 1986 the Weser-Ems regional council notified the applicant that she had been temporarily suspended from her post. “Although you knew the views of your superiors and the case-law of the disciplinary courts you have nevertheless, over a considerable period of time, deliberately violated your duty of oyalty. For a permanent civil servant that is anextraordinarily serious breach of duty.” From October 1986 Mrs Vogt was paid only 60 per cent of her salary (Dienstbezüge). The applicant, who by her own account has been a member of the DKP since 1972, argued that her conduct could not amount to a failure to fulfil her duties as a civil servant. The DKP's aims were clearly opposed to the free democratic constitutional system of the Federal Republic of Germany. A party could be held to be anti-constitutional even if it had not been banned by the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) under Article 21 para. 2 of the Basic Law (Grundgesetz - see paragraph 25 below) The Disciplinary Division held that the applicant had failed to comply with her duty of political loyalty and ordered her dismissal as a disciplinary measure. It granted her a sum equivalent to 75 per cent of her pension entitlement at that date, to be paid for a six-month period. The division found that neither ILO Convention No. 111 nor the recommendations made in the Commission of Inquiry's report of 20 February 1987 constituted a bar to the opening of disciplinary proceedings. Mrs Vogt was dismissed for having betrayed the relationship of trust between herself and her employer. The Disciplinary Division finally ordered that Mrs Vogt should be paid 75 per cent of her pension allowance for a period of six months. It did so in recognition of the fact that apart from her breach of the duty of loyalty Mrs VogT had always performed her duties unexceptionably and enthusiastically and needed some income to be protected from immediate hardship. The fact that she had done her work satisfactorily for many years was immaterial. The applicant lodged an appeal against the above judgment with the Lower Saxony Disciplinary Court, reiterating her previous arguments (see paragraph 18 above). In a judgment of 31 October 1989 the Dis disciplinary Court dismissed Mrs Vogts appeal and upheld the Administrative Court's judgment in all respects. The applicant had failed to satisfy requirements of Article 5 para. 5 of the Basic Law, taken together with section 61 (2) of the Lower Saxony Civil Service Act. By holding such a senior political post within the DKP, she necessarily espoused anti-constitutional aims and had therefore to be considered to be opposed to the Constitution herself. It was not possible to support both systems at the same time, even though Mrs Vogt sought above all to support the constitutional system. The court held that the applicant's reference to the right to freedom of expression was not relevant as the provisions governing the civil service were general laws. The DKP's aims were admittedly not all anti-constitutional; some of them were compatible with the Basic Law. However, civil servants could not, as a means of furthering their own political objectives, make use of a party with anti- constitutional aims and help it to come to power. The former Communist Party (KPD) employed 'tactics of conflict' employed by the former KPD to achieve its final objective of 'socialist rule' [sozialistische Herrschaft]. The Federal Constitutional Court held that intensive propaganda and persistent unrest aimed at establishing - even if this was not to be achieved in the near future - a socialist order. The court also considered that the applicant's commitment to changing the DKP's policies could not exculpate her. The court added that such a breach of duty was especially serious in the case of a teacher, who was supposed to teach the children entrusted to her care the fundamental values of the Constitution. Parents, who because of compulsory education had to send their children to State schools, were entitled to expect the State to expect them to do the same. Mrs Vogt had knowingly breached her professional obligations. Her dismissal had therefore been justified, since a civil servant who thus persisted in breaching her duties and refusing to see reason (unbelehrbar) was no longer capable of serving the State. The State was under a duty to dismiss teachers who played an active role in an anti-constitutional organisation. The court added that a radical change in a civil servant's attitude could affect its assessment of the seriousness of professional misconduct. It followed that a more lenient disciplinary measure, aimed at persuading her to abandon her political activities within the DKP, was bound to fail. Her otherwise blameless conduct in carrying out her teaching tasks did not change the situation in any way, since the basis of trust that was essential for her to continue as a civil servants was lacking. The applicant's dismissal had therefore not amounted to a breach of the principle of proportionality as regards her constitutional rights. From 1987 to 1991 the applicant worked as a playwright and drama teacher at the North Lower Saxony regional theatre (Landesbühne) in Wilhelmshaven. From 1 February 1991 she was reinstated in her post as a teacher for the LowerSaxony education authority. The Land government had beforehand repealed the decree on the employment of extremists in the Lower Saxon civil service. Subsequent developments in Germany have seen the number of extremists at the lower Saxony civil service halved since the decree was repealed in 1991.
