It originated in an application (no. 17851/91) lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a German national, Mrs Dorothea Vogt, on 13 February 1991. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention. The applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent her (Rule 30). The President gave her lawyers leave to use the German language. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 February 1995. The Grand Chamber comprised as ex officio members the President and the Vice-President, Mr Bernhardt, who in this case was already sitting as national judge. The names of the remaining ten judges were drawn by lot by the President in the presence of the Registrar on 27 January 1995, namely Mr F. Gölcüklü, Mr R. Macdonald, Mr A. Spielmann, Mr J. De Meyer, Mr I. Foighel, Mr M. Loizou, Mr F F. Bigi, Mr L.A. Lopes Rocha, Mr D. Gotchev and Mr P. Kuris. Dorothea Vogt, a German national born in 1949, lives in Jever in the Land of Lower Saxony. She studied literature and languages at the University of Marburg/Lahn for six years. She became a member of the German Communist Party (Deutsche Kommunistische Partei - “DKP’) In November 1975 she sat the examination to become a secondary-school teacher. On 1 February 1979, before the end of her probationary period, she was appointed a permanent civil servant (Beamtin auf Lebenszeit) She taught German and French. In an assessment report drawn up in March 1981 her capabilities and work were described as entirely satisfactory and it was stated that she was held in high regard by her pupils. Weser-Ems regional council issued an order (Verfügung) on 13 July 1982 instituting disciplinary proceedings against the applicant. She had failed to comply with the duty of loyalty to the Constitution (“duty of political loyalty“ - politische Treuepflicht) that she owed as a civil servant under section 61 (2) of the Lower Saxony Civil Service Act (Niedersächsisches Beamtengesetz - see paragraph 28 below). She had, it was said, engaged in various political activities on behalf of the DKP since the autumn of 1980 and in particular had stood as a DKP candidate in the 1982 elections to the Landtag. The Weser-Ems regional council notified the applicant that she had been temporarily suspended from her post. “Although you knew the views of your superiors and the case-law of the disciplinary courts you have nevertheless, over a considerable period of time, deliberately violated your duty of oyalty” For a permanent civil servant that is anextraordinarily serious breach of duty. The applicant, who by her own account has been a member of the DKP since 1972, argued that her conduct could not amount to a failure to fulfil her duties as a civil servant. She had always carried out such activity within the law and within the limits laid down in the Constitution. Her action to promote peace within the Federal Republic of Germany was in no way indicative of an anti-constitutional stance. In its judgment of 15 October 1987 the Disciplinary Division dismissed applications by Mrs Vogt to have the proceedings stayed and witnesses examined. It considered that active membership of a political party that pursued anti-constitutional aims was incompatible with a civil servant's duty of political loyalty. The DKP's aims, as described in the Mannheim programme of 21 October 1978 (see paragraph 22 below), were clearly opposed to the free democratic constitutional system of the Federal Republic of Germany. Through the active role which she played within the DKP the applicant had clearly supported aims that were contrary to the Constitution. It granted her a sum equivalent to 75 per cent of her pension entitlement at that date, to be paid for a six-month period. Mrs Vogt was dismissed for having betrayed the relationship of trust between herself and her employer. She repeatedly indicated that she intended to continue her political activities for the DKP despite the warnings she had received. The fact that she had done her work satisfactorily for many years was immaterial. The Disciplinary Division finally ordered that Mrs Vogt should be paid 75 per cent of her pension allowance for a period of six months. It did so in recognition of the fact that apart from her breach of the duty of loyalty Mrs VogT had always performed her duties unexceptionably and enthusiastically and needed some income to be protected from immediate hardship.  DKP's political aims were incompatible with that system. The court held that the applicant's reference to Article 5 para. 1 of the Basic Law, which secured the right to freedom of expression, was not relevant. By holding such a senior political post within the DKP, she necessarily espoused anti-constitutional aims and had therefore to be considered to be opposed to the Constitution herself. Even though Mrs Vogt sought above all to support both systems at the same time, it was not possible to support the two systems. The same approach applied in cases where a person had already been appointed to a permanent civil service post. The DKP's aims were admittedly not all anti-constitutional; some of them were compatible with the Basic Law. However, civil servants could not, as a means of furthering their own political objectives, make use of a party with anti- constitutional aims and help it to come to power. The former Communist Party (KPD) employed 'tactics of conflict' that were incompatible with the free democratic constitutional system. The DKP also aimed to establish a 'socialist rule' [sozialistische Herrschaft], namely proletarian revolution by peaceful or violent means and the triumph of the working class. It appears doubtful whether the view of the Constitution espoused by the official and described above reflects accurately the principles enshrined in the Basic law. The court also considered that the applicant's commitment to changing the DKP's policies could not exculpate her. The political loyalty owed by civil servants entailed a duty for them to dissociate themselves unequivocally from groups which criticised or cast aspersions on the State and the existing constitutional system. The attitude of civil servants who, even if they campaigned within the. DKP for the renunciation of aims that were contrary to the Constitution, showed outside the. party, through the political offices they held, that they unreservedly supported its programme and policy, was incompatible with. such a duty. Mrs Vogt had knowingly breached her professional obligations. The State was under a duty to dismiss teachers who played an active role in an anti-constitutional organisation. The court added that a radical change in a civil servant's attitude could affect its assessment of the seriousness of professional misconduct. Mrs Vogt had herself stated that there was no point, section or part of the DKP's programme of which she disapproved, thus endorsing unconditionally the party's aims set out in the Mannheim programme. The Federal Constitutional Court decided on 7 August 1990 not to entertain the constitutional complaint, on the ground that it had insufficient prospects of success. The dismissal had therefore not amounted to a breach of the principle of proportionality as regards her constitutional rights. From 1987 to 1991 the applicant worked as a playwright and drama teacher at the North Lower Saxony regional theatre (Landesbühne) in Wilhelmshaven. From 1 February 1991 she was reinstated in her post as a teacher for the LowerSaxony education authority. The Land government had beforehand repealed the decree on the employment of extremists in the Lower Saxonic civil service (Ministerpräsidentenbeschluß - also known as the Radikalenerlaß - see paragraph 32 below) See paragraph 33 below for more information on the case. And see paragraph 36 below for further information on this case.

name: Adnan Levent Çamlar
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was arrested in London on suspicion of trafficking of illegal drugs in 1997. On 15 September 1998, after having heard witness statements and evaluated all relevant evidence, the Crown Court acquitted the applicant of all charges and ordered his release. On 24 June 2013 the complaints under Article 6. 1 and 3(d) were communicated to the Government and the. remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The application was lodged by a Turkish national, Mr Adnan Levent Çamlar (“the applicant”), on 4 August 2004. On an unspecified date in 1997, the Magistrates’ Court ordered the applicant’s detention on remand in absentia. dated 13 June 1997. The public prosecutor stated that the British authorities had provided him with the tapes of the applicant's police statements as well as other evidence on the alleged offence. At a hearing on 24 February 1998 the İzmir State Security Court joined the proceedings against the applicant with the proceedings. against the other persons involved in the same offence. The applicant contested the incriminating statements of B.Ӧ. and F.A. and requested to have certain witnesses, including his counsel in the United Kingdom, heard. The court rejected that request, finding that the statements of the witnesses called by the applicant would not contribute to the case. On 27 March 2003, on the basis of the investigation conducted by the British authorities, the İzmir State Security Court found the applicant guilty as charged and sentenced him to twenty four years’ imprisonment and a fine. On 31 March 2003 the applicant appealed against that judgment. In June 2005, the applicant requested the reassessment of his case and the application of the more favourable clauses in the new Code. On 3 July 2008 the applicant was sentenced to twenty years and ten months of imprisonment. Finally, on 9 April 2009 the Court of Cassation held a hearing and heard the submissions of the applicant’s lawyer. The higher court upheld the judgment with a minor procedural correction.

The case originated in an application (no. 28226/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Adnan Levent Çamlar (“the applicant”) was arrested in London on suspicion of trafficking of illegal drugs in 1997. On 15 September 1998, after having heard witness statements and evaluated all relevant evidence, the Crown Court acquitted the applicant of all charges and ordered his release. On 24 June 2013 the complaints under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) were communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The applicant was arrested in 1997 on suspicion of trafficking illegal drugs in Turkey. The applicant denied his involvement in the trafficking of illegal drugs. He was placed in detention on remand in absentia. In 2003 the applicant submitted his written defence to the court and requested his acquittal. The court rejected his request, finding that the statements of the witnesses called by the applicant would not contribute to the case in view of the information already available concerning the proceedings in the United Kingdom. The case was adjourned and the applicant was released pending trial. He has since left Turkey and is now living in the U.S. with his wife and children. The applicant was sentenced to twenty four years' imprisonment and a fine. He argued that he could not be found guilty on the basis of evidence which according to a British court was insufficient to prove his involvement in the alleged acts. The higher court indicated that the offence at issue concerned the exportation of illegal drugs and accordingly the case differed from that concluded in the United Kingdom. The high court dismissed the applicant’s remaining grounds for appeal without further elaboration. On 9 April 2009 the Court of Cassation held a hearing and heard the submissions of the applicant's lawyer. Finally, the higher court upheld the judgment of the İzmir Assize Court with a minor procedural correction.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national. The applicant was arrested in London on suspicion of trafficking of illegal drugs in 1997. He was acquitted of all charges and ordered his release in 1998. The application was declared inadmissible on 24 June 2013 because of the independence and impartiality of the İzmir State Security Court and the applicant’s inability to examine or have examined witnesses. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent. The applicant was charged with the trafficking of illegal drugs in 1997. In 1998 he was acquitted by the Crown Court. The applicant returned to Turkey and was placed in detention on remand in absentia. He denied his involvement in the alleged offence. In 2003 the applicant submitted his written defence to the court and requested his acquittal. The court rejected this request, finding that the statements of the witnesses called by the applicant would not contribute to the case in view of the information already available concerning the proceedings in the United Kingdom. The application was rejected and the applicant was released pending trial. The case has been referred to as the ‘Turkish War of Drugs’. The applicant was found guilty as charged and sentenced to twenty four years' imprisonment and a fine. On 31 March 2003 the applicant appealed against that judgment. He argued that he could not be found guilty on the basis of evidence which according to the British court was insufficient to prove his involvement in the alleged acts. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the İzmir State Security Court on 4 March 2004. The higher court indicated that the offence at issue concerned the exportation of illegal drugs and accordingly the case differed from that concluded in the United Kingdom. The high court dismissed the applicant’s remaining grounds for appeal without further elaboration.

name: Bożenna Wiśniewska
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42401/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was granted, in particular, the ownership of the common apartment together with the furniture and was obliged to pay R.W. a certain amount of money. Between October 1995 and March 2007 the Warsaw District Court scheduled approximately 25 hearings. At least eight of them were adjourned – on three occasions because of the absence of a witness, on two occasions because the illness of the judge, on one occasion because the court had to deal with the request of the applicant's former husband. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Warsaw Regional Court under section 5 of the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. The applicant sought a ruling that the length of the proceedings before the Warsaw District Court had been excessive and an award of just satisfaction in the amount of 10,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) The court held that the 2004 Act had taken full legal effect on the date of its entry into force, i.e. 17 September 2004. On 9 June 2009 the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) refused to examine the applicant's cassation appeal.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36757/97) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 8 of the Convention that a residence prohibition imposed on him by the Austrian authorities violated his right to respect for his private and family life. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted. By a decision of 15 November 2001 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber having decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The applicant was convicted of burglary and sentenced to five months' imprisonment, suspended for a probationary period of three years. The Vöcklabruck District Administrative Authority (Bezirkshauptmannschaft) issued a ten year residence prohibition against the applicant. The Constitutional Court declined to deal with the matter for lack of prospects of success and remitted the case to the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) The applicant's mother, his brother and two half sisters were living in Austria and he appealed against the residence prohibition. On 21 June 1996 the applicant filed a complaint with the Constitutional Court. Court which dismissed it on 19 February 1997. It found that authorities had correctly found that the residence prohibition was necessary in the public interest and did not constitute a disproportionate interference with the applicant's family situation. The applicant was taken into detention with a view to his expulsion and, on 9 April 1997, he was deported to Sarajewo. He was sentenced to 15 years in prison but was released in April 1998. He is currently serving a 15-year prison sentence for attempting to kill a police officer in 1995. The conviction was later quashed on appeal and he is serving a 5-year sentence for attempted murder. He has also been sentenced to a 10-year jail sentence for failing to pay a fine.

name: İsmail Şencan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 7436/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights. The applicants signed contracts with third persons before the notary public to acquire de facto possession (zilyedlik) of a plot of land in Gökçeada. On 1 June 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The Court held that the fact that the land in question appeared as “meadow’ was not an issue. The Court of Cassation quashed the three judgments of the first-instance court. The cases were remitted to the Gökçeada Civil Court of General Jurisdiction. All three cases were joined on 26 September 1994. In its judgment, the court stated that the plot in question was not designated as “meadowland” in the land registration records and that, therefore, it could be subject to private ownership. The court further held that the land should be officially designated as a second degree conservation area. On 6 April 2001 the Court ofCassation dismissed the applicants' request for rectification. This decision was served on the applicants’ representative on 30 April 2001.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 19583/05) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Ms R. Orlikowska-Wrońska, a lawyer practising in Sopot. The Polish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was charged with twelve offences, including aggravated robbery, kidnapping and illegal possession of a weapon. The Gdańsk Regional Court convicted the applicant of nine offences, acquitted him of the remaining three and sentenced him to 15 years’ imprisonment. The applicant appealed against the decisions extending his detention on several occasions. Only one of his appeals was allowed to the effect that the period of extension of his detention was reduced by two months (the Gda ńsk Court of Appeal decision of 17 August 2005). The court’s exceeding the permissible period of the length of intervals between hearings, the proceedings had to be conducted anew. The Court of Appeal found that the length of proceedings had been excessive in the applicant’s case and awarded him compensation. In its reasoned grounds the court stated that as a result of the fact that the trial court had exceeded the permissible length of time between the hearings of 26 March 2001 and 6 June 2001, the proceedings had to be conducted anew. On 27 December 2005 the Gdansk Regional Court sentenced the applicant to 15 years’ imprisonment. The applicant expressed his intention to lodge an appeal. The reasoned grounds for this judgment are being drawn up. It is not yet clear whether the applicant will appeal the sentence. We are happy to clarify this.

It also finds that it is in the public interest in protecting the cultural heritage of the neighbourhood that the application be rejected. 10 February 1999 to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Skåne. The applicant obtained extensions of time-limits for filing his written submissions in April and May 1999, and in September he asked the court to give priority to the case. In November 2000 the applicant appealed against both judgments to the Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten), in Gothenburg. The Supreme Administrative Court refused the applicant leave to appeal in both cases on 15 September 2004. In separate proceedings in 1997, the applicant requested for a declaratory judgment establishing liability in the case of the building permit. The applicant asked the District Court (tingsrätten) of Lund to declare that the Municipality of Lund was liable to pay him compensation. The Municipality denied responsibility. The District Court found that the Building Committee had disregarded a clear and unambiguous provision in the 1987 Act, i.e. Chapter 8 section 34, which stated that a tentative approval was binding if an application for a building permit was made within two years from the date on which it was granted. The Court considered that the building committee’s handling of the case had involved such fault and neglect in its exercise of public authority that the municipality was liable. The applicant sought compensation in an amount of SEK 3,000,000 for the damage he had suffered due to the refusal to grant him the building permit. The District Court of Lund noted that the proceedings relating to the permit were still pending and that it was improbable that he would be granted such a permit. Even if he were to be granted a permit, the decision would most likely be quashed on appeal. The Court of Appeal upheld the District Court’s judgment of 4 March 2003. The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Supreme Court, which on 23 May 2005 refused the applicant leave to appeal. It found that the applicant had not been able to demonstrate that the consideration of his application for a tentative approval by the Municipality of Lund, while blameworthy, had led to his being denied a definite right to divide and build a new house.

name: Stephen Arthur Perry
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that the police covertly videotaped him for identification purposes and used the material in the prosecution against him. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 26 September 2002, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Court decided that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The case was decided in favour of the applicant and the application was dismissed. An important part of the prosecution's case rested almost entirely on the ability of the witnesses to visually identify the perpetrator. Given the applicant's failure to attend the arranged identification parades, the police decided to arrange a video identification parade. Permission to covertly video the applicant for identification purposes was sought from the Deputy Chief Constable for the West Midlands Police Force. A compilation tape was prepared in which eleven volunteers imitated the actions of the applicant as captured on the covert video. This video was shown to various witnesses of the armed robberies, of whom two positively identified the applicant. The applicant was acquitted of all charges against him on 1 August 1997. The applicant's trial commenced in January 1999. Neither the applicant nor his solicitor were informed that a tape had been made or used for identification parade purposes or given an opportunity to view it prior to its use. The judge concluded that there had been no unfairness arising from the use of the video. Eleven persons had been filmed for comparison purposes rather than the required eight and were all within comparative height, age and appearance. Even though the applicant's solicitor was not present to verify the procedures adopted when the witnesses were shown the videos, the entire process had been recorded on video. This had been shown to the court which had the opportunity of seeing exactly how the entire video identification process was operated. TheJudge ruled that the evidence was therefore admissible. Jury convicted applicant of three counts of robbery and acquitted him of two others. He was sentenced to five years' imprisonment. He applied for leave to appeal against conviction. Leave was granted by a single judge of the Court of Appeal. House of Lords rejected his appeal on 14 April 2000. Claimed that they were informed on 7 July 2000 that the trial judge had erred in not excluding the evidence obtained as a result of the covert identification video. Jury were also made aware of the complaints about the honesty and fairness of his treatment by the police and the alleged breaches of the code of practice relating to identification parades. The jury were told that if it was not a fair test they should not give much weight to the identifications.

The applicant complained that the police covertly videotaped him for identification purposes and used the material in the prosecution against him. The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine) The case was heard by a Chamber that would consider the case. An important part of the prosecution's case rested almost entirely on the ability of the witnesses to visually identify the perpetrator. Given the failure of the applicant to attend the arranged identification parades, the police decided to arrange a video identification parade. Permission to covertly video the applicant for identification purposes was sought from the Deputy Chief Constable for the West Midlands Police Force under the Home Office Guidelines on the Use of Equipment in Police Surveillance Operations 1984. This video was shown to various witnesses of the armed robberies, of whom two positively identified the applicant as the robber. The applicant was acquitted on this count on 1 August 1997 and later acquitted on the other counts. The trial lasted 17 days, the applicant and 31 witnesses giving live evidence. Neither the applicant nor his solicitor were informed that a tape had been made or used for identification parade purposes or given an opportunity to view it prior to its use. The judge concluded that there had been no unfairness arising from the use of the video. Eleven persons had been filmed for comparison purposes rather than the required eight and were all within comparative height, age and appearance. Even though the applicant's solicitor was not present to verify the procedures adopted when the witnesses were shown the videos, the entire process had been recorded on video and this had been shown to the court. The jury convicted the applicant of three counts of robbery and acquitted him of two others. The judge sentenced him to five years' imprisonment. The applicant applied for leave to appeal against conviction. Leave was granted by a single judge of the Court of Appeal. On 14 April 2000, the House of Lords rejected the appeal. The appeal was not heard again until 2 July 2000. The case was settled at the High Court in London on 17 March 2001. The trial judge ruled that the evidence was admissible and that the jury had been directed to give the evidence little or no weight if it was in any way unfair. The jury was also made aware of the complaints about the honesty and fairness of his treatment by police.

The Court declared the application partly admissible on 26 September 2002. The case was heard by a Chamber that would consider the case under Article 27 of the Convention. The applicant was arrested on 1 August 1997 and later acquitted on this count. An important part of the prosecution's case rested almost entirely on the ability of the witnesses to visually identify the perpetrator. Given the failure of the applicant to attend the arranged identification parades, the police decided to arrange a video identification parade. Permission to covertly video the applicant for identification purposes was sought from the Deputy Chief Constable for the West Midlands Police Force under the Home Office Guidelines on the Use of Equipment in Police Surveillance Operations 1984. This video was shown to various witnesses of the armed robberies, of whom two positively identified the applicant as the alleged robber. Neither the applicant nor his solicitor were informed that a tape had been made or used for identification parade purposes or given an opportunity to view it prior to its use. The judge concluded that there had been no unfairness arising from the use of the video. Eleven persons had been filmed for comparison purposes rather than the required eight and were all within comparative height, age and appearance. Even though the applicant's solicitor was not present to verify the procedures adopted when the witnesses were shown the videos, the entire process had been recorded on video and this had been shown to the court which had the opportunity of seeing exactly how the entire video identification process had be operated. Jury convicted him of three counts of robbery and acquitted him of two others. The judge sentenced him to five years' imprisonment. The applicant applied for leave to appeal against conviction, inter alia, alleging that the trial judge had erred in not excluding the evidence obtained as a result of the covert identification video. Leave was granted by a single judge of the Court of Appeal. On 14 April 2000, the House of Lords rejected the application. The solicitors claimed that they were informed on 7 July 2000. The appeal was rejected on 3 April 2000. And the case was thrown out of court on 13 March 2001. The trial judge ruled that the evidence was admissible and that the jury had been directed to give the evidence little or no weight if it was unfair.

On the same date the President of Chamber III of the Supreme court informed the Detention Centre that a session on prolongation of the applicant's detention had been scheduled for 1 October 1999. On 27 September 2000 the Gdansk Court of Appeal granted the application. The applicant was arrested by the police in connection with criminal proceedings pending against him. The trial court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment. On 17 June 2003 the Gdansk Court of Appeal allowed the appeals and quashed the impugned judgment. The case was remitted to the Bydgoszcz Regional Court which, on 14 January 2004, stayed the proceedings because the other set of criminal proceedings before the Zielona Góra Regional Court were pending and the applicant could not be transported. name: Peter Maxwell
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 12 July 1993 by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and on 3 August 1993 by. the Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (“the Government’), within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 3 (c) (Art. 6-3-c). Peter Maxwell, a British citizen born in 1944, was found guilty of assault in 1990. He was sentenced to five years' imprisonment. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 18 April 1994. The Court heard addresses by Mr Loucaides and Lord Rodger as well as replies to its questions. The applicant received the Government’s memorial on 10 January 1994 and lodged written observations in reply to it on 23 February 1994. On 15 April 1994 the Secretary to the Commission informed the Registrar that the Delegate would not submit written observations. The application was heard by the President of the Chamber, Mr Ryssdal, acting through the Registrar. The applicant lodged with the court a note of appeal setting out grounds which he formulated himself. The grounds of appeal can be summarised as follows: (a) the applicant had not been able to substantiate his contention that a crucial witness was giving false evidence against him because to do so would have involved revealing to the jury a previous conviction; (b) a number of witnesses had not be called by the Crown or by the Defence; (c) crucial evidence had been entirely fabricated; (d) the verdict of the jury was not supported by the evidence; (e) his legal advisers had disregarded instructions which he had given them and had not defended him in accordance with his instructions. Mr Maxwell's solicitors advised him that he should abandon his appeal but he chose not to accept their advice. The applicant decided to proceed with his appeal personally. On 21 March 1991, the applicant addressed the High Court of Justiciary on his grounds of appeal. The Crown was represented by counsel but there is no indication that he intervened at the hearing. Presiding over the three-judge bench was the Lord Justice Clerk, one of the two most senior judges in Scotland. On the same date the court dismissed the appeal. In his judgment the Lord justice Clerk noted that detailed grounds of Appeal had been put forward and that the applicant had addressed the court at some length upon those grounds. He was satisfied that they had no substance and that there had been no miscarriage of justice.

name: Morten Sørensen
train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained that the existence of closed-shop agreements in Denmark in their respective areas of employment had violated their right to freedom of association. The applications were allocated to the First Section of the Court. In a decision of 25 November 2004, a Chamber constituted within the First section relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber, none of the parties having objected (Article 30 of the Agreement and Rule 72). The Grand Chamber was fixed in accordance with Article 27 §§ 2 and 3 of the convention and Rule 24. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 June 2005. The Court heard addresses by Mr Lego Andersen and Mr Taksøe-Jensen, as well as their replies to questions from judges. The first applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Århus, Denmark. He applied for a job as a holiday relief worker in a company, FDB Distributionen (‘FDB’). In a letter of 20 May 1996, the applicant was offered the job from 3 June until 10 August 1996 and informed that his terms of employment would be regulated by an agreement concluded between FDB and a trade union called SID. At the time of his appointment he had applied for membership. The applicant did not want to pay the subscription to SID because he had been told that, as a holiday relief employee, he would not be given full membership of SID. He alleged that section 2(2) of the Protection against Dismissal due to Association Membership Act of 9 June 1982 (Lov om beskyttelse mod afskedigelse på grund af foreningsforhold) violated Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights. On 18 November 1998 the High Court found for FDB, stating as follows: “The High Court finds it established that the applicant was aware that membership of the SID was a condition for his employment in the company” On appeal, the Supreme Court (Højesteret) upheld the High Court's judgment on 8 June 1999. A decision abolishing or limiting the existing possibility of entering into closed-shop agreements will have far-reaching consequences for the Danish labour market. The second applicant was born in 1959 and lives in Haderslev, Denmark. He is a gardener by profession. He became a citizen of Denmark in 1997. In his application, he said that the domestic courts should disregard section 2(2) of the Protection against Dismissal due to Association Membership Act. The starting-point must be taken from the Act of 1992 incorporating the European Convention on Human Rights. He became a member of SID in the mid-1980s, but resigned his membership after a few years as he felt unable to support its political affiliations. He then rejoined SID, although he still did not agree with its political views. In 1999 he was offered a job at a nursery on condition he joined SID as the employer had entered into a closed-shop agreement with that trade union. The applicant commenced the job on 17 May 1999 and rejoined the union. He resigned from SID on 31 May 1999, but re-joined the union in 2004. He died on 17 July 2006. He is survived by his wife, two children and two grandchildren.

His terms of employment would be regulated by an agreement concluded between FDB and a trade union called SID, which was affiliated to LO, and of which the applicant was obliged to become a member. From his first payslip on 20 June 1996 the applicant became aware that he was paying a subscription to SID. Instead, at the time of his appointment he had applied for membership. Denmark's Free Trade Union (Danmarks Frie Fagforening) was the subject of the case. The applicant did not want to pay the subscription to SID because he had been told that, as a holiday relief employee, he would not be given full membership of SID. He alleged that section 2(2) of the Protection against Dismissal due to Association Membership Act of 9 June 1982 violated Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights. On 18 November 1998 the High Court found for FDB, stating as follows: “The High Court finds it established that the applicant was aware that membership was a condition for his employment in the company” The High Court upheld the Supreme Court's judgment on 8 June 1999. The starting-point must be taken from the Act of 1992 incorporating the European Convention on Human Rights. A decision abolishing or limiting the existing possibility of entering into closed-shop agreements will have far-reaching consequences for the Danish labour market. The second applicant was born in 1959 and lives in Haderslev, Denmark. He is a gardener by profession. He became the applicant in the case against Danish rail operator Danish Rail. The case is still under appeal. It is expected that the appeal will be heard by the Danish Supreme Court in the next few months. A former member of the Christian Trade Union (Kristelig Fagforening I/S) joined SID in the mid-1980s. He resigned his membership after a few years as he felt unable to support its political affiliations. After being unemployed for a while, he was offered a job at a nursery on condition that he became a member of SID. The applicant commenced the job on 17 May 1999 and rejoined SID, although he still did not agree with its political views. He died in November 2006, aged 82. He is survived by his wife, four children and a daughter-in-law.
eval_texts: Case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained that the existence of closed-shop agreements in Denmark in their respective areas of employment had violated their right to freedom of association. The applications were allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) by decisions of 20 March 2003, the applications were declared partly admissible. In a decision of 25 November 2004, a Chamber constituted within the First. Section relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber, none of the parties having objected (Article 30 of the. Convention and Rule 72). A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 June 2005. The Court heard addresses by Mr Lego Andersen and Mr Taksøe-Jensen, as well as their replies to questions from judges. The first applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Århus, Denmark. He applied for a job as a holiday relief worker in a company, FDB Distributionen (‘FDB’). The applicant was offered the job from 3 June until 10 August 1996 and informed that his terms of employment would be regulated by an agreement concluded between FDB and a trade union called SID. The applicant was dismissed for not satisfying the requirements for obtaining the job as he was not a member of a trade union affiliated to LO. The applicant, represented by Denmark's Free Trade Union, instituted proceedings before the High Court of Western Denmark (Vestre Landsret) against FDB. The High Court found for FDB, stating as follows: “The High Court finds it established that the applicant was aware that membership of SID was a condition for his employment in the company. Thus, since the applicant did not comply with this requirement the conditions for dismissing him are fulfilled in accordance with section 2, subsection (2), in conjunction with subsection (1)” On appeal, the Supreme Court (Højesteret) upheld the High Court's judgment on 8 June 1999. In its reasoning the Supreme court stated as follows: “The Protection against Dismissal due to Association Membership Act (Law no. 285 of 9 June 1982) was passed notably in order to comply with the negative right to freedom of association” The second applicant was born in 1959 and lives in Haderslev, Denmark. He is a gardener by profession. He became a plaintiff in the case against the Danish government. He argued that section 2(2) of the Protection against dismissed was at variance with Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant was a member of SID in the mid-1980s, but resigned his membership after a few years as he felt unable to support its political affiliations. The applicant commenced the job on 17 May 1999 and rejoined SID, although he still did not agree with its political views. He later joined the Christian Trade Union (Kristelig Fagforeningning I/S), but continued to belong to SID until his death in 1999. He was killed on 18 May 1999 in a car crash in the city of Stuttgart, Germany. He died of a suspected heart attack on 25 May 1999.

name: Roy H.W. Johnston
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 9697/82) against Ireland lodged with the Commission in 1982 under Article 25 (art. 25) by Roy H.W. Johnston, an Irish citizen, Janice Williams-Johnston, a British citizen, and Nessa Williams- Johnston, their daughter. The request sought a decision from the Court as to the existence of violations of Articles 8, 9, 12 and 13. The Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, having been informed by the Registrar of their right to intervene, did not indicate any intention of so doing. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr B. Walsh, the elected judge of Irish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. On 24 January 1986, the Chamber decided under Rule 50 to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. oral proceedings should open on 23 June 1986. The hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 and 24 June 1986, Immediately before they opened, the Court had held a preparatory meeting. The Court heard addresses by Mr. Gleeson and Mr. O’Reilly for the Government, by Mr Gaukur Jörundsson for the Commission and by Senator M. Robinson and Dr. Duncan for the applicants. It also heard replies to questions put to the applicants’ representatives. Roy H.W. Johnston married a Miss M in 1952 in a Church of Ireland ceremony. Three children were born of this marriage, in 1956, 1959 and 1965. The first applicant is unable to obtain, in Ireland, a dissolution of his marriage to enable him to marry the second applicant. He has taken the following steps to regularise his relationship with her and with his wife and to make proper provision for his dependents. The matter has therefore not been pursued in England. (b) On 19 September 1982, he concluded a formal separation agreement with his. wife, Nessa Doreen Williams-Johnston. He consented to his name being included in the Register of Births as the father. The third applicant has, under Irish law, the legal situation of an illegitimate child. Her parents are concerned at the lack of any means by which she can, even with their consent, be recognised as their child. They are also concerned about the possibility of a stigma attaching to her by virtue of her legal situation. She has adopted the first applicant’s surname, which she uses amongst friends and neighbours, but for business purposes continues to use the name Williams. According to her, she has felt inhibited about telling employers of her domestic circumstances. She would like to become an Irish citizen by naturalisation, but has been reluctant to make an application, not wishing to put those circumstances in issue. She received a lump-sum of IR£8,800 and provision was made for maintenance of the remaining dependent child of the marriage.

name: Mehmet Pehlivan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4233/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the applicant’s right to be released pending trial, to a fair hearing within a reasonable time and to be informed promptly of the nature and cause of the accusations against him. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of affiliation to the PKK (the Kurdistan Workers’ Party), an illegal organisation, and of having committed homicide. On 4 September 2007 the Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was charged under Article 125 of the former Criminal Code, and with killing B.C. in 1992. The applicant made statements before the first-instance court, denying the charges against him. The court subsequently postponed the hearings until 24 December 1998 on account of the failure of the gendarmerie command to submit the relevant information. On 22 November 1999 the First Division of the Diyarbakır State Security Court ordered the applicant’s continued detention on remand in view of the nature of the offence, the state of evidence and the content of the case file. The judge said that there were strong indications that he had committed the offence defined in Article 125. The applicant was convicted under Article 448 of the Criminal Code of homicide and sentenced to 15 years’ imprisonment. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of 26 March 2002 because the applicant had been unable to examine three witnesses against him during the trial. The case was subsequently remitted to the First Division of the Diyarbakır State Security Court. The court found no convincing evidence that the offence committed by the applicant was linked to terrorist activities. The applicant was released from prison in view of the length of his detention during judicial proceedings. He was sentenced to a further 15 years' imprisonment on 14 July 2003.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4233/03) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the applicant’s right to be released pending trial, to a fair hearing within a reasonable time and to be informed promptly of the nature and cause of the accusations against him. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Pehlivan, a lawyer practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 25 April 1996 the applicant was brought before the Diyarbakır public prosecutor, where he alleged that he was not involved in the activities of the PKK. The applicant further contended that in 1992 he had killed B.C. in his village as he had suspected that his partner had had a relationship with him. The statements that he had made at the gendarmerie command were read to him. Furthermore the statements of three other suspects, Ş.B., S.B. and Ţ.C., who maintained that the. applicant was a member of the Kurdistan Workers' Party, were also read to the applicant. The judge remanded the applicant in custody, holding that there were strong indications he had committed the offence. The applicant was convicted under Article 448 of the Criminal Code of homicide and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. The court found no convincing evidence that the offence committed by the applicant was linked to terrorist activities. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of 26 March 2002 because the applicant had been unable to examine three witnesses against him during the trial. The case was subsequently remitted to the First Division of the Diyarbakır State Security Court. On 14 July 2003 the first-instance court convicted the applicant once more of homicide. The applicant was sentenced to 15 years' imprisonment. On 8 April 2004 the Court ofCassation upheld this judgment.

name: Jens Olaf Jersild
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 9 September 1993 by the European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 15890/89) against Denmark lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Danish national on 25 July 1989. The object of the request and of the Government’s application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10 (Art. 10) of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr I. Foighel, the elected judge of Danish nationality, and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President. On 23 February 1994 the President of the Chamber granted leave to Human Rights Watch, a New York based non-governmental human rights organisation, to submit observations on specific aspects of the case. The latter’s comments were filed on 23 March. On 23 February the Chamber had authorised (Rule 41 para. 1) the applicant to show the video-recording of the television programme in issue in his case to the judges taking part in the proceedings. A showing was held shortly before the hearing on 20 April. On various dates between 22 March and 15 April 1994 the Commission produced a number of documents and two video-cassettes. The applicant submitted further details on his claims under Article 50 (art. 50) of the Convention. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 April 1994. There appeared before the Court: Mr T. Lehmann, Ambassador, Legal Adviser, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Agent, Mr M.B. Elmer, Deputy Permanent Secretary, Chief Legal Adviser,. Ministry of Justice, Ms J. Rechnagel, Minister Counsellor. Mr Jens Olaf Jersild, a Danish national, is a journalist and lives in Copenhagen. He was at the time of the events giving rise to the present case, and still is, employed by Danmarks Radio (Danish Broadcasting Corporation), assigned to its Sunday News Magazine (Søndagsavisen) Interview was broadcast by Danmarks Radio on 21 July 1985. Interview lasted between five and six hours, of which between two and two and a half hours were video-recorded. The applicant subsequently edited and cut the film of the interview down to a few minutes. The transcript of the Greenjackets item reads as follows: ‘It’s good being a racist. We believe Denmark is for the Danes.’ ‘The flag on the wall is the flag of the Southern States from the American Civil War, but today it is also the symbol of racism’. ‘I just ran into a petrol station with a ... gun and made them give me some money. Then I ran out again. That's all’ There are 20-25 young people from STUDSEN in the same group. They meet not far away from the public housing area near some old houses which are to be torn down. The group meet here to reaffirm among other things their racism, their hatred of immigrants and their support for the Ku Klux Klan. A nigger is not a human being, it’s an ape. People should be allowed to keep slaves, I think so anyway. You can also see that from their body structure, man, big flat noses, with cauliflower ears etc., man. Broad heads and very broad bodies,. man, hairy, you are looking at a gorilla and compare it with an ape, man. Henrik is one of the strongest supporters of the Klan. He hates the foreign workers, ‘Perkere’ [a very derogatory word in Danish for immigrant workers]. ‘They come up here, man, and sponge on our society,’ he says. ‘We don’t like their mentality - I mean they can damn well, I mean ... what’s it called ... I mean if they feel like speaking Russian in their homes, right, then it's okay, but what we don't like is when they walk around in those Zimbabwe-clothes and then speak this hula-hula language in the street’ Per Axholt, known as ‘Pax’ [(P)], is employed in the youth centre in Studsgårdsgade. He has worked there for several years, but many give up a lot sooner because of the tough environment. He feels that the reasons why the young people are persecuting the immigrants is that they are themselves powerless and disappointed. What do you think they would say that they want, if you asked them? (P) Just what you and I want. Some control over their lives, work which may be considered decent and which they like, a reasonable economic situation, a reasonably functioning family, a wife or a husband and some children. Gentleman tells how he has been involved in crime since the age of 14. He says he has had a criminal career but doesn't know if it can be called a career. He explains why people are involved in criminal activities as they have nothing better to do. "If people want to be out here and have a nice time and be racists and drink beer, and have fun, then it’s quite obvious you don’t want to sit in the slammer," he says. "It’'s not prison, that doesn't frighten people. If you really get into the joint it would be such a ridiculously large place" G: "Last time we caused some trouble over at the pub, they let us out the next day. Nothing really comes of it. It doesn’t discourage us, but there were five of us, who just came out and then we had a celebration for the last guy, who came out yesterday" The Bishop of Ålborg complained to the Minister of Justice. The Public Prosecutor instituted criminal proceedings in the City Court of Copenhagen (Københavns Byret) against the three youths interviewed by the applicant. They were charged with a violation of Article 266 (b) of the Penal Code (straffeloven) “A nigger is not a human being, it’s an animal, that goes for all the other foreign workers as well, Turks, Yugoslavs and whatever they are called.“ “Half of the prison population in ‘Vestre’ are in there because of drugs ... they are the people who are serving time for dealing drugs ...” “What we don’t like is when they walk around in those Zimbabwe-clothes and then speak this hula-hula language in the street ...“ The applicant was charged, under Article 266 (b) in conjunction with Article 23, with aiding and abetting the three youths; the same charge was brought against the head of the news section of Danmarks Radio, Mr Lasse Jensen. Three youths were convicted of making racist statements on a television programme. The applicant was convicted of aiding and abetting them, as was Mr Jensen, in his capacity as programme controller. They were sentenced to pay day-fines (dagsbøder) totalling 1,000 and 2,000 Danish kroner, respectively, or alternatively to five days’ imprisonment (hæfte) The applicant and Mr Jensen appealed against the City Court’s judgment to the High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret) The application was dismissed on the grounds that there had been no consistent prosecution policy in the case. The High Court, by five votes to one, dismissed the appeal. The Supreme Court (Højesteret), which by four votes toOne dismissed the Appeal in a judgment of 13 February 1989. The majority held: “The defendants have caused the publication of the racist statements made by a narrow circle of persons and thereby made those persons liable to punishment’ The dissent said the programme had a fair degree of news and information value. Although it concerned a relatively small group of people holding extreme views, the programme was to contribute to information on an issue which was the subject of extensive and sometimes emotional public debate. The fact that the defendants took the initiative to disseminate such views is not of paramount importance for the assessment of their conduct. The majority had attached importance to the fact that the applicant and Mr Jensen had caused the racist statements to be made public. The statements would hardly have been punishable under Article 266 (b) of the Penal Code had they not been made to a wide circle (“videre kreds“) of people. It was therefore beyond doubt that they had aided and abetted the dissemination of the statements. Their news or information value was not such as to justify their dissemination and therefore did not warrant acquitting the defendants. This did not mean that extremist views could not be reported in the press, but such reports must be carried out in a more balanced and comprehensive manner than was the case in the television programme. Justice Hermann noted that the compatibility of the impugned measures with Article 10 (art. 10) of the Convention was not raised during the trial. The minority, on the other hand, considered that the right to information overrode the interests protected by Article 266 (b) The minority also thought that the. also be permitted. Also, Justice Hermann said that the protection of the rights to information and to freedom of expression should be protected. Also noted that, according to Article 10 of the convention, the. right to know should also be protected by the same rules as the right of the public to be informed, and that the access to information should not be a violation of these rights.

The case originated in an application (no. 15890/89) against Denmark lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Danish national, Mr Jens Olaf Jersild, on 25 July 1989. The object of the request and of the Government’s application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr I. Foighel, the elected judge of Danish nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. As President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 5), Mr Ryssdal, acting through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Government, the applicant’s lawyers and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and 38). Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the. the Registrar received the Government's memorial on 18 February 1994 and the applicant's memorial. on 20 February. On 23 February 1994 the Chamber had also decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of a Grand Chamber. The names of the additional nine judges were drawn by lot by the President in the presence of the Registrar on 24 February (Rule 51 para. 2 (a) to (c)), namely Mr F. Gölcüklü, Mr C. Russo, Mr A. Spielmann, Mr N. Valticos, Mr S. Martens, Mr J.M. Morenilla, Mr L. Wildhaber and Mr B. Repik. The court heard evidence from Mr Jens Olaf Jersild, a Danish national. The hearing was held in Strasbourg on 20 April 1994. The Greenjackets were a group of young people who called themselves “the Greenjacket’s” The application was brought by a Danish journalist who was employed by Danmarks Radio at the time. The newspaper Information had published an article describing the racist attitudes of members of the group. The editors of the Sunday News Magazine decided to produce a documentary on the GreenJackets. During the interview, which was conducted by the applicant, the three Green Jackets were asked to give their side of the story. The Greenjackets made derogatory remarks about immigrants and ethnic groups in Denmark. The documentary was about a group of young people, calling themselves “the Greenjacket’s” (“grønjakkerne’) Interview with an extremist group in Copenhagen. They made abusive and derogatory remarks about immigrants and ethnic groups in Denmark. "I mean, for instance fights and stabbings and smashing up things ... If you really get into the joint it would be such a ridiculously crazy place," she adds. I just wouldn’t accept it, if she was mugging old women and stealing their handbags" "Just take a picture of a gorilla, man, and then look at a nigger, it’s. it's a nigger" "They are not human beings, they are animals.“ “A nigger is not a human being, it’s an animal, that goes for all the other foreign workers as well, Turks, Yugoslavs and whatever they are called.“ “They are in there, all the ‘Perkere’, because of drugs ...” “What we don’t like is when they walk around in those Zimbabwe-clothes and then speak this hula-hula language in the street ...’’ “It was by no means the intention of Danmarks Radio to persuade others to subscribe to the same views as the Greenjackets.” The applicant was convicted of aiding and abetting the Greenjackets. The applicant had himself taken the initiative of making the television programme. He had been well aware in advance that discriminatory statements of a racist nature were likely to be made during the interview. The interview had lasted several hours, during which beer, partly paid for by Danmarks Radio, was consumed. The statements were broadcast without any counterbalancing comments, after the recordings had been edited by the applicant. He was accordingly found guilty of aiding the violation of Article 266 (b) of the Penal Code. The High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret) upheld the conviction. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1799/07) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) The applicant alleged that his conviction for insult had been in breach of his right to freedom of expression. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz, succeeded by Ms J. Chrzanowska, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was represented by Ms K. Zakrzewska, a lawyer practising in Radomsko. Quail breeding and mushroom growing will not solve the unemployment problem in the villages of Radomsko, writes the author. ‘I will continue calling the actions of dim-witted officials and their dull bosses pretentious and populist, and no numbskull will convince me that I am wrong,’ the author says. The article was published in a local newspaper, and the author was accused of defamation by the district's mayor and his spokesperson of using words such as ‘numbskull’, ‘dull boss’ and ‘poser’ The case was eventually dismissed, but not before the application was brought before the Radomska District Court, where the judge found the author guilty. The court held that the use of the words “numbskull”, “poser” and “dim‑witted official” in respect of K.H., had amounted to insult (zniewaga) committed through the mass media. The court convicted the applicant under that provision and ordered him to pay a fine of PLN 10,000 (approximately 2,630 euros (EUR) The court also ordered the applicant to reimburse the private prosecutors’ costs (PLN 900, approximately EUR 236) and the costs of the State Treasury (PLn 1,000, approximately Euro 263) The trial court rejected the applicant’s argument that the impugned article had been a simple weekly column in which any similarity to actual persons had been purely coincidental. It found that the article in issue had been part of a campaign carried out by the newspaper against the private prosecutors. The trial court noted that a journalist had the right to criticise the actions of public officials, but was not entitled to use media in a manipulative way to wage private wars. The latter behaviour was not only unethical and unprofessional, but also incompatible with the role of the media, which was to serve the State and society.“The fair criticism and objective coverage, free from personal emotions, which is desired in journalism, gave way to the private interest of the defendant, pursued through expressions which, in common understanding, remain offensive and disrespectful,” the court said. Maciej Ziembiński was found guilty of insulting district officials in a newspaper article. The court found that the impugned words had the effect of lowering the private prosecutors in public esteem. The judge imposed a fine of PLN 10,000, which it considered proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of the applicant’s guilt. The trial court noted that the present case involved a conflict between constitutionally guaranteed freedom of speech and the right of each citizen to have his reputation protected. However, it found that. the acts had constituted a blatant abuse of free speech and professional ethics and that a fine would be the most appropriate penalty. The applicant appealed. He contested the factual findings of the first‑instance court. He argued that the impugned article had presented in a sarcastic light people who achieved personal gain by pretending to work. The Regional Court held that the lower court had correctly established the facts of the case. It endorsed the trial court’s findings that the words used in the article had been insulting and harmful to the private prosecutors’ dignity. It ordered the applicant to pay PLN 1,000 (approx. EUR 256) in respect of the costs of the appeal proceedings. The judgment was served on the applicant on 29 May 2006.

Case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Polish national Maciej Ziembiński alleged that his conviction for insult had been in breach of his right to freedom of expression. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz, succeeded by Ms J. Chrzanowska, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. In issue no. 33 of 18 August 2004 the applicant published an article entitled “Elegantly wrapped dung” (“Łajno – elegancko opakowane”). It read: “A poser is someone who does everything to produce external effects by his conduct, speech and, in particular, with the populism he preaches”. Radomsko District's mayor and two other officials accused of defamation. They accused the author of using words such as ‘numbskull’, ‘dull boss’ and ‘dim-witted official’ They also accused him of being a ‘poser’ who ‘sells his dull bosses dung nicely wrapped in words.’ The article has since been removed from the internet and replaced with an image of the Radomsko district’s mayor and the head and spokesperson of the district”s marketing department. The article can be read here: http://www.dailymailonline.co.uk/news/article-284536/Radomska-District-officials-accused-of-defamation.html#storylink=cpy. The Radomsko District Court ruled that it did not have jurisdiction in the case, and transmitted the private bill of indictment to the Piotrków Trybunalski District Court. The trial court held two hearings. The court convicted the applicant under that provision and ordered him to pay a fine of PLN 10,000 (approximately 2,630 euros (EUR) The court further noted that, since March 2004, the applicant’s newspaper had been publishing articles which were critical of M.D., the mayor of the Radomska District, and his officials. In April 2004 the applicant had published an article in which he had made ironic remarks about K.H.'s initiative to develop quail farming in order to tackle the impoverishment of the local population. The trial court rejected the applicant’s argument that the impugned article had been a simple weekly column in which any similarity to actual persons had been purely coincidental. It found that the article in issue had been part of a campaign carried out by the newspaper against the private prosecutors. The trial court noted that a journalist had the right to criticise the actions of public officials, but was not entitled to use media in a manipulative way to wage private wars. The latter behaviour was not only unethical and unprofessional, but also incompatible with the role of the media, which was to serve the State and society. It is difficult not to agree with the position that the word “numbskull” (“palant”) in the analysed context, although its literal meaning is legally irrelevant. The court found no grounds to hold that the impugned words had the effect of lowering the private prosecutors in public esteem. The court imposed a fine of PLN 10,000, which it considered proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of the applicant’s guilt. By doing so in a newspaper, he fell within the scope of Article 216 § 2 of the Criminal Code, acting unlawfully, reprehensibly, and, in the absence of circumstances capable of precluding or mitigating his guilt, also culpably.“Dull” meaning not sharp, unintelligent, intellectually retarded. “poser”, “dim-witted official” and “dull boss’ are equally offensive. The Regional Court held that the lower court had correctly established the facts of the case. It endorsed the trial court’s findings that the words used in the article had been insulting and harmful to the private prosecutors’ dignity. It further held that, although fair criticism of public authorities and officials was socially desirable and legally accepted, the protection afforded by law did not extend to the use of insulting words which offended human dignity. The applicant was ordered to pay PLN 1,000 (approx. EUR 256) in respect of the costs of the appeal proceedings. The judgment was served on the applicant on 29 May 2006 and he appealed.

It is difficult not to agree with the position that the word “numbskull” (“palant”) in the analysed context, although its literal meaning is legally irrelevant, The court found no grounds to hold that the impugned words had the effect of lowering the private prosecutors in public esteem. The court found that, having regard to the circumstances of the case, it would be disproportionate to impose a prison sentence. It imposed a fine of PLN 10,000, which it considered proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of the applicant’s guilt.“Dull” meaning not sharp, unintelligent, intellectually retarded. “Dung” used in the title of the article has a cruder equivalent, and undoubtedly that equivalent was meant to describe K.H.’S contribution to the development of local entrepreneurship. The applicant appealed. He contested the factual findings of the first‑instance court. He argued that the impugned article had presented in a sarcastic light people who achieved personal gain by pretending to work. The applicant emphasised that criticism of the quail farm project as a solution to a decline in agriculture in the region had been entirely legitimate. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1799/07) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Maciej Ziembiński alleged that his conviction for insult had been in breach of his right to freedom of expression. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz, succeeded by Ms J. Chrzanowska, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was represented by Ms K. Zakrzewska, a lawyer practising in Radomsko. The Radomsko District in Poland is considering a scheme to breed quail eggs. The district's mayor and two other officials accused the author of defamation. The applicant called the officials 'dim-witted officials and their dull bosses pretentious and populist' The application was dismissed and the case is now pending in the court of appeal. The author says he will continue to call the actions of the district's officials 'pretentious' and 'populist' and says that no 'numbskull' or 'dull boss' will convince him that he is wrong. The application is still pending at the Court of Appeal of Appeal. The court held that the use of the words “numbskull”, “poser” and “dim‑witted official” had amounted to insult (zniewaga) committed through the mass media. The court convicted the applicant under that provision and ordered him to pay a fine of PLN 10,000 (approximately 2,630 euros (EUR) The court further noted that, since March 2004, the applicant’s newspaper had been publishing articles which were critical of M.D., the mayor of the Radomsko District, and his officials. In April 2004 the applicant had published an article in which he had made ironic remarks about K.H., the head of the marketing department. In June 2004 a journalist at the same newspaper had published a detailed article on the same subject. The trial court rejected the applicant’s argument that the impugned article had been a simple weekly column in which any similarity to actual persons had been purely coincidental. It found that the article in issue had been part of a campaign carried out by the newspaper against the private prosecutors. The trial court noted that a journalist had the right to criticise the actions of public officials, but was not entitled to use media in a manipulative way to wage private wars. The latter behaviour was not only unethical and unprofessional, but also incompatible with the role of the media, which was to serve the State and society. It is difficult not to agree with the position that the word “numbskull” (“palant”) in the analysed context, although its literal meaning is legally irrelevant. The court found no grounds to hold that the impugned words had the effect of lowering the private prosecutors in public esteem. It imposed a fine of PLN 10,000, which it considered proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of the applicant’s guilt. The trial court noted that the present case involved a conflict between constitutionally guaranteed freedom of speech and the right of each citizen to have his reputation protected. The court observed that his acts and motivation had been reprehensible, since he had been settling a private conflict with the officials and transgressing basic professional standards. By doing so in a newspaper, he fell within the scope of Article 216 § 2 of the Criminal Code. The Regional Court held that the lower court had correctly established the facts of the case. It endorsed the trial court’s findings that the words used in the article had been insulting and harmful to the private prosecutors’ dignity. It ordered the applicant to pay PLN 1,000 (approx. EUR 256) in respect of the costs of the appeal proceedings. The judge ruled that fair criticism of public authorities and officials was socially desirable and legally accepted. But the protection afforded by law did not extend to the use of insulting words which offended human dignity. The judgment was served on the applicant on 29 May 2006 and he appealed.

name: Wojciech Figiel
train_texts: The case stems from an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) by a Polish national, Mr Wojciech Figiel (“the applicant”), on 29 January 2005. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Government requested that the present application be joined to application no. 38190/05, which was lodged by the applicant (Figiel v Poland (no. 1) and which concerned the length of another and unrelated set of civil proceedings. On 6 May 2008 the President of the Chamber decided not to join the applications. The applicant made use of the complaint provided for by the 2004 Act. He sought a ruling declaring that the length of the proceedings before the Warsaw District Court had been excessive and that just satisfaction should be awarded to him. On 9 November 2004 the Warsaw Regional Court. gave a decision in which it acknowledged the excessive length of. the proceedings (36 months and 7 days of inactivity on the part of the Warsaw. Those proceedings lasted 5 years at one level of jurisdiction.

name: Bogusław Tekiela
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35785/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 19 February and 27 March 2007 hearings were held. On 23 May 2007 the court gave a judgment and allowed the applicant’s claim in part.

name: Jadwiga Marszał
train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 63391/00) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) Mrs Jadwiga Marszał (“the applicant”) was dismissed from her job in August 1994. On 21 November 2001 the Regional Court dismissed the defendant's appeal. On 5 December 2000 the Bytom District Court gave judgment. The court granted the applicant compensation and dismissed her claim for reinstatement. The judgment is final. The case is referred to as the Rozbark coal mine criminal case. The investigation was resumed on 2 July 2001. April 2001 the expert on management submitted his opinion to the Prosecutor. On 28 December 2001 the District Prosecutor submitted to the Bytom District Court a bill of indictment against the applicant and three other persons. In August 2003 the By tom District Court discontinued the criminal proceedings against the. applicant. The investigation was continued until 28 August 2003 when it was discontinued by the District Court of Bytom. The case was closed in October 2003 and the investigation was closed on 30 November 2003.
