name: Hüseyin Karataş
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court, as established under former Article 19 of the Convention, by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 17 March 1998. It originated in an application (no. 23168/94) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Commission underFormer Article 25. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (former Rule 30). The lawyer was given leave by the President of the Court at the time, Mr R. Bernhardt, to use the Turkish language in the written procedure (Former Rule 27 § 3) The Grand Chamber included ex officio Mr R. Türmen, the judge elected in respect of Turkey, the President of the Court, the Vice-Presidents of Sections and other members of the Grand Chamber. The Grand Chamber took the decision to exempt Mr Türman from sitting after his withdrawal from the case in the light of the decision in the case of Oğur v. Turkey. The Government notified the Registry that Mr F. Gölcüklü had been appointed ad hoc judge (Rule 29 § 1) and Mrs Botoucharova was appointed judge ad hoc. The decision was made in accordance with Rule 28 § 4 of the Rules of Court. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 5 March 1999, the case being heard simultaneously with that of Polat v Turkey. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr D. Tezcan, Mr M. Özmen, Co-Agents, Mr B. Çalışkan, Ms G. Akyüz, Ms A. Günyaktı, Mr F. Polat and Mrs Batmaz Keremoğlu. For the applicant Ms T. Tuncer, of the Istanbul Bar, Counsel and for the Commission Mr H. Danelius, Delegate. "Freedom is the law of the clan" is one of the poems in an anthology of the Kurds. "We will sacrifice our heads, drunk on the fire of rebellion" is another. "There is a rebellion in the mountains can we hear and do nothing? let the festivities and celebrations begin let flames as high as the rooftops reach for the sky" "We have been the close acquaintance of the most barbaric cruelties" is a poem written by a member of the Kurdish diaspora in the U.S. and published in the anthology "Kurdish Voices" It was written in response to a letter from a Turkish journalist to the editor of the magazine "This is the Voice of Kurdistan" Kurds have been under siege in our besieged land for thousands of years. We have hauled behind us a sword but never have we been conquered by the sword. The venerable Sheikh Alişer of Hasanan was brave enough to know how to die for his honour, his homeland and his freedom. ‘I invite you to freedom, to death in these mountains, in this sacred spring with death we march, freedom is blessed with death, I invites you to die’ ‘The young Kurd shall take vengeance’ when life leaves this body my heart shall not cry out What happiness to live this day to join the martyrs of Kurdistan.’ The National Security Court entirely accepted the submissions of the public prosecutor and found, inter alia, that the poems in issue referred to a particular region of Turkey as “Kurdistan’ Mr Karataş was sentenced to one year and eight months’ imprisonment and a fine of 41,666,666 Turkish liras (TRL), to be paid in ten monthly instalments. On an appeal by the applicant, the Court of Cassation upheld that decision on 1 December 1997. On 30 October 1995 Law no. 4126 of 27 October 1995 came into force, it reduced the length of prison sentences that could be imposed under section 8 of law no. 3713.

The case was referred to the Court, as established under former Article 19 of the Convention, by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 17 March 1998. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 10 and 6 § 1 of the convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (former Rule 30). The lawyer was given leave by the President of the Court at the time, Mr R. Bernhardt, to use the Turkish language in the written procedure. The Grand Chamber constituted for that purpose included ex officio Mr R. Türmen, the judge elected in respect of Turkey. Mr Wildhaber, the President of the Court, Mrs E. Palm, Vice-President, and Mr J.-P. Costa and Mr M. Fischbach were Vice-Presidents of Sections. The other members appointed to complete the Grand Chamber were Mr A. Pastor Ridruejo, Mr G. Bonello, Mr J. Makarczyk, Mr P. Kūris, Mrs F. Tulkens, Mrs V. Strážnická, Mr V. Butkevych, Mrs H.S. Greve and Mrs S. Botoucharova. Hüseyin Karataş is a Turk of Kurdish origin and was born in 1963. He lives in Istanbul and works as a psychologist. In November 1991 he published an anthology of poems in Istanbul entitled “The song of a rebellion – Dersim0” (“Dersim – Bir İsyanın Türküsü”). He requested, inter alia, application of section 8 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713 – see paragraph 18 below) and the confiscation of the copies of the work concerned (see paragraph 16 below) He relied on the following passages from the applicant’s work. ‘A great passion is taking shape in our holy hands – the light of ancient Kurdistan for as long as the Munzursuyu is not reddened by our blood we shall not let the whelps of the Ottoman whore trample upon it after all for thousands of years we have obeyed the law freedom is the law of the clan’ ‘On the head of Hızır[0], my brave one we have never seen nor heard anything like this I ask you, brother, what Scripture would accept such cruelty? … and now cruelty is spreading apace our blood will mix with the blood shed. resistance and betrayal freedom and surrender side by side’ ‘I invite you to freedom, to death in these mountains, in this sacred spring with death we march, freedom is blessed with death.’ ‘I am seventy-five years old I die a martyr I join the martyrs of Kurdistan Dersim has been defeated but Kurdism and Kurdistan shall live on the young Kurd shall take vengeance’ When life leaves this body my heart shall not cry out What happiness to live this day to join themartyrs of Kurdistan. … [Alişer is dead too] … we have lived for centuries without a State, in exile, during massacres for centuries along the paths we have hauled behind us a sword.” He was sentenced to one year and eight months’ imprisonment and a fine of 41,666,666 Turkish liras (TRL), to be paid in ten monthly instalments. The National Security Court entirely accepted the submissions of the public prosecutor and found, inter alia, that the poems in issue referred to a particular region of Turkey as ‘Kurdistan’ The expression of praise apparent throughout the work amounted to separatist propaganda that was detrimental to the unity of the Turkish nation and the territorial integrity of theTurkish State, the court said. On an appeal by the applicant, the Court of Cassation upheld that decision on 1 December 1997. Mr Karataş was at that time still serving his sentence in Ümraniye Prison.

Botoucharova. Mr Gölcüklü was appointed ad hoc judge. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 5 March 1999, the case being heard simultaneously with that of Polat v. Turkey. The Court heard addresses by Mr Danelius, Ms Tuncer, Mr Tezcan and Mr Özmen. The judge who was unable to take part in the further consideration of the case, was replaced by Mr K. Traja, substitute judge (Rule 24 § 5 (b)). The applicant and his publisher were accused of disseminating propaganda against the “indivisible unity of the State’. The prosecutor requested, inter alia, application of section 8 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713) “A great passion is taking shape in our holy hands – the light of ancient Kurdistan for as long as the Munzursuyu is not reddened by our blood we shall not let the whelps of the Ottoman whore trample upon it after all for thousands of years we have obeyed the law freedom is the law of the clan’s. The heart of Dersim is torn to pieces its serpentine streets explosions of dynamite the noise of excavators the soldiers’ boots … a phial of medicine in one hand of poison in the other the towers of Babel in others the Turks are coming with their schools” “In the corridors of Parliament in the galleries in the garrisons they are preparing genocide like those who know no bounds” ‘An unbounded anger in my heart a speechless hatred … the laws do not give way rebellion comes from the mountains’ ‘When life leaves this body my heart shall not cry out What happiness to live this day to join the martyrs of Kurdistan. … [Alişer is dead too] … we have lived for centuries without a State, in exile, during massacres for centuries along the paths we have hauled behind us a sword but never have we been conquered by the sword' ‘The venerable Sheikh Alişer of Hasanan[0] was brave enough to know how to die for his honour, his homeland and his freedom’ The National Security Court found that the poems in issue referred to a particular region of Turkey as ‘Kurdistan’ and had glorified the insurrectionary movements in that region. In the court’s view, the expression of praise apparent throughout the work amounted to separatist propaganda that was detrimental to the unity of the Turkish nation. Mr Karataş was sentenced to one year and eight months’ imprisonment and a fine of 41,666,666 Turkish liras (TRL), to be paid in ten monthly instalments. name: Hroar Anton Hansen
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 15319/09) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) The applicant was represented by Mr A.C. Ryssdal, a lawyer practising in Oslo. The Norwegian Government were represented by their Agent, Mr M. Emberland, Attorney, Attorney General’s Office (Civil Affairs) The application was communicated to the Government on 31 August 2011. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant sought an order that Ekheim Invest convey 50% of the property to him and that he held a pre-emption right with respect to the remaining 50%. The question was how to interpret the former spouses’ joint ownership agreement of 3 November 1995. According to legal doctrine, such a contract was not dependent on any condition as to form. The applicant further submitted that in its 2001 judgment. the City Court had not reviewed the validity of the joint ownership. agreement. The legal force of that judgment extended only to the relationship. between Mrs B. and the applicant, not between Ekheim. Invest and the. applicant. In the period since 2001 the estate had increased so greatly in value that the City. Court now had to assess the ownership issue independently of the conclusion reached in the 2001. judgment. The applicant appealed against the City Court’s judgment of 21 January 2008 to the Borgarting High Court. The High Court refused to admit the appeal (‘Anken nektes fremmet’) on 12 June 2008. The applicant appealed the decision to the Supreme Court, who rejected the appeal. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that the applicant did not have title to the property in question as the respondent company had derived its rights from Mrs B. and had ruled in her favour in its 2001 judgment. It would be unreasonable if Mrs B or her successors should be able to profit from the tremendous increase in the property's value. The 2005 Code of Civil Procedure (Tvisteloven) entered into force on 1 January 2008. The conditions for the High Court granting leave to appeal and for refusing the admission of an appeal (“Krav til samtykke Nektelse”) were set out in Article 29-13. An appeal against a City Court judgment could not be admitted if the value of the subject-matter was less than NOK 125,000 (approximately EUR 15,000) The provision did not come into play in the instant case, where the appeal related to pecuniary interests ( approximately EUR 1,780,000), exceeding by far that minimum threshold. Unless an appeal had been decided under Articles 29-12 or 29-13, the proceedings were to continue, according to Article 29-14. The type of decision (beslutning) at issue in the present case was not mentioned. The committee submitting draft statutory provisions recognised that there was a need to stop clearly unmeritorious appeals to the High Court in order to avoid additional considerable costs being incurred by the parties and by the judiciary. The Ministry of Justice observed that, whilst the right to appellate review of a decision on the merits was an important safeguard, an unlimited and extensive right in this respect could be counterproductive to the rule of law. The High Court's role in appeal proceedings in a civil case was not to examine the case afresh but to review the first-instance court’s decision that formed the subject of the appeal. It was sufficient that the High Court found it clear that the outcome would be upheld, possibly on a different reasoning than that given by the City Court (Ot.prp. nr. 51 (2004‑2005), p. 475). It was moreover a condition in Article 29-13 (5) that the three judges taking part in the decision to refuse admission unanimously found that the appeal would not succeed (ibid., p. 476). The Norwegian Supreme Court held that every High Court decision refusing admission of an appeal under the Code of Criminal Procedure ought to be reasoned. It concluded that from Article 14 § 5 of the Covenant it followed that every high Court decision under Article 321 § 2 of the code of criminal Procedure must bereasoned. Omitting to provide reasons “impair[ed] the effective exercise of the right to have one’s conviction reviewed’ The requirement of reasons was a necessary safeguard for ensuring a substantial review. By requiring the court to explain why the appeal would not succeed, one could ensure that the decision was reached on the basis of a thorough and sound assessment. The Supreme Court quashed a High Court decision refusing admission of an appeal on the basis of Article 29-13 (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The majority observed that this provision left the legislator great latitude in organising the national system of judicial remedies as it deemed appropriate. A filtering system for appeals would not as such be incompatible with Article 88. The extent of the reasoning required would vary considerably, depending on the nature of the particular case, ranging from a couple of sentences to more extensive reasoning. There were also other mechanisms that could ensure the Supreme Court the necessary control over the judicial system, the majority of seven members said. Supreme Court’s competence to review the High Court procedure encompassed questions of whether a breach had occurred of expressly stated rules of procedure. The Supreme Court was empowered to fully examine the application of the law and the assessment of the evidence in relation to questions of procedure and, if necessary, determine whether an error of procedure had materialised. This also covered whether in the light of the points of law raised in the case was justifiable for the High court to refuse admission of the appeal. No constitutional obligation to give reasons for a High Court refusal to admit an appeal could be justified by the interests of the Supreme Court procedure. This ought to be sufficient to satisfy Article 88 of the Constitution. The Supreme Court’s majority found it unnecessary to consider the alternative plea that the decision had to be quashed in view of the requirements of Article 6 of the Convention and Article 14 of the Covenant that national decisions be reasoned. Two dissenting members disagreed with the majority view that the obligation to state reasons for a refusal of admission of an appeal in criminal cases also extended to civil cases. With effect from 10 December 2010, Article 29-13 (5) of the Code of Civil Procedure was amended to include a requirement that a decision refusing admission of a criminal appeal under that law must be reasoned (“begrunnet”).

The United Nations Human Rights Committee communicated its “Views” on a communication lodged by Mr Abdel Kereem Hassan Aboushanif under the Protocol to the 1966 International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. A decision by the Norwegian Supreme Court on 9 December 2008 (Norsk Retstidende – “Rt.” – 2008 at pp. 1764, 1783 and 1786) in criminal proceedings led to the requirement of reasons being made part of Norwegian national law. A majority of seven members considered the subject matter in relation to Article 88 of the Constitution, according to which the Supreme Court was to adjudicate in final instance. The majority observed that this provision left the legislator great latitude in organising the national system of judicial remedies as it deemed appropriate. The Supreme Court could in addition review whether the state of the evidence before the High. Court suggested that the subject matter could be adequately dealt with on the. basis of the written case-file in a simplified procedure. The relevant High Court should therefore have given reasons for its impugned decision in that case. With effect from 10 December 2010, the requirement was amended to include a requirement that a refusal of admission under the same article had to be reasoned (“begrunnet”). The financial and administrative consequences of the proposed changes for High Courts should be manageable, according to the Ministry of Justice. name: Havva Kaba
train_texts: The case was brought by three Turkish nationals, Ms Havva Kaba, Miss Edanur Kaba and Miss Elif Kaba. In their application, the applicants complained that Mr Kaba's death was the result of the asbestos levels at Hasköy Dock and that he had not received adequate medical treatment at the GATA military hospital. The applicants also requested legal aid for the court fees. The Military Supreme Administrative Court, without giving any reason, decided that the applicants did not qualify for legal aid. On 15 September 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applications at the same time. The applicants were requested to pay the fees due within one month in order to be able to continue the proceedings. They were warned that failure to do so would result in the discontinuation of the Proceedings. The court also decided to discontinue the compensation proceedings because the applicants had not paid the necessary court fees. This decision was served on the applicants on 4 June 2004. The applicants' lawyer referred to the relevant statements of means provided by the domestic authorities. He further stated that while lodging the case he had submitted the relevant medical records concerning Mr Yusuf Kaba, a report on the asbestos levels at Hasköy Dock and an expert report, and that this evidence should be sufficient to prove that they had a well-founded case.

The case originated in an application (no. 1236/05) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were born in 1978, 2001 and 1997 respectively and live in Istanbul. The first applicant is the wife and the second and third applicants are the children of Mr Yusuf Kaba, who was an officer in the Turkish Navy and died of cancer in 2003. According to the applicants, Mr Kaba's exposure to asbestos at Hasköy Dock had caused his cancer. They were also concerned about allegedly inadequate treatment he received at the GATA military hospital.  applicants were notified that they had to pay TRL 8,758,870,000 (approximately EUR 5,000) in court fees within one month for the proceedings to be continued. Failure to do so would result in the discontinuation of the proceedings. In January 2004 the applicants again requested legal aid to pay the court fees. The applicants' lawyer also lodged a request with the Military Supreme Administrative Court and requested clarification (tavzih) of the decision dated 21 January 2004. The court examined both requests and decided that a rectification or a clarification request was not possible under domestic law. This decision was served on the applicants on 4 June 2004.

name: Martin Zumtobel
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 1 September 1992. It originated in an application (no. 12235/86) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by the firm of F.M. Zumtobel. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them (Rule 30) and who was given leave by the President to use the German language. The case concerns expropriation proceedings instituted with a view to the construction in the province of Vorarlberg of a provincial highway, the L 52. It appears that the scheme in question dated back to 1960, but that opposition from local landowners had prevented its realisation. The authorities conducted an investigation into inter alia whether the projected road was compatible with the requirements of environmental protection (Landschaftsschutz). The proposed route was published (zur öffentlichen Einsichtnahme aufgelegt) and the file made available for consultation at the Rankweil council offices from 1 to 31 October 1984. The Zumtobel partnership applied for expropriation of 2,140m2 of land to build a new highway. The authorities consulted several experts and made an order for the land to be expropriated. The first applicant repeatedly but unsuccessfully requested to be allowed to study various documents in the file, namely a report of the Court of Audit (Rechnungshof) and an expert report on the environmental implications. On 13 February 1986 the Office of the Provincial Government (Amt der Landesregierung) made a decision to expropriate the land and fixed compensation at 620 schillings per square metre. It claimed that the proceedings had violated its right of access to a court with full jurisdiction. The Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 22 September 1989, after a purely written procedure; the applicants had not asked it to hold a hearing. In the court’s opinion, the complaint that the scheme objected to was not based on any reasonable overall plan was not enough to establish that the contested decision had been unlawful. The court held that the applicant partnership had also failed to cast doubt on the official experts’ reports such as could disclose a procedural irregularity capable of affecting the decision. The Administrative Court cannot hold to be unlawful the fact that the respondent authority had regard to road traffic requirements and based its decision principally on the consideration that no other more appropriate solution was possible. The court considered that mere general remarks on the independence of official experts were not enough to prove a specific legitimate doubt. The fact that such an expert took part in proceedings to which the Province was a party did not, unless there were special circumstances, constitute a serious reason within the meaning of the 1950 Law to doubt his complete impartiality. The court stated that it could not find that the Office had disregarded procedural rules, compliance with which could have led to a different decision. As the applicant partnership had not been a party to the environmental protection proceedings (Landschaftsschutzverfahren), it couldn't claim a right to compensation. The Administrative Court also found that there had been no breach of Article 6 (art. 6) of the Convention and declined to refer the matter to the Constitutional Court. The first applicant had meanwhile applied to the Feldkirch District Court (Bezirksgericht) to determine the amount of compensation. On 17 December 1987 this was set at 9,963,032.50 Austrian schillings (ATS) On 28 May 1988, on appeal (Rekurs) the amount was reduced to ATS 4,560,000.50. On 6 June 1988, the court ruled that the first applicant was entitled to the compensation. The first applicant’s appeal on points of law (Revisionsrekurs) against this decision was dismissed by the Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) October 1988. The first applicant's appeal against the decision of the first judge was dismissed in 1988. It was the first appeal to be dismissed by a German court of appeals. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that the decision was based on errors of law. The case was appealed to the German Supreme Court of Appeal. The decision was upheld by the Court of Appeals of appeal in 1988, and the appeal was rejected on appeal in 1989, with the appeal dismissed in 1990.

The proposed route was published (zur öffentlichen Einsichtnahme aufgelegt) and the file made available for consultation at the Rankweil council offices from 1 to 31 October 1984. Expropriation proceedings relating to a parcel of land of 2,140m2 belonging to the Zumtobel partnership were opened on 28 February 1985. The authorities consulted several experts. According to the highways expert and the road traffic expert, the proposed section of highway was important because it would improve traffic links between Rankweil and Feldkirch, which went through densely populated built-up areas. On 13 February 1986 the Office made an order for expropriation and fixed compensation at 620 schillings per square metre. The first applicant repeatedly but unsuccessfully requested to be allowed to study various documents in the file, namely a report of the Court of Audit (Rechnungshof) and an expert report on the environmental implications. The court held that the applicant partnership had also failed to cast doubt on the official experts’ reports such as could disclose a procedural irregularity capable of affecting the decision.“ As can be seen from the findings of fact in the contested decision, the respondent authority took the view that it was in the interests of road users to divert through- traffic from the Rankweil-Brederis built-up area. The fact that the Government Office had not made the commencement of construction work for the L 52 subject to a final decision on the length of the route was not incompatible with the Provincial Highways Law. Contrary to the applicant partnership’s arguments, the Office had indeed taken environmental protection into account when assessing the various relevant interests. As for compensation in kind (Naturalersatz) or an exchange of land (Tauschanbot), the documents in the case showed that these had not been available as alternative solutions. The court also rejected the complaints relating to the hearing of the official experts. The fact that such an expert took part in proceedings to which the Province was a party did not constitute a serious reason within the meaning of the 1950 Law to doubt his complete impartiality. The Administrative Court also found that there had been no breach of Article 6 (art. 6) of the Convention and declined to refer the matter to the Constitutional Court. On 17 December 1987 this was set at 9,963,032.50 Austrian schillings (ATS). On 28 May 1988, on appeal (Rekurs), the amount was reduced to ATS 4,560,000.50Austrian schillens (ATS) The court cited a judgment given by an enlarged chamber in 1978 and stated: “[That judgment shows that] the Administrative Court is not allowed, in a case which has been before the respondent administrative authority, to take evidence, which the latter may have omitted to take” The first applicant’s appeal on points of law (Revisionsrekurs) against this decision was dismissed by the Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) October 1988 the first applicant's appeal onPoints of Law was dismissed. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal against the decision of the Court of Appeal. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that it was not a legal appeal. The case was decided by the German Supreme Court and the appeal was decided on the basis of the law of the country, not the principles of the case. The decision was upheld by the High Court of Justice in October 1988 and the case was dismissed in November 1988.

name: Herbert Tuma
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 22833/07) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant was arrested on 11 October 2001 on suspicion of fraud. He was in pre-trial detention until 18 October 2001. The Austrian Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Tichy, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for European and International Affairs. The Vienna Regional Criminal Court acquitted the applicant on 28 June 2007. The applicant was charged with embezzlement on 15 March 2006. The court held a second hearing on 26 April 2007 and acquitted him on the same day. The judgment was served on the applicant’s counsel on 28June 2007. His trial was scheduled to commence on 10 August 2006 but had to be postponed because the applicant was in hospital. The trial was finally held on 2 November 2006 and the judge's verdict was delivered on 26 June 2007, after a further hearing on 6 February 2007. He was found not guilty by reason of innocence or guilt. The judge's decision was published in the Austrian edition of this article on 8 August 2007.

The case originated in an application (no. 22833/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) The applicant was arrested on 11 October 2001 on suspicion of fraud. He was in pre-trial detention until 18 October 2001. On 29 June 2005 the investigating judge decided nevertheless to obtain an expert opinion on various transactions in respect of which the applicant was suspected of embezzlement. The expert’s opinion was submitted on 14 November 2005 and transmitted to the Public Prosecutor’S Office and the Government. On 24 March 2009 the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government and to rule on the admissibility and merits at the same time. The Vienna Public Prosecutor issued the bill of indictment charging the applicant with embezzlement on 15 March 2006. The applicant lodged objections against the indictment on 12 April 2006. By decision of 11 May 2006 the Court of Appeal rejected the objections and upheld the indictment. The court held another hearing on 26 April 2007. On that date it acquitted the applicant. The judgment was served on the applicant’s counsel on 28 June 2007. The Vienna Regional Criminal Court, sitting with two professional and two lay judges, then held the first hearing on 2 November 2006. During this hearing the expert was ordered to supplement his opinion, taking into consideration further documents.

name: Duncan Lustig-Prean
train_texts: The case originated in two applications against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Both applicants complained that the investigations into their homosexuality and their discharge from the Royal Navy on the sole ground that they are homosexual constituted violations of Article 8 of the Covention taken alone and in conjunction with Article 14. The applications were adjourned pending the outcome of a reference to the European Court of Justice (“ECJ”) pursuant to Article 177 of the Treaty of Rome by the English High Court on the question of the applicability of the Council Directive on the Implementation of the Principle of Equal Treatment for Men and Women. On 13 July 1998 the High Court delivered its judgment withdrawing its reference of the above question given the decision of the ECJ in the case of R. v. Secretary of State for Defence, ex parte Perkins (13 July 1998) The applications fall to be examined by the Court following the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 on 1 November 1998. The High Court decided to disjoin them from the Smith and Grady cases. It was also decided to hold a hearing on the merits of the case. On 4 May 1999 the President of the Chamber decided to grant Mr Lustig-Prean legal aid. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 18 May 1999. The first applicant joined the Royal Navy Reserve as a radio operator in 1982. He became a midshipman in the executive branch of the navy in 1983. In 1994 the applicant attained the rank of lieutenant-commander. The applicant was interviewed on 13 June 1994 by personnel from the service police about his sexual orientation for approximately twenty minutes. He confirmed that he was homosexual, acknowledging that he had been a practising homosexual since his teenage years. He was then asked, inter alia, whether he had had homosexual contact with service personnel (at least four questions on this subject), what type of sexual relations he hadHad with a particular person, when and where this had occurred, about his current relationship and whether his parents knew of his homosexuality. The applicant was asked about an anonymous letter alleging that the applicant had had a relationship with a serviceman. The applicant was told that it would ‘come back’ on the applicant’s interviewer if the latter did not properly follow up on the anonymous letter. In December 1994, the Admiralty Board informed the applicant that it had decided to terminate his commission and to discharge him, administratively, from the navy with effect from 17 January 1995. The ground for his discharge was his sexual orientation. His commission was removed and most of the bonus which he had received with that promotion was recouped by the naval authorities (£4,875 out of £6,000) In May 1993 the applicant had been refused time off to deal with a personal matter (he wished to collect his Aids test results) to whom he admitted his sexual orientation. On 10 May 1993 he was asked by his lieutenant-commander to repeat what he had told the chaplain. He again admitted his homosexuality to that officer and was then called for interview by the service police. He was cautioned in the same terms as the first applicant and told that he would not be questioned on the above admissions prior to a search of his locker. His consent to the search was requested and given. During the search, slides (of himself, his partner and some of his service friends) and personal postcards were seized. On 28 July 1993 the applicant’s administrative discharge was approved on the basis of his homosexuality. The applicants argued that the policy of the Ministry of Defence against homosexuals in the armed forces was ‘irrational’ The applicants’ judicial review proceedings (R.C. v. MoD, ex parte Smith and Others 2 Weeky Law Reports 305) were successful on 7 June 1995. On 6 December 1994 the Admiralty Board dismissed the applicant's complaint against the decision to discharge him. The application was brought by Ms Smith and Mr Grady who, along with Ms Grady, obtained leave to apply for judicial review of the decisions to discharge them. Four men were discharged on the sole ground of sexual orientation. All were devastated by their discharge. High Court dismissed the application for judicial review. Lord Justice Simon Brown gave the main judgment of the court. He noted that the cases illustrated the hardships resulting from the absolute policy against homosexuals in the armed forces. In his view, the tide of history was against the Ministry of Defence. He further observed that it was improbable, whatever the High Court would say, that the policy could survive for much longer and added, “I doubt whether most of those present in court throughout the proceedings now believe otherwise.” He concluded that the conventional Wednesbury principles, adapted to a human rights context, should be applied. The primary decision was for him. Simon Brown LJ also found that the Equal Treatment Directive was not applicable to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. He also observed that the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, Israel, Germany, France, Norway, Sweden, Austria and the Netherlands permitted homosexuals into the forces. A brief analysis of the Convention’s case-law led the judge to comment that he strongly suspected that, as far as the United Kingdom’S obligations were concerned, the days of the policy were numbered. It followed that the applications had to be rejected “ albeit with hesitation and regret”. The Master of the Rolls, Sir Thomas Bingham, delivered the main judgment. The court may not interfere with the exercise of an administrative discretion on substantive grounds save where the court is satisfied that the decision is unreasonable. The more substantial the interference with human rights, the more the court will require by way of justification before it is. satisfied that a decision is reasonable in the sense outlined above” He went on to quote from, inter alia, the. Human rights context is important. The Court of appeal dismissed the appeals on 3 November 1995. The case was appealed to the Court of Justice of the European Court of Human Rights. The appeal was dismissed on 8 December 1995. Master of the Rolls noted that the case concerned innate qualities of a very personal kind. He considered that the greater the policy content of the decision and the more remote the subject matter of a decision from ordinary judicial experience, the more hesitant the court had to be in holding a decision to be irrational. While the court must properly defer to the expertise of responsible decision-makers, it must not shrink from its fundamental duty to ‘do right to all manner of people’ He concluded that the policy could not be considered “irrational” at the time the applicants were discharged from the armed forces, finding that the threshold of irrationality was “a high one” and that it had not been crossed. Henry LJ of the Court of Appeal agreed with the judgment of the Master of the Rolls. He questioned the utility of a debate as to the likely fate of the ‘longstanding’ policy of the Ministry of Defence before the European Court of Human Rights. In Henry LJ’s view, the only relevance of the Convention was as “background to the complaint of irrationality’ Thorpe LJ agreed with both preceding judgments and, in particular, with the views expressed on the rationality test to be applied and on its application in the particular case. He also found that the Equal Treatment Directive did not apply to complaints in relation to sexual orientation. In December 1995 Mr Lustig-Prean issued proceedings in the Industrial Tribunal claiming unfair dismissal and sexual discrimination contrary to the Sexual Discrimination Act 1975. Those proceedings were adjourned pending the application for leave to appeal to the House of Lords. On 19 March 1996 the Appeals Committee of the House. of Lords refused leave to Appeal to the Lords. Mr Beckett requested the withdrawal of his Industrial Tribunal proceedings and those proceedings were dismissed by the. Industrial Tribunal on 25 April 1996. In the light of subsequent decisions of the ECJ and of the domestic courts, the second applicant subsequently requested the. withdrawal of those proceedings which were, on 27 August 1998, dismissed.

The case originated in two applications against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Both applicants complained that the investigations into their homosexuality and their discharge from the Royal Navy on the sole ground that they are homosexual constituted violations of Article 8 of the Covention taken alone and in conjunction with Article 14. The Government, represented by Mr M. Eaton and, subsequently, by Mr C. Whomersley, submitted their observations on 17 October 1997. The applications were adjourned pending the outcome of a reference to the European Court of Justice (“ECJ”) pursuant to Article 177 of the Treaty of Rome by the English High Court. On 13 July 1998 the High Court delivered its judgment withdrawing its reference of the above question given the decision of the ECJ in the case of R. v. Secretary of State for Defence, ex parte Perkins. the Commission granted Mr Beckett legal aid. The hearing in this case took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 18 May 1999. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr C. Whomersley, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr J. Eadie, Counsel, Mr. Betteley, Ms J. Pfieffer, Adviser. The ground for his discharge was his sexual orientation. The second applicant joined the Royal Navy, enlisting for twenty-two years’ service. He was then called for interview by the service police. Detailed questions were put as to how they had sex and whether they used condoms and other sex aids. The service police report completed after the applicant’s interview included several internal documents where it was noted that the applicant, in openly declaring his homosexuality and his relationship with a civilian, had effectively disposed “of any immediate potential security concern” For that reason, it was considered in the report that “no cause was identified for conducting a security interview with Beckett”. That report also accepted that a case for fraudulent entry into the armed forces would be inappropriate given the date when the applicant had discovered his homosexuality. All four of the applicants had exemplary service records, some with reports written in glowing terms. In his view, the tide of history was against the Ministry of Defence. He further observed that it was improbable, whatever the High Court would say, that the policy could survive for much longer and added, “I doubt whether most of those present in court throughout the proceedings now believe otherwise.” However, having considered arguments as to the test to be applied in the context of these judicial review proceedings, he concluded that the conventional Wednesbury principles, adapted to a human rights context, should be applied. He emphasised that, even where the most fundamental human rights were being restricted, “the threshold of unreasonableness is not lowered’. The court may not interfere with the exercise of an administrative. discretion on substantive grounds save where the court is satisfied. that the. decision is unreasonable. But in judging whether the decision-maker has exceeded this margin of appreciation the human rights context. is key. The Master of the Rolls noted that the case concerned innate qualities of a very personal kind. He considered that the greater the policy content of the decision and the more remote the subject matter of a decision from ordinary judicial experience, the more hesitant the court had to be in holding a decision to be irrational. However, he concluded that the policy could not be considered “irrational” at the time the applicants were discharged from the armed forces, finding that the threshold of irrationality was “a high one” and that it had not been crossed in this case. “The court must properly defer to the expertise of responsible decision-makers, it must not shrink from its fundamental duty to ‘do right to all manner of people’ …” Henry LJ of the Court of Appeal agreed with the judgment of the Master of the Rolls. He found that to dismiss a person from his or her employment on the grounds of a private sexual preference, and to interrogate him or her about private sexual behaviour, would not appear to show respect for that person’s private and family life. He held that there might be room for argument as to whether the policy answered a “pressing social need” and, in particular, was proportionate to the legitimate aim pursued. However, he held that these were not questions to which answers could be properly or usefully proffered. Thorpe LJ agreed with both preceding judgments. Lustig-Prean issued proceedings in the Industrial Tribunal claiming unfair dismissal and sexual discrimination contrary to the Sexual Discrimination Act 1975. On 19 March 1996 the Appeals Committee of the House of Lords refused leave to appeal to the Lords. Beckett requested the withdrawal of his Industrial Tribunal proceedings and those proceedings were dismissed on 25 April 1996. In the light of subsequent decisions of the ECJ and of the domestic courts, the second applicant subsequently requested the. withdrawal of those proceedings which were, on 27 August 1998, dismissed by the Industrial. Tribunal. The case originated in two applications lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Both applicants complained that the investigations into their homosexuality and their discharge from the Royal Navy constituted violations of Article 8 of the Covention taken alone and in conjunction with Article 14. The Government, represented by Mr M. Eaton and, subsequently, by Mr C. Whomersley, both Agents, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, submitted their observations on 17 October 1997. On 17 January 1998 the Commission decided to adjourn the applications pending the outcome of a reference to the European Court of Justice (“ECJ”) pursuant to Article 177 of the Treaty of Rome by the English High Court. The High Court delivered its judgment withdrawing its reference of the above question given the decision of the ECJ in the case of R. v. Secretary of State for Defence, ex parte Perkins (13 July 1998). The applications fall to be examined by the Court. On 4 May 1999 the President of the Chamber decided to grant Mr Lustig-Prean legal aid. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 18 May 1999. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr C. Whomersley, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr J. Eadie, Counsel and Ms J. Pfieffer, Adviser. The first applicant joined the Royal Navy Reserve as a radio operator in 1982. On 27 April 1983 he became a midshipman in the executive branch of the navy. His evaluation of November 1989 noted that he was an officer with “great potential” and the “sort of person that the Navy needs to attract and retain” In 1994 the applicant attained the rank of lieutenant-commander. The applicant was interviewed on 13 June 1994 by personnel from the service police about his sexual orientation for approximately twenty minutes. He was asked, inter alia, whether he had had homosexual contact with service personnel (at least four questions on this subject) He was also asked about his current relationship and whether his parents knew of his homosexuality. The second applicant joined the Royal Navy in 1989 and served for 22 years. He was discharged in 1995 because of his sexual orientation. The Admiralty Board decided to terminate his commission and to discharge him, administratively, from the navy with effect from 17 January 1995. The applicant’s commission was removed and most of the bonus which he had received with that promotion was recouped by the naval authorities (£4,875 out of £6,000). His term of service would otherwise have terminated in 2009, with the possibility of renewal. Mr Beckett now works as a weapons engineering mechanic for a private company in Newcastle. In May 1993 the applicant had been refused time off to deal with a personal matter (he wished to collect his Aids test results) and consequently he spoke with the chaplain, to whom he admitted his sexual orientation. He was then called for interview by the service police. The applicant immediately confirmed his homosexuality, later clarifying that he first had “niggling doubts’ about his orientation approximately two and a half years previously. The interview, which had lasted approximately five minutes, was suspended pending the search. During the search, slides (of himself, his partner and some of his service friends) and personal postcards were seized. The service police report completed after the applicant’s interview included several internal documents where it was noted that the applicant, in openly declaring his homosexuality and his relationship with a civilian, had effectively disposed “of any immediate potential security concern” For that reason, it was considered in the report that “no cause was identified for conducting a security interview with Beckett” That report also accepted that a case for fraudulent entry into the armed forces would be inappropriate given the date when the applicant had discovered his homosexuality.Prior to his discharge, the applicant completed his duties and remained in communal sleeping accommodation with no reported difficulties. The applicant then complained about the decision to discharge him to the Admiralty Board. The applicants’ judicial review proceedings (R.C. v. Ministry of Defence, ex parte Smith and Others 2 Weeky Law Reports 305) Lord Justice Simon Brown gave the main judgment of the court. He noted that the cases illustrated the hardships resulting from the absolute policy against homosexuals in the armed forces. All four of the applicants had exemplary service records, some with reports written in glowing terms. In none of the cases before him was it suggested that the applicants’ sexual orientation had in any way affected their ability to carry out their work or had any ill-effect on discipline. All were devastated by their discharge. In his view, the tide of history was against the Ministry of Defence. He said it was improbable, whatever the High Court would say, that the policy could survive for much longer. Simon Brown LJ also found that the Equal Treatment Directive was not applicable to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and that the domestic courts could not rule on Convention matters. He emphasised that, even where the most fundamental human rights were being restricted, ‘the threshold of unreasonableness is not lowered’. He also observed that the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, Israel, Germany, France, Norway, Sweden, Austria and the Netherlands permitted homosexuals into the armed services. A brief analysis of the Convention’s case-law led the judge to comment that he strongly suspected that, as far as the United Kingdom’S obligations were concerned, the days of the policy were numbered. It followed that the applications had to be rejected ‘ albeit with hesitation and regret’ In August 1995 a consultation paper was circulated by the Ministry of Defence to “management’s levels in the armed forces relating to the policy against homosexuals in those forces. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal on 3 November 1995. The Master of the Rolls, Sir Thomas Bingham, delivered the main judgment (with which the two other judges of the Court of appeal agreed) The court may not interfere with the exercise of an administrative discretion on substantive grounds save where the court is satisfied that the decision is unreasonable in the sense that it is beyond the range of responses open to a reasonable decision- maker. But in judging whether the decision-maker has exceeded this margin of appreciation the human rights context is important. The more substantial the interference with human rights, the more the court will require by way of justification. Master of the Rolls says it is not the role of the courts to regulate the conditions of service in the armed forces. The court has the constitutional role and duty of ensuring that the rights of citizens are not abused by the unlawful exercise of executive power, he says. But he concludes that the policy could not be considered “irrational” at the time the applicants were discharged from the armed force. He finds that the threshold of irrationality was “a high one” and that it had not been crossed in this case. He says the court must properly defer to the expertise of responsible decision-makers but it must not shrink from its fundamental duty to ‘do right to all manner of people' Henry LJ of the Court of Appeal agreed with the judgment of the Master of the Rolls and, in particular, with the latter’s approach to the irrationality test. He questioned the utility of a debate as to the likely fate of the ‘longstanding’ policy of the Ministry of Defence before the European Court of Human Rights with which the primary adjudicating role on the Convention lay. He also found that the Equal Treatment Directive did not apply to complaints in relation to sexual orientation. Thorpe LJ agreed with both preceding judgments and with the views expressed on the rationality test to be applied and on its application in the particular case. The applicants’ challenge to the arguments in support of the policy was ‘completely persuasive’ and ‘impressive’ But the attack on the Secretary of State’s rationality fell ‘a long way short of success’ The policy was, in his view, ‘ripe for review and for consideration of its replacement by a strict conduct code’. The application for leave to appeal to the House of Lords was rejected. The second applicant requested the withdrawal of his Industrial Tribunal proceedings and those proceedings were dismissed by the Industrial Tribunal on 25 April 1996. In the light of subsequent decisions of the ECJ and of the domestic courts, the second applicant subsequently requested the withdrawing of those proceedings which were dismissed in 1998.

name: Paweł Kurczewski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18157/04) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the excessive length of the applicant's detention to the Government. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was born in 1979 and lives in Gdańsk, Poland. On 16 April 2002 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of having committed robbery. The applicant was indicted before the Gdańsk District Court on 25 March 2003. He was charged with robbery and illegal possession of firearms and ammunition. The trial court held the first hearing in the case on 5 June 2003. Four of the sixteen hearings scheduled were cancelled for various reasons. The judge convicted the applicant on 28 July 2004 and sentenced him to four years' imprisonment. His detention was subsequently extended on several occasions. His appeals and applications for release lodged by the applicant were to no avail. In all those decisions the courts stated that the grounds originally given for the applicant's detention were still valid. They repeated the grounds previously given for his continued detention. Appeal hearings scheduled for 12 October and 12 December 2005 and 2 February 2006 were cancelled for various reasons, such as illness or absence of defence lawyers, and the need to obtain evidence. On 3 February 2006 the Gdańsk Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) quashed the applicant's detention order. He was released on the same date. It appears that the first-instance judgment was upheld by the GdaŚsk Regional Court on 11 July 2007. The appeal hearing was scheduled for 11 October 2005, but was cancelled because of illness or absence of defence lawyers.

The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 4 May 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the excessive length of the applicant's detention to the Government. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The application was filed by a Polish national, Mr Paweł Kurczewski (‘the applicant’), on 7 May 2004. The applicant was indicted before the Gdańsk District Court on 25 March 2003. He was charged with robbery and illegal possession of firearms and ammunition. The bill of indictment concerned five defendants and, in all, twelve charges were brought against them. Hearings scheduled for 9 October and 11 December 2003 were cancelled due to, among other things, the failure to bring the co-accused to trial from prison. The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to four years' imprisonment in July 2004. His detention was subsequently extended on several occasions. All the appeals and. applications for release lodged by the applicant were to no avail. Appeals scheduled for 12 October and 12 December 2005 and 2 February 2006 were cancelled for various reasons, such as illness or absence of defence lawyers, and the need to obtain evidence. On 3 February 2006 the Gdańsk Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) quashed the applicant's detention order. He was released on the same date. It appears that the first-instance judgment was upheld by the GdaŹska Regional Court on 11 July 2007. It is not known if the application will be heard in court again in the future. The applicant's case is currently being heard in the Polish Court of Appeal in Warsaw.

name: Melahat Filiz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 34481/97) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Two Turkish nationals, Melahat Filiz and Nadir Kalkan (“the applicants”) complained that their detention in police custody lasted eight days without being brought before a judge or other officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power. The applicants were represented before the Court by Mr İşeri, a lawyer practising in İzmir. The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. The charges were brought under Articles 125 and 168 of the Criminal Code. Ms Melahat Filiz was acquitted of the charges, holding that there was insufficient evidence to convict her. The court found Mr Nadir Kalkan guilty of the offences under Articles125 and 168 and sentenced him to capital punishment. He lodged an appeal with the Court of Cassation. The applicant did not submit any information concerning the outcome of the criminal proceedings against him. He has never been found guilty of any of the crimes against which he was charged. He is believed to have been a member of the PRK-Rızgari. He was accused of joining and undertaking actions against the indivisible integrity of the state.

Mr Türmen, the judge elected in respect of Turkey, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The Government accordingly appointed Mr F. Gölcüklü to sit as an ad hoc judge (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 29 § 1). The charges were brought under Articles 125 and 168 of the Criminal Code. Ms Melahat Filiz was acquitted of the charges, holding that there was insufficient evidence to convict her. He lodged an appeal with the Court of Cassation, but the applicant did not submit any information concerning the outcome of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was dismissed and he was not sentenced to death. The case is now referred to as 'The PRK-Rızgari case' and is being investigated by the Turkish National Police.

name: Jutta Huber
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights and by the Government of the Swiss Confederation. It originated in an application (no. 12794/87) against Switzerland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mrs Jutta Huber, a Swiss national, on 27 February 1987. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 5 para. 3 ( art. 5-3) of the Convention. The applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent her (Rule 30). The applicant lodged her claims for just satisfaction on 13 February 1990. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr Jacot-Guillarmod and Mr Levi for the Government, by Mr Schermers for the Commission and by Mr Schönenberger and Mr Mäder for the applicant. Following the hearing and at the Court’s request, the Delegate produced the copy of a document. On 30 March 1990, pursuant to Rule 51, the Chamber decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. On 24 May 1990, the Court decided to proceed to judgment without holding a further hearing. Jutta Huber, a Swiss national, resides in Zürich. She admitted making a living from prostitution, but maintained that she knew Mr K. and Mr B. by name and that she did not pass on to them any of her earnings. The District Attorney signed a detention order (Verhaftsverfügung) remanding the applicant in custody on grave suspicion of having given false evidence. When appearing as a witness, she had denied any contact with the “Hell’s Angels“, which appeared unlikely to be true. The order referred in particular to the danger of collusion and the possibility that evidence might be tampered with. Mrs Huber was released on 19 August 1983. District Attorney J. instituted proceedings before the Judge in Criminal Cases. Trial took place on 10 January 1985, after the indictment had been accepted. Mrs Huber acquitted on the ground that she had never been validly summoned to appear as a witness. The Court of Appeal of the Canton of Zürich fined the applicant 4,000 Swiss francs for attempting to give false evidence. The appeal court found that the accused’s testimony was not unlawfully obtained and could therefore be used in evidence. In addition, it referred to the monitoring of telephone conversations. carried out by the German authorities who had communicated the transcript thereof to the Swiss judicial authorities. Mrs Huber's appeal to the Court of Cassation of the Canton of Zürich was dismissed on 1 July 1986. On 22 August 1986 Mrs Huber lodged a public-law appeal with the Federal Court. She complained, inter alia, that, notwithstanding Article 5 para. 3 (art. 5-3), the same District Attorney had both ordered her detention on remand and drawn up the indictment. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal by a judgment of 24 November 1986, which was served on 18 December. As to the complaint based on Article 5. para. 4 of the Convention, it held as follows (translation): “As the appellant has long since been released from detention on. remand, she no longer has a current, practical interest in a ruling on [her] complaint, for which reason the Court can no longer deal with it.” The Zürich District Attorney qualifies as an ‘officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power’ within the meaning of Article 5 para. 3 (art. 5-3) of the Convention. The status and powers of District Attorneys were laid down in the Courts Act of 13 June 1976 (Gerichtsverfassungsgesetz, “GVG’). The District Attorney may make a detention order (Verhaftsbefehl - Article 55 StPO), the grounds for which he must state. He has to hear an arrested suspect within 24 hours (Article 64 StPO). Detention on remand ordered by the District attorney may not exceed 14 days. District Attorney is the prosecuting authority before the “Judge in Criminal Cases’ and before the District Courts in cases concerning petty offences and misdemeanours. For the higher cantonal courts (the Court of Appeal and the Assize Court - section 72 GVG), this function is performed by the Principal Public Prosecutor. The combination of the functions of investigation and prosecution has given rise to case-law - at cantonal and federal level - which has recently been confirmed. In a judgment of 13 June 1988 (Ante Djukic geg geg), the Zürich court ruled that there was no case to answer in the case. Cantonal Court of Cassation stated that the District Attorney of the Canton of Zürich exercises judicial power. What is decisive is whether at the time of the arrest the decision was taken by an official who satisfied the requirements of Article 5 para. 3 (art. 5-3) of the European Convention on Human Rights. This question has been answered in the affirmative by the eminent courts referred to above. train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant complained about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court ruled in favour of the applicant. The application was joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaint (applications nos. 28291/95, 29280/95 and 26699/95) (Rule 43 § 2) The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation. He was convicted of his involvement in the THKP/C in 1984. The applicant appealed to the Military Court of Cassation (Askeri Yargıtay) in 1988. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections. This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1) The case-file was sent to the İzmir Assize Court (ağır ceza mahkemesi) on 17 August 1990. It was decided to join the two criminal proceedings against the applicant. Following promulgation of the Law of 27 December 1993, which abolished the jurisdiction of the Martial Law Courts, the Court of Cassation (Yargıtay) acquired jurisdiction over the case. The criminal proceedings against the applicant should be discontinued since the prosecution was time‑barred. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Military Court ofCassation against this decision. The case file was transmitted to it on 4 January 1994. The application was dismissed on 18 April 1995 under Article 322 of the Criminal Code, that the prosecution should be stopped since the case was time-barred; the applicant appealed against the decision; the appeal was dismissed.

The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The judge elected in respect of Turkey withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28) and the Government appointed Mr Feyyaz Gölcüklü to sit as an ad hoc judge, in his place. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaint. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits. The Court declared the application admissible. The case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1) The case-file was sent to the İzmir Assize Court (ağır ceza mahkemesi) in August 1990. The applicant appealed to the Military Court of Cassation (Askeri Yargıtay) on 12 April 1988. In November 1984 the  İstanbul Martial Law Court convicted the applicant of his involvement in the THKP/C. However, the court did not indicate the applicant’s sentence in its judgment. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Military Court of Cassation against this decision. The criminal proceedings against the applicant should be discontinued since the prosecution was time‑barred. The case file was transmitted to the Court ofCassation on 4 January 1994. The applicant appealed the decision, but the decision was upheld on 18 April 1995. The application was settled by the Supreme Court of Justice on 7 November 1996. The appeal was dismissed on 9 October 1997. The judge ruled that the applicant was not guilty of any crime and that the case should be dismissed. The decision was appealed again on 11 October 1998. The appeals were dismissed on 10 October 1998 and 9 November 1998.

The case originated in an application (no. 29912/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaint. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court ruled that the application against Turkey was not valid. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation, the THKP-C (Turkish People’s Liberation Party/Front). The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59): the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant appealed to the Military Court of Cassation (Askeri Yargıtay), which quashed the first instance court's judgment in 1988. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25): the case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52): the application was dismissed and the case-file joined. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Military Court of Cassation against this decision. The criminal proceedings against the applicant should be discontinued since the prosecution was time‑barred. The applicant was found not guilty of all charges and his appeal was dismissed. The case file was transmitted to the Court ofCassation on 4 January 1994. The judge ruled that the case should be dropped because the prosecution had already been discontinued. The application was dismissed on 18 April 1995 and the case was settled out of court. The appeal was dropped on 20 April 1995. The hearing was adjourned until 20 April 1997. The verdict was returned on 24 April 1997 and the applicant was cleared.

train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were represented by Mr H. Graupner, a lawyer practising in Vienna. The Austrian Government (“the Government”) was represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Winkler, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The first applicant was convicted under section 209 of the Criminal Code of having committed homosexual acts with an adolescent and sentenced to a fine of ATS 4,500 (approximately EUR 330) with 75 days’ imprisonment in default. The second applicant was arrested on suspicion of having committed homosexual acts with an adolescent contrary to section 209 of the Criminal Code. He was convicted and sentenced to 15 months' imprisonment, 14 of which were suspended on probation. On appeal the Vienna Court of Appeal dismissed the second applicant’s appeal on points of law. On 7 July 2002 he requested a pardon and a further stay of execution pending the decision on his request for pardon. On 23 September 2002 the Federal President granted him a remission of the remaining sentence. The second applicant has since been released from detention on remand. The case is still pending in the Federal Court of Justice.

train_texts: A juror complained that the jury had been racially prejudiced. The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained that his case had not been heard by an impartial tribunal. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 of the Rules of Court) The applicant and the Government each filed written observations on the merits. By a decision of 29 June 1999, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The judge discussed the case with the jury and asked the juror who had written the complaint not to join the other jurors. The jury acquitted the applicant of the charge of conspiracy to defraud. The defence asked the judge to dismiss the jury on the ground that there was a real danger of bias. The judge decided to call the jury back into court and read out the complaint. The jury wrote two letters in response to the complaint, the first of which was signed by all the jurors. The second letter was written by a juror who appeared to have thought himself to have been the one who had been making the jokes. The juror in question explained at length that he might have done so, that he was sorry if he had given any offence, and that he thought he had been the only one making the joke. The judge decided that he would not discharge the jury and told them the following: “Ladies and gentlemen, the events of yesterday afternoon were clearly distressing for you, but I am sure you will see and realise that when a judge receives a note from one of your number raising those sort of issues it is the judge's duty to bring it to the attention of the whole jury” The jury found the applicant guilty, but acquitted G.C., who was also Asian. On 20 April 1995 the judge imposed on the applicant a sentence of five years' imprisonment. The applicant was given leave to appeal against conviction. In his appeal he raised, inter alia, the following ground: The judge should have reacted to the juror's complaint by dismissing the jury. The juror who had written the complaint should not have been segregated from the other members of the jury in the early stages. Judge dealt with possibility of tensions among the jurors perfectly sensibly in the direction he gave to them. However, it would be unrealistic to suppose that the jury would not have wanted to know who the author of the complaint was. Other members of the jury, as this led to his identification, were also asked to take part in the investigation into the death penalty. The jury was told they would be able to vote on the question of whether to convict or acquit the killer if they wanted to. The verdict was returned in favour of the prosecution, and the jury was then told they could decide whether or not to convict the killer.

The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained that his case had not been heard by an impartial tribunal because, allegedly, the jury had been racially prejudiced. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). By a decision of 29 June 1999, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Government of the United Kingdom were represented by their Agent, Ms S. Langrish, of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The judge discussed the case and ruled that the application was not admissible and that the jury's actions had been fair and just. The judge received a complaint from one of the jurors. He discussed the. complaint with counsel in chambers and then adjourned and listened to submissions in open court. The defence asked the judge to dismiss the jury on the ground that there was a real danger of bias. The judge, however, decided to call the jury back into court, at which stage the juror who had written the complaint joined the others. The next morning the judge received two letters from the jury. The first letter, which was signed by all the jurors, stated that we intend to reach a verdict solely according to the evidence and without racial bias. A second letter was written by a juror. who appeared to have thought himself to have been the one who had been making the jokes. The judge decided that he would not discharge the jury and told them the following: “Ladies and gentlemen, the events of yesterday afternoon were clearly distressing for you, but I am sure you will see and realise that when a judge receives a note from one of your number raising those sort of issues it is the judge's duty to bring it to the attention of the whole jury’ The jury found the applicant guilty, but acquitted G.C. who was also Asian. On 20 April 1995 the judge imposed on the applicant a sentence of five years' imprisonment. On 1 March 1996 the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal. Judge dealt with the possibility of tensions among the jurors perfectly sensibly in the direction he gave to them. However, it would be unrealistic to suppose that the jury would not have wanted to know who the author of the complaint was. Other members of the jury, as this led to his identification, were also asked to identify themselves. The judge dealt with this possibility of tension among the jury in the same way as he dealt with tensions among other members of it. He gave them the option of identifying themselves in a way that would have led them to identify each other. The jury were asked to name themselves and identify themselves to the judge.
