name: Einar Strömblad
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 3684/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that the Swedish courts’ protracted custody proceedings, including their handling of his. request for the return of his daughter under the Hague Convention, violated Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the. the Convention. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fifth Section of the Court on 1 February 2011. The application was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The proceedings relating to custody and rights of contact relating to the applicant’s daughter, N., were heard in the Fifth Section. The applicant and his wife sought sole custody of their daughter. He wanted contact rights to be exercised on a regular basis according to a specific schedule. The court found it to be in the child’s best interest to live with L. even though L., by moving to Prague, had made it more difficult for N. to see her father. The parties were left to agree on where it would be best for the applicant and the applicant to meet. On 13 December 2005 the Court of Appeal upheld the lower court's decision in full. It found that no circumstances had been presented which indicated that the District Court's decision was not in the best interests of the child. The applicant requested the District Court to change its interim decision, inter alia, in respect of N’s place of residence and the contact rights. He claimed that the interim decision in force had made it impossible for him to create meaningful contact with N., since it was too expensive to travel to Prague every other weekend. The Court of Appeal rejected the appeal, noting that it was not legally possible for it to decide where a child should live; it could only decide with whom. The court found it to be in the best interests of N. to keep the interim arrangements until final judgment was delivered in the case. The hearing was cancelled and the applicant and N. did not therefore meet as scheduled in Sweden. The applicant applied to the Swedish Ministry for Foreign Affairs for assistance for the return of N. to Sweden in accordance with the Hague Convention of 25 October 1980 on the Civil Aspects of International Child Protection. The Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal on 29 September 2010. On 8 December 2010 the Supreme Court refused leave for the applicant to appeal. The applicant appealed against the judgment on 27 July 2010. The court decided that L. should have the sole custody of N and granted the applicant a right of contact with N. four days in a row on a monthly basis, which should gradually be increased. The District Court held that both the applicant and L. were suitable parents. It concluded that the fact that N. had not seen her father for the last five years was to a large extent caused by L’s behaviour. The applicant contacted the Ministry for Foreign Affairs in May 2006 expressing his concern and requesting that the Ministry put some pressure on the Czech Central Authority. The application was forwarded to the District Court in Kristianstad. The District Court declared that L.’s retention of N. in the Czech Republic was not unlawful within the meaning of Article 3 of the Hague Convention. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal, claiming that the. District Court should have focused on the actual removal of N from Sweden by L. and not on the retention. In his view, the removal had been unlawful and the Hague. Convention was therefore applicable. The Supreme Court rejected the application on 1 February 2007. The applicant appealed against the decision to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Skåne, demanding that the Tax Authority’s decision be repealed. The applicant lodged a further appeal to the Supreme Administrative Court, maintaining his claims and invoking Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention. The Court of Appeal in Gothenburg refused leave to appeal. On 18 December 2006 theSupreme Administrative Court refused leave for the appeal to be heard. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that both parents, since they had joint custody, had to agree on the appeal. The case is still pending in the Supreme Court of Sweden.

This was a violation of his rights under Article 8 and, consequently, he had a right under Article 13 to have an effective remedy.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 3684/07) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that the Swedish courts’ protracted custody proceedings, including their handling of his request for the return of his daughter under the Hague Convention, violated Articles 6, 8 and 13. The Swedish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr B. Sjöberg, of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The application was assigned to the newly composed Fifth Section of the Court on 1 February 2011. The proceedings relating to custody and rights of contact relate to the case of Mr Einar Strömblad and his daughter N. L. agreed to the divorce but opposed the applicant’s requests in relation to their daughter. She wanted sole custody of N. but agreed, pending the final outcome of the proceedings, that the applicant could visit N. in Prague for a few hours every other weekend with her or her mother (N.'s maternal grandmother) present. The applicant appealed against the decision to the Court of Appeal (hovrätten) of Skåne and Blekinge, maintaining his requests for sole custody and for her to live with him. In the alternative, he wanted his right of contact with N. to be exercised in southern Sweden. The applicant requested the District Court to change its interim decision, inter alia, in respect of N.’s place of residence and the contact rights. He claimed that the interim decision in force had made it impossible for him to create meaningful contact with N. The Court of Appeal rejected the appeal, noting that it was not legally possible for it to decide where a child should live; it could only decide with whom. No appeal lay against the decision. The hearing was cancelled and, apparently, the applicant and N. did not therefore meet as scheduled in Sweden. On 13 March 2008 the District. Court decided that N. should meet with the applicant for four hours on 8 December 2007 and for 4 hours on 9 December 2007 in. Sweden. The date for the main hearing in the case was fixed for 11 and 12 December 2007. The applicant applied to the Swedish Ministry for Foreign Affairs for assistance for the return of N. in accordance with the Hague Convention of 25 October 1980 on the Civil Aspects of International Child Rights. On 27 July 2010 the District Court, after having held an oral hearing, delivered its judgment. The court decided that L. should have the sole custody of N and granted the applicant a right of contact with N. four days in a row on a monthly basis, which should gradually be increased. The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Court of Appeal, which refused leave to appeal on 29 September 2010. On 8 December 2010 the Supreme Court refused left to appeal. The applicant contacted the Ministry for Foreign Affairs in May 2006 expressing his concern and requesting that the Ministry put some pressure on the Czech Central Authority. The application was forwarded to the Swedish Central Authority in charge of matters falling under the Hague Convention. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal, claiming that the District Court should have focused on the actual removal of N. from Sweden by L. and not on the retention. In his view, the removal had been unlawful and the Hague convention was therefore applicable. On 1 February 2007 the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) for re-opening of the case rejected the application. The applicant opposed the change of N’s place of residence in the Swedish population register (folkbokföringen) since he considered the removal of N. to be unlawful and the custody proceedings were still ongoing. He considered that since the custody case and the proceedings relating to his demand under the Hague Convention were still pending, the Tax Authority should not prejudge those proceedings by removing N. from the population register as having emigrated. The applicant appealed against the decision to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Skåne, demanding that the decision be repealed. The Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal.

name: Bolesław Dudek
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was born in 1959 and lives in Hamburg, Germany. On 25 July 2001 the applicant was arrested by the police. On 16 April 2002, the Bielsko-Biała Regional Court again prolonged the applicant’s detention. The court considered that, given the fact that the applicant had been living in Germany, there was a real risk that he might go into hiding. In addition, it found that the case was complex as it concerned an organised criminal group. The applicant’s detention on remand was prolonged and his applications for release dismissed. The applicant was acquitted of the charges of being a member of an organised criminal group. The remaining part of the proceedings, which was remitted by the Katowice Court of Appeal, is pending. The appeal was partly allowed on 16 December 2004 and the applicant was released from detention on 30 January 2004. He was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment, but this was quashed and remitted. The case is pending at the Supreme Court of Poland, which has yet to issue a decision. The application has been brought by a man whose name has been changed to protect his identity.

The court repeated grounds given previously: the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offences, the severity of the anticipated sentence, the complexity of the case and the risk that the applicant might go into hiding. name: Vereinigung Bildender Künstler
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 68354/01) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant association alleged that the Austrian courts' decisions forbidding it to continue exhibiting a painting by Otto Mühl had violated its right to freedom of expression. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Court declared the application admissible in a decision of 30 June 2005. The case was settled in favour of the applicant association and the Austrian Government in August 2005.  FPÖ member of the National Assembly (Nationalratsabgeordneter) Mr Meischberger was shown in sexual positions with two other politicians and ejaculating on Mother Teresa. The painting was damaged by a visitor, who covered with red paint the part which showed him. He sought an injunction prohibiting it from exhibiting and publishing the painting. The Vienna Commercial Court dismissed his action on 6 August 1999. It noted that it had initially been intended to show a picture of a group of men in sexual situations with Bishop Groer and Mother Teresa, and had been changed to show the former FPÄ general secretary of the Austrian National Assembly. The Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) issued an injunction against the applicant association prohibiting it from continuing to display the painting at exhibitions. It ordered it to pay the costs incurred by Mr Meischberger in the proceedings and ATS 20,000 (EUR 1,453.46), plus 4% interest with effect from 8 July 1998, in compensation. The court further added that there appeared to be no danger of recurrence (Wiederholungsgefahr) as the painting had been partly covered by red paint and Mr Meischerberger was therefore no longer recognisable on it. The limits of artistic freedom were exceeded when the image of a person was substantially deformed. The painting in the present case was not intended to be a parable or even an exaggerated criticism conveying a basic message. It therefore did not fall within the scope of Article 10 of the Convention, but in fact constituted a debasement of Mr Meischberger's public standing. The applicant association could not justify the exhibition of the painting under the artistic freedom protected by Article 17a of the Basic Law (Staatsgrundsgesetz) The Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) rejected an appeal by the applicant association as it did not concern a legal question of considerable interest. The Court of Appeal had not contradicted the documents contained in the court file and there was therefore no need for a rectification.

He did not feel like working and financed his very costly lifestyle through crime. He had caused substantial material damage and had acted with considerable criminal energy. As confirmed by the convincing report of a psychiatric and neurological expert, Sa., it was to be expected that the applicant would commit further offences against the property of others if released. He confessed to the police that he had been involved in the murder of a certain İ.G. The applicant’s detention in police custody and the medical reports issued in his respect have not been found to show signs of physical ill-treatment. He is currently serving his prison sentence in Muğla Prison. The application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant was taken before the public prosecutor and the judge. Still waiving his right to legal assistance, the applicant repeated the statement he had given to the police. The judge ordered his pre-trial detention and the applicant was placed in Fethiye Prison. The other co-accused, Y.A., who had allegedly killed İ.G. according to the applicant’s statement, was arrested. The applicant complained of pain in his left ear and that he should therefore be examined by an ear, nose and throat specialist. According to the medical report, the doctor found two bruises 5-6 cm wide and 30 cm long. The doctor noted that the bruises had been caused by a blunt object 24 to 48 hours before. Y.A. and the applicant were convicted of the murder of İ.G. in Fethiye, Turkey in 2004. They were sentenced to life imprisonment commuted to sixteen years and eight months’ imprisonment. The trial was adjourned until 17 December 2004, and the appeal was rejected on 20 December 2004. It was the first time a Turkish man had been sentenced to more than three years in jail.

name: Mehmet Erdagöz
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the Government of the Republic of Turkey (“the Government”) on 18 September 1996. It originated in an application (no. 21890/93) against Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) under Article 25 by a Turkish national, Mr Mehmet Erdagöz, on 1 May 1993. The object of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 5 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent him (Rule 30). The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 26 June 1997. The Court heard addresses by Mr Martínez, Mr Kaplan, Mr Yılmaz and Mrs Akçay. As Mr Walsh was unable to take part in the deliberations on 22 September 1997, Sir John Freeland, substitute judge, replaced him as a member of the Chamber. The outcome of these proceedings is not known. The circumstances of the case are as follows: Mr Mehmet Erdagöz, a Turkish national, was the owner of a shop in Adana. On 3 June 1992 a brawl broke out between the applicant and members of his family and a Mr H.A. and his friends on the other. The applicant returned to the police station to have the premises searched again before he opened the shop. He also named the persons he suspected of the attack, including H.A., but decided against lodging a complaint and left the station. A police squad conducted a fresh search of the scene of the crime. According to the report drawn up at the time, at 11.30 a.m., no bullet marks were found. In a judgment of 28 June 1993 the Criminal Court acquitted him for lack of sufficient evidence. The Court of Cassation upheld this judgment on 28 February 1994. The applicant was transferred to security police headquarters for detailed questioning. The applicant lodged a criminal complaint against the chief inspector and Deputy Inspector S.K. with the public prosecutor. He alleged that during the inquiries into the altercation of 3 June 1992 the former had abused his authority by drawing up a biased report. Mr Erdagöz was released the same day, at a time which has not been specified. The Adana public prosecutor, after conducting an investigation, concluded that the allegation of abusing authority was unfounded and decided not to pursue the investigation concerning the chief. inspector. The applicant’s complaints against the police were dismissed by the prosecutor. The first complaint was that the applicant had falsely reported a criminal offence. The second was that he had been subjected to ill-treatment. Mehmet Erdagöz accused of falsely reporting a criminal offence. Allegations that police insulted him and took him into police custody for forty-eight hours. Adana public prosecutor discontinued proceedings against two officers in December 1993. The applicant appealed against the discontinuation order to the President of the Tarsus Assize Court, who dismissed the appeal on 23 February 1993. On 8 March 1993 the applicant petitioned the Minister of Justice to lodge an appeal in the interests of the law. On 29 March 1993, the minister of Justice refused. The second complaint was dismissed on 17 September 1992. The third complaint against the chief inspector and another policeman, A.K., was dismissed in December 1992. ‘Mr Erdagöz was suspected of falsely reporting a criminal offence and the object of the inquiry was therefore modified and an investigation in two branches conducted. As the police had not found any pertinent evidence that the offence had been committed, the complainant was referred to the public prosecutor’s office by an order of 17 September 1992. Contrary to his allegations, he was not taken into police custody for forty-eight hours but necessarily held for twenty-four hours so that the inquiry could be completed. Moreover, there is no evidence to support the allegations of defamation.’ ‘On 15 February 1994 the applicant appealed against the above discontinuation order to the President of the Assize Court. He alleged in particular that his detention in police custody had lasted for two days and had been due to the resentment the police felt towards him on account of his previous complaints’

The Court heard addresses by Mr Martínez, Mr Kaplan, Mr Yılmaz and Mrs Akçay. The outcome of these proceedings is not known. The case was brought by a Turkish national, Mehmet Erdagöz, a shop owner in Adana, who was accused of throwing stones at his shop during a brawl in 1992. The Turkish national was charged with armed assault, attempted murder and offences under the Firearms Act. The applicant returned to the police station and handed over two spent cartridge cases which he claimed to have found inside his shop. He also lodged a complaint and demanded the arrest of H.A., who had allegedly organised the attack out of animosity towards the applicant. A police squad conducted a fresh search of the scene of the crime. According to the report drawn up at the time, at 11.30 a.m., no bullet marks were found. In a judgment of 28 June 1993 the Criminal Court acquitted him for lack of sufficient evidence. The Court of Cassation upheld this judgment on 28 February 1994. Deprivation of the applicant’s liberty. The applicant’s complaints against the police were made on 17 September 1992. He alleged that during the inquiries into the altercation of 3 June 1992 the former had abused his authority by drawing up a biased report of the incident. He accused S.K. of inflicting ill-treatment on him when he first went to the police station, at 5.30 a.m., following the events of the night of 15 to 16 September. The next day, at the request of the police, Mr Erdagöz had a medical examination at the social security hospital in Adana. The provisional report mentions the following injuries: superficial grazing on the left side of the back and bruises and swelling below both knees. Mehmet Erdagöz accused of falsely reporting a criminal offence. Complainant was taken into custody for forty-eight hours even though he was the complainant. The case was dismissed on appeal by the President of the Tarsus Assize Court on 23 February 1993. There is no conclusive evidence that the lesions noted in the report were the result of blows inflicted by the deputy inspector; there is therefore insufficient evidence to prosecute him. The Minister of Justice refused to lodge an appeal in the interests of the law on 29 March 1993. The second complaint was dropped on 6 December 1993 after the Adana public prosecutor discontinued the proceedings against two officers. Mr Erdagöz was suspected of falsely reporting a criminal offence and the object of the inquiry was modified and an investigation in two branches conducted. As the police had not found any pertinent evidence that the offence had been committed, the complainant was referred to the public prosecutor’s office by an order of 17 September 1992. He alleged in particular that his detention in police custody had lasted for two days and had been due to the resentment the police felt towards him on account of his previous complaints to the European Commission of Human Rights and the domestic courts. On 7 March 1994 the President of the Tarsus Assize Court dismissed the appeal and on 24 June 1994 the Minister of Justice refused a petition in which he had asked him to lodge an appeal.

The applicant was suspected of falsely reporting a criminal offence and the object of the inquiry was therefore modified and an investigation in two branches conducted. name: Susan Anne Allen
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18837/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the fact that she was not allowed to attend the hearing of the prosecution's appeal against her being granted bail had breached her rights under Article 5 and 6. The application was given notice to the Government on 14 May 2008. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The applicant was granted legal aid and was represented by a lawyer practising in Liverpool. The Government were represented by their Agent, Ms E. Willmott, of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London. Judge Globe refused the applicant's request to be present at the appeal hearing. He said it would set a precedent for any defendant in custody wishing to attend an appeal against bail in the future. The applicant's counsel said she was a respectable woman of good background and a vulnerable person. The judge said he was not going to alter his view in relation to the applicant being present during the hearing and would listen to her submissions. He added that the basis for his application was “common humanity” and “not technical”. The application was dismissed on a technicality and the application was rejected on the basis that the applicant was being dealt with fairly. The applicant applied for permission to apply for judicial review of the decision not to allow her to attend the hearing on the ground that her rights under the Convention had been breached. On 9 November 2005 Mr Justice Sullivan refused the applicant's application for permission. The applicant's first application to the Court of Appeal was rejected on the grounds that she was not entitled to be present. The application was later rejected on grounds that the judge had not given her enough time to prepare for the hearing. The appeal was dismissed on the basis that the decision to refuse her bail was not unreasonable. The hearing was adjourned and the application was rejected. The case was heard again on 12 November 2005, and the decision was upheld. The applicant's grounds for applying for permission to seek judicial review did not explain why hers was an exceptional case or why the interests of justice required her attendance whilst she was legally represented. Mr Justice Sullivan took into account Judge Globe's clear indication that he would be prepared to reconsider his view and allow the applicant to be present if there was anything that would require him to hear evidence from her in person. But counsel representing the applicant had not been able to identify what would be gained by producing the applicant. The judge left open the possibility of altering his decision if, for example, it became apparent that oral evidence might be required from the applicant in support of her application. Mr Justice Gibbs said. was authorised to exercise judicial power as required by Article 5 § 3 of the Convention and clearly had exercised it, even though his decision was subject to immediate appeal. The legal framework covering applications for bail, including appeals, did in Mr Justice Gibbs view enable her to take proceedings whereby the lawfulness of her detention could be decided speedily by a court, he said. There was, in his judgment, nothing even arguably to be found in the wording of Article 5§ 4 which entitled an applicant to be present at such proceedings in all instances. Rule 19.17 (4) provided a Convention compatible procedure to ensure that no injustice was caused to an applicant in cases in which he or she was not permitted to bePresent.

The case originated in an application (no. 18837/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the fact that she was not allowed to attend the hearing of the prosecution's appeal against her being granted bail had breached her rights under Article 5 and 6. The application was examined by the Court at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The case was heard by the Supreme Court of England and Wales on 14 May 2008. The decision was made to allow the application to be heard. The case is adjourned until 11 October 2009, when it will be heard again. Judge Globe refused the request, reasoning that the applicant could be given a full report of what had happened from her counsel. He emphasised that this was a re-hearing and rather unusual as it was the prosecution which had sought to appeal the Deputy District Judge's ruling on bail. In refusing the applicant permission to attend, Judge Globe stated: “I am not going to alter my view in relation to [the applicant] being present during the hearing. I will listen to your submissions.” If there is anything during your submissions that causes me to hear evidence from her or to have to do something different to what I am doing at the moment, I will reconsider it. The applicant applied for permission to apply for judicial review of the decision not to allow her to attend the hearing on the ground that her rights under the Convention had been breached. On 9 November 2005 Mr Justice Sullivan refused the application. The application was the applicant's first application to the Court of Appeal for a judicial review. She was denied permission to attend because the judge believed she was at risk of absconding and giving information about the case which would obstruct the course of justice. The appeal was heard in the absence of the applicant, and the judge ruled that she was entitled to be present in court in an exceptional circumstances. The applicant appealed again and was granted permission to appear in court. Mr Justice Sullivan took into account Judge Globe's clear indication that he would be prepared to reconsider his view and allow the applicant to be present if there was anything that would require him to hear evidence from her in person. But counsel representing the applicant had not been able to identify what would be gained by producing the applicant. The applicant's grounds for applying for permission to seek judicial review did not explain why hers was an exceptional case or why the interests of justice required her attendance whilst she was legally represented. Mr Justice Gibbs found that the Deputy District Judge had not fulfilled the first exception to Rule 19.17 (4) as the applicant was not acting in person as the case was of an exceptional nature. Mr Justice Gibbs said the judge was authorised to exercise judicial power as required by Article 5 § 3 of the Convention and clearly had exercised it. He said there was nothing even arguably to be found in the wording of Article 5 ° 4 which entitled an applicant to be present at such proceedings in all instances. Mr Justice Gibbs also said that Rule 19.17 (4) provided a Convention compatible procedure to ensure that no injustice was caused to an applicant in cases in which he or she was not permitted to bePresent. He added that the ruling was subject to immediate appeal and was not put into effect pending appeal. The judge's decision was upheld by the Court of Appeal.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the fact that she was not allowed to attend the hearing of the prosecution's appeal against her being granted bail had breached her rights under Article 5 §§ 3 and 4 and Article 6. On 14 May 2008 the President of the Chamber decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The application was brought by Ms Susan Anne Allen (“the applicant”), who had been granted legal aid, on 2 May 2006. Judge Globe refused the request, reasoning that the applicant could be given a full report of what had happened from her counsel. Judge Globe explained that if he allowed the applicant to be present it would set a precedent for any defendant in custody wishing to attend an appeal against bail in the future. He emphasised that this was a re-hearing and rather unusual as it was the prosecution which had sought to appeal the Deputy District Judge's ruling on bail. As the applicant was already present in the building, her production would cause little inconvenience. In refusing the applicant permission to attend, Judge Globe stated: “I am not going to alter my view in relation to [the applicant] being present during the hearing.” The applicant's first application for permission to apply for judicial review was refused in 2005. Mr Justice Sullivan refused the applicant's request to review the decision not to allow her to attend the hearing. The applicant then applied to the European Court of Human Rights for review of the decision to refuse bail. The application was refused on the grounds that her rights under the Convention had been breached. On 9 November 2005 the application was finally granted and the appeal was heard. The hearing was held in the person of the applicant, who was not in court at the time. Judge Globe refused to allow the prosecution appeal and refused bail. He ruled that the applicant was entitled to be present if, in an exceptional circumstances, she was in fact in the court. Mr Justice Sullivan took into account Judge Globe's clear indication that he would be prepared to reconsider his view and allow the applicant to be present if there was anything that would require him to hear evidence from her in person. The applicant's grounds for applying for permission to seek judicial review did not explain why hers was an exceptional case or why the interests of justice required her attendance whilst she was legally represented. Mr Justice Gibbs found that the Deputy District Judge had made a mistake when he refused the applicant's renewed application for. permission to bring judicial review proceedings. The judge had referred to the position of the co-defendant and had made an enquiry as to whether there was any particular reason to believe that injustice would occur. Mr Justice Gibbs said that he was authorised to exercise judicial power as required by Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. However, his decision was subject to immediate appeal and was not put into effect pending appeal. There was, in his judgment, nothing even arguably to be found in the wording of Article 5§ 4 which entitled an applicant to be present at such proceedings in all instances. Where prosecution appeals against refusal of bail were concerned, Rule 19.17 (4) provided a Convention compatible procedure to ensure that no injustice was caused to an applicant in cases in which he or she was not permitted to be at the hearing. Mr Justice Gibbs ruled that the applicant was entitled to take proceedings whereby the lawfulness of her detention could be decided speedily by a court.

name: Colin Laskey
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 11 December 1995. It originated in three applications (nos. 21627/93, 21826/93 and 21974/93) lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 14 December 1992 by three British nationals. The late Mr Laskey’s father and the two other applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent them (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President. Rights International, a New York-based non-governmental human rights organisation, submitted written comments on specified aspects of the case. The comments were received on 16 August 1996. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 21 October 1996. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr I. Christie, Assistant Legal Adviser, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr D. Pannick QC, Mr M. Shaw, Counsel, Mr S. Bramley, Ms B. Moxon, Advisers. For the applicants Lord Lester of Herne Hill QC, Ms A. Worrall QC, Counsel,. Mr D D. Jonas, Mr A. Hamilton,Mr I. Geffen, Solicitors, Mr J. Wadham, Adviser. The activities took place at a number of locations, including rooms equipped as torture chambers. Video cameras were used to record events and the tapes copied and distributed amongst members of the group. The infliction of pain was subject to certain rules including the provision of a code word to be used by any “victim’s” to stop an “assault’ The defendants pleaded guilty to the assault charges after the trial judge ruled that they could not rely on the consent of the ‘victims’ as an answer to the prosecution case. The trial judge commented that the unlawful conduct now before the court would be dealt with equally in the prosecution of heterosexuals or bisexuals. The applicants appealed against conviction and sentence. Since they did not appreciate that their actions in inflicting injuries were criminal, reduced sentences were imposed. The applicants appealed to the House of Lords on the following certified point of law of public importance. On 11 March 1993, the appeal, known as the case of R. v. Brown ([1993] 2 All England Law Reports 75), was dismissed. Lord Templeman, in the majority, held after reviewing the case-law that: “... the authorities dealing with the intentional infliction of bodily harm do not establish that consent is a defence to a charge under the Act of 1861’ It is an offence for a person to abuse his own body and mind by taking drugs. Although the law is often broken, the criminal law restrains a practice which is regarded as dangerous and injurious to individuals. Lord Jauncey of Tullichettle found that the line falls properly to be drawn between assault at common law and the offence of assault occasioning actual bodily harm created by section 47 of the 1861 Act. Society is entitled and bound to protect itself against a cult of violence. Pleasure derived from the infliction of pain is an evil thing. Cruelty is uncivilised.‘I am not prepared to invent a defence of consent for sado-masochistic encounters which breed and glorify cruelty’ There is no suggestion that the appellants and their associates are the only practitioners of homosexual sado-masochism in England and Wales. Wounds can easily become septic if not properly treated, the free flow of blood from a person who is HIV-positive or who has AIDS can infect another. An inflicter who is carried away by sexual excitement or by drink or drugs could very easily inflict pain and injury beyond the level to which the receiver had consented. The possibility of proselytisation and corruption of young men is a real danger even in the case of these appellants. The taking of video recordings of such activities suggests that secrecy may not be as strict as the appellant claimed to your Lordships. Lord Slynn of Hadley found that as the law stood adults were able to consent to acts done in private which did not result in serious bodily harm. He agreed that it was in the end a matter of policy in an area where social and moral factors were extremely important and where attitudes could change. It was however for the legislature to decide whether such conduct should be brought within the criminal law and not for the courts. All the applicants lost their jobs and Mr Jaggard required extensive psychiatric treatment. The proceedings were given widespread press coverage and were given extensive coverage by the BBC and ITV. The case was heard in the House of Lords on Tuesday.

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 11 December 1995. It originated in three applications (nos. 21627/93, 21826/93 and 21974/93) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 14 December 1992. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 8 of the Convention. The late Mr Laskey’s father and the two other applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent them. Rights International was granted leave to submit written comments on specified aspects of the case. The comments were received on 16 August 1996. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 21 October 1996. Three men were charged with a series of offences, including assault and wounding, relating to sado-masochistic activities that had taken place over a ten-year period. One of the charges involved a defendant who was not yet 21 years old - the age of consent to male homosexual practices at the time. Although the instances of assault were very numerous, the prosecution limited the counts to a small number of exemplary charges. name: Fikret Çetin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 24829/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the criminal proceedings brought against him had not been fair. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The case was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicant was born in 1969 and lives in Diyarbakır. The first trial of the applicant was held in 1994 and he was acquitted in 1999. On 6 June 2000 the applicant was released from police custody and was brought before a prosecutor and then before a judge, who questioned him further. The applicant denied the statements taken from him by police officers the previous day, and added that he had not been involved in any bombing. On 6 November 2001 the trial court found the applicant guilty of offences of membership of an illegal organisation and planting explosives. He was sentenced to seventeen years, four months and ten days' imprisonment. In his appeal against his conviction the applicant appealed against the conviction and was found not guilty on 13 November 2001. The application is now on appeal at the Supreme Court of Justice of Turkey. The Court of Cassation rejected the appeal and upheld the applicant's conviction. The decision was deposited with the registry of the trial court on 16 December 2002. The applicant argued, inter alia, that he had been subjected to ill-treatment in police custody and that he was forced to sign a number of documents. The prosecutor's observations were not communicated to the applicant. In his written observations submitted to the Court of. Cassation the prosecutor referred to the. applicant's allegations of ill- treatment. On 20 June 2002 the Court. of Cassated to reject the appeal. and uphold the applicant’s conviction. For more information on the appeal, visit www.cassation.org.

name: Wojciech Depa
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was made by a Polish national, Mr Wojciech Depa (‘the applicant’), on 26 May 1999. On 1 December 2005 the President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. It was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Kraków, Poland. On 13 July 1998, the applicant was indicted before the Kraków Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy). At a hearing held on 16 February 1999, at which the applicant, his lawyers were present, the court prolonged the applicant’s detention on remand. The court relied on the strong probability that the applicant had committed the offences and the advanced stage of the trial. The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. On 13 April 2000, the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, quashed the impugned judgment and remitted the case. On 24 August 2000 the K.R.C. extended the applicant's detention. The applicant was convicted of attempted murder and sentenced to 15 years' imprisonment. His numerous requests for release were to no avail. His appeals against the decisions to prolong his detention were dismissed at court sessions. The decisions were upheld on appeal by the Kraków Court of Appeal. The applicant’s court-appointed lawyer lodged on his behalf a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court (S.C.I.R). On 19 September 2002, the court partly allowed the appeal and the applicant was acquitted of the charge and his sentence was reduced to five years’ imprisonment. The case is now being heard in the High Court of Justice in Warsaw. The Supreme Court partly allowed the cassation appeal, quashed the appeal court’s judgment and remitted the case. On 24 June 2004 the Krakow Court of Appeal gave a judgment. The court amended its judgment of 19 September 2002 but it upheld the applicant's sentence. The judgment became final. The case was decided by the Supreme Court on 3 June 2003. The appeal court's judgment was quashed on 2 June 2003 and the case was remitted. The applicant received a sentence of 10 years in prison. The sentence was later reduced to five years and three months. The application was dismissed on 6 June 2004.

The case originated in an application (no. 62324/00) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Kraków, Poland. On 14 January 1998 the applicant was arrested by the police. On 16 January 1998 he was detained on remand in view of the reasonable suspicion that he had committed offences of kidnapping, sequestration, attempted murder and theft. On 1 December 2005 the President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. On 13 July 1998, the applicant was indicted before the Kraków Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy). At a hearing held on 16 February 1999, at which the applicant and his lawyers were present, the court prolonged the applicant’s detention. The court relied on the strong probability that the applicant had committed the offences and the advanced stage of the trial. The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. On 13 April 2000, the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, quashed the impugned judgment and remitted the case. The application for release and appeals against the decisions to prolong the detention were to no avail. Kraków Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s request to attend the session at which his appeal against the decision of 27 July 2000 was to be examined. The Court found that the severity of the anticipated penalty was a sufficient ground (“samodzielna przesłanka”) for his continued detention and was consistent with the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights. The applicant was acquitted of the charge of attempted murder and his sentence was reduced to five years’ imprisonment. The decisions were upheld on appeal by the Krakow Court of appeal. The applications and appeals against the decisions to prolong his detention were dismissed at court sessions. On 3 June 2003 the Supreme Court partly allowed the cassation appeal, quashed the appeal court’s judgment and remitted the case. On 24 June 2004 the Krakow Court of Appeal gave a judgment. The court amended its judgment of 19 September 2002 but it upheld the applicant's sentence. The judgment became final. The case is still pending in the Polish Supreme Court. It is the most high-profile case of its kind in modern Polish history. It was the subject of the film "Unguarded" (2003) by Polish director Arkadiusz Mladyk. The film is based on a novel by Polish writer Piotr Wojciechowski, which was published in 2003.

He appealed against those decisions arguing that there was no evidence that once released he would obstruct the proper course of the proceedings or abscond. Krakow Regional Court prolonged the applicant’s detention. The court relied on the strong probability that. the applicant had committed the offences and the advanced stage of the trial. The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. On 13 April 2000, the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, quashed the impugned judgment and remitted the case. The trial court held in total thirteen hearings in 1999 and 2000. Kraków Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s request to attend the session at which his appeal against the decision of 27 July 2000 was to be examined. The Court found that the severity of the anticipated penalty was a sufficient ground (“samodzielna przesłanka”) for his continued detention and was consistent with the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights. The applicant was acquitted of the charge of attempted murder and his sentence was reduced to five years’ imprisonment. The applications and appeals against the decisions to prolong his detention were dismissed at court sessions. The decisions were upheld on appeal by the Krakow Court of appeal. Subsequently, the applicant's court-appointed lawyer lodged on his behalf a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court. The Krakow Court of Appeal gave a judgment on 24 June 2004. name: Grzegorz Michal Braun
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30162/10) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his right to freedom of expression was breached in violation of Article 10. The Government contested that the applicant could be considered a journalist. The case has now been settled by the European Court of Human rights in Strasbourg. The verdict will be delivered on October 25, 2014, at 11.30am GMT (4.30pm ET) and is expected to last for up to four days. The judge will deliver the verdict by the end of the month. The court considered that the applicant had clearly used several expressions indicating that the claimant had been a secret collaborator with the communist-era secret services. The court noted that Mr J.M. was a distinguished linguist and well‑known person in Poland. He was a member of the Polish Language Council and for many years had been presenting a programme on television. Between 1975 and 1984 he had been summoned by agents of the secret services on five occasions for interviews in connection with applications he had made for passports and returns from stays abroad. This was not contested by the claimant, who had himself made this information public. Other notes from the Institute of National Remembrance (“IPN”) archives indicated that until 1989 a two-volume file on the claimanthad existed. The applicant submitted that once he had discovered that Mr J.M. was on the list of secret collaborators with the secret services it had been his duty to inform the public about it. He argued that he had not alleged that the claimant had caused harm to other people or had been paid for his services. The applicant lodged an appeal against the judgment. The court referred to the definition of collaboration contained in the 1997 Lustration Act and reiterated that collaboration had to be intentional, secret and consist of passing on information. It concluded that registration by the. secret services alone was not sufficient to consider that someone had been a secret. collaborator. The Wrocław Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. The Supreme Court announced the judgment and gave an oral summary of the reasons. The applicant was ordered to reimburse the claimant a further PLN 2,000 for the costs of the cassation proceedings. The text of the apology to be published by the applicant was as follows: “I apologise to Professor J.M. for having made, on 20 April 2007, the untrue assertion that he had been an informer of the [communist-era] political police’”. The court considered that the applicant had not fulfilled his duty to act with particular diligence and caution in making serious allegations. The court agreed with the facts as established by the lower courts in particular as regards the conclusion that the statement made by the applicant had not been true. Imposing an obligation on a journalist to prove the veracity of each statement would unjustifiably limit the freedom of the press in a democratic society. The applicant could not be considered to be a journalist with a socially necessary duty to inform. The court considered that making an untrue statement that offended the personal rights of a person would always be contrary to the law. An untrue statement would remain illegal even if all efforts had been made to diligently collect and examine its factual basis. The question of due diligence would be taken into account only when assessing the fault of the defendant.

Case originated in an application (no. 30162/10) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention. Polish linguist claimed he was a secret collaborator with the communist-era secret services. Warsaw Regional Court allowed the action. The applicant was also ordered to publish an apology for having damaged the claimant’s good name in six national and regional newspapers, on three national TV channels and on Radio Wrocław. The court noted that Mr J.M. was a distinguished linguist and well‑known person in Poland. He had been summoned by agents of the secret services on five occasions between 1975 and 1984. The applicant submitted that once he had discovered that Mr J.M. was on the list of secret collaborators with the secret services it had been his duty to inform the public about it. The court referred to the definition of collaboration contained in the 1997 Lustration Act and reiterated that collaboration had to be intentional, secret and consist of passing on information. It concluded that registration by the. secret services alone was not sufficient to consider that someone had been a. secret collaborator. The applicant lodged an appeal against the judgment and the court noted that no documents confirming that the claimant had agreed to be a collaborator or that he had actively reported to the secret. services were available. Wrocław Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. The Supreme Court announced the judgment and gave an oral summary of the reasons. The applicant was ordered to reimburse the claimant a further PLN 2,000 for the costs of the cassation proceedings. The text of the apology to be published by the applicant was as follows: “I apologise to Professor J.M. for having made, on 20 April 2007, the untrue assertion that he had been an informer of the [communist-era] political police’“. The court considered that the applicant had not fulfilled his duty to act with particular diligence and caution in making serious allegations. The court agreed with the facts as established by the lower courts in particular as regards the conclusion that the statement made by the applicant had not been true. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 53645/10) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant claims that the police officers pulled his ears and he was beaten and subjected to falaka (beating on the soles of his feet) The applicant was represented by Mr O. Gündoğdu, a lawyer practising in Kars. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent. The application was communicated to the Government on 29 November 2012. The case was heard by the European Court of Justice on 14 July 2013. On 9 May 2002 the Kars Criminal Court declared that it lacked jurisdiction, holding that the proceedings should be initiated before the Assize Court on account of torture under Article 243 of the former Criminal Code. The court found it established that the police officers had intentionally ill-treated the applicant to extract a confession. The officers were sentenced to one year imprisonment and banned from public service for six months. The sentence was later reduced to ten months' imprisonment and five months’ ban from publicService. The applicant joined the proceedings as a civil party and the case was heard by the Assizes Court on 15 June 2010. The police officers were found guilty of inflicting torture pursuant to Article 243. of the Former Criminal Code and sentenced to a year imprisonment.

name: Geoffrey Robins
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 16 September 1996. It originated in an application (no. 22410/93) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and sought leave to present their own case. However, the President of the Chamber, Mr R. Bernhardt, declined to grant the requested leave and the applicants subsequently designated the lawyer who would represent them. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality. The applicants, Mr and Mrs Robins, are resident in Crediton, Devon and in London. The background to the case is a dispute between neighbours over sewerage. Initially the applicants’ neighbours instituted proceedings seeking damages for problems experienced with their sewerage, allegedly caused by work carried out by the applicants. On 1 May 1991, Judge Clarke gave judgment against the applicants and their appeal was subsequently dismissed by the Court of Appeal. On 25 April 1997 the Chamber decided to dispense with a hearing in the case, having satisfied itself that the conditions for this derogation from its usual procedure had been met (Rules 26 and 38). The Government, applicants and Commission were invited to submit written comments. The applicants first applied for legal aid in November 1991. A report was sent to the parties on 14 January 1992. A fresh Department of Social Security assessment of the applicants’ means was required in view of the fact that they had separated. The DSS later explained, in a letter filed with the court on 10 November 1992, that a delay of nine months had been caused because of a misapprehension in this respect. The applicants sought legal aid to appeal against this decision. On 11 January 1993 they applied for an extension of time, since the time-limit for appealing the costs order had expired on 11 December 1992. Subsequently queries were raised by a lawyer in the Civil Appeals Office as to whether leave to appeal was required. The applicants were requested to lodge the relevant documents by 2 May 1994. Extensions of this time-limit were granted on 25 April, 24 May, 16 June, 6 July and again on 27 July 1994 at the request of the applicants. It later transpired that Judge Clarke’s notes had been either lost or did not exist. On 6 October 1994, the applicants’ request that transcripts of the judgment of Judge Darwall-Smith be produced at public expense. Another extension of the time- Limit for the submission of documents was granted, upon the applicants' request, on 16 February 1995. On 29 March 1995 the application was listed for hearing. After the hearing on 19 June 1995, the Court of Appeal confirmed Judge Dar wall Smith's judgment of 13 November 1992 and dismissed the appeal.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 12050/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the sum set for bail in his case had been excessive and had been fixed without his personal circumstances being taken into consideration. The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court. On 1 February 2008 the Court changed the composition of its Sections. The case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section. On 8 January 2009 the Chamber, composed of Josep Casadevall, President, Elisabet Fura, Corneliu Bîrsan, Boštjan M. Zupančič, Egbert Myjer, Ineta Ziemele, judges, and Alejandro Saiz Arnaiz, ad hoc judge, delivered a judgment. The case was referred to the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights on 5 June 2009. A hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 September 2009. The Court heard addresses by Mr Fitzgerald and Mr Blasco. in which it held unanimously that there had been no violation of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. The applicant was born in 1935 and lives in Greece. The ship Prestige, flying the flag of the Bahamas, was sailing in the Spanish exclusive economic zone off the coast of Galicia, carrying 70,000 tonnes of fuel oil. At a distance of 28 miles from the applicant, the ship came into contact with the vessel. The oil spill blackened beaches and cliffs, destroyed marine life, adversely affected water quality and had an immediate environmental impact on numerous animal species. The spillage of the ship’s cargo caused an ecological disaster whose effects on marine flora and fauna lasted for several months and spread as far as the French coast. The applicant's conduct could constitute an offence of causing damage to natural resources and the environment and one of failing to comply with the instructions of the administrative authorities. A judge remanded the applicant in custody and set bail at 3,000,000 euros (EUR), after finding that the facts of the case disclosed sufficient indicative evidence to justify opening a criminal investigation. The investigation has produced sufficient indicative evidence to suggest that Mr Apostolos Mangouras could be criminally responsible for the offences in question. It is clear at this stage that the Prestige did not have any emergency towing equipment or that if it did, it was not in working order, as demonstrated by the recordings of conversations. The ship’s Master, by repeatedly ignoring the instructions of the port authorities, hampered meaningful joint efforts to lessen the extremely serious risks. Without prejudice to all of the above, the accused's detention could be dispensed with subject to bail being furnished in the amount of. under Article 556 of the Code. The judge took the view that the seriousness of the offences of which the applicant stood accused justified his continued pre-trial detention. The judge stated that the applicant’s appearance at trial was vital in order to elucidate the sequence of events following the leak in the vessel. An appeal by the applicant was dismissed on 3 January 2003 by the Corunna Audiencia Provincial on the ground that there was sufficient evidence to charge the applicant with serious offences and that the amount of bail was justified by the unusual circumstances of the case. The applicant had been remanded in custody on account of his “alleged involvement in his ‘alleging involvement in the leak’ The Audiencia Provincial dismissed the ground of appeal based on the applicability of Article 230 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea of 10 December 1982. The judge ordered the applicant’s provisional release after eighty-three days in detention, subject to the following conditions. It referred in that regard to the category of offences in question and the severity of the likely sentence, the fact that the accused's presence was essential to the investigation, the possibility that the trial might collapse if he absconded and the public outcry surrounding the established facts. On 6 February 2003 the Corcubión (Corunna) no. 1 investigating judge recorded the lodging of a bank guarantee in an amount corresponding to the sum set for bail, which was provided as a one-off humanitarian gesture. On 28 May 2003 the London P and I Club and the ship’s owner, Mare Shipping Inc., paid out EUR 22,777,986 in compensation for the damage for which they were civilly liable within the limits laid down by Article V of the 1992 International Convention on Civil Liability for Oil Pollution Damage. The applicant lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court. While he did not appeal against his pre-trial detention, he complained of the amount set for bail. He alleged that the amount had been fixed without account being taken of his personal circumstances. The Constitutional Court declared the appeal inadmissible in a reasoned decision (auto) of 29 September 2003. The judge took into account the national and international disaster caused by the oil spill, the fact that the accused is a non‑national and that he has no ties in Spain. In March 2005, the Spanish authorities authorised the applicant’s return to his country of origin, where he is now living. The criminal proceedings are currently pending before the Corcubión (Corunna) no. 1 investigating judge. The applicant is therefore required to report every two weeks to a police station on the island of Icaria. or in Athens, where his children live. The exceptional amount reflects the exceptional nature of the situation.”

The ship’s Master, by repeatedly ignoring the instructions of the port authorities, hampered meaningful joint efforts to lessen the extremely serious risks. Without prejudice to all of the above, the accused's detention could be dispensed with subject to bail being furnished in the amount of under Article 556 of the Code. The applicant complained of the amount set for bail, arguing that it had been excessive and disproportionate in view of his financial circumstances and had made any prospect of provisional release unrealistic. He alleged that the amount had been fixed without account being taken of his personal circumstances, in disregard of the requirements of the court's case-law. By a reasoned decision (auto) of 29 September 2003 the Constitutional Court declared the appeal inadmissible. The court took into account the national and international disaster caused by the oil spill, the fact that the accused is a non‑national and that he has no ties in Spain. The court also took into consideration the accused’s personal and financial circumstances and his professional environment. It follows that bail was fixed on the basis of criteria of proportionality ... It also referred to the fact that the accused's presence was essential to the investigation, the possibility that the trial might collapse if he absconded and the public outcry surrounding the established facts. The Audiencias Provincial dismissed the ground of appeal based on the applicability of Article 230 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea of 10 December 1982, holding that the provision in question referred only to administrative offences relating to pollution of the marine environment. London P and I Club and the ship’s owner, Mare Shipping Inc., paid out EUR 22,777,986 in compensation for the damage for which they were civilly liable. name: Tuan Tran Pham Hoang
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 7 June 1991. It originated in an application (no. 13191/87) against the French Republic lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of that State, Mr Tuan Tran Pham Hoang, on 20 August 1987. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 paras. 1, 2 and 3 (c) (Art 6-1, art. 6-2, 6-3-c). The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 21 April 1992. The Court heard addresses by Mrs Belliard for the Government, Mr Schermers for the Commission and Mr Lestourneaud for the applicant, as well as replies to its question. Mr Hoang, a French national who was born in Saigon in 1963, was unemployed and living at Auln. The applicant’s lawyer on the organisation of the procedure (Rules 37 para. 1 and 38) was represented by Mrs Potiez-Lestournaud. The hearing was adjourned until 16 April 1992, at which point the applicant was allowed to leave Strasbourg. On 3 January 1984 he was arrested in Paris with four other people from Hong Kong, Cambodia or Vietnam. They were carrying two bags containing 2,750 grams of heroin base and 85 grams of almost pure heroin, together with a pair of scales, one pan of which bore traces of heroin. Two other people, Mr Jip Quang Duong and Mr Hanh Phuoc, were arrested after weapons and 5kg of caffeine were discovered by police while searching a flat visited by the applicant. He was charged with an offence under the drugs legislation and remanded in custody. He and the six others mentioned above were convicted on the charge that they had ‘conspired in Paris during 1983-84 to produce, possess and supply drugs, namely heroin’ The Director-General’s submissions included the following details: “The defendants’ statements and the police surveillance disclosed the following: Cheng Man Ming and Fu Wing Kin left Bangkok together by air on 26 december 1983 carrying a suitcase with a false bottom containing the heroin subsequently seized. When they arrived in Athens, Cheng continued his journey by air to Paris and instructed Fu to bring the suitcase by rail in order to avoid the thorough checks made at airports in Paris. In France Ngo Pan accompanied Cheng to make a number of purchases: the receptacle which would have served to mix the heroin and the caffeine [and] the secateurs for cutting open the hidden compartment in the suitcase. The heroin was to be transported in Pham’S motor vehicle, and Tran was to drive with it to the home of Jip Quang Duong and Hanh Phuoc, where the 5kg of caffeine were seized.”

name: Halil Kızılöz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32962/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the criminal proceedings brought against him had not been concluded within a “reasonable time” The Court declared the remainder of the applicant’s complaints inadmissible. The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998. Mr Rıza Türmen, the judge elected in respect of Turkey, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The Government accordingly appointed Mr Feyyaz Gölcüklü to sit as an ad hoc judge, in his place. The applicant was suspected of membership of an illegal organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) The applicant was remanded in custody until trial in the Ankara Martial Law Court. He was found guilty as charged and sentenced to 13 years and 4 months’ imprisonment and permanently debarred from practicing law. The case was brought before the Turkish Military Public Prosecutor's Office. The application was dismissed after the prosecutor. filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The applicant. was released on bail and returned to Turkey. He is now living in an undisclosed location in Turkey. The applicant’s appeal was denied by the Turkish government and his appeal was rejected. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Military Court of Cassation (askeri yargıtay) The case was transferred to the Court after the Law of 27 December 1993 abolished the jurisdiction of the martial law courts. The applicant was sentenced to ten years’ imprisonment. On 27 December 1995 the Court ofCassation reviewed the judgment of the Martial Law Court and reduced the applicant’s sentence to 10 years' imprisonment. The appeal was rejected and the applicant was released from prison. The case has not been heard in court since the 1995 appeal was dismissed and the case was dismissed. It is unclear whether this has happened in the current case.

The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the criminal proceedings brought against him had not been concluded within a ‘reasonable time’ and that his right to a fair hearing had been breached on account of his conviction by the Ankara Martial Law Court which lacked independence and impartiality. The Court declared the remainder of the applicant’s complaints inadmissible. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 of the Rules of Court. The applicant was suspected of membership of an illegal organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) He admitted that the weapons and bullets found in his possession belonged to him. He was sentenced to 13 years and 4 months’ imprisonment and permanently debarred from working. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the applicant had not shown that he was a member of a criminal organisation. The applicant was conditionally released pending trial in the Ankara Martial Law Court in 1985. The decision to acquit the applicant was made after the prosecution filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The decision was overturned on appeal on 14 July 1989. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Military Court of Cassation (askeri yargıtay). Following promulgation of the Law of 27 December 1993, the Court ofCassation acquired jurisdiction over the case. The applicant’s sentence was reduced to ten years’ imprisonment. The case was settled in court on 27 December 1995. The ruling was upheld by the Supreme Court of Justice of Turkey and the case was quashed. The respondent was sentenced to 10 years in prison. The sentence was later reduced to five years. The decision was overturned on 29 November 1997. The appeal was dismissed on 13 November 1998. The judge ruled in favor of the applicant and the sentence was quashes.

The Chamber retained the applicant’s complaints concerning his right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal and his further complaints that he was not informed promptly of the nature and cause of the accusation against him. The Court declared the remainder of the applicant's complaints inadmissible. He was remanded in custody and released on bail pending trial. The application has been dismissed by the Court of Appeals of Turkey and the appeal was dismissed on 30 December 1995.

name: M. Wojtunik
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 64212/01) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 4 June 1999. The applicant brought an action against his former employer before the Szczecin Regional Court for payment of 88,674 zlotys in compensation for refraining from undertaking any professional activity in competition to that of the former employer. The Polish Government was represented by their Agent, Mr. J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The case was brought against the Polish government for unreasonable delays in a trial. The case was settled in 1999 and the applicant received 61,000 zlotys. The 2004 Act laid down various legal means designed to counteract and/or redress the undue length of judicial proceedings. A party to pending proceedings may ask for the acceleration of those proceedings and/ or just satisfaction for their unreasonable length under section 2 read in conjunction with section 5(1) of the 2004 Act. The law was passed on 17 September 2004 and came into force on 18 January 2005. The provisions applied retroactively to proceedings in which delays had occurred before that date but only when they had not yet been remedied.

name: Armand Atlan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36533/97) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 10 October 2000 the Chamber declared the application admissible and decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The application is the result of a case brought by two French nationals, Armand Atlan and his son, Thierry Atlan, against the UK Government. A man named Willi Smolny flew from Brazil to London via Copenhagen. He had with him a black suitcase containing 18 kilograms of cocaine. Mr Terrasson and Thierry were arrested by customs officers at Heathrow. The two men were found to be carrying a black and a grey suitcase. The suitcase containing Mr Smolney's cocaine was twice as heavy as the one checked in by Mr Terrassing. The pair were arrested and charged with possession with intent to smuggle and possession of a controlled substance. They were released on bail in November 1990 after serving four years in prison. The case is currently being prosecuted in the UK by the British authorities in connection with the 1990 drug bust. Armand Terrasson, Thierry and Mr Smolny were arrested at Heathrow Airport. They all denied any knowledge of or participation in the offence. Armand was an emerald and diamond dealer in England for a short time on his way to Antwerp. He claimed not to know his son’s trip to Copenhagen and that he did not know anything about his son's trip to Denmark. Mr Terrassin said that he had travelled alone to Copenhagen, taking with him a black suitcase, to meet a married woman friend. He was unable to meet her because her husband was home, so he returned immediately to London and claimed to have taken his own suitcase from the carousel. All four defendants pleaded not guilty and gave evidence. The applicants maintained that Armand worked principally as a jewel trader, but that he did not keep written records because he systematically avoided paying taxes and duties in Brazil. The illegality of his jewel trading had motivated their lies during their initial interviews with customs officers. The defence centred around a dispute between Armand and a rival jewel trader based in Brazil called Rudi Steiner. They claimed that, in order to avoid repaying his debt, he had arranged falsely to implicate them in the importation of cocaine. However, they had no evidence to connect Mr Steiner to Mr Molny’s suitcase full of drugs or to substantiate the suggestion he was a Customs and Excise informer. Steiner 'got Armand Atlan to believe that it was worthwhile going for the third time to Copenhagen for a delivery of the diamonds' 'It would be difficult for Steiner to ask the British Customs and Excise about Terrasson’s suitcase for that purpose, you may think, without revealing that he himself was engaged in setting them up' 'You may want to consider whether they would agree to co-operate on that basis in framing an innocent group of foreigners of good character at the behest of an unknown Brazilian businessman like Steiner' 'His costs: he provided initially some samples [of diamonds] worth seven or eight thousand ... US dollars. ... He lost the cost of sending [his representative] diagonally across the world and back with the sample' On 5 July 1991 the jury, by a majority of ten to one, convicted the applicants and Mr Terrasson of importing the cocaine. Mr Smolny was acquitted. In spring 1994 the applicants learned from the French press (Libération) that a Swiss undercover police officer, Commissioner Cattaneo, had written a report. In early 1995 the applicants’ solicitor obtained a copy of the report. It mentioned Rudi Steiner, describing him as one of three regular informers of the Brazilian, Danish and French police. He was said to have an interest in stolen jewels and a long-term involvement in the traffic from Brazil to Europe of large quantities of cocaine. The applicants added a further ground of appeal coupled with an application for leave to call fresh evidence. The Court of Appeal indicated its view that the Mato Grosso Report would not be admissible in evidence because, inter alia, its author could not be found to vouch for its accuracy and be cross-examined on its contents. It decided not to rule on the application unless or until such time that, having considered the applicants’ application to introduce new evidence, it became necessary to do so.
