train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of effective access to court in contravention of Article 6 § 1. The Government submitted a unilateral declaration which did not offer sufficient basis for finding that respect for human rights as defined in Article 37 § 1 the Convention had been fulfilled. The Court was therefore required to continue the examination of the case. The application was assigned to the newly composed Fifth Section of the Rules of Court on 1 February 2011. The court ruled on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The Enforcement Authority distributed and paid the attached money to the creditor, in this case, the State itself. The decision was open to appeal within three weeks from the date of the decision. The applicant was on holiday at the time and did not receive the Proof of Attachment until he returned home on 8 September 2005 and was formally served. He appealed against the decision to the Svea Court of Appeal (hovrätten) requesting that it quash the lower court’s decision. On 19 October 2005 the District Court dismissed the appeal after first having noted that the decision as regarded the payment of the attached funds had gained legal force on 15 September 2005. Thereafter the court, with reference to case-law from the Supreme Court, stated that an appeal against an attachment decision that was lodged after a decision regarding the payment was made could not be considered by the court. The Court of Appeal upheld the District Court’s decision in full. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) which, on 28 February 2006, refused leave to appeal. Authority, five days after the attachment decision, had distributed and paid the attached money. In his view, it should not have been permitted to distribute attached money until the actual attachment decision had gained legal force. He also argued that the money should have been returned to the rightful owner of the money, not to the Receiver of Pensions. The Supreme Court refused to hear his appeal, so the money was returned to its rightful owner.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 10434/08) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were born in 1941, 1946 and 1948 respectively and live in Bursa. In 2004 the General Directorate of Highways seized a plot of land belonging to the applicants without any formal expropriation, for the construction of a highway. They requested 6,500 Turkish liras (TRY) as compensation from the court and reserved their right to increase this claim in due course. The court awarded the applicants TRY 158,626.30, plus interest. On 16 October 2007 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the Karacabey Civil Court. On 20 March 2009 the administration paid TRY 10,297.75. According to the information provided by the applicants, there has been no outstanding debt in the execution files. They requested 6,500 Turkish liras as compensation from the court and reserved their right to increase this claim in due course. The applicants were represented by Mr A.F. Demirkan, a lawyer practising in Bursa, and the Turkish Government (“the Government’s” Agent) was represented by their Agent. The President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government in June 2009. On 20 March 2009 the administration paid TRY 10,297.75. The decision was upheld by the court of cassation.

The administration paid TRY 10,297.75. According to the information provided by the applicants, there has been no outstanding debt in the execution files. On 16 October 2007 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the Karacabey Civil Court. On 20 March 2009 the administration paid the outstanding sum of TRY 8,936.73. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) for legal advice. The ECHR ruled that the case should be thrown out because there were not enough grounds for it. The decision was upheld by the ECHR on 18 October 2007. The appeal was heard by the Supreme Court of Appeal on 21 October 2007 (No. 182).

name: Yash Pal Kansal
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the statements obtained under compulsion in bankruptcy proceedings should not have been admitted in criminal proceedings against him. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine) The case has been described as a case of self-incrimination. The case was decided by the Court of Appeal and the decision was published on 19 June 2012. The applicant's wife collected part of the advance, GBP 104,000, and took it to India in a bin liner. The applicant was charged with two offences of obtaining property by deception contrary to section 15(1) of the Theft Act 1968. On 18 February 1992, the applicant was convicted of the four offences charged and was sentenced to 15 months' imprisonment. On 27 June 1995, the Royal Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain decided to remove the applicant's licence to practise as a pharmacist on the grounds of unfitness due to his involvement in the deception connected with his bankruptcy proceedings. Leave to appeal was refused by the Court of Appeal and by the House of Lords. The European Court of Human Rights ruled that the answers given by the official receiver were in breach of Article 6 of the Convention. The Court of Appeal overturned the conviction on the grounds that the answer given had been wrongly admitted. The House of Lords ruled in 2001 that the Human Rights Act 1998 could apply retrospectively to the case. The case was appealed to the Supreme Court of England and Wales, but was not heard until after the case had been decided in the court of appeal. The appeal was dismissed on the basis that the decision to overturn the conviction was based on a change in the law. The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the applicant, and the appeal was thrown out.

The case originated in an application (no. 21413/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the statements obtained under compulsion in bankruptcy proceedings should not have been admitted in criminal proceedings against him. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. The Court declared the remainder of the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant but not the Government filed observations on the merit of the case. The decision was made in favour of the applicant. The applicant misled the building society into advancing money by false representations. On 23 March 1988, the applicant's wife collected part of the advance, GBP 104,000, and took it to India in a bin liner. The applicant was convicted of the four offences charged and was sentenced to 15 months' imprisonment. He appealed against conviction and on 12 May 1992, the Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal deciding, inter alia, that the transcript of the bankruptcy examination was admissible under section 433 of the Insolvency Act 1986. On 27 June 1995, the Royal Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain decided to remove his licence to practise as a pharmacist on the grounds of unfitness due to his involvement in the deception. The Court of Appeal ruled that the admission of answers under compulsion had breached Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The House of Lords ruled in favor of the appeal, saying that the Human Rights Act 1998 could not apply retrospectively. The appeal was rejected by the Supreme Court, which said that the act could not be applied retrospectively to individuals whose trial took place before the Act came into force. The case is now being heard by the European Court of Human Rights, which will decide whether the case can be re-examined or not. The application is expected to be heard in October or November 2014, and the decision will be made on whether or not to overturn the conviction.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36801/06) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. In the alternative, she requested that the court declare her entitled to disability benefits as from June 1999. train_texts: The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the criminal proceedings brought against him had not been concluded within a “reasonable time” The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. The Court declared the application admissible on 10 February 2004. The case was referred to the Military Court of Cassation. It was ruled that the application was not admissible by the Court on 1 November 2001. The application and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court ruled that both observations were meritorious and that the case was allowed to stand. The applicant was arrested in 1986. The Martial Law Court in Diyarbakır dismissed the case in 1990. The applicant was released from detention on 29 July 1990. On 13 July 1998, the Diyarbakir Assize Court held that the offence fell within the scope of Article 168 § 2 and that the statutory time limit under Articles 102 and 104 of the Criminal Code had expired. It accordingly ordered that the criminal proceedings against the applicant be terminated. On 10 September 1998 the judgment became final in respect of the applicant. The case was decided by a jury in a trial that took place in front of a panel of judges. The jury decided that the applicant was not guilty.

name: Lella Christodoulidou
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 16085/90) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Turkish occupation of the northern part of Cyprus had deprived her of her properties. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 7 December 1999 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The case was heard by the European Court of Human rights in Strasbourg, France, between 7 and 14 January 2011. The decision was made by the Court of Appeal on behalf of the applicant. The applicant's properties were located in the area under the occupation and control of the Turkish military authorities. The applicant joined an anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia in which the applicants in the Chrysostomos and Papachrysostomou v. Turkey also took part. Since the 1974 Turkish intervention, the applicant has been deprived of her properties, which were located under Turkish occupation. The application was filed in April 2000. The case was heard in March and April 2007. The judge ruled in favor of the applicant on July 4, 2008. The appeal was dismissed on July 9, 2008, and the case was adjourned until July 14, 2009. The applicant was injured during a demonstration in Nicosia in 1989. She claims she was hit with a bayonet by a Turkish soldier. The wound was stitched internally and externally. For the next six months, the applicant suffered considerable pain in her leg. She could not walk or even put weight on the leg and was forced to use crutches. She continued to have problems climbing stairs and the scar on her leg remained visible. The applicant produced a medical certificate issued on 27 March 2000 by Doctor Stelios Georgiou, a specialist orthopaedic surgeon. The certificate states that the wound was caused with a sharp object. Three of the witnesses who saw the wound being inflicted had already died. The applicant was arrested by the Turkish-Cypriot police after crossing the UN buffer zone in the Ayios Kassianos area of Nicosia. The Government alleged that the applicant had participated in a violent demonstration with the aim of inflaming anti-Turkish sentiment. No force was used against demonstrators who did not intrude into the “TRNC” border area and, in the case of demonstrators who were arrested for violating the border, no more was used than was reasonably necessary in the circumstances in order to arrest and detain the persons concerned. No one was ill-treated. It was possible that some of the demonstrators had hurt themselves in the confusion or in attempting to scale barbed wire or other fencing. Turkish-Cypriot police and security forces elements forced their way into the area and apprehended 111 persons, 101 of them women. The Ayios Kassianos school complex is situated in the UN buffer zone. However, the Turkish forces claim it to be on their side of the cease-fire line. On 21 July, I expressed my concern at the events that have taken place and stressed that it was vital that all parties keep in mind the purpose of the UNbuffer zone. I also urged the Turkish- Cypriot authorities to release without delay all those who had been detained. On 24 July, the President of the Security Council announced that he had conveyed to the representatives of all the parties, on behalf of the members of the Council, the Council's deep concern.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 16085/90) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant claimed that the Turkish occupation of the northern part of Cyprus had deprived her of her properties. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 7 December 1999 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The decision was published in full on 17 December 1999. The original article was amended on 18 January 2001 to make clear that the case was brought by a Cypriot national, Mrs Lella Christodoulidou. The applicant joined an anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia on 19 July 1989. The applicant's properties were located in the area under the occupation and control of the Turkish military authorities. Since the 1974 Turkish intervention, the applicant has been deprived of her properties. The applicants in the Chrysostomos and Papachrysostomou v. Turkey and Loizidou v Turkey cases (see below) also took part in the demonstration. The application was dismissed on the basis of the grounds that the applicant's version of events did not meet the requirements of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant was injured in 1989 following an attack on women near Ayios Kassianos. Three of the witnesses who saw the wound being inflicted (two friends and the editor of a local newspaper) had already died. However, an affidavit sworn by a witness, Mrs Olga Nicolaidou, corroborated her version of events. The applicant produced a medical certificate issued on 27 March 2000 by Doctor Stelios Georgiou, a specialist orthopaedic surgeon practising in Nicosia, which reads as follows: “The [applicant] was injured on 19.7.1989 by Turks following an assault on women in Ayios Cassianos Primary School. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 55434/00) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his detention on remand pending his trial by court martial was in breach of Article 5 § 3 of the convention. By a decision of 25 October 2005, the Court declared the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine), and the parties replied in writing to each other's observations. A certificate dated 6 November 1999 and signed by the applicant confirms that the applicant received the pamphlet “The Rights of a Soldier Charged with an Offence under the Army Act 1955” A short note by the CO (“referred to Higher Authority”) constitutes the sole record before the Court of that hearing. The final report dated 7 February 2000 recorded for the first time an additional charge against the applicant pursuant to section 70 of the 1955 Act: rape contrary to section 1(1) of the Sexual Offences Act 1956. The applicant was given a four-page document immediately before that hearing, which document was taken back from him immediately thereafter. The applicant's parents instructed a solicitor on 12 January 2000. The solicitor sought a review of the applicant's detention by the general officer commanding 4th Division. The applicant's representative applied for a writ of habeas corpus to the High Court. On 22 February 2000 the CO of the MCTC released the applicant from close arrest and he was posted to the 47th Regiment Royal Artillery. On 2 March 2000, the same CO swore an affidavit setting out the reasons for the applicant’s release. He stated: 'I decided, on balance, following a thorough review, that following the seriousness of the alleged offence it was undesirable in the interests of discipline that he be allowed to consort with his comrades' The applicant and his two co-defendants were tried by Army General Court Martial on a joint charge of rape between 14 May and 25 May 2001. All three defendants were acquitted. 'I decided that the Applicant should be posted with immediate effect to a different unit in a different country namely the UK, and issued with specific orders preventing him from being able to influence the witnesses,' the judge said. 'The applicant should be sent back to his home country of origin where he can be with his family and friends' 'He should be placed under house arrest and not allowed to leave the country.' 'The Applicant should not be allowed to return to his native country and should be kept out of the public eye' 'I believe that the interests of justice could be met by releasing the Applicant into open arrest even though he had committed rape and indecent assault'

The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The decision was made not to hear the case on the merit of the allegations against the applicant. The case was decided in favour of the applicant and the Government. The applicant was transferred to the Military Correctional Training Centre (“the MCTC”) in the United Kingdom on 16 November 1999. A certificate dated 6 November 1999 and signed by the applicant confirms that the applicant received the pamphlet “The Rights of a Soldier Charged with an Offence under the Army Act 1955” The CO referred the case to the Higher Authority and remanded the applicant in close arrest. The final report dated 7 February 2000 recorded for the first time an additional charge against the applicant pursuant to section 70 of the 1955 Act: rape contrary to section 1(1) of the Sexual Offences Act 1956. No reasons were noted as to why the applicant had been detained except in the last form (dated 7 February 2000) which recorded the same reasons as in the above-noted 8-day reports. It is undesirable in the interests of discipline that he be allowed to consort with his comrades due to the seriousness of the alleged offence. name: Abdurrahman Dilipak
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29680/05) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Abdurrahman Dilipak (“the applicant”), on 22 July 2005, made the application. He published an article on the front page of issue 84 of the weekly magazine Türkiye’de Cuma, which came out on 29 August 2003. His article contained criticisms of high-ranking officers who were about to retire. He suggested that the officers in question should set up a political party on retirement and present their political projects to the people. The Military Court declined jurisdiction in favour of the Bakırköy Assize Court on the grounds that the offence at issue was not military in nature. The commanding officer of the Third Army Corps lodged an appeal on points of law against the decision to decline jurisdiction. The Military Court of Cassation quashed the decision declining jurisdiction and referred the case back to the Military Court. In its reasoning the Court ofCassation mentioned the need to reclassify the facts and to assess them under Article 95 § 4 of the Military Criminal Code. It specified that the provisions of Article 95§ 4 and (the former) were not relevant to the case. The case was referred to the Bakırköy 24th Criminal Court. Law No. 5530 of 29 June 2006 made a series of amendments to the Military Criminal Code, abolishing military court jurisdiction for trying civilians for offences such as those with which the applicant was charged. By a judgment of 14 November 2006 the military court once again decline jurisdiction and referred the case to the Bağcılar 2nd Criminal Court, which held jurisdiction for offences committed via the press. The Prosecutor with the Military Court of Cassation pointed out that the provisions of the Military criminal Code (Law No. 353) enabling civilians to be tried by military courts had not been amended. Bakırköy 2nd Criminal Court referred the case to the BakırKöy 16th Criminal Court on the grounds that that court was the former Bağcılar 2nd criminal Court. By a judgment of 12 March 2009 the BakTurkish 16th criminal court referred a jurisdictional dispute to the  Bak Turkey Assize Court. Finally, the Bak Turkish Assize Court decided in favour of the Bak Turkey 2nd Criminal Court in the jurisdictional dispute, and referred the case to that court. The case was then subsequently referred to the Bak Turkey 2nd Criminal Court, which declared the proceedings statute-barred under Article 95 of the Military Criminal Code.

name: Osman Koşti
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 74321/01) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were arrested and taken into custody on 19 and 20 February 1999 respectively on suspicion of their involvement in the throwing of Molotov cocktails at various public buildings. On 25 August 2005 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaint concerning the length of the applicants' remand in custody and the criminal proceedings brought against them. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purpose of the proceedings before the Court. The Diyarbakır Security Court held fifteen hearings between 12 May 1999 and 22 December 2000. The court decided to secure the testimony of those who had attended the arrest and the reconstruction of events and the submissions of the accused who were not detained. It further ordered that the birth date of Hışman Öngör and another accused be determined since they had claimed that they were actually born in 1986. The first instance court dismissed the applicants' requests until 29 May 2001, having regard to the nature of the offence with which they were charged and the state of the evidence. The public prosecutor appealed. On 20 September 2001 the Court of Cassation upheld the decision.

name: Hasan Öztunç
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1936 and lives in Van. In 1985 the applicant obtained a contract from the Provincial Administration of Van to carry out repair work in twelve public schools in Başkale. At a later date, he noticed that some of the schools had not yet been fully constructed. He applied to the Governor's Office in Van and requested the contract to be annulled. He submitted that the payment agreed on for the repairs was too low, given the amount of work needed to complete the construction of those schools. The Van Civil Court awarded the applicant TRL 47,273,000 plus interest calculated at three different rates depending on the relevant period of time. In his petition to the Court of Cassation he complained about the loss that he had suffered as a result of the high rate of inflation during the proceedings before the civil court. On 23 July 2001 the applicant was paid the total amount of TRL 282,795,000, consisting of the capital plus interest incurred until the payment date. The applicant appealed the decision. On 9 April 2001 the same court dismissed the applicant's request for rectification. The case was referred to the European Court of Justice.

name: Milenko Stojakovic
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30003/02) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Mr Milenko Stojakovic complained about the lack of a public oral hearing before a tribunal. Since 1984 the applicant was the head of the Federal Bacteriological Serological Research Institute (Bundesstaatiche bakteriologisch-serologische Untersuchungsanstalt) in Linz. According to the activity profile submitted by the Government the tasks of the Institute involved carrying out various examinations, namely examinations upon official request under the relevant Health Acts. The applicant, as head of the Institute, was responsible for all tasks entrusted to it. Under section 3 of the Civil Servants Act (Beamten-Dienstrechtsgesetz) he was further responsible for certain matters concerning the regulation of its service. On 22 November 1999 the Disciplinary Commission at the Ministry for Work, Health and Social Affairs found the applicant guilty of having violated his professional duties under the Non-Discrimination Act. It found that the applicant inter alia had made statements about some of his employees amounting to sexual harassment. He was sentenced to a fine of approximately 2,400 euros (EUR) On 4 September 2003 the Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's complaint. The applicant was transferred from the Institute for Public Service and Sport in 2000. He appealed the decision to transfer him. The Appeals Commission dismissed his appeal without holding a hearing. The applicant filed a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) in 2001. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant's complaint. It found that rights and obligations which resulted from an employment as a civil servant could not be considered as being relevant to the transfer case. The court also ruled that the transfer did not need to wait for the outcome of pending disciplinary proceedings. It confirmed the Federal Minister's finding that the applicant could no longer be trusted to perform the tasks of a head. The European Court of Human Rights ruled that Article 6 of the Convention was not applicable to the applicant's case. It further found that there was no indication of arbitrariness in the proceedings at issue. The applicant's counsel was served with the decision on 13 February 2002. The case was heard at the Geneva Convention on Human Rights in Geneva, Switzerland, on 16 June 2001. The decision was delivered on 13 July 2001 and the case was dismissed on 17 July 2001. name: Wiktor Kucharczyk
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 3464/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Polish national, Mr Wiktor Kucharczyk. The applicant was born in 1952 and lives in Kielce. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the Application at the same time. The case was brought by an ex-member of the Świętokrzyski trade union. The case has been ongoing since 1991. In 2005 the applicant revoked the power of attorney of his lawyer, G.P. The Kielce Regional Court dismissed the applicant's appeal on the grounds that he had terminated his legal-aid lawyer with effect on 12 July 2005 and voluntarily relinquished free legal aid. The appeal was dismissed again on 25 July 2005. The applicant appealed against that decision on 18 August 2005, but the appeal was also dismissed by the Regional Court. The application was finally dismissed on 9 July 2006, after it had gone to a higher court. The applicant lodged a complaint under section 5 of the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. Kielce Regional Court rejected the appeal as inadmissible in law. The court found that in the remaining periods the proceedings had been conducted without undue delays. The applicant was granted PLN 2,000 in just satisfaction. The appeal was rejected by the court on 1 March 2005 and the appeal was dismissed. The case was settled out of court and the application was dismissed on appeal. The appeals were dismissed by the Court of Appeal of Poland and the Appeal Court of Poland.

name: David Adetoro
train_texts: David Adetoro claimed that he did not have a fair trial as a result of the trial judge's misdirection to the jury on the drawing of adverse inferences as regards his refusal to answer questions during police interviews. The evidence against the applicant was almost entirely circumstantial and the case relied heavily on evidence from a police surveillance exercise carried out over a period of about one year. The applicant was born in 1972 and is currently detained in HMP Whitemoor, Cambridgeshire. He denied any involvement in the conspiracy to rob and was interviewed under caution in March and June 1997. The terms of the caution were that he didn't have to say anything but that it might harm his defence if he didnot mention when questioned something on which he later sought to. The applicant pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to rob and other offences arising out of the conspiracy. During the interviews, he was asked to give an explanation for his movements as recorded by the police in their surveillance exercise, his association with a variety of individuals and his whereabouts at the time of the robberies. On each occasion, he replied “no comment’. The applicant also provided answers to all the questions which he had declined to answer during the police interviews in March and June 1997. The judge directed them as to the burden of proof and the standard of proof in the case: “...The burden [of proof] lies upon the prosecution throughout the case, to prove their case against the defendant. The defendant does not have to prove anything at all, there is no burden upon him to prove Anything” The judge went on to deal with the questioning of the applicant by the police. He noted that the applicant had not answered questions put to him during the police interviews, replying ‘no comment’ to each of the questions posed. The judge concluded with the following direction: ‘Any such lie can be evidence going to support the prosecution's case. A defendant may lie for many reasons. He may lie because he doesn't want to disclose something or out of confusion, panic or something of that sort.’ The applicant admits that he failed to mention any of the facts to which I have just referred, when he was interviewed and he says his reason for that, was that although well knowing that others had been arrested for the much more serious offence of armed robbery. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal arguing that the summing up contained a Lucas direction (a direction to the jury in relation to lies – see paragraph 33) He was found guilty of the offences charged and sentenced to 26 years' imprisonment. The trial judge described Mr Adetoro as a dangerous, cunning and intelligent man and he was satisfied that after he had joined the conspiracy, he had played a commanding role. He was a 'rather clever and determined liar' and his alibi 'fell apart' The judge was not prepared to place reliance on anything he said and made no finding in respect of Mr Shearer and Mr Stephenson's presence or absence in the circumstances of the sixth robbery. The applicant's appeal against conviction was dismissed. However, his sentence was reduced to 22 years' imprisonment. The Criminal Cases Review Commission referred the applicant's conviction to the Court of Appeal on the basis of the trial judge's direction to the jury. The main ground of appeal was that the direction on adverse inferences was defective in that the jury were not directed that an adverse inference could only be drawn where it was satisfied that the real reason for the applicant’s silence was that he had no answer to the questions asked, or no answer that would hold up to scrutiny. The Court of appeal disagreed and found that, despite the misdirection by the judge, the conviction was safe. The court found that the jury had rejected the applicant's defence. It also noted that the judge had given the jury an unnecessary Lucas direction. The jury were told that if they thought there was an innocent explanation for any such lie told by the appellant they should not hold it against him. So, as the jury must have concluded that the appellant's explanation for his silence ('I wanted to protect others') was a lie, following the judge's direction they would have had to consider whether there was a innocent explanation before they could have used it as supportive of the Crown's case. This is not a case in which one cannot say what the jury would have done if such a direction had been given. The applicant's appeal against conviction was dismissed on 7 June 2006. the earlier judgment of the Court of Appeal, which found the evidence against the applicant to be overwhelming, and concluded: “This was not therefore a case in which one could say that the correct direction would have tipped the balance” The appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 17 May 2006. The applicant was acquitted of all charges and was allowed to leave the country. The application was dismissed after a hearing in June 2006, when it was rejected by the High Court. The judge said that the case was not one that should be decided on the basis of a single verdict. He said the evidence was overwhelming and that he could not reach a verdict.

The case originated in an application (no. 46834/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The evidence against the applicant was almost entirely circumstantial and the case relied heavily on evidence from a police surveillance exercise carried out over a period of about one year. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms J. Gladstone, of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The applicant pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to rob and other offences arising out of the conspiracy. During interviews, he was asked to give an explanation for his movements as recorded by the police in their surveillance exercise, his association with a variety of individuals and his whereabouts at the time of the robberies. On each occasion, he replied “no comment’. At trial before the Crown Court, the applicant gave evidence in his own defence. He claimed that he was not even aware of the robbery conspiracy or his associates' involvement. However, he admitted being involved in the buying and selling of stolen cars and argued that the police observations showed his involvement in that business. The judge noted that the applicant had not answered questions put to him during the police interviews, replying ‘no comment’ to each of the questions posed. The applicant did not suggest that he was advised by his lawyer not to comment but said that he did not want to incriminate people in relation to stolen vehicles. The judge concluded with the following direction: “If you think that the defendant has lied in evidence, then ignore it, take no notice of it at all.”‘A defendant may lie for many reasons. He may lie because he doesn't want to disclose something or out of confusion, panic or something of that sort’ On 18 June 1998 the jury found the applicant guilty of the offences charged. He was sentenced to 26 years' imprisonment. Court of Appeal rules that there was no need for a Lucas direction. The applicant's appeal against conviction was dismissed. However, his sentence was reduced to 22 years' imprisonment. The Court of Appeal disagreed and found that, despite the misdirection by the trial judge, the conviction was safe. The main ground of appeal was that the direction on adverse inferences was defective in that the jury were not directed that an adverse inference could only be drawn where it was satisfied that the real reason for the applicant's silence was that he had no answer to the questions asked, or no answer that would hold up to scrutiny. The court distinguished between cases where an accused exercised his right to silence pursuant to legal advice or because he was tired or ill and those where the reason for not answering questions was linked to the accused's silence. The court found that the jury had rejected the applicant's defence. It also noted that the judge had given the jury an unnecessary Lucas direction. The jury were told that if they thought there was an innocent explanation for any such lie told by the appellant they should not hold it against him. But the jury must have concluded that the lie was not innocent – in other words the reason he was lying about why he had not answered the questions was because he had no answer to them or none which would withstand scrutiny. This is not a case in which one cannot say what the jury would have done if such a direction had been given. The court referred to the accused's defence itself. The applicant's appeal against conviction was dismissed on 7 June 2006. The Court of Appeal found the evidence against the applicant to be overwhelming. The applicant was convicted of three counts of perverting the course of justice and was sentenced to 30 years in prison. The conviction was quashed on appeal in June 2006, and the conviction was overturned on appeal again in June 2009. The case was described as "one of the most complex criminal cases in British history" by the Supreme Court of England and Wales. The judge ruled that the evidence was 'overwhelming' and that the 'correct direction would have tipped the balance' in the applicant's favour.

train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, that their conviction for propaganda in favour of a terrorist organisation had entailed a violation of Article 9 of the convention. The applications were brought by two Turkish nationals, Mr İhsan Güler and Mr Sinan Uğur. They were active members and regional leaders of the Party for a Democratic Society (Demokratik Toplum Partisi (DTP), which was subsequently dissolved by the Constitutional Court. On 21 August 2006 the applicants took part in a religious ceremony (mevlût)0 on the premises of the DTP in Altındağ (Ankara), in which they paid tribute to three members of the PKK who had been killed. The court added that for treatment to be qualified as torture under domestic law, the victims needed to have been charged with a particular crime. In the present case the applicants had only been suspects and were later released without charge. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment on the ground that the provisions applicable to the police officers and the doctor were contained in Articles 243 and 230 of the Criminal Code which concerned the offences of torture and negligence in the performance of public duties respectively. Cassation (Criminal Divisions) quashed. the Mersin Assize Court’s judgment and held that the evidence in the case file showed that the applicants. had been subjected to torture. The application was lodged with the Court. It concluded that as the proceedings had eventually been discontinued, the complaint lodged by the applicant pursuant to the2004 Act had served its purpose and had to be dismissed.

name: Beneficio Cappella Paolini
train_texts: The San Marinese government issued an expropriation order in respect of certain plots of land belonging to the applicant church. The latter was awarded 114,790,590 Italian lire (about 59,284 euros) in compensation. The land, which was earmarked for urban development projects that were scheduled for completion by 31 December 1987, was only partially used. The applicant church applied to the government seeking to recover possession of the unused land. On 20 October 1987 the government refused the application on the ground that the land in question could still be used in the interests of the community. On 12 March 1992 the applicantChurch brought an action before the judge of civil appeals (Giudice delle Appellazioni Civili) to establish title to land. The first hearing was held on 9 April 1992. On 21 May 1992 the applicant church filed a number of documents. The parties lodged their final submissions on 10 February and 24 March 1994. Preparation of the case was concluded on 27 April 1994. In December 1994 the appeal Judge C.P. died. No other judge could replace him, as the organisational structure of the court of civil appeals provided for only one judge. On 25 April 1995 the General Grand Council appointed Judge P.G.P to replace the deceased judge. However, P.g.P asked the Council of the XII for leave to withdraw from the proceedings on the ground that he had been involved as the first-instance civil judge. The applicant church had asked the government on 3 March 1992 to return its assets. On 20 April 1993 it applied to the first-instance administrative court. A hearing took place on 3 August 1993. By a judgment of 17 August 1993, the court stated that it did not have jurisdiction to “recognise the existence of a possible right to restitution of unused land”. It found that the General Grand Council alone was entitled to rule on what was to be done with the said property. Noting finally that the new land-use plan had changed the designated use of the unused land, it declared the expropriation order of 7 March 1985 void in so far as it had lapsed. The case of Beneficio Cappella Paolini was heard in the administrative court of appeal. The judge found that the State had acquired ownership of the plots of land in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law. He concluded that the applicant church’s request of 20 April 1993 was inadmissible, since the government's behaviour could not be described as an implied refusal. Finally, he stated that, in declaring the expropriation order partially void – an order which, moreover, had never been contested – the first-instance administrative court had exceeded its jurisdiction. On 27 September 1994 the Council of the XII upheld the appeal court's judgment.

On 7 March 1985 the San Marinese government issued an expropriation order in respect of certain plots of land belonging to the applicant church. The applicant church applied to the government seeking to recover possession of the unused land. On 20 October 1987 the government refused the application on the ground that the land in question could still be used in the interests of the community. The judge found that the State had acquired ownership of the plots of land in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28388/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the civil proceedings. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). The applicant was represented by Mrs İ. İlimoğlu, a lawyer practising in Ankara. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The case was subsequently remitted to the Ankara Commercial Court. The applicant and Global A.Ş. and B.G. appealed the decision of 7 November 2001. The Court of Cassation partially granted the applicant’s request and ordered them to pay her TRL 1,512,000,000 with simple interest. On 13 January 2003 the applicant requested rectification of the Court of. Cassation’S decision of 10 October 2002. On 11 April 2003 the Court Of Cassation dismissed the applicant's request. The case was settled at the European Court of Human Rights in 2003. The judge ruled in favour of the applicant and ordered the parties to pay back the money.

Mrs Bindschedler-Robert, the first substitute judge, replaced Mr. Pallieri on 21 November. The oral hearings took place in public at the Human Rights Building, Stras. Three applicants were charged before the German courts with the commission of various criminal offences. Since they were not sufficiently familiar with the language of the country, they were assisted by an interpreter in accordance with German law. They consider that the inclusion of this latter item is contrary to, inter alia, Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention. After conviction they were ordered, amongst other things, to pay the costs of the proceedings, including the interpretation costs. The Commission produce to the Court certain documents referred to by the Principal Delegate at the hearings; these documents were the subject of a letter, received on 16 August, from the Agent of the Government. If the individual concerned is convicted, he has to pay the costs, but only such proportion thereof as relates to the criminal charges upheld by the court. The obligation to employ an interpreter is, however, subject to one exception, namely when all the participants are familiar with the foreign language (section 185 para. 2 of the Constitution of the Courts Act). He appealed against the decision, arguing that it violated Article 6 para. 3 (e) of the Convention. The appeal was rejected and the case was referred to the Bielefeld Regional Court. The applicant was awarded DM 1,330.90, made up of the fine of DM 900, the fees (Gebühren) due in respect of the criminal proceedings (DM 90) and the withdrawal of his driving licence (DM 30), together with police costs and interpretation costs (DM 225.40) Algerian Mohammed Belkacem is an Algerian citizen, born in 1954. After completing his apprenticeship as a locksmith in Algeria, he rejoined his father in the Federal Republic of Germany where he followed various occupations. In December 1973, he was involved in a dispute in a Berlin night-club during which another client lost his coat. He paid the costs of the proceedings, including the interpretation costs, on 4 May 1973. On 10 April 1974, Mr. BelKacem filed an “immediate appeal’ against the order as to costs insofar as the interpretation costs had been included in the award. On 29 May 1975, his appeal was dismissed by the District Court. Arif Koç, a Turkish citizen born in 1940, has been employed in the Federal Republic of Germany in various trades, including mining and the construction industry. He was convicted in 1973 of causing grievous bodily harm and sentenced to a year's imprisonment. On 12 April 1976, he notified the relevant authorities in Alsdorf, near Aachen, his last place of residence in Germany, of his intention to return to Turkey. On 5 May 1977, following a request by Mr. Belkacem, the Berlin Justizkasse allowed him to defer payment ‘until the decision of the Commission of Human Rights be known’ The Cologne Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht), in a fully reasoned decision delivered on 5 June 1975, set aside the Assize Court’s judgment insofar as it related to the interpretation costs. The court ordered the applicant to bear the costs of the proceedings “with the exception, however, of the costs occasioned by the assistance of the Turkish-language interpreter, which costs are to be borne by the Treasury’. The object of the Convention is to secure human rights and fundamental freedoms against arbitrary State action and to place them under the protection of supranational law. The intention was to enshrine rights of the citizen and duties of the State which ensure a fair trial. In July 1975, Mr. Koç applied to the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) which declined to hear the application on the ground that it did not offer sufficient prospects of success. It cannot be assumed that the Convention is intended to provide a piecemeal solution of the question of costs in criminal proceedings. Nor does the consideration that a foreigner should not receive worse treatment in the matter of costs than a national, dictate the conclusion that permanent exemption from costs is necessarily implied by the object of the Convention. The Convention would not have come appreciably nearer to achieving its aim by prohibiting a financial disadvantage of such a kind. They alleged discrimination by reason of the fact that a foreigner not speaking German was in a less favourable position than a German person. If the individual concerned is convicted, he has to pay the costs, but only such proportion thereof as relates to the criminal charges upheld by the court. The obligation to employ an interpreter is subject to one exception, namely when all the participants are familiar with the foreign language. Gerhard W. Luedicke was convicted of a road traffic offence in 1972. He was fined DM 900 and ordered to pay the costs of the proceedings. He appealed against the decision, claiming that it was contrary to Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention in so far as it concerned payment of the interpretation costs. The decision was upheld by the Court of Appeal for the Federal Republic of Germany. The application was returned to the European Court of Human Rights in May 2013. The European Court's decision was made on 26 May 2013, and the application has now been reinstated. Algerian citizen Mohammed Belkacem sued for not paying costs of interpreters. Court said German law does not forbid awarding costs of proceedings against a person convicted of an offence. Court interprets Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) ... as a provisional exemption from paying the interpretation costs. Mr. Belkcem paid the costs of the proceedings, including interpretation costs, on 4 May 1973, including the costs. He was involved in a dispute in a Berlin night-club in December 1973 during which another client lost his coat. Mr Belcacem is an Algerian citizen, born in 1954. He is a locksmith. Berlin-Tiergarten Juvenile Court convicted him of assault occasioning bodily harm. He was sentenced to four weeks’ imprisonment (Dauerarrest) and a fine of DM 500. The Berlin Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 13 June 1974. The Regional Court reasoned that, since no assessment of costs had yet been made, there had been no decision capable of being challenged on appeal. On 29 May 1975, his appeal was dismissed by the District Court which held, inter alia, that Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention did not prohibit a convicted person being made to bear interpretation costs. Arif Koç, a Turkish citizen born in 1940, has been employed in the Federal Republic of Germany in various trades, including mining and the construction industry. On 6 December 1973, the Assize Court attached to the Regional Court (Schwurgericht beim Landgericht) at Aachen convicted Mr. Koç of causing grievous bodily harm. He was sentenced to a year’s imprisonment, but the balance of his sentence remaining after allowance had been made for his detention on remand was commended. On 5 May 1977, following a request by Mr. Belkacem, the Berlin Justizkasse allowed him to defer payment “until the decision of the Commission of Human Rights be known’ The Cologne Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht), in a fully reasoned decision delivered on 5 June 1975, set aside the Assize Court’s judgment insofar as it related to the interpretation costs. The court ordered the applicant to bear the costs of the proceedings ‘with the exception, however, of the costs occasioned by the assistance of the Turkish-language interpreter, which costs are to be borne by the Treasury’. The aim of the Convention is to secure human rights and fundamental freedoms against arbitrary State action and to place them under the protection of supranational law. ... It is not its purpose to go further and alter the national legal systems. “It cannot be assumed that the Convention is intended to provide a piecemeal solution of the question of costs in criminal proceedings. Nor does the consideration that a foreigner should not receive worse treatment in the matter of costs than a national, dictate the conclusion that permanent exemption from costs is necessarily implied by the object of the Convention.” “The applicant was not served with a notice to pay the costs for which he was liable, including the interpretation costs, since it was noted that he had a wife and four children to support, that his income was modest and that there was thus no prospect of recovering the costs.“ Three men claimed to be victims of a violation of Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention in that they had been ordered by the German courts to bear interpretation costs. The application was initially represented by Ms M. Kronfeldner, his sister, and subsequently by Mr A. Ahmed, a lawyer practising in Munich. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin. Regensburg Regional Court convicted the applicant of rape. It sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment and ordered his placement in preventive detention pursuant to Article 66 § 1 of the Criminal Code (see paragraphs 32-33 below) The court found that in July 1989, some four months after his release from prison, the applicant had raped a woman whom he had come across in Regensburg at night. The court considered that owing to his propensity to commit serious sexual offences, theApplicant was dangerous to the public. On 25 October 2007 the Regensberg Regional Court prolonged the execution of the applicant’s preventive detention in a psychiatric hospital. The applicant had served ten years in preventive detention by 11 May 2008. The court took the view that the applicant’s dangerousness had not diminished. There was a risk that he might commit further violent sexual offences, in particular rapes, the court said. The reintegration into society of the applicant, who did not suffer from a psychiatric illness, could not better be furthered in that hospital. The therapy in the psychiatric hospital, in which he might become even more dangerous, had not yielded any success. The applicant was accordingly transferred from Straubing Psychiatric Hospital to Straubed Prison on 19 June 2008. On 22 July 2008 the Nuremberg Court of Appeal quashed the decision of 26 October 2005 to execute the applicant's preventive detention in a psychiatric hospital. The Court of Appeal added that the reasons why the applicant’s therapy in Straubing Psychiatric Hospital had not been successful were irrelevant for the question whether there was still a risk that the applicant, if released, might commit further sexual offences. The court further referred to the leading judgment dated 5 February 2004 of the Federal Constitutional Court, in which the latter had considered the retroactive extension of a convicted person's preventive detention beyond a period of ten years to be constitutional. It found, accordingly, that the applicants’ continued preventive detention was lawful and proportionate. The decision of the federal court was upheld by the Regional Court. The applicant was considered by the Straubing Prison authorities to be a self-confident, demanding and mistrustful person. Since July 2009 he has been working in the prison’s furniture factory. The applicant did not make any of the therapies available – notably a group or possibly individual social therapy for sexual offenders – for lack of motivation. He consistently refused the treatment offered, questioning the therapists’ expertise. He was not granted any relaxations in the execution of the preventive detention order against him for fear of abuse. The Federal Court of Justice decided to adjourn the case pending a decision of its grand senate on the legal question at issue. It remitted the case-file to the Nuremberg Court of Appeal in order to review whether, applying a stricter standard of proportionality, the applicant's preventive detention was to continue. The Nuremberg Court of Appeal quashed the decision of the Regensburg Regional Court of 26 July 2010. It found that, having regard to the criteria set up by the Federal Constitutional Court in its judgment dated 4 May 2011, the applicant’s preventive detention was disproportionate. On 28 November 2011 the applicant was ordered the provisional detention in a suitable institution pending a decision on his placement under the Therapy Detention Act (see paragraph 40 below). The applicant had not previously been placed in a psychiatric hospital under section 1 of the Bavarian (Mentally Ill Persons’) Placement Act. The court ordered preventive detention in addition to the penalty if someone is sentenced for an intentional offence to at least two years’ imprisonment and if the following further conditions are satisfied. The court may review at any time whether the further execution of the preventive detention order should be suspended and a measure of probation applied or whether it should be declared terminated. For persons in preventive detention, this time‑limit is two years (paragraph 2 of Article 67e). The first period of preventive detention may not exceed ten years. If the maximum duration has expired, the detainee shall be released (Article 67d § 3). The case of M. v. Germany (no. 19359/04, §§ 45-78, 17 December 2009) The former maximum duration of a first period of preventive detention was abolished. The detention of mentally ill persons is provided for, first of all, in the Criminal Code as a measure of correction and prevention if the detention is ordered in relation to an unlawful act committed by the person concerned. The decision at issue in the case of M. v. Germany, cited above, was subsequently reversed (see paragraphs 41-45 below). The court may quash that decision if it later emerges that no success can be achieved by placing the person in a psychiatric hospital or a detoxification facility (Article 67a § 3). The duration of the placement is determined by the provisions which apply to the measure ordered in the judgment. A court may order a person’s placement in a psychiatric hospital at the request of the authorities of a town or county if the person concerned is mentally ill and thereby poses a severe threat to public security and order. Such an order may only be executed as long as no measure under Article 63 of the Criminal Code has been taken. The Federal Constitutional Court held that all provisions on the retrospective prolongation of the complainants’ preventive detention beyond the former ten-year maximum period were valid. The person concerned must further suffer from a mental disorder owing to which it is highly likely that he will considerably impair the life, physical integrity, personal liberty or sexual self-determination of another person. The Federal Constitutional Court held that all provisions of the Criminal Code on the imposition and duration of preventive detention at issue were incompatible with the fundamental right to liberty. The provisions did not satisfy the constitutional requirement of establishing a difference between preventive detention and detention for serving a term of imprisonment (Abstandsgebot). These provisions included, in particular, Article 66 of the criminal Code in its version in force since 27 December 2003. The court ordered all provisions to remain applicable until the entry into force of new legislation and until 31 May 2013 at the most. It stressed that the fact that the Constitution stood above the Convention was not an obstacle to an international and European dialogue between the courts. In its reasoning, the Federal Constitutional Court relied on the interpretation of Article 5 and Article 7 of the Convention. It stressed, in particular, that the constitutional requirement of establishing a difference between preventive detention and detention for serving a term of imprisonment required an individualised and intensified offer of therapy and care. In line with the Court’s findings in the case of M. v. Germany, it was necessary to provide a high level of care by a team of multi-disciplinary staff. It was also necessary to offer the detainees an individualising therapy if the standard therapies available in the institution did not have prospects of success (see§ 113 and 113).

The case was heard in the Court of Appeal of Germany. The court ruled that preventive detention should be ordered in addition to the penalty. The order of preventive detention must be based on the fact that the perpetrator has been shown to be a danger to the public. The maximum duration of the preventive detention is two years. The sentence must be suspended and a measure of probation applied. If the maximum duration has expired, the detainee shall be released (Article 67d § 3). The case was decided in the Supreme Court of Germany and was heard on 17 December 2009. The decision was made by the court of appeal of Germany, and the decision was handed down in the case of M. v. Germany (no. 19359/04) The detention of mentally ill persons is provided for, first of all, in the Criminal Code as a measure of correction and prevention if the detention is ordered in relation to an unlawful act committed by the person concerned. The former maximum duration of a first period of preventive detention was abolished. Transfer for enforcement of a different measure of corrections and prevention is allowed. The detention of the mentally ill is allowed to be extended for a period of up to five years if there is a risk of serious harm to the victims. The courts can transfer a person in preventive detention to a psychiatric hospital or to a detoxification facility if the person’s reintegration into society can be better promoted thereby. A court may order a person’s placement in a psychiatric hospital at the request of the authorities of a town or county if the person concerned is mentally ill and thereby poses a severe threat to public security and order. Such an order may only be executed as long as no measure under Article 63 of the Criminal Code has been taken. On 1 January 2011 the Act on Therapy and Detention of Mentally Disturbed Violent Offenders (Therapy Detention Act – Gesetz zur Therapierung und Unterbringung psychisch gestörter Gewalttäter) entered into force. The Federal Constitutional Court held that all provisions on the retrospective prolongation of the complainants’ preventive detention beyond the former ten-year maximum period were valid. All provisions of the Criminal Code on the imposition and duration of preventive detention at issue were incompatible with the fundamental right to liberty of the persons in preventive detention. Federal Constitutional Court ordered that all provisions remained applicable until the entry into force of new legislation and until 31 May 2013 at the most. In relation to detainees whose preventive detention had been prolonged or ordered retrospectively, the courts had to examine without delay whether the persons concerned were highly likely to commit the most serious crimes of violence or sexual offences. If the above pre-conditions were not met, those detainees had to be released no later than 31 December 2011. The other provisions could only be further applied in the transitional period subject to a strict review of proportionality. In its reasoning, the Federal Constitutional Court relied on the interpretation of Article 5 and Article 7 of the Convention. It stressed, in particular, that the constitutional requirement of establishing a difference between preventive detention and detention for serving a term of imprisonment required an individualised and intensified offer of therapy and care. In line with the Court’s findings in the case of M. v. Germany (cited above, § 129), it was necessary to provide a high level of care by a team of multi-disciplinary staff and to offer the detainees anindividualised therapy if the standard therapies available in the institution did not have prospects of success.

name: Kurt Nielsen
train_texts: The case originated in an application against Denmark lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained that civil proceedings instituted by him had not been heard within a reasonable time. On 22 June 1999, the Court declared the application admissible. The case now falls to be examined by the Court of Justice of the European Union. The application was filed by Mr Kurt Nielsen (“the applicant’s” case) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) The applicant is a Danish citizen, born in 1966, and resides in Skanderborg, Denmark. The applicant claimed that the defendant companies should be held liable to pay, jointly and severally, a specified amount in compensation for permanent disablement and loss of working capacity. The case was adjourned pending the outcome of the applicant’s request to the National Board of Industrial Injuries (Arbejdsskadestyrelsen, hereinafter called the NBI), to give an opinion on the degree of disablement. The applicant was hereafter examined by two medical experts at the request of the N BI which also, on 2 February 1989, requested the Municipality of Skanderborg to provide certain information. The High Court of Western Denmark upheld the decision on 1 October 1992. The case was heard by the City Court on 25 January 1995. By judgment of 15 February 1995 the defendant companies were held liable to pay 950,803.60 DKK plus interest to the applicant. The defendants appealed against the judgment to the High Court of Western Denmark. The High Court fixed the trial to commence on 1 August 1996. It was later rescheduled to start on 5 September 1996. The judgment of 9 September 1996 was upheld and the judgment has become final. The applicant was accordingly examined again by medical experts following which the NBI submitted its opinion as to the applicants degree of disablement and working capacity on 30 June 1994.

name: Ingo Hentschel
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) by two German nationals. The applicants alleged they had been beaten and pepper spray had been used on them by police officers who, owing to an inadequate investigation, had been neither identified nor punished. They also complained under Article 13 that they had had no judicial remedy at their disposal to challenge the discontinuation and the ineffectiveness of the investigation. On 26 February 2016 the application was communicated to the Government of the Federal Republic of Germany and the case was heard. Police cordoned off the stands of the supporters of one of the teams, including both applicants, to prevent them from leaving the stadium and encountering supporters of the other team. The first applicant himself was hit with a truncheon on the head, which resulted in a bleeding laceration of 3 cm behind his ear. Both applicants were able to identify their attackers as police officers, but were not able to distinguish them further, owing to their identical uniforms and the lack of identifying signs or name tags. Both uniforms did not include any name tags or other signs identifying the individual officers. On the back of the helmets an identification number of the squad was displayed. Munich police used truncheons and pepper-spray to control supporters of Bayern Munich against Borussia Monchengladbach in December 2007. Two people filed criminal complaints against police officers. The Munich public prosecutor’s office instigated a preliminary investigation. The investigating division was also provided with a DVD showing excerpts of the video surveillance recorded by the riot control police at the football match. On 10 September 2008 the competent public prosecutor discontinued the investigation. He found that the investigation had produced evidence that some of the police officers had used. trunchetons against spectators, including women and children, in a disproportionate way and without an official order or approval. The applicants appealed against the decision to discontinue the investigation and argued that the public prosecutor had not identified all the officers involved in the operation and deployed in the area of the stadium at issue. The public prosecutor reopened the investigation on 14 October 2008 and ordered further enquiries. A further twenty-two witnesses were interviewed including fourteen platoon leaders, squad leaders and video officers of the deployed police units. The individual squad members of the three squads of the Munich riot control unit were not interviewed. The applicants had requested that they be interviewed, as the evidence had suggested that the alleged perpetrators had belonged to one of these three squads. It was established that the original video tapes and possible digital copies had already been deleted and that only the excerpts were still available. On 4 August 2009 the Munich general public prosecutor discontinued the investigation. The applicants appealed and pointed out that the members of the deployed squads had still not been questioned and that the inspected videos were fragmentary. The Munich Court of Appeal declared the applicants’ application to force further enquiries inadmissible. On 25 October 2011 the applicants lodged a constitutional complaint, relying on Articles 2, 19, 4 and 103 of the German Basic Law. The application was dismissed as it did not provide specific facts or evidence that would have allowed the court to identify an accused. Only in a case where a public prosecutor’s office had entirely refrained from investigating a crime had a court the possibility to order an investigation. The Federal Constitutional Court (hereinafter ‘the Constitutional Court’) refused, in a reasoned decision (2 BvR 1304/12), to admit the applicants’ constitutional complaint. In essence they complained that the investigation had not been effective and that the Court of Appeal had not evaluated the effectiveness of the investigation. The court held that the investigations had been conducted diligently, but had not established sufficient suspicion of criminal conduct on the part of specific police officers. The investigation against the five police officers was discontinued by the Munich public prosecutor’s office. The applicants alleged that several relevant parts of the video material, showing disproportionate police violence, had been deleted.

On 26 February 2016 the application was communicated to the Government of the Federal Republic of Germany. The applicants were represented by Mr M. Noli, a lawyer practising in Munich, and Ms A. Luczak, a law practise in Berlin. The German Government was represented by their Agents, Mr H.‑J. Behrens and Ms K. Behr. Police cordoned off the stands of the supporters of one of the teams, including both applicants, to prevent them leaving the stadium and encountering supporters of the other team. The first applicant himself was hit with a truncheon on the head, which resulted in a bleeding laceration of 3 cm behind his ear. Both applicants were able to identify their attackers as police officers, but were not able to distinguish them further, owing to their identical uniforms and the lack of identifying signs or name tags. The Government’s version of the subsequent events was that the blockade was lifted due to the aggressive behaviour of some of the spectators. The Munich public prosecutor’s office instigated a preliminary investigation into the alleged police violence. The Government challenged the accounts of the applicants and submitted that there was no credible evidence that the applicants had deliberately been hit or harmed by police officers. The investigation was conducted by the unit of the Munich police responsible for offences perpetrated by public officials. The investigating division was also provided with a DVD showing excerpts of the video surveillance recorded by the riot control police at the football match. On 10 September 2008 the competent public prosecutor discontinued the investigation. He found that the investigation had produced evidence that some of the police officers had used truncheons against spectators, including women and children, in a disproportionate way. The applicants appealed against the decision to discontinue the investigation. A further twenty-two witnesses were interviewed including fourteen platoon leaders, squad leaders and video officers of the deployed police units. The individual squad members of the three squads of the Munich riot control unit were not interviewed. The applicants had requested that they be interviewed, as the evidence had suggested that the alleged perpetrators had belonged to one of these three squads. The investigating police unit was also provided with video surveillance recorded by the 23rd platoon of the 6th Dachau public-order support force battalion. Upon the request of the applicants to secure the entire video material of the police operation, it was established that the original video tapes and possible digital copies had already been deleted. The Munich general public prosecutor confirmed the decision of the public prosecutor’s office of 4 August 2009 to discontinue the investigation. The applicants appealed and pointed out that the members of the deployed squads had still not been questioned and that the inspected videos were fragmentary, but nonetheless contradicted certain parts of the statements made by the squad leaders. The Munich Court of Appeal declared the applicants’ application to force further enquiries inadmissible on 19 September 2011. On 25 October 2011 the applicants lodged a constitutional complaint, relying on Articles 2 § 2, 19 § 4 and 103 § 1 of the German Basic Law (Gylageerzwingungsverfahren) The Federal Constitutional Court refused, in a reasoned decision (2 BvR 1304/12), to admit the applicants’ constitutional complaint. The court held that the investigations had been conducted diligently, but had not established sufficient suspicion of criminal conduct on the part of specific police officers. In its decision the Constitutional Court referred to the Court’s case-law concerning the procedural obligation of Article 2 of the Convention and, in particular, to the cases of McCann and Others v. the United Kingdom (27 September 1995, Series A no. 324) and Grams v Germany (dec., no. 33677/96, ECHR 1999‑VII)

The court held that the investigations had been conducted diligently, but had not established sufficient suspicion of criminal conduct on the part of specific police officers. A subsequent appeal before the Munich general public prosecutor was to no avail. The investigation against the five police officers was discontinued by the Munich public prosecutor’s office. name: Mehmet Tanay
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18753/04) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that a factual error made by the Court of Cassation had infringed his right of access to court. On 20 November 2007 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. The Court also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the convention) The application was filed by Mr Mehmet Tanay (“the applicant”) on 11 February 2004. The Tunceli Court accepted the medical report and began examining the merits of the case. The Court of Cassation quashed the decision, quoting the applicant’s name, instead of that of his representative, as the person who had been ill. In an application for rectification Mrs Demirdaş argued that it was she who was ill, not her client. On 13 November 2003 the Court ofCassation upheld the final ruling. The Directorate appealed, but the case was dismissed on 4 July 2003 and upheld on 14 November 2003. The case is still pending in the High Court of Justice of Turkey, which has the power to overturn the ruling.

name: Hermann Kammerer
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32435/06) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant alleged that his right to be heard had been infringed. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The case was settled by the Austrian Court of Appeal in September 2008. The applicant was granted a stay of the decision and the appeal was dismissed. The court ruled that the Austrian Government had breached the right to a fair hearing. The IAP dismissed the applicant's appeal and only amended a citation of the DAA's decision. It found that even though the car was used by somebody else the applicant, as the registered owner, has to check that the car undergoes regular inspections. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court in which he complained, inter alia, that the IAP had convicted him in absentia. The Administrative Court refused to deal with the complaint under section 33a of the Administrative Court Act since the amount of the penalty did not exceed EUR 750 and no important legal issue was at stake. The case was transferred to the Supreme Court on 29 July 2005.
