name: Thomas John Crompton
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The parties requested an oral hearing. However, the Chamber decided not to hold a hearing in the case. The applicant, Mr Thomas John Crompton, is a British national who was born in 1954 and lives in Stalybridge, Cheshire. He joined the Territorial Army in 1989 as a pay and accounts clerk, a military post, carrying out duties such as filing, photocopying and maintaining a stationery store. In July 1993 he was informed that he was to be made redundant, following organisational changes in the TA pursuant to a process of civilianisation. The applicant complained about his redundancy to the Industrial Tribunal, but his claim was rejected because the Tribunal did not have jurisdiction over military personnel. The matter was then placed before the Army Board. The Army Board met to reach a determination on 11 April 2001. It issued its decision on 16 July 2001, ordering that the applicant be offered compensation in respect of the failure to offer him alternative employment within the Army. The sum was made up of three parts: loss of salary (minus the applicant's actual earnings during the relevant period); a redundancy payment estimated on the basis of the Army Act 1955. On 10 August 2001, an award of compensation was notified to the applicant but he disputed the calculation of the compensation. The High Court rejected the claim in 2003, and again in 2004. The judge said the claim did not meet the requirements of the Act. The High Court finally accepted the claim on 18 February 2005. The bill was settled out of court in March 2005. At the time of the decision, the cost of the award was estimated at £15,000. The award was then reduced to £12,000, but not paid until the claim had been settled. The case was eventually settled for £9,000 by the Court of Appeal in 2007. The appeal was dismissed, and the decision was upheld by the Supreme Court. The decision was made to pay the full amount, plus an additional £2,500, for the cause of the case. The applicant was awarded compensation of GBP 153,864.47. The Army Board issued its decision awarding the applicant compensation on 24 May 2005. The applicant's application for judicial review was refused on 24 June 2005 on the ground that the Army Board's decision had brought the finality which the applicant had been seeking. The application was refused again on 22 September 2005. Following the applicant's renewed application and an oral hearing, permission was finally refused on 14 November 2005. It is believed that the award was incorrectly reached on the day of the awarding of the compensation. The case has been referred to as "The Soldier's Compensation Case"

The case originated in an application (no. 42509/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The parties requested an oral hearing. However, the Chamber decided not to hold a hearing in the case. The applicant, Mr Thomas John Crompton, is a British national who was born in 1954 and lives in Stalybridge, Cheshire. His discharge from the Army, dated 18 February 1994, was formally made, incorrectly, on the basis that his services were no longer required. He later discovered that his former duties were being carried out by an untrained civilian, while the technical store-man post remained vacant. In 1994 the applicant complained about his redundancy to the Industrial Tribunal. His claim was rejected because the Tribunal did not have jurisdiction over matters involving military personnel. The matter was then placed before the Army Board of the Defence Council. The Army Board found in the applicant's favour as regards his argument that he ought to have been, but was not, given priority before five selection boards. An award of compensation was notified to the applicant on 10 August 2001, but he disputed the calculation of the compensation. In November 2001 a further offer of settlement was made to him, which he rejected. In April 2003 the Army board made a further compensation offer of GBP 94,016.67. The High Court ruled that the award did not cover the full cost of the service. A further offer of GBP 147,000 was made, but it was refused. The case was adjourned for two years. The High Court finally ruled in favor of the claimant on 6 October 2004. The award was made on 9 October 2004, but the compensation was not paid. The appeal was dismissed on 9 November 2005, and the case was settled out of court on 10 November 2005. The claimant's case was rejected on 9 December 2005, after a delay of six months. The compensation was paid out of the total cost of his service, not from the total amount of the award. On 24 May 2005 the Army Board issued its decision awarding the applicant compensation of GBP 153,864.47. The applicant's application for judicial review was refused on 24 June 2005. The application was refused again on 22 September 2005. Following the applicant's renewed application and an oral hearing, permission was finally refused on 14 November 2005. train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The application was declared partially inadmissible and the complaint concerning the applicants’ right to have effective review proceedings, by which they could challenge the lawfulness of their continued detention, was communicated to the Government. The applicants were born in 1947, 1976, 1973, 1983 and 1987 respectively. At the time of the application they were being held in detention in Buca F‑Type prison in İzmir. They were held on suspicion of making threats, of fraud and of smuggling, the offences that they were suspected of having committed. The applicants were charged with committing fraud, making threats, and carrying out raids and smuggling, under Article 220 and other related articles of the Criminal Code. The first hearing was scheduled for 24 June 2008. The trial court decided to release the applicants from pre-trial detention on the same day. The applicants’ representative appealed. The appeal court dismissed the appeal without holding an oral hearing. The applicant’s representative appealed to the İzmir Assize Court to release them. The court dismissed this appeal on 9 May 2008 without holding a hearing. On 2 May 2008 the applicants objected to that decision in respect of the first four applicants and applied for them to be released. The objection was dismissed on 7 May 2008.

name: Andrzej Pakos
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 3252/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his detention on remand exceeded a “reasonable time’ within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the convention. He was arrested on suspicion of having been involved in drug trafficking as a member of an organised criminal group. In their decisions, the courts repeatedly relied on the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged, the serious nature of the offences and the severity of the likely sentence. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The prosecutor lodged a bill of indictment with the Katowice Regional Court against the applicant and 32 other co-accused. The prosecutor requested 22 witnesses to be heard. The applicant's detention was extended three more times and the measure has still not been lifted. The judge in charge of the case has refused to lift the detention order. The court has ordered that the trial of the applicant will begin by 15 March 2006. However, the judge says that the applicant's family situation is not so different from that of most families where a husband and father is imprisoned. The case will be heard in the Regional Court on 15 January 2007. The applicant is still detained and the proceedings before the first-instance court have not yet been terminated. The suspicion was justified, in the court’s view, by the charge of acting in an organised criminal group. The applicant was charged with two counts of attempted murder and one count of attempted theft. The charges were confirmed by the Court of Appeal but the applicant was not allowed to leave the country to face the charges. He is currently being held in a detention centre in the city of Krakow, Poland. He was also charged with three counts of attempting to steal a car in Poland in 2009. The court of appeal found that the charges against him were not proven and he was released on bail. However, he was allowed to travel to Poland to continue his legal battle.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29913/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. name: Makbule Özalp
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32457/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The petition asked for a copy of the arrest and autopsy reports as well as the publicProsecutor's decision of non-prosecution. It also asked for the decision of the investigation that had been commenced into the death of Cavit OzalP and the decision of non- Prosecution. The application was denied by the public Prosecutor. On 24 August 1995 Cavit Özalp was taken into custody by the gendarmes from the Bismil Gendarme District Command on suspicion of membership of the PKK. He was suspected of aiding and abetting the PKK terrorists. Cavit guided the soldiers to the shelter near the Şedat road in the Kamberli village. While protecting themselves in a secure distance, the soldiers asked him to open the cover of the shelter. As he opened the cover,. the soldiers witnessed a big explosion, which tore Cavit's body into pieces. The explosives had been placed in the entrance to the. shelter by other members of the. PKK. Cavit Özalp was killed on 26 August 1995. His legs were severed as a result of the explosion. No other signs of injury were observed on the dismembered body. An incident report was drafted by the gendarmes and was signed by three non-commissioned officers and the village mayor Mr Kütbettin Altunç. The public prosecutor at the Diyarbakır State Security Court decided that no prosecution should be brought against Cavit ÖZalp on account of his membership of the PKK. The case file was transferred to the Bismil District Administrative Council. Cavit Özalp was killed in an explosion after being asked to open the cover of a bomb shelter. The explosives had been previously placed there by the terrorists. The report concluded that the security forces had performed their duty with diligence and it was recommended that no prosecution be brought against the members of the security force. On 2 April 1996 the Diyarbakır Regional Administrative Court upheld the decision of the Bismil District Administrative Council to not bring charges against security forces. The court ruled that no charges should be brought in connection with the incident. The case is still pending in the Turkish Supreme Court of Justice, which is expected to rule in the case in the near future. Cavit Özalp was sentenced to three years in prison in 1996. The sentence was handed down by the Diyarbakır State Security Court Public Prosecutor's Office. The case was originally brought by the applicants' representatives to the public prosecutor's office. The application was rejected on 5 February 1996 and the subsequent rejection of the publicProsecutor's office was upheld on 2 April 1996. In addition, the application was also rejected by the Bismil District Administrative Council on 28 February 1996. It was upheld by the Regional Administrative Court on 2 March 1996, upholding the decision of the Council. The appeal was dismissed on 5 April 1996, and the appeal was dropped on 10 July 1996.

name: Abdülkerim Ağrakçe
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29059/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Abdülkerim Ağrakçe (“the applicant”) was arrested and taken into custody for his suspected involvement in terrorist activities in 1980. He was acquitted of all charges in 1990. In 1996 the applicant applied to the Diyarbakır Assize Court, seeking compensation pursuant to Law no. 466. This Law provides, inter alia, for an award of damages to any person who has been unlawfully deprived of his or her liberty. In the course of the proceedings the assize court held investigatory sittings on a regular basis. Only on four occasions did it decide to notify the applicant’s lawyer of the date of its next session (30 April 1997, 10 February 1999, 1 June 2000 and 6 June 2001). However, no session was postponed on account of the applicant's lawyer's failure to attend. In 2000 the first-instance court handed down its third ruling where it awarded a certain amount of compensation. On 27 March 2001 the Court of Cassation quashed this judgment on the ground that the amount awarded was too low. On 6 September 2001 theAssize court awarded the applicant TRL 3,000,000k in respect of non-pecuniary damage.

name: Henrik Hasslund
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36244/06) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Acting President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government on 5 September 2007. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applicant's application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). The applicant was represented by Mr Tyge Trier, a lawyer practising in Copenhagen. The Danish Government were represented by their Agent, Ms Nina Holst-Christensen of the Ministry of Justice. The applicant was arrested and charged with aggravated debtor fraud on 19 September 1995. He was charged with 15 counts out of a total of fifty-nine committed between March 1992 and May 1993. His responsibility related to an amount of DKK 9,890,000 (approximately 1,300,000 euros (EUR) out of the total amount of tax evaded in the case which came to approximately EUR 19,000,000. The applicant, the five co-accused and more than seventy witnesses were heard, including state-registered public accountants. A judgment of 6 April 2001, which ran to 220 pages, the City Court convicted the applicant in accordance with the indictment. The City Court dismissed the applicant’s claim that the length of the proceedings had been at variance with Article 6 of the Convention. The applicant was sentenced to two years’ imprisonment. but on one count he was acquitted. The co-accused were also convicted. An amount of DKK 2,200,000 was seized, and he was deprived for an indefinite period of his right to establish a private limited company or a company or an association requiring public approval, or to become a manager and/or member of a directors’ board of such companies. The City Court found no violation of Article 6, although there were longer periods of inactivity during one part of the case, while investigation was going on in another. The High Court upheld the City Court’s judgment. A total of about 90 hearings were held in the case. The closing speeches were held over ten days in April, May, and June 2004. In January 2005 the cases were sent to the prosecution, which gave its opinion on 29 March 2005. The applicant and the co‑defendants gave their comments in reply and at a meeting on 5 August 2005 the Leave to Appeal Board decided to refuse the requests. The case was not heard again until 2 May 2006, when the police telephoned the leave to appeal board and drew attention to the case's existence. The Court records comprised 861 pages. The applicant and the co-defendant were informed on 21 June 2006 that their requests for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court had been refused. Subsequently, on his request, counsel for the relevant co-Defendant who had wanted to submit supplementary comments did so on 2 and 13 June 2006. the case. The applicant was found not guilty of all charges against him. The co- Defendant was found to be guilty of the most serious charges against the applicant. The case was adjourned until 6 July 2006 for further proceedings to be heard by the Court of Appeal. The appeal was eventually dismissed on 14 July 2006. The application was later dismissed on 9 August 2006.

name: İlkay Barış
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant was born in 1967 and lives in Istanbul. She was taken into police custody on suspicion of membership of the Revolutionary Left (the “DEV-SOL”), an illegal organisation. On 24 December 2002 the Istanbul State Security Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced her to death, subsequently commuted to life imprisonment. On 15 November 2006 the Istanbul Assize Court convicted her under Article 146 of the former Criminal Code. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the assize court. On 16 April 2007 the court ruled that the judgment was correct. The court of cassation was the highest court in the country. The case was heard in the Supreme Court of the European Court of Justice, which heard the case in 2007. The decision was upheld by the court of appeals on 13 April 2008. The appeal was dismissed on 15 April 2008, and the case was returned to the assizes court for further proceedings. The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was brought before a single judge at the Istanbul State Security Court who ordered her detention on remand in 1992. She was charged with attempting to undermine the constitutional order, proscribed by Article 146 of the former Criminal Code. The case against the applicant was joined to another brought against five other persons. The court dismissed her requests for release pending trial on each occasion, having regard to the nature of the offence, the state of evidence and the content of the case file. On 15 November 2006 the Istanbul Assize Court convicted the applicant under Article 146 and sentenced her to life imprisonment. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the assize court. On 16 April 2007 the court upheld the decision of the court of assize. The decision was made by the High Court of Justice and Justice of the Peace. The case is still pending in the Supreme Court of the United States of America. The verdict is due back in October 2007. name: Sławomir Raban
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 24254/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant's detention to the Government. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was born in 1962 and lives in Warszawa. He is currently serving a prison sentence in Włodawa Prison. He was arrested on suspicion of several counts of extortion on 28 June 2001. The Lublin Regional Prosecutor decided to amend the charges against the applicant. He was suspected of several counts of extortion committed while acting in an organised criminal gang. The court relied on a strong suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences in question, which was supported by evidence from witnesses and experts. The applicant was charged with crimes for which he was liable to a sentence of imprisonment exceeding eight years, and that the circumstances of the case indicated that there was a reasonable risk that he might obstruct the proceedings. The Lublin Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's detention until 11 May 2004. The judge noted that the prolongation of the investigation was not attributable to the prosecuting authorities, but resulted from the fact that other suspects had been identified and arrested. The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to six years' imprisonment (case no. IX K 2252/01) The applicant appealed on 20 January 2006. According to the applicant the appellate court remitted the case for re-examination. The applicant is currently serving a prison sentence imposed by the judgment of the Płońsk District Court of 3 September 2004 (case file no. II K 282/03). It appears that the judgment has become final. The application was dropped on 2 December 2005, and the applicant was also found guilty of the offences he had been charged with in another set of criminal proceedings conducted by the Lublin District Court. He was sentenced to 3 year's imprisonment.

The case originated in an application (no. 24254/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Sławomir Raban (“the applicant”) is currently serving a prison sentence in Włodawa Prison. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of several counts of extortion on 28 June 2001. On 29 June 2001 the Lublin District Court remanded him in custody, relying on the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offence in question. On 6 October 2005 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the applicant's detention to the Government. The applicant was charged with several counts of extortion committed while being a member of an organised crime group. The court relied on a strong suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences in question, which was supported by evidence from witnesses and experts. The applicant was hospitalised following a medicine overdose in a suicide attempt. He could not attend the hearing on 16 July 2002. The Lublin Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's detention until 11 May 2004. It observed that the fact that the trial had not been terminated could not be attributed to the authorities, given the volume of evidence and the fact  that some hearings had had to be cancelled as the defendants' counsels or witnesses had not appeared. The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to six years' imprisonment. The applicant appealed on 20 January 2006. According to the applicant the appellate court remitted the case for re-examination. The court relied on the fact that almost all witnesses had been heard and thus the applicant ceased to pose a threat to the proper conduct of the proceedings. He is currently serving a prison sentence imposed by the judgment of the Płońsk District Court of 3 September 2004 (case file no. II K 282/03). It appears that the judgment has become final. He was also found guilty of the offences he had been charged with in another set of criminal proceedings conducted by the Lublin District Court in 2005.

The hearing was held in the German language because the Court had authorised the person assisting the Delegates of the Commission to use the. German language (Rule 27 para. 3). Peter Sutter, a Swiss national born in 1949, was a student and resident in Basel. He was subjected to five and seven days’ strict arrest for refusing to comply with Article 203 bis of the service regulations, relating to hair-cuts. On 16 May 1977, at the close of a public hearing, Divisional Court no. 5 delivered in public a judgment sentencing the applicant to ten days' imprisonment for the two offences. name: Mirosław Palewski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32971/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of his right of access to a court. The application was brought by Mr Mirosław Palewski (“the applicant”). The Polish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The case was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The court was told that the applicant had already received PLN 360,572.68 from the insurance company Warta S.A. The court further considered that this in itself justified the refusal to exempt him from court fees as he could have put money aside for that purpose. “It is therefore not clear what type of business activities the applicant is involved in at Morska Street in Koszalin (...) The documents submitted by the applicant show that he has already received £90,000 [EUR 90,142] as partial compensation. According to the applicant, this amount did not compensate him for the damage actually incurred.” The applicant applied for compensation of PLN 545,918.65 and asked to be exempted from court fees. He submitted that the business’s assets had been attached in enforcement proceedings against him, that his bank accounts had been frozen and that he had substantial debts. His wife did not work and their children were students. On 3 December 2003 the Koszalin District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) declared the applicant's company insolvent. The Gdańsk Court of Appeal gave a decision exempting the applicant from any fees exceeding PLN 10,000 (approx. EUR 2,500) on 14 May 2004. The Koszalin Regional Court ordered the applicant to pay a court fee of PLN 10,000 for lodging his statement of claim on pain of having it returned. The court further found that, while it was true that the applicant was in debt and that his tax return for the period from January to October 2003 had shown a loss in the amount ofPLN 68,538.74 (approx. EUR 7,134) “The previous decisions concerning the exemption from court fees, based on the different facts, are irrelevant for the present finding.” On 27 August 2004 the Koszino Regional Court returned the statement of claims to the applicant since he had failed to pay the required court fee.

name: A. Mackay
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 10734/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged they were unable to challenge a court order prohibiting reporting of a criminal trial in violation of Articles 6, 10 and 13. The application was lodged by a British national, Mr A. Mackay, and the British Broadcasting Corporation in Scotland (BBC Scotland) (“the applicants”) on 23 March 2005. It was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The Crown appealed against the decision of the trial judge to desert the trial diet simpliciter. The appeal was scheduled to be heard by the High Court of Justiciary (sitting as an appeal court in Edinburgh) on 15 February 2005. The High Court made a section 4(2) order prohibiting the publication of a report of any part of the appeal hearing until the appeal was completed. The order was posted on the Scottish Courts Service website and circulated to the Scottish media. BBC Scotland was told verbally by court officials that no opportunity would be made available for it to make representations in court. The Government maintain that BBC Scotland did not challenge that decision. Government maintain that BBC Scotland did not contest the decision not to hold a hearing before 18 February 2005. Appeal Court deferred consideration of BBC Scotland's application for the recall of the section 4(2) order made on 15 February 2005 until 21 June 2005. On the basis of further information provided by the prosecution as to who had been watching the trial proceedings in the remote viewing room, the Appeal Court recalled the order of the trial judge and substituted an order for desertion pro loco et tempore, which allowed for the re-indictment of one of the original accused. If the High Court dismissed the prosecution's appeal, then BBC Scotland would be heard by the court.

name: Ewa Glesmann
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’s Convention”) by a Polish national. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr T. Kochanowski, a lawyer practising in Berlin. The German Government were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Polish Government, having been informed of their right to intervene in the proceedings, did not indicate that they wished to exercise that right. The applicant was not informed about the foster parents’ place of residence for almost two years and was thus prevented from exercising access rights. On 9 February 1998 the expert E. submitted her expert opinion. She considered that the child S. suffered from a serious emotional disorder which had been caused by family tensions and that S. should be offered psychotherapy in order to overcome her traumata. The decision on custody and access rights should be suspended until the child had stabilised. The applicant consented to the child’s remaining with the foster family for the duration of the necessary psychotherapy, which she estimated at one year. On 29 October 1998, during the hearing on the parents' divorce, both parents‘ counsels unanimously declared that they presently did not lodge any motions regarding parental authority. On 9 September 1999 the District Court ordered the parents to advance their share of the costs. On 6 March 2000 the judge ruled that the parents should be allowed to return the child to their care. On 28 June 2000 the court ruled that both parents could return their child to care for him or her. On 23 October 2000 the mother and father agreed that the child should be returned to the care of the parents. The child was returned to his mother on 24 October 2000. The parents were allowed to keep the child until the end of the year when they could return him to his father. The father and daughter were then allowed to leave the house without fear of losing their child. The child was supposed to stay with her parents for a period of time. Her parents wanted to continue to care for her. The court ruled that the child should stay with them until she was older. The child was eventually released to her mother. She has since lived with her mother and other family members. She is now living with a new family. Her mother and father are no longer involved in the child's care. She no longer needs to be seen by her parents. She does not need to see them regularly. She should not be left alone with her father. She needs to have regular visits to see her mother, sister and other relatives. She also needs to see the carer regularly. The child’s curator told the court that S. wished to live with the foster family and was seriously opposed to contacts with her parents. The curator recommended that this wish be respected. The court requested the Youth Office to report on the child's present life circumstances and on the discontinuation of therapy. The applicant rejected this proposal and submitted that recent visiting contacts between herself and her daughter had developed in a more positive way. On 24 April 2003 the Pankow-Weissensee District Court, following a hearing attended by the applicant, decided that the child should stay with her foster family until she reached the age of majority. However, it was essential that visiting contact were not discontinued completely. The District Court considered that the applicant was unable to accept the child’s wishes and her present life circumstances within the foster family. It followed that parental authority had to be withdrawn from both parents and transferred to the Youth Office. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Berlin Court of Appeal (Kammergericht) and considered the measures taken by the District Court to be disproportionate. The Court of appeal held a hearing in the presence of S. and her curator ad litem, her parents, her foster parents, two representatives of the Youth. Office and the foster parents and withdrew parental authority from the parents. Furthermore, visiting contacts between the child and her parents were suspended for one year. The Court of Appeal quashed the District Court’s decision, transferred sole parental authority to the child’S father and granted the applicant visiting rights once per month for five and a half hours each. All parties heard in the proceedings had confirmed that the child found a sense of security and stability in the foster family, where she had been living for six and ahalf years. The child had consistently expressed the wish to live with the fosterFamily as a full family member. The Court of appeal conceded that the alienation between the applicant and her daughter had to a substantial degree been caused by the period of time which had elapsed since her placement. The applicant was ordered to contribute to costs incurred by the accommodation of her daughter in the foster family from 25 June 1997 until 31 December 1998. She alleged that the impugned decision was disproportionate and violated her right to the enjoyment of her family life under Article 6 of the Basic Law. The Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant’s constitutional complaint for adjudication without giving any further reasons. The applicant's appeal was rejected by the Berlin-Brandenburg Administrative Court of Appeal (Oberverwaltungsgericht) on 19 September 2005. If the applicant. should wish to do so, she can appeal the decision.

name: Juri Maslov
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the imposition of an exclusion order on him and his expulsion to Bulgaria violated his right to respect for private and family life. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. On 22 March 2007 a Chamber of that Section delivered a judgment in which it held, by four votes to three, that there had been a violation of Article 8. The respondent Government should pay the applicant 5,759.96 euros in respect of costs and expenses. The Bulgarian Government did not make use of their right to intervene. The applicant was sentenced to eighteen months’ imprisonment, thirteen of which were suspended on probation. The sentence was accompanied by an order to undergo drug therapy. The Court heard addresses by Mr Deuretsbacher and Mr Trauttmansdorff, as well as their answers to questions put by a number of judges. András Sajó, substitute judge, replaced Riza Türmen, who was unable to take part in the further consideration of the case (Rule 24 § 1). The applicant was granted an unlimited settlement permit (Niederlassungsbewilligung) on 8 March 1999. On 11 February 2000 the applicant was arrested and further criminal proceedings were opened against him relating to a series of burglaries committed between June and January 2000. The applicant, who moved to Austria at the age of six, was convicted of aggravated burglary and attempted aggravated burglary in 2000. The Vienna Federal Police Authority imposed a ten-year exclusion order on the applicant. The applicant appealed, saying the order violated his rights under Article 8 of the Convention. The appeal was dismissed by the Vienna Public Security Authority (Sicherheitsdirektion) on 19 July 2001. He served his prison term, but was not allowed to stay in Austria any longer as it was contrary to the public interest to allow him to stay any longer. The application was eventually rejected by the Administrative Court and the Constitutional Court. The applicant came to Austria only at the age of six, had attended school in Austria and could not speak Bulgarian. He had no relatives or other social contacts in Bulgaria and stressed the fact that he was still a minor. The Administrative Court dismissed the complaint and found that the exclusion order was justified under Article 8 § 2 of the Convention. On 22 December 2003 the applicant was deported to Sofia. According to information given by counsel at the hearing, the applicant did not commit any further offences in Bulgarian and has found employment there. The Government informed the Court that the order will expire on 3 January 2011, that is ten years after its issue.

On 22 March 2007 a Chamber of that Section delivered a judgment in which it held, by four votes to three, that there had been a violation of Article 8. The respondent Government should pay the applicant 5,759.96 euros in respect of costs and expenses. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 6 February 2008 (Rule 59) The applicant was born in October 1984 and currently lives in Bulgaria. He was sentenced to eighteen months’ imprisonment, thirteen of which were suspended on probation. The sentence was accompanied by an order to undergo drug therapy. The applicant was granted an unlimited settlement permit (Niederlassungsbewilligung) on 8 March 1999. On 11 February 2000 the applicant was arrested and further criminal proceedings were opened against him relating to a series of burglaries committed between June 1999 and January 2000. The Court heard addresses by Mr Deuretsbacher and Mr Trauttmansdorff, as well as their answers to questions put by a number of judges. On 25 May 2000 the Vienna Juvenile Court convicted the applicant on eighteen counts of aggravated burglary and attempted aggravated burglary. On 3 January 2001 the Vienna Federal Police Authority (Bundespolizeidirektion) imposed a ten-year exclusion order on the applicant. The applicant appealed the exclusion order, claiming it violated his rights under Article 8 of the Convention. On 17 August 2001 the applicant lodged complaints both with the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) and the Constitutional Court. On 19 July 2001, the Vienna Public Security Authority (Sicherheitsdirektionsverfassung) dismissed the appeal. The applicant came to Austria only at the age of six, had attended school in Austria and could not speak Bulgarian. He had no relatives or other social contacts in Bulgaria and stressed the fact that he was still a minor. The Administrative Court dismissed the complaint and found that the exclusion order was justified under Article 8 § 2 of the Convention. The Constitutional Court declined to deal with the applicant’s complaint for lack of prospects of success. On 22 December 2003 the applicant was deported to Sofia. According to information given by counsel at the hearing, the applicant did not commit any further offences in Bulgaria. The Government informed the Court that the inclusion order will expire on 3 January 2011, ten years after its issue.

name: Michael Thaler
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 58141/00) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the Regional Appeals Commission which decided on his claims for doctor’s fees lacked independence and impartiality. By a decision of 15 September 2003 the Court declared the application admissible. The case was assigned to the newly composed First Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26:1. The Court ruled in favour of the applicant and the Austrian government. The applicant lodged a complaint against the Tyrol Regional Health Insurance Board. He claimed that it had to pay some ATS 18 million (about 1,3 million euros) as the doctor’s fees provided for in the general agreement between the Association of Social Insurance Boards and Tyrol Medical Association were far too low. The Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint. It did not accept that the Regional Appeals Commission's decision had violated the applicant's constitutional rights. However, referring to its constant case-law, the Constitutional Court found that the applicant’S constitutional rights were not violated. The second set of proceedings took place in 1999. Constitutional Court found no indication that the members of the Regional Appeals Commission lacked independence or impartiality. ‘A violation of the required impartiality could, thus, ... be due to specific circumstances in the individual case resulting, for example, from an official or organisational dependence of the appointed member of the Commission,' said the court. “A constellation affecting the appearance of independence and impartiality ... could only exist if the appointed assessors had been involved in the preparation of the general agreement or if there were other specific reasons raising legitimate doubts about their independence, impartiality in determining certain legal matters,’ the court said.

On 17 December 1999 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint. It did not accept that the Regional Appeals Commission's decision had violated the applicant's constitutional rights. The second set of proceedings was heard at the Supreme Court of Justice of Germany. The applicant claimed that it had to pay some ATS 18 million (about 1,3 million euros) as the doctor's fees provided for in the general agreement were far too low and, therefore, his contract with the Regional Health Insurance Board was null and void. Constitutional Court found no indication that the members of the Regional Appeals Commission lacked independence or impartiality. Members were not bound by any instructions and could not be forced to act in a certain way. ‘A constellation affecting the appearance of independence and impartiality could only exist if the appointed assessors had been involved in the preparation of the general agreement or if there were other specific reasons raising legitimate doubts about their impartiality in determining certain legal matters,’ the court said in its ruling. The case was Hortolomei v. Austria (cited above) in which the court ruled that the European Court of Human Rights had a right to hear the case in Strasbourg.

name: Istvan Herczegfalvy
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 19 April 1991. It originated in an application (no. 10533/83) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr Istvan Herczegfalvy, a Hungarian national, on 27 November 1978. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b) The applicant is Istvan Herczegfalvy, a Hungarian citizen who has lived in Austria since 1964. He had served two prison sentences in succession, following convictions pronounced by the Vienna Regional Criminal Court and confirmed in part by the Supreme Court. He was declared partly incapacitated (beschränkt entmündigt) and appointed an adviser. The Court heard addresses by them by them in Strasbourg on 21 April 1992. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 21 October 1991. The applicant's memorial incorporated his claims for just satisfaction (Article 50 of the Convention) (art. 50), on 16 October and 20 December. In the meantime, further prosecutions were brought against Mr Herczegfalvy for assaults on warders and fellow prisoners and for serious threats against judges. The applicant unsuccessfully appealed to the Review Chamber (Ratskammer) of the Regional Court and to the Vienna Court of Appeal. On 9 August 1983 the District Court appointed a new adviser, who has acted as such since then. According to a ruling of the guardianship court of 19 July 1984, his position was equivalent as from 1 July 1984 to that of a curator (Sachwalter) within the meaning of Article 273 (3), sub-paragraph 3, of the Civil Code. The hearing before the Regional Court took place on 9 and 10 January 1979. The court found that the charges against Mr Herczegfalvy had been proved and ordered him to be detained under Article 21 (1) of the Criminal Code. The Vienna Court of Appeal, to which the applicant had appealed, held on 29 August 1979 that it had no jurisdiction. On 5 September 1979 the Review Chamber upheld the detention in issue. Applying Article 429 (4) ofThe Code of Criminal Procedure, it ordered Mr Herzenfalvy to be sent to the Vienna psychiatric hospital. He stayed there from 29 June to 23 July 1979 and was then returned to the prison. Mr Herczegfalvy went on hunger strike since 2 August 1979. On 10 September 1979 he was admitted to ward 23 of a psychiatric hospital. He stayed there until his release on 28 November 1984. The application was dismissed by the Vienna Court of Appeal on 8 October 1979. The Supreme Court had on 3 October 1979 varied the judgment of 10 January 1979 in part (see paragraphs 14-15 above), quashed the detention order and remitted the case to the Regional Court. Pursuant to Article 429 (4), the Review Chamber and the Court of appeal extended the detention in question in 1980. The applicant subsequently challenged the validity of his declarations. He said that he had made them only with a view to his repatriation to Hungary. A court ordered the detention of Mr Herczegfalvy after a psychiatric report stated that he was a dangerous person. A psychiatrist recommended his release subject to supervision. He was conditionally released on 28 November in accordance with a court’s decision of 14 November, itself based on a psychiatric. report dated 14 September (see paragraph 34 below) The court found that the applicant's paranoia had admittedly worsened, but that it was primarily due to his detention (Haftquerulanz) He was still suffering from paranoia querulans, and if released would undoubtedly refuse to follow the necessary course of treatment. He would consequently be likely to bring numerous complaints or even carry out the threats he had made, in particular those against the prison staff. Mr Herczegfalvy had begun a hunger strike on 2 August 1979 as a protest against his detention and the refusal to give him his files. He collapsed on 28 August and was transferred to a clinic where he received intensive medical care. On 10 September 1979 he was transferred back to the Vienna psychiatric hospital, where he remained until his release on 28 November 1984 (see paragraph 23 above). The director of the hospital ordered him to be force fed, pursuant to section 8 (3) of the Hospitals Law. The applicant refused all contact and refused to have any medical examination or treatment. He was also given sedatives against his will (three doses of 30mg each of Taractan IM) Mr Herczegfalvy. made a complete recovery when he left, and he still needed treatment with antibiotics and neuroleptics. On his return to the closed unit he was handcuffed and a belt placed around his ankles because of the danger of aggression and the death threats he was making. The restraints were not removed until 14 February 1980. The applicant continued his hunger strike without interruption, and had been artificially fed throughout this period. On 22 February he was given paper and a ballpoint pen. He was forbidden on 27 December 1980 to watch television. name: Günther Paul Litwin
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been denied access to the appeal courts, contrary to Article 6 of the convention. The court, following a proposal made by the applicant’s counsel, promised a maximum penalty of nine‑and‑a‑half years’ imprisonment in exchange for the applicant's waiver of his right to appeal. The Government did not take part in the agreement reached between the applicant and the public prosecutor. The application was decided on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant was convicted of aggravated extortion, aggravated robbery and attempted aggravated robbery (two counts of each offence) and dangerous bodily injury (one count) and sentenced to nine-and-a-half years’ imprisonment. The court considered the fact that the applicant had eventually waived his right to the confiscated assets and had thus delivered a major proportion of his criminal profits as a mitigating factor. The applicant's new counsel applied for restitution of the status quo ante and lodged an appeal on points of law, arguing that the waiver of the right to appeal had been invalid because it had not complied with the requirements of the Federal Court of Justice's case-law. The Second Chamber of the Federal Court of Justice dismissed the applicant’s request for restitution of the status quo ante and rejected his appeal on points of law as inadmissible. Relying on its own settled case-law, the court observed that a waiver of the right to appeal could not be revoked, rescinded or withdrawn. The court did not find it necessary to establish whether the waiver had been part of a negotiated agreement, as this fact did not call into question the validity of the waiver as such. The only decisive factor was whether the accused had been unduly influenced when waiving hisright to appeal. In the present case, there was no indication that there had been such undue influence. The applicant complained he had been unduly influenced when waiving his right to appeal in exchange for a maximum penalty of nine-and-a-half years’ imprisonment. The Federal Court of Justice had failed to consider the fact that his wife, who had not been involved in the trial, had also been asked to waive any rights she had to the confiscated assets. This procedural method had been arbitrary and not been in accordance with the statutory provisions governing the confiscation of assets in criminal proceedings, he said. The court refused to admit the constitutional complaint for examination without giving further reasons. This decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 4 December 2003.

The case originated in an application (no. 29090/06) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been denied access to the appeal courts, contrary to Article 6 of the convention. The Government was represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The court, following a proposal made by the applicant’s counsel, promised a maximum penalty of nine‑and‑a‑half years’ imprisonment in exchange for his waiver of his right to appeal. The Fulda Regional Court convicted the applicant of aggravated extortion, aggravated robbery and attempted aggravated robbery (two counts of each offence) and dangerous bodily injury (one count) The court, stating that the applicant had not entered a plea, based its findings on DNA expert evidence pointing to a high probability that the. applicant had been the person that had caused marks found at the crime scenes. The applicant subsequently appointed new counsel. On 12 April 2001 the applicant’s new counsel applied for restitution of the status quo ante and lodged an appeal on points of law, arguing that the waiver of the right to appeal had been invalid because it had not complied with the requirements of the Federal Court of Justice's case-law. The applicant argued that the actual waiver of the right to appeal had been declared before delivery of the judgment. The Court of Justice did not find it necessary to establish whether the waiver had been part of a negotiated agreement. The only decisive factor was whether the accused had been unduly influenced. The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) by a stateless person, Mr Günther Paul Litwin (“the applicant’), on 14 May 2004. The Government was represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. On 29 March 2010 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the case at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicant and his wife, who was present in the courtroom, declared that they waived any rights to the assets confiscated by the prosecution service. The court considered the fact that the applicant had eventually waived his right to the confiscated assets and had thus delivered a major proportion of his criminal profits as a mitigating factor. The Fulda Regional Court convicted the applicant of aggravated extortion, aggravated robbery and attempted aggravated robbery (two counts of each offence) and dangerous bodily injury (one count) and sentenced him to nine-and-a-half years’ imprisonment. The applicant subsequently appointed new counsel. On 12 April 2001 the applicant’s new counsel applied for restitution of the status quo ante and lodged an appeal on points of law. The applicant argued that the actual waiver of the right to appeal had been declared before delivery of the judgment and had been invalid for this reason as well. The only decisive factor was whether the accused had been unduly influenced when waiving his right to Appeal. In the present case, there was no indication that there had been such undue influence. The applicant could not be granted restitution of the status quo ante. The decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 5 July 2001. A man accused of embezzling money was sentenced to nine-and-a-half years in prison. He filed a constitutional complaint claiming that he had been unduly influenced by the court. The case was settled out of court and the assets were returned to the owner. The man was released on bail and returned to his home in the north of the country. The court ruled that the confiscation of the assets had been arbitrary and constituted a violation of the right to an effective remedy.

The applicant was living with his family in Germany, where his father was an Army Corporal serving in the Support Unit of the Rhine Garrison. His father was discharged from the army in November 1994. Trial by court-martial ended with the applicant’s conviction on 3 May 1995. The applicant appealed to the Courts-Martial Appeal Court, which had the power to quash the conviction if it considered it unsafe. The Lord Chief Justice, Lord Bingham of Cornhill, giving judgment on 30 July 1996, held, dismissing the appeal. We are satisfied that these proceedings were not an abuse of process. Had the appellant been held in Germany to await trial, as he could have been, his claim to trial in England would have appeared weaker. The appeal court certified a question of law for law for the benefit of the public. House of Lords granted leave to appeal on 9 July 1997. On 16 December 1997 the House of Lords unanimously dismissed the appeal. Lords Slynn of Hadley and Hope of Craighead expressed the view that at first sight the decision to prosecute the applicant—a civilian aged only 17 at the time of the murder—by court-martial had been inappropriate. Lord Hope explained: “It is not difficult to understand the utility of [section 209 of the Army Act 1955: see paragraph 24 below], in view of the greatly increased opportunities which were by then available for families and other civilian personnel to accompany the forces when serving overseas.” In his letter of 14 June 1994 to the Attorney General the Director of Army Legal Services had stated that many of the witnesses were German and that they could not be forced to attend a trial in England. The defence had not yet indicated what evidence would be agreed. The Director thought that, while some of their evidence might be agreed, it was unlikely that this would include the police and forensic experts. He added that one of the forensic scientists who was responsible for examining secretions and bloodstains was being difficult to deal with and would only attend meetings if they were arranged through the German public prosecutor in the nearest large town. This account of what happened strongly suggests that no agreement was reached, despite several written requests and reminders, about any of the evidence until the commencement of the trial. There is no sound basis for thinking that a prosecution in the English courts within a reasonable time would have been seen to be practicable. The Army Act 1955 provides that a person subject to military law who commits a civil offence, whether in the United Kingdom or elsewhere, shall be guilty of an offence against this section. A person shall not be charged with an offence under this section committed in the UK if the corresponding civil offence is ... murder. ...” A person won’t be charged for an offence committed in Britain if the equivalent civil offence in Britain is murder.” “The Army Act 1950 provides that military authorities of the sending State shall have the primary right to exercise jurisdiction over a member of a force or a civilian component in relation to (i) offences solely against property or security of that State, or (ii) offences arising out of an act or omission done in the performance of official duty”. Trial of those who have ceased to be subject to military law is expressly provided for by section 131 of the Act. In practice, most criminal offences allegedly committed by a civilian dependent would be tried by a Standing Civilian Court. An exception is provided by section 9 of the 1861 Act, which gives jurisdiction to British courts in respect of alleged murders and manslaughters committed by British citizens anywhere in the world. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 8400/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had not had a fair trial as there were insufficient guarantees to exclude legitimate doubt regarding the independence and impartiality of the tribunal which tried him on criminal charges. The Crown case was that D.G. had been summoned to the scene by the applicant and another co-accused, M.H., using a mobile telephone. D.M. survived but suffered permanent brain damage after being shot in the back of the head in 2004. An important part of the Crown case involved video recordings from closed circuit television (CCTV) cameras near the scene. From a combination of video recordings and mobile telephone records, the Crown contended that the applicant could be seen making certain calls. There was also eye witness evidence of him making at least one of the critical calls. The applicant's case at trial was that he had made no calls on M.H.'s mobile telephone. However, he said that he was a drug dealer using his own telephone and that the calls were made for his own criminal purposes and were nothing to do with the summoning of D.G. or one of his associates. A compilation of the CCTV footage was shown a number of times during the trial. The jury asked to see the videos again after the first day of deliberations. They wanted to see them in the jury room, not in court. The prosecution argued that the jury should be able to view the videos on their own. The jury retired after the second day of their deliberations. The case was adjourned until the next day, at which point it was decided that the videos could be shown to the jury in the court room. The judge said the jury would have to pass a note to the prosecution if they wanted to watch the video again. The trial was concluded on the third day, with the jury deciding not to convict the defendant. No assent was recorded from junior counsel for the applicant but no objections were raised to the course of action proposed. The judge instructed the jury to return and directed them as follows: “We are going to leave [Officer M] in this court with you, and he will play any part of the video that you have seen.” “There is to be no other communication with him – or any communication from him – than simply asking him to play you what you want to see – and I think it is probably better,” the judge said. “He will play it as you think fit. Remember that there is more than one camera that operates – that sometimes you are viewing camera no. 1, and at other times camera No. 2.’ Jury was left alone in the court room with Officer M at 2.05 p.m. to begin reviewing the video evidence. When the court reconvened, leading counsel for the applicant directed the judge's attention to various authorities, including Archbold's Criminal Pleading, Evidence and Practice. The jury spent almost two hours viewing the video recordings in the presence of Officer M. The judge agreed to reconvene the court at 4 p.M. as he did not wish to interrupt the jury's viewing of the video footage. The case was adjourned until the next day at 11.30 a.m., when the jury were allowed to continue their deliberations. Counsel for the applicant then suggested that the police officer could continue to operate the equipment but the presence of a jury bailiff in the jury room would ensure that there was no communication between the parties. The judge agreed that the bailiff was duty bound to stop all communication, and essentially, that communication can only be complained of if it came from the officer. The jury were put on trust in relation to the officer's lack of communication, the judge said, and there is no reason why they should feel that they can trust the officer to that extent. Judge: 'I am merely looking at the peculiar situation that arises here, and the simple fact of the matter is quite simply this' The judge observed that there was a need to protect the privacy of the jury while preserving the integrity of the situation. However, he pointed out that “the die had been cast” and that: “... either the procedure in the circumstances of this particular case is acceptable, or it is not. I am not sure I would want to change it now.” It was then suggested by counsel for M.H. that the jury themselves be instructed how to use the equipment or that the video be played in open court in the presence of the judge. A solution was agreed which would allow the jury to operate the equipment themselves, with information provided to assist them in locating the part of the recordings that they wished to view. The jury viewed the video recordings alone for about an hour. They continued their deliberations for the rest of the day and into the following morning. The jury found the applicant guilty of attempted murder and making threats to kill. He was sentenced to 25 years in prison for attempted murder. His co-accused, M.H., was found not guilty. The applicant appealed, arguing that the approach taken to the viewing of video recordings amounted to a fundamental infringement of the integrity of the jury's deliberations. On 20 June 2006, the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal. The court summarised the matter before it as follows: ‘This was not a case in which there was any challenge to the credibility or propriety of the officer in question’ Court of Appeal refused to receive witness statement which had not been seen by the applicant or his lawyers. Court of Appeal: 'This was not that kind of a case. There was no challenge whatever to the manner of investigation. The issue at the trial was what the evidence, which the police were accepted properly to have gathered, did or did not prove.’ 'No further enquiry, for example of jurors, would in a case of this kind be proper' 'We do not think that we should be invited to receive partial evidence of what occurred' 'The court agreed that a fair trial required that a jury should not be improperly influenced during its deliberations' The court noted that the approach adopted in the present case occurred with the authority of the judge and with the consent of all parties. The safeguard of the integrity of the jury system lies in the respect that jurors have for the serious oath that they have taken, reinforced by the directions and warnings that they are given by trial judges, rather than in requiring formal rules. Jurors approach what is a difficult and often anxious task with a remarkable sense of duty.” The court noted the “careful direction” given to the jury that there was to be no communication between them and the officer operating the equipment except for the purposes of finding the correct place on the video. The court noted that the jury had been in any way inhibited by the presence of the police officer: they spent considerable time viewing the recordings. The court concluded that on the facts of this case, whether or not what occurred should have happened – and we will come to that in a moment – the hypothetical informed and fair minded observer would be aware of all the factors to which we have called attention. We do not, however, think that anybody needed to be concerned that a jury would betray its thinking by identifying a piece of evidence. We firmly suggest that this is a course which is not followed in future with or without the consent of the parties. Jurors commonly ask questions on all manner of topics. Some of them call for the jury to be reminded of a particular area of evidence. We do not believe that anybody who has any experience of jury trials supposes that anything can be read into the questions which a jury asks. The judge in this case, we are satisfied, was absolutely right not to permit them to be given a substitute poorer quality VHS recording. If the necessary equipment can be provided in any particular court by agreement as to compatibility of machinery between parties and the court, then so much the better. It is not desirable that equipment should be provided which can only be used in open court, because in many courts the courtroom will by then be in use in the next trial. On 22 August 2008, the applicant was denied leave to appeal to the House of Lords. The case was heard in the Lords for the first time on 21 August 2008. The judge ruled that the case should have been heard in open court. The application was dismissed on 23 August 2008 and the case was settled on 24 August. The appeal was heard again on 25 August 2008 at the Lords Court of Appeal. The hearing was returned to the Lords and the appeal was dismissed again on 28 August 2008 with the result that the appeal could not be heard in court. It was decided the appeal should be heard by the Lords of Appeal instead of the Lords.

name: Brian Curley
train_texts: The case originated in an application (32340/96) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant, Brian Curley, is a British national, born in 1961 and serving a sentence of detention during Her Majesty's Pleasure. The Government of the United Kingdom were represented by their Agent, Mr Ian Christie of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The application principally concerned the applicant’s complaints that he has had no review of the lawfulness of his continued detention in compliance with Article 5 of the Convention. On 1 December 1998, the Court declared the application admissible and decided that it was not necessary to hold a hearing. The applicant's case was the subject of review by the Parole Board on a number of occasions. Following the fourth review in January 1991, the applicant absconded from prison. Following his recapture on 6 July 1993 it was decided that his case should be reviewed again in January 1995. At this, the fifth review, which in fact took place in August 1995, theParole Board recommended that the applicant be given a provisional release date of 12 months hence. These were rejected by the Secretary of State by letter dated 2 January 1996. The applicant was advised by counsel who represented him at the hearing that there was no tenable basis for appeal against the decision refusing leave.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Ms Louise O’Keeffe complained that the system of primary education had failed to protect her from sexual abuse by a teacher in 1973. The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court. The Chamber, unanimously, struck out the complaints regarding the length of the domestic proceedings and the lack of an effective domestic remedy in that regard, given the friendly settlement reached between the parties on those issues. It also declared admissible the remaining complaints. On 20 September 2012 that Chamber (Angelika Nußberger, substitute judge, replaced Ganna Yudkivska) relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber. The applicant attended Dunderrow National School from 1968. The school was owned, through trustees, by the Catholic Bishop of the Diocese of Cork and Ross. The manager (S.), acting on behalf of the bishop, was the local parish priest. The applicant was born in 1964 and lives in Cork, Ireland. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 6 March 2013 (Rule 59 § 3). The Court heard addresses by Mr Holland and Mr McDonagh. The Court also heard from the Irish Human Rights Commission and the European Centre for Law and Justice. The parties objected to relinquishment (Article 30 of the Convention and Rule 72). In 1971 a parent of a child complained to the manager that L.H. had sexually abused her child. That complaint was not reported to the police, to the Department or to any other State authority and was not acted upon by the manager. In September 1973 other parents brought to the applicant’s parents’ attention similar allegations. Those allegations were not reported at that time. In 1996 she was contacted by the police who were investigating a complaint made in 1995 by a former pupil of Dunderrow National School. The applicant made a statement to the. police in January 1997 and was referred for counselling. During the investigation a number of other pupils made statements. L.h. was charged with 386 criminal offences of sexual abuse involving some twenty-one former pupils of the school. In 1998 he pleaded guilty to twenty-one sample charges and was sentenced to imprisonment. His licence to teach was withdrawn by the Minister for Education. The applicant accepted the offer by letter of 5 November 2002 and gave the standard undertaking to repay the CICT award from any other award she may receive, from whatever source, in relation to the same injury. The award was made on an ex gratia basis. Since the State is never a party to CICT proceedings, it became aware of this award later before the High Court (see directly below).C.B.R. v. Ireland (No. 1998/10555P) The High Court awarded damages payable by L.H. in the sum of EUR 305,104. The first payment was received in November 2007 so that she has been paid in the region of EUR 31,000 to date. She registered a judgment mortgage against that part of the family home owned by L.-H. L. claimed he had insufficient means and she obtained an instalment order of EUR 400 per month. Professor Ferguson agreed that if the child-protection protocols existing in 2003 had been in place in 1973, it was very likely that the applicant’s abuse would have been acted upon in a manner which would have ensured the promotion of her welfare. He feared that pleading the case on the basis of what the State should have known at the time would be unsuccessful. The High Court accepted the State Defendants’ application on 9 March 2004. It found that the action was not statute barred. It also concluded that the State was not vicariously liable for the sexual assaults perpetrated by L.H. The costs of the proceedings were awarded against the applicant. In May 2006 the applicant appealed to the Supreme Court. Her Notice of Appeal challenged the finding on vicarious liability. By a majority judgment of 19 December 2008 (Hardiman J and Fennelly J, with whom Chief Justice Murray and Mr Justice. Mr JusticeFennelly ruled), the High Court found that no action lay for a breach of a constitutional right where existing laws protected that right. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal. Hardiman J described in detail the legal status of national schools. State funding was accorded on a proportionate basis to all denominational schools. The population was at the time overwhelmingly Catholic so that the majority of national school had Catholic patrons and managers. The Catholic Church had responded that there could be no interference whatever with the “inherited tradition of managerial rights of schooling”. The court heard evidence of one expert witness (in the history of education in Ireland) who described the position after the inception of the Irish Free State in 1922. He noted that the Catholic managers in this “managerial” system “were very clearly articulate and very absolutely ... precise” Hardiman J referred to the “urgent desire” of the denominations to maintain their role in primary education. As a result there were approximately 3,000 national schools in Ireland. Most were under the control of Catholic patrons and managers. The Constitution reflected this managerial structure: the obligation on the State to “provide for” free primary education reflected a largely State-funded, but entirely clerically administered, system of education. Hardiman J noted that, in recent times and after more than a century and a half, the provision of education was belatedly and at least partially placed on a statutory basis by the Education Act 1998. Hardiman J concluded that, having regard to the relevant test for vicarious liability and to the above-described arrangements for the control and management of national schools, the State Defendants were not liable to the applicant for the wrongs committed against her. The relationship of L.H. and the State – a “triangular one with the Church” – was entirely sui generis and a product of Ireland’s unique historical experience. The manager was “the nominee of the patron, that is of a power other than the Minister and he did not inform the Minister of any difficulties with, or complaints about, [L.H.] or of his resignation and appointment to teach elsewhere” Hardiman J said the Minister was simply providing assistance and subvention to private and corporate (i.e. Roman Catholic) endeavour, leaving the running of the school to the private or corporate entities. He concluded by pointing out that nothing in the judgment could be interpreted as suggesting liability on the part of the Church. Cases of sexual abuse had preoccupied the criminal courts and the Supreme Court for many years and it was surprising that that court was confronted for the first time with questions relating to the liability of institutions including the State for sexual abuse of schoolchildren in a national school by a teacher. Fennelly J also described in some detail the history and consequent circumstances of the case. Fennelly J accepted the expert’s evidence that it was not a State system but rather a “State-supported system’ He noted the clear division of power between the State (funding and fixing the curriculum) and the manager (day-to-day running of the school including hiring and firing teachers) The different religions were determined to preserve and guard their own distinct religious education so that national schools developed on a denominational basis. He concluded that the State was not vicariously liable for the acts of L.H. or the failure of the manager to report the 1971 complaint to the State.Geoghegan J dissented. He accepted that neither the Department nor its inspectors had any knowledge of the assaults. Geoghegan J relied, notably, on the role of school inspectors. He noted that if an allegation of sexual assault by a teacher on a national-school pupil was considered well-founded by an inquiry set up by the Department, it could lead to the withdrawal of recognition or to a police investigation. The Supreme Court vacated the High Court order for costs against the applicant since it was not disputed that hers was an important and complex test case. It determined that each party had to bear its own costs related to the action against the State Defendants. The applicant was legally represented throughout the civil proceedings, although she did not have legal aid.

name: Ali İhsan Pekdaş
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties, the Court ruled in favour of the applicant. The decision was published in The European Court of Justice (ECJ) on 8 November 1999. The ECJ’s decision is published in the book, ‘The European Courts of Justice: A Handbook for the Implementation of the European Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms’, published by the ECJ. The case was brought against the applicant on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way). The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The applicant appealed to the Military Court of Cassation (askeri yargıtay), which quashed the conviction in 1995. The application was declared admissible on the basis of the Government’s observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The application has now been dismissed by the High Court of Justice. The case was heard by the International Criminal Court (ICC), which heard the case in 2002. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that the prosecution was time-barred.
