The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties the parties had agreed to join the case. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way). The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The applicant appealed to the Military Court of Cassation (askeri yargıtay). The Court quashed the applicants’ conviction on 27 December 1995. It held that the criminal proceedings against the applicant should be discontinued since the prosecution was time‑barred. The application was declared admissible by the Court. The case file was transmitted to the Court on 26 December 1994. The judge ruled that the application was admissible and that the applicant’s case should be dismissed.

name: Ali Ümit Alkes
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was taken into police custody on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation. On 2 April 1998 he was placed in detention on remand. On 28 March 2001 the Istanbul State Security Court convicted the applicant under Articles 168 (2) and 497 (2), and sentenced him to eight years and four months' imprisonment. On 29 April 2002 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment, finding that the classification of the applicant's offence had been erroneous. On 5 February 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. The applicant was convicted under Article 146 (1) of the former Criminal Code for attempting to undermine the constitutional order. He was sentenced to 16 years and eight months' imprisonment. The applicant appealed against this judgment arguing, inter alia, that his acquired rights had not been protected. On 2 December 2003 the Court of Cassation upheld the reasoning in the judgment of the Istanbul State Security Court, and dismissed the appeal. In the meantime, following his release, the applicant fled to Switzerland, where he currently resides. The Istanbul Assize Court reopened the proceedings against the applicant in order to review his sentence, pursuant to the provisions of the new Criminal Code. As an interim measure, on 11 October 2005 the applicant was conditionally released pending the outcome of the proceedings.

name: Dariusz Karwowski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29869/13) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms J. Chrzanowska of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application alleged that the imposition of the “dangerous detainee” regime on the applicant amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment. On 7 July 2014 the complaint was communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The applicant was kept in a cell which was constantly monitored via closed‑circuit television. He was subjected to a body search every time he left or entered the cell. He had to strip naked in front of prison officers. On 21 November 2013 the commission lifted the dangerous detainee regime applied to the applicant. The court held that the decision had been lawful. The applicant is still being held in prison in Poland. The charges against him and his highly deficient moral character have led to him being held as a dangerous detainee on several occasions. The Warsaw Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 30 January 2013. The decision was made to extend the period of imposition of the regime in respect of the applicant on 3 January 2013 and was upheld by the court.

name: Karlheinz Schmidt
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 7 April 1993. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. Mr Karlheinz Schmidt, a German national who was born in 1939, lives at Tettnang, in the Land of Baden-Württemberg. On 30 April 1982 the relevant municipal authorities required him to pay a fire service levy (Feuerwehrabgabe) of 75 German marks (DM) for 1982. This decision was based on section 43 of the Land Fire Brigades Act, as amended on 27 November 1978. On 7 February 1994 the Commission produced various documents as requested by the Registrar on the President's instructions. The decision was contrary to the constitutional principle of equality before the law. Tettnang at the beginning of the budget year (1 January) were liable to pay the contribution in question. The Administrative Appeals Court dismissed the appeal. The case raised no issue of principle (grundlegende Bedeutung) and there were no new facts to present to the Constitutional Court. It would only be possible to refer the case back to the Administrative Court. The Constitutional Court refused to refer it to the Appeals Court again. The issue was resolved in 1986. The decision was not appealed to the Supreme Court of Germany, which has the power to overturn the decision if it is not in conformity with the Constitution. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to accept the appeal for adjudication, on the ground that it did not have sufficient prospects of success. It noted, inter alia: “... The Federal Constitutional court has already held, in its judgment of 17 October 1961 ..., concerning the provision which corresponds to the present section 43 para. 2, first sentence, of the Baden-Württemberg Fire Brigades Act’’ The court said there had still been no general change in legal opinion; the fact that the obligation to serve in the fire brigade was limited to the male residents of a municipality still continued to be objectively justified.

train_texts: Cases originated in two application (nos. 26766/05 and 2228/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. A preliminary hearing was held to determine whether the statement should be read to the jury. The judge allowed the evidence to be admitted at trial. The jury heard evidence from a number of different witnesses and the defence were given the opportunity to cross-examine other witnesses who had produced similar evidence. On three occasions the jury asked for clarification of points raised in the read statement of S.T. account when considering her evidence. On 6 September 2005 the appeal was dismissed. The Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords but certified that a point of law of general public importance was involved in the decision. The court also considered that the applicant had been able to attack the accuracy of the deceased complainant's statement by exploring the inconsistencies between it and the evidence given by witnesses and experts. The applicant was charged with wounding with intent and also with attempting to pervert the course of justice by telling the police that he had seen two black men stab S. When witnesses were questioned at the scene, no-one claimed to have seen the applicant stabbed S. Two days later, however, one of the witnesses, T., made a statement to police. In S.'s statement to the police, it is clear that he did not see who stabbed him. T.'s statement was read to the jury under section 116(2) (e) and (4) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 (the “CJA 2003”) The prosecution argued under the CJA 2003 that T. was too fearful to attend trial before the jury and that he should qualify for special measures. The trial judge heard evidence from a police officer conducting the case who testified that the Iranian community was close-knit and that T.'s fear was genuine. T. himself gave evidence to the judge from behind a screen and said he could not give evidence because he was 'genuinely in fear' The judge ruled that leave should be given for the statement to be read. T.'s witness statement was read to the jury in his absence. The applicant also gave evidence. He was later sentenced to nine years' imprisonment to be served concurrently with a term of fifteen months' imprisonment for doing an act intended to pervert the course of justice. Cases originated in two application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 22 March 2004, a preliminary hearing was held to determine whether the statement should be read to the jury. The judge allowed the evidence to be admitted at trial. The jury heard evidence from a number of different witnesses and the defence were given the opportunity to cross-examine other witnesses who had produced similar fact evidence. In his summing up, the trial judge directed the members of the jury as to how they should regard the read statement of the deceased complainant. The applicant was convicted by a unanimous verdict on both counts of indecent assault. The Court of Appeal concluded on 3 November 2005 that the applicant's right to a fair trial had not been infringed. Relying on Doorson v. the Netherlands, judgment of 26 March 1996, Reports of Judgments and Decisions 1996‑II p 66, the court held that admissibility of evidence is primarily a matter of domestic law. It then found: “Where a witness who is the sole witness of a crime has made a statement to be used in its prosecution and has since died, there may be a strong public interest in the admission of the statement in evidence so that the prosecution may proceed” The Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords but certified that a point of law of general public importance was involved in the decision. The applicant was charged with wounding with intent and also with attempting to pervert the course of justice by telling the police that he had seen two black men stab S. When witnesses were questioned at the scene, no-one claimed to have seen the applicant stabbed S. Two days later, however, one of the witnesses, T., made a statement to police that the applicant had stabbed him three times in the back. In S.'s statement to the police, it is clear that he did not see who stabbed him. Both S. and T. were members of the Iranian community. T. was too fearful to attend trial before the jury and should qualify for special measures. T. himself gave evidence to the judge from behind a screen. In ruling that leave should be given for the statement to be read to the jury, the trial judge stated: “I am satisfied in those circumstances upon the criminal standard of proof that this witness is genuinely in fear.” The judge ruled that the defendant's evidence, if he chooses to give it, would be sufficient to rebut and to challenge the evidence in the statement. The judge warned the jury about the danger of relying on the evidence of T. T.'s witness statement was then read to the jury in his absence. On 29 April 2005, the applicant was convicted by a majority verdict, principally of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm. He was later sentenced to nine years' imprisonment to be served concurrently with a term of fifteen months' imprisonment for doing an act intended to pervert the course of justice. The applicant's appeal was referred directly before the full Court of Appeal. The appeal judges were satisfied that if they were to refuse leave, under the CJA 2003, to have T.’s statement read at trial there would be unfairness to the prosecution. The applicant's sentence was reduced to seven years' imprisonment. The trial judge had explicitly warned the jury in detail as to how they should treat this evidence and properly directed them as toHow they should consider it in reaching their verdict. The application was rejected on the grounds that even a proper direction by the judge could not cure the unfairness of the jury's decision to convict the applicant of a crime he did not commit. name: İzzet Belge
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 50171/09) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that there had been an unjustified interference with his right to freedom of expression. On 7 July 2014 the complaint concerning the applicant’s right of expression was communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The application was brought by a Turkish national, Mr İzzet Belge (“the applicant”), on 10 September 2009. The public prosecutor submitted that the following passages in the speech constituted propaganda in favour of an illegal organisation. “... We want peace in this country. Those who wish for war prevent us from having peace. Mr Abdullah Öcalan has not been able to meet his lawyers or members of his family for the last three months. We believe that that sanction is harmful to the peace process.” “We have once again started to receive the bodies of guerrillas and soldiers. We want an end to the crying of the mothers of guerillas and. soldiers.’ “ “The slogans chanted by the crowd during his speech had promoted peace” According to the report, dated 21 May 2007, on the examination of the police video-recordings of the gathering of 5 September 2005, the applicant had referred to Abdullah Öcalan as the leader of the Kurdish people. He further noted that there had been no violent incidents during or after his speech. Following his speech the demonstrators had dispersed quietly and the slogans that had been chanted while he spoke had been peaceful. We were kept in police custody for one night and then taken before a court. The court released us. However, it took a decision to place me under judicial control. I have to go to give my signature every Monday and I am banned from travelling abroad. Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan called for a ceasefire six years ago. He has not been able to meet his lawyers or members of his family for three and a half months. We believe that that sanction is harmful to the peace process. The demonstration organised by Tuhay-Der will contribute to peace because a one-month ceasefire has been declared. We want an end to the crying of the mothers of guerrillas and soldiers in this country. We will continue our struggle for peace. I thank you all. You can disperse now in silence ...” For confidential support call the Samaritans in the UK on 08457 90 90 90, visit a local Samaritans branch or click here for details. The Diyarbakır Assize Court delivered its judgment on 19 February 2008. The court noted that those who disseminated propaganda in favour of the PKK were expressing their support and approval for the PKK, whose methods were those of terrorism and violence. The first-instance court convicted the applicant of disseminating propaganda in favor of a terrorist organisation under section 7(2) as well as referring to PKK members who had been killed as ‘guerrillas’ The court also found it established that the applicant had directed the demonstrators who had chanted slogans in favour the PKK and waved yellow, red and green pieces of cloth and carried photographs of Abdullah Öcalan. The Court of Cassation upheld the Diyarbakır Assize Court’s judgment. The court also ordered that Article 53 §§ 1, 2 and 3 of the Criminal Code should apply in respect of the applicant (see paragraph 20 below). On 13 July 2010, the court sentenced the applicant to ten months’ imprisonment. The sentence was imposed under Law no. 3713, as amended by Law No. 5532, and sentenced him to 10 months in prison. The verdict was handed down by the Court of Assize on 11 June 2010. The appeal was heard on 16 June 2010 and the case was settled on 17 July 2010.

name: Edward Skałka
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 43425/98) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr Adam Bezucha, a lawyer practising in Kłodzko. The Polish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent, Mr Krzysztof Drzewicki, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) "I am not going to be afraid of any such clown who wants to intimidate me," he writes. "Not only does [the judge] write rubbish about my alleged request for a pardon, which my request was absolutely not, but he also intimidates me" The judge was charged with proffering insults against a State authority at its headquarters or in public. "Such a cretin should not take the post of a reliable lawyer who would know how to reply to a letter. A cretin he will remain and I see no reason to be fearful of any legal consequences," he says."You know, you understand, shut up” – that is all the education he has, as a fool does not need any better.” The Sosnowiec District Court convicted the applicant of insulting a State authority and sentenced him to eight months' imprisonment. The court found that on 15 November 1994 the applicant had sent a letter to the President of the Regional Court in which he referred to all judges of the Penitentiary Division as ‘irresponsible clowns’ The court further observed that the applicant, as a citizen, had a constitutional right to criticise the State authorities. However, the impugned letter had largely exceeded the limits of acceptable criticism and was directly aimed at lowering the court in the public. Accordingly, it had to be understood that the. applicant had insulted the court as the State authority, and the unidentified judge could be regarded as a symbol of that court. The Katowice Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on the grounds that the conviction had been in flagrant breach of Article 237 of the Criminal Code. The Bielsko-Biała Regional Court upheld the contested judgment on 10 September 1996. The applicant's lawyer lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court on 2 June 1997. The Supreme Court dismissed the Appeal and confirmed the contested ruling. The appeal was dismissed because the grounds of the appeal had been laconic and limited in their reasoning. The Appeal was dismissed on the basis that the appeal was not supported by the facts of the case and that the sentence imposed was commensurate with the degree of the applicant's guilt. The Supreme Court went on to state that the applicant's abusive letter, referred to and quoted by the Regional Court, had clearly exceeded the limits of acceptable criticism. No new arguments had been submitted to the Supreme Court to show that there had been any procedural shortcomings in the proceedings. The Supreme Court therefore dismissed the cassation appeal as unfounded. It was also pointed out that the appeals court had examined all complaints submitted in the appeal, including those concerning the assessment of evidence and the factual findings of the first-instance court. The appeal was dismissed as not being in compliance with the requirements laid down by the applicable procedural provisions. The court emphasised, it was worth noting, that the purpose of the appeal was only to bring procedural complaints to the attention of the Supreme court.

name: Arnaldo Otegi Mondragon
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 2034/07) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the decision of the Supreme Court finding him guilty of serious insult against the King of Spain amounted to an unjustified infringement of his right to freedom of expression. In view of the information available to it, the Court decided that no hearing was necessary. The case was decided in favour of the applicant on 7 June 2009. The decision was made on the basis of the evidence given by the applicant and the Spanish Government. Basque Country High Court of Justice has jurisdiction to try the applicant because of his status as a member of parliament. The applicant argued that his remarks had constituted political criticism directed against the Head of the government of the Basque Country. The public prosecutor lodged a criminal complaint against the applicant for “serious insult against the King” within the meaning of Article 490 § 3 of the Criminal Code read in conjunction with Article 208. On account of his remarks made on 26 February 2003, the applicant was charged with ‘insulting the King of Spain’ and sentenced to two years in prison. The application was dismissed in April 2003. In a judgment of 18 March 2005, the High Court of Justice found the applicant not guilty of the charges against him. After stating that his remarks had been “clearly offensive, improper, unjust, ignominious and divorced from reality”, the court found as follows: “... This is not an issue concerning the private life of the Head of State but one of rejection of the ties of political power deriving from the hereditary nature of the institution which he personally symbolises’. The Constitution does not guarantee the right to freedom of expression solely in relation to certain points of view that are considered correct, but in. relation to all ideas, subject to the limits which it lays down. The public prosecutor lodged an appeal on points of law to the Supreme Court. He argued that the law protected the honour of the King as a specific individual possessed of personal dignity. The seriousness of the offence could be inferred from the fact that the legislature had sought to afford increased protection to the dignity of the king. The Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the lower court, making several references to the Court’s case-law. It sentenced the applicant to one year's imprisonment, suspended his right to stand for election for the duration of the sentence and ordered him to serve his sentence in prison.‘It was clear that the King had been performing official duties, but that did not deprive him of the right to respect for his honour’ The Supreme Court considered the impugned remarks to have been value judgments rather than statements of fact. The judge agreed with the Basque Country High Court of Justice that the remarks had not targeted the King’s private life or his personal honour but had been directed solely at his institutional role as Commander-in-Chief of the Spanish armed forces. The applicant had not claimed that the King was responsible for actual acts of torture, only that he was strictly liable as Head of the State apparatus. Judge P.A.I. issued a dissenting opinion in which he argued that the comments complained of had been of a political nature, in view of the applicant's status as a member of parliament. In a decision (auto) of 3 July 2006, the Constitutional Court declared the applicant’s amparo appeal inadmissible as manifestly devoid of constitutional content. The right to freedom of expression did not encompass a right to proffer insults. The statements in question had not been disproportionate in the context in which they had been uttered, namely the warm welcome extended to the King of Spain by the government of the Basque Country in the wake of the closure of the daily newspaper Euskaldunon Egunkaria. The Constitutional Court considered that the weighing of the competing rights at stake had been carried out in an appropriate manner by the Supreme Court. The King occupied a neutral position in political debate. This implied that he was owed institutional respect of a kind that was ‘substantively’ different from that due to other State institutions. Constitutional Court held that the applicant’s remarks, on account of their obviously derogatory nature, had clearly gone beyond what could be considered legitimate. It agreed with the Supreme Court that the remarks had expressed open contempt for the King and the institution he embodied, affecting the essential core of his dignity. Such statements could manifestly not fall within the exercise of the right to freedom of expression. He is currently in pre-trial detention in connection with other criminal proceedings.

The right to freedom of expression did not encompass a right to proffer insults. The statements in question had not been disproportionate in the context in which they had been uttered, namely the warm welcome extended to the King of Spain by the government of the Basque Country. name: Sławomir Wierzba
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 20315/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the excessive length of the applicant’s detention and the length of criminal proceedings to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3) The application was filed by a Polish national, Mr Sławomir Wierzba (“the applicant”), on 17 May 2004. The applicant was born in 1980 and lives in Gdańsk. The case was heard in the Gdańsk District Court. The bill of indictment concerned five defendants and, in all, twelve charges were brought against them. Hearings scheduled for 9 October and 11 December 2003 were cancelled due to, among other things, the failure to bring the applicant to trial from prison, and the fact that a trial judge was on mission. The applicant made numerous, but unsuccessful, applications for release and appealed, likewise unsuccessfully, against refusals to release him and against decisions extending his detention. The first-instance judgment was upheld by the Gdańsk Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) on 11 July 2007. In the meantime, between 3 October 2002 and 5 January 2005 the applicant served prison sentences which had been imposed on him in other criminal proceedings. name: Robert Głowacki
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1608/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, a violation of Article 3 on account of the imposition of the ‘dangerous detainee’ regime on him. He also complained about the length of criminal proceedings against him. The Polish Government were represented by their then Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was communicated to the Government on 17 November 2010. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant was arrested in May 2007 and placed in the Warsaw Białołęka Detention Centre. He was convicted of armed robbery, burglary and causing serious bodily harm and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment. The applicant lodged an appeal against the last of those decisions and was released from custody on 10 April 2010, at the applicant’s request, the detention was lifted and he was released in March 2011. He has since been living in hiding in Poland and is believed to be in his late 30s. He is currently serving a five-year prison sentence for armed robbery and burglary. He had been charged with illegal possession of weapons and robbery in 2005 and 2007. The applicant was placed in the Warsaw Białołęka Remand Centre (Areszt Śledczy) on 21 May 2007. On 18 December 2008 the Płock Regional Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to seven years and six months’ imprisonment. On 1 September 2009 the applicant lodged a complaint with the Warsaw Court of Appeal under the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. The applicant sought a ruling that the length of the proceedings before the Warsaw Regional Court (see paragraphs 6-19 above) had been excessive, and also sought an award of just satisfaction. The court considered that there had been no significant delays in the proceedings. Every three months the Warsaw Remand Centre Penitentiary Commission reviewed and upheld its decision classifying the applicant as a ‘dangerous detainee’ The commission considered that it was necessary to place the applicant in solitary confinement as he had been charged with numerous offences, including armed robbery. The commission also referred to his ‘serious lack of moral character’ and long history of criminal convictions. The applicant appealed to the penitentiary courts against most of those decisions, arguing that he was suffering from various health problems including hemiparesis and discopathy. The courts gave decisions on 26 May, 29 August and 17 October 2008, 15 April and 24 June 2009, and 4 March 2010. The applicant argued that the living conditions in the detention centres in which he was detained were inadequate. He failed to lodge a claim for compensation for damage to his health sustained as a result of inadequate conditions of detention. The applicant was detained in the following detention centres: Warsaw Białołeka Detention Centre, Lublin Remand Centre, Warsaw Mokotów Remand Center, and Płock Prison. The Government submitted that during the applicant’s detention in all four of the penal establishments listed above all standards of detention were respected. The judge ruled that the applicant was held in solitary confinement after his initial complaint.

name: Bünyamin İnan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 39428/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties, the Court ruled in favour of the applicant (Rule 43 § 2) and the respondent (Rule 44 § 1) The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way). The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The applicant was convicted in 1989 and sentenced to 15 years' imprisonment. In 1995 the Court of Cassation quashed the conviction and referred the case to the Ankara Assize Court. The criminal proceedings are still pending before the latter court. The case is being heard by the Turkish Supreme Court of Justice (Bektas), which has jurisdiction over the case. The application is expected to be heard in October or November 2014. For more information about the case, please visit: http://www.kim.com/kim-kim/2013/07/25/kamil-kumil-trial-case.html#storylink=cpy

The case originated in an application (no. 39428/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties, the Court ruled in favour of the applicant. The case was joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints (applications nos. 26480/95, 28291/95 and 29280/95) (Rule 43): The Court decided that this was in the interests of the proper administration of justice. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The Court of Cassation quashed the applicant’s conviction on the ground that he should have been convicted of the offence. The criminal proceedings are still pending before the Ankara Assize Court (ağır ceza mahkemesi). The applicant appealed the conviction. The case file was transmitted to it on 26 December 1994. On 27 December 1995 the case was referred to the Court of. Cassation (yargıtay) It acquired jurisdiction over the case and the case. was transferred to it. On 14 September 1988 the applicant was released pending trial.

The case originated in an application (no. 39428/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 18 August 1997. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. Mr Rıza Türmen, the judge elected in respect of Turkey, withdrew from sitting in the case. The Government appointed Mr Feyyaz Gölcüklü to sit as an ad hoc judge, in his place. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints. The applicant was arrested in 1980 on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The Court of Cassation quashed the applicant’s conviction on the ground that he should have been convicted of the offence. The criminal proceedings are still pending before the Ankara Assize Court (ağır ceza mahkemesi). The applicant appealed. The case file was transmitted to it on 26 December 1994. The applicant was sentenced to 15 years’ imprisonment, permanently debarred him from employment in the civil service.

By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties, the Court ruled in favour of the applicant. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way). The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. He was convicted and sentenced to 15 years’ imprisonment. The criminal proceedings are still pending before the Ankara Assize Court (ağır ceza mahkemesi). The case file was transmitted to the latter court on 26 December 1994. The applicant appealed the conviction but it was quashed in December 1995. The case is still pending.

name: Max Myer Kingsley
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of a hearing before an independent and impartial tribunal. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. On 7 November 2000 the Chamber delivered its judgment in which it held, unanimously, that there had been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Chamber decided, by six votes to one, that the finding of a violation constituted sufficient just satisfaction for the non-pecuniary damage sustained by the applicant. Apart from a unanimous award of 13,500 pounds sterling in respect of Strasbourg legal costs and expenses, it dismissed the remainder of the applicant's claims for just satisfaction. The applicant and the Government each filed written observations concerning the issues under Article 41 of the Convention. Third-party comments were received from Liberty, a non-governmental organisation based in London. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 7 November 2001 (Rule 59 § 2) The Court heard addresses by Lord Goldsmith and Mr Greenwood, and also their replies to questions from its individual members. The composition of the Grand Chamber was determined according to the provisions of Article 27 §§ 2 and 3 of the convention and Rule 24 of Rule 24. The applicant was the sole managing director of London Clubs Limited (“LCL”) between 1984 and 1992. London Clubs applied for new licences via reconstituted operating companies. If the applications were successful, LCL would surrender its existing licences. The Gaming Board issued LCL with certificates of consent. LCL was statutorily obliged to obtain these as a prerequisite to making an application to the Licensing Magistrates. Objections to the issuing of new licences were made by a rival casino owner. New licences were granted in October 1992, after a three day hearing before the Lic licensing magistrates. Lady Littler, the Chairman of the Gaming Board, addressed the British Casino Association at its annual luncheon in November 1992. Her speech referred to London Clubs and commented that the practices we and the Police had regarded as unacceptable had ceased. The Gaming Board was considering whether the applicant was a fit and proper person to hold the Board's certificate of approval. The applicant's legal advisers objected to the Gaming Board presiding the section 19 hearing, suggesting that an independent tribunal be set up as an alternative. The Gaming Board informed the applicant formally that it was “minded to revoke” the applicant's section 19 certificates and that the applicant would be given the opportunity to state his case against revocation either in writing or orally at an interview. The application for cancellation of LCL's licences had, in fact, never taken place and no reference was intended to the applicant. The Gaming Board rejected the request for an independent tribunal. The application for judicial review was dismissed on 11 January 1996 by Mr Justice Jowitt after a hearing lasting over sixteen days. The effect of the revocation of the section 19 certificates was that the applicant was unable to obtain employment in any sector of the gaming industry. The first judgment dealt with the applicant's appeal. The decision was challenged on the grounds that the Panel was biased, or had the appearance of bias, and that its findings were vitiated by errors of law and were irrational. The case was settled by a three-judge panel of the Supreme Court of England and Wales. Mr Justice Jowitt found that the Board was entitled to reach its conclusion. The applicant's claim that he had a “legitimate expectation” that the Gaming Board would be precluded from taking account of any breaches of its guidelines ran to 165 pages. The judge described the test of bias under English law in the following terms (pp. 93-96 of the judgment): “[Counsel for the applicant] submits that the decision to revoke the applicant's section 19 certificates of approval should be quashed because the Panel was biased.” The judge found that what took place amounted to an agreement between Mr S. and LCL, such that section 16 was breached. There was no evidence that the cheques were shams. There is a two-stage test. The applicant has first to show from the evidence that there is an appearance of bias (R. v. Inner West London Coroner, ex parte Dallaglio [1994] 4 All England Law Reports 139) The question on which the court must reach its own factual conclusion is this: is there a real danger of injustice having occurred as a result of bias? By “real” is meant not without substance. A real danger clearly involves more than a minimal risk, less than a probability. One could, I think, as well speak of a real risk or a real possibility. Mr Justice Jowitt applied the test of bias which he had set out to the facts of the case, and concluded that, on the evidence before him, he could not say that the applicant had established that there was a real danger of injustice having occurred as a result of bias. He stated further that if, contrary to his finding, there was unconscious bias on the part of the Panel, the “doctrine of necessity” fell to be considered. Counsel for the applicant submitted that the Board had failed to take the reasonable steps to minimise the risk of bias affecting them. The decision was upheld by the Court of Appeal. Mr Justice Jowitt rejected the submission, on the grounds that no useful reference could have been made to an independent tribunal which did not involve an impermissible delegation. Lord Justice Morritt (with whom Lord Justice Hobhouse agreed) held that there was a real risk that the decision of the tribunal had been actuated by bias even though they were not in fact biased against him. The decision for the Board was, at the end of the day, whether or not Mr Kingsley was a fit and proper person. That could not be delegated to anindependent panel and if they were actuated. by bias, apparent or real, then the decision would still have to be made by them. "It seems to me that there is no arguable point, susceptible on this part of the case, which would justify giving leave to appeal," he said. "There is no meaningful independent panel and the decision would stand because the decision has to be made by the Board and could not be delegated to the independent tribunal," he added. The decision to appeal was made by a panel of five judges, including two women, and was made in the absence of an independent panel. The case has now been referred to the European Court of Human Rights, which has the power to overturn the decision if it is found to be unlawful. The hearing is due to take place on Tuesday.

name: Uli Lutz
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 28 January 1986. It originated in an application (no. 9912/82) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of that State, Mr. Uli Lutz, on 14 June 1982. The President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the Englert and Nölkenbockhoff cases should be considered by the same Chamber. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr R. Bernhardt, the elected judge of German nationality. The Court heard addresses from the Government, the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for the applicant. The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg on the appointed day. The Court decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. The President granted the members of the Government’s delegation leave to speak in German (Rule 27: 2). The Court heard. addresses by Mrs. Maier, Ministerialdirigentin, Federal Ministry of Justice, Agent, Mr. P.-G. Pötz and Mr. H. Stöcker, Minister for Justice and Advisers. Uli Lutz, a German national born in 1959, lives in Heilbronn-Horkheim. On 10 October 1980, he was riding a motor cycle and was involved in a road accident. According to the police report (Verkehrs-Ordnungswidrigkeiten-Anzeige), he had attempted to overtake a car, although the traffic situation was unclear. The result had been a collision which caused damage to both vehicles. Mr. Lutz was fined DM 125, to which were added costs of DM 14, for “joint responsibility for a road crash due to overtaking in an unclear traffic situation’ The decision was based on section 24 of the Road Traffic Act (Strassenverkehrsgesetz) and Regulations 1(2), 5 and 49. The driver of the car was likewise fined for a “regulatory offence’ (Ordnungswidrigkeit) on 9 December 1980. On 24 August 1981, the District Court stayed the proceedings on the ground that they were time-barred. The court informed the applicant that it intended to discontinue the proceedings and order costs against the Treasury (Staatskasse) The applicant would have to bear his own necessary costs and expenses (notwendige Auslagen) On 9 December 1980, the Heilbronn Police Authority took a decision to impose a fine (Bussgeldbescheid) on the defendant for a breach of the Road Traffic Regulations. Uli Lutz appealed against this decision. By an order made on 27 January 1981, the public prosecutor’s office in Heil bronn forwarded the case to a district court for a decision. After the case had been submitted, prosecution of the ‘regulatory offence’ became time-barred under section 26(4) of the road traffic Act. The proceedings must therefore be stayed by reason of there being a technical bar to prosecution (Verfolgungshindernis) The costs of the proceedings shall be borne by the Treasury. The defendant shall bear his own necessary costs and expenses. Mr. Lutz then applied to the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) but on 2 February 1982 a bench of three of that court’s judges refused to entertain the application. The Constitutional Court held that the decisions of the District Court and the Regional Court did not offend the presumption of innocence, which was founded on the principle of the rule of law. The court held that in such circumstances it would have been unjust to award the defendant's necessary costs and expenses against the Treasury, especially as the prosecution had become time-barred only during the course of the court proceedings. Mr Lutz had thus broken the basic rule in Regulation 1(2) of the Road Traffic Regulations and disregarded his duty under Regulation 5(3)(1) not to overtake where the traffic situation was unclear. The decision not to order the Treasury to pay the costs and expenses of the party concerned obviously cannot be regarded as a punishment (Bestrafung) or even be equated with such. The reasons for the order as to costs in the impugned decisions are therefore rightly confined to the finding that the defendant would most probably have been found guilty. The decision as to cost and expenses does not make any find that the person concerned is guilty. It derives merely from the suspicion falling on him, which had given rise to his being prosecuted for a ‘regulatory offence’. The ruling was made in line with the European Convention on Human Rights.

name: Uğur Eşim
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 59601/09) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant was born in 1969 and lives in İstanbul. He was severely wounded by gunshots during a clash between the security forces and a group of terrorists in 1990. He claimed that, on account of medical negligence, the bullet in his head had remained unnoticed and he had sustained further pecuniary damage as this fact had not been taken into account in calculating his disability pension. The Supreme Military Administrative Court, by a majority, rejected both actions as being out of time. In both decisions the court held that notwithstanding the fact that the applicant had not been aware of the bullet in his head until 2007, pursuant to section 43(1) of the Supreme Military. Administrative Court Act, his compensation claims should have been lodged within five years of the incident. Its decision was served on the applicant on 6 May 2009. The court rejected a rectification request lodged by the applicant in April 2009, and the case was closed. The applicant appealed against the decision, but the appeal was rejected by the High Court.

Since the relevant disciplinary file was lost, the Government could not provide a copy. of the form acknowledging receipt. name: Gerhard Lang
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28648/03) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been discriminated against in the exercise of his rights on the ground of his religion. He was liable for military or alternative civilian service whereas members of recognised religious societies holding religious functions comparable to his functions were exempted. The application was dismissed by the Upper Austrian Military Authority in 2000. On 17 November 2005 the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) In 2000 the Federal Minister for Defence (Bundesminister für Landesverteidigung) refused the applicant’s appeals on the ground that he did not belong to a recognised religious society. On 25 January 2001, the applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof), requesting it to repeal the wording ‘recognised religious societies’ in section 24(3) of the Military Service Act. On 23 May 2003 the Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's complaint. The applicant asked the Federal Ministry for Defence to take no action until the European Court of Human Rights had decided on his application.

It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The applicant asked the Federal Ministry for Defence to take no action until the European Court of Human Rights had decided on his application. The applicant was informed that an instruction had been issued to the Upper Austrian Military Authority not to call him up until further notice. On 23 May 2003 the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) dismissed the applicant’s complaint. It found that exemption from the obligation to perform military service merely applied to members of recognised religious societies and could not be extended to registered religious communities. This decision was served on the applicant's counsel on 4 July 2003. On 25 September 2001 the Constitutional Court refused to deal with the complaint for lack of prospects of success.

name: Yaşar Kanbur
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28291/95) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court ruled in favour of the applicant. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) He was then taken to Ankara for questioning in relation to his activities in the organisation. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. In a judgment of 19 July 1989 the Martial Law Court convicted the applicant of membership. It sentenced the applicant to 15 years’ imprisonment, permanently debarred him from employment in the civil service and placed him under judicial guardianship. In 1995 the Court of Cassation quashed the applicant’s conviction. It referred the case to the Ankara Assize Court. The criminal proceedings are still pending before the latter court.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the administrative courts had failed to hold an oral hearing in proceedings relating to his request for life annuity. The Swedish Government were represented by their Agent, Ms G. Isaksson, of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The application was communicated to the Government on 2 February 2011. The case is currently before the Court of Appeal and the appeal is expected to take place within the next few weeks. The appeal will be heard by the Court on 13 December 2013. The applicant’s legal counsel appealed to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Södermanland, claiming that the applicant had a right to a life annuity since his illnesses had been work-related. At times he had had up to three different jobs, each one of which, had been hectic and thereby created a difficult and very stressful situation. He produced a medical opinion by Dr. C-G.E., dated 5 February 2003, which stated that known risk factors for arteriosclerosis and heart attack were, among other factors, diabetes, smoking and high blood pressure. Recently, the feeling of severe stress had been shown to be an element that increased the risk of developing heart and vascular disorders as well. The applicant requested an oral hearing to deal with his case as a whole, including the question of leave to appeal. He also wanted to be heard himself about his work situation and the stressful environment. The court found that no such grounds were at hand, it refused leave to Appeal. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten), reiterating the grounds of appeal already presented before the lower instances. He again invoked Article 6 of the Convention in relation to his right to an oral Hearing. The Supreme Administrative court rejected the request on 29 October 2007. The case was referred back to the Administrative Court of Appeal for an Oral hearing or to the court itself. Supreme Administrative Court refused the applicant leave to appeal. It found no reason to hold an oral hearing. The applicant was requested to complete his written submissions. The court ruled there was no need to hold a hearing in order to decide on the question of leave to appealed. He produced a medical opinion by Dr. C-G.E., dated 5 February 2003, which stated that known risk factors for arteriosclerosis and heart attack were, among other factors, diabetes, smoking and high blood pressure. In reaching its decision, the court had regard to the medical certificates by Dr B.M., which established no link between the work situation and the applicant's illness. The applicant requested an oral hearing to deal with his case as a whole, including the question of leave to appeal. He also wanted to be heard himself about his work situation and the stressful environment. He invoked Article 6 of the Convention in relation to his right to an Oral hearing. The court found that no such grounds were at hand, it refused leave to Appeal. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten), reiterating the grounds of appeal already presented before the lower instances and requesting the court either to refer the case back to the Administrative Court of Appeal for an oral Hearings or to hold an oral Hearing itself. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47114/99) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant, Sean Marc Taylor-Sabori, was granted legal aid, but never actually claimed it. The application was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections. This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, to dispense with a hearing (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The applicant was arrested and charged with conspiracy to supply a controlled drug. He was tried, along with a number of alleged co-conspirators, at Bristol Crown Court in September 1997. The Court of Appeal, dismissing the appeal on 13 September 1998, upheld the trial judge’s ruling that the messages had been intercepted at the point of transmission on the private radio system, so that the 1985 Act did not apply. The messages were admissible despite having been intercepted without a warrant. The applicant appealed against conviction and sentence. One of the grounds was the admission in evidence of the pager messages. The appeal was dismissed and he was sentenced to ten years’ imprisonment.

name: Zbigniew Dyller
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 39842/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his pre-trial detention had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the. Convention. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicant was born in 1961 and lives in Tczew. On 15 October 2003 the applicant was arrested by the police for the robbery of a homeless person. It appears that on 29 July 2004 the trial court held the first hearing. Subsequently, hearings were held at regular intervals. The applicant was sentenced to three years and six months’ imprisonment. It appears that the applicant failed to lodge a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) and that the judgment became final. On 14 April 2007 the applicant was released from detention, having served the totality of his sentence. The case was transferred to the Starogard Gdański District Court, to which the case had been transferred, in September 2005. The court found the applicant guilty of the robbery of a watch worth not less than PLN 3, committed within five years of his previous conviction.

name: Franz Weber
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’s) on 12 April 1989 and by the Government of the Swiss Confederation (‘the Government’) on 3 July 1989. It originated in an application (no. 11034/84) against Switzerland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of that State, Mr Franz Weber, on 15 May 1984. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6. The hearing was held on 23 January 1990 in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg. The Court heard addresses by Mr Boillat and Mr Vautier for the Government, by Mr Trechsel for the Commission and by Mr Schaller for the applicant, as well as their replies to its questions. The applicant and one of the associations he runs, Helvetia Nostra, lodged a complaint alleging defamation against R.M., who had written a letter published in the letters column of the newspaper L’Est vaudois under the headline ‘Franz Weber is fooling you’. In a letter he received on 13 December 1989 the Registrar was informed by the Secretary to the Commission that the Delegate would submit his observations at the hearing. The list of municipal taxpayers is not published and it is easy to hide behind that sort of censorship and live by devious means. May everyone have the courage to tell Helvetia Nostra (there’s a fine name to fleece you with!) that we have had enough of playing into the hands of people who sponge off us and whose behaviour borders on the criminal. ...“▬▬ ”. “ĉ.” “ ’’.  ”“’,  ,  ,”, ‘’;’ ’‘‘, ’,’ and ’'’ as well as the names of the members of the associations’ who have been accused of defaming R.M. Weber’ On 3 March 1982 the daily newspapers Gazette de Lausanne, 24 heures and Tribune/Le Matin reported what the applicant had said. Mr Weber had already divulged the first three items of information at a press conference in Berne on 11 May 1981. He also stated that he had lodged a challenge and a complaint against the investigating judge. On 27 April 1982 the President of the Cassation Division imposed a fine of 300 Swiss francs on him, together with a probationary period of a year for the purposes of deletion of the fine from the cantonal register. He based his decision on the following grounds: “II. He relied on Article 6 (art. 6) of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) and impugned the procedure provided for in Article 185 § 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure’. Criminal proceedings will shortly be time-barred. Breach of the confidentiality of an investigation means ‘disclosing’ a matter which ought to be kept confidential. The actus reus of the offence punishable under Article 185 CC is therefore made out. This offence is punishable even if it has been committed inadvertently (s. 4 of the Vaud Criminal Justice Act, s. 6 of the Minor Offences Act). In the instant case it is plain that Mr Weber acted deliberately. His submission based on a kind of necessity is devoid of merit since it was open to him to appeal to the Indictment Division against the orders for the sequestration of his accounts. Article 185 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP) is therefore not applicable to the disclosure that the first complaint had been lodged, because this was punishable as defamation. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32771/96) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he did not receive a fair trial on account of the absence of interpretation at his hearing on sentencing. The application was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court, which declared it admissible on 26 June 2001. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The case was heard by the Fourth Section, which was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. In September 1994 the applicant was declared bankrupt as a result of civil proceedings brought by the Inland Revenue to recover unpaid tax. The various companies were all registered for Value Added Tax (VAT) purposes but failed to make any VAT payments or returns to the Customs and Excise authorities. The resulting loss of VAT was assessed at approximately 460,000 pounds sterling (“GBP”) and the accumulated losses in respect of Income Tax and National Insurance contributions were assessed at GBP 360,000. The applicant was represented throughout the proceedings by a Queen's Counsel, who was also a Recorder, a very experienced junior counsel and two different firms of solicitors. The applicant was convicted of fraud and sentenced to four years' imprisonment. He applied to the Court of Appeal Criminal Division seeking leave to appeal against his sentence. In his application, the applicant was represented by the same legal team that had defended him at trial. The applicant did not maintain in his application that he had been unable to understand the proceedings at the trial or to communicate effectively in court. He did not allege that he should have been provided with the services of an interpreter. The court agreed to make use of the applicant's brother, if need be, but he was never requested to translate any statement during the course of the hearing. Leave to appeal was refused by the Single Judge on 3 May 1996 and by the full Court of Appeal on 15 July 1996. The applicant wrote to the Home Secretary, admitting that he had not declared GBP 2,000 per week for staff wages due to the recession, and claiming that the real amount of the fraud was GBP 140,000 and not GBP 800,000. He further complained that his counsel had failed to secure him the services of an interpreter at the trial on 26 January 1996 and that this was of ‘paramount importance’ for the purposes of the plea in mitigation. The Commission observed that the applicant's solicitor and counsel at trial did not accept that he lacked understanding either of the language or of the nature of the case against him. The Commission accepted that the applicant would have been able to understand the generality of the prosecution case but expressed the view that an interpreter ought to have been present. The Commission concluded that there were grounds for finding that the plea was uninformed. In the view of the Commission, whilst the applicant's conviction was arguably unsatisfactory, it could not be said to be unsafe. Since the Commission did not consider that there was a real possibility that, if referred to the Court of Appeal, the conviction and sentence would not be upheld, it decided not to make such reference. The applicant was released from prison on licence on 25 November 1996.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 37222/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. He contended that because he held a vocational high school diploma, the new selection system had put him at a disadvantage in relation to candidates from ordinary high schools. On these points he relied on Article 14 of the convention in conjunction with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30943/96) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the German court decisions dismissing his request for a right of access to his child, born out of wedlock, amounted to a breach of his right to respect for his family life. On 11 October 2001 the Chamber delivered its judgment in which it held, by five votes to two, that there had been a violation of Article 8 of the convention. The applicant, born in 1950, was a Turkish national at the time of the events complained of. He subsequently obtained German nationality. The applicant is the father of G., born out of wedlock on 29 June 1988. In a document dated 15 June 1988, he acknowledged paternity of the unborn child, and in a further document, dated 15 August 1988,. he undertook to pay maintenance. The Government requested, in accordance with Article 43 of the Convention and Rule 73, that the case be referred to the Grand Chamber, contending that the Chamber should not have found violations of Article 8 and 14 of the convention. On 27 March 2002 a panel of the Grand. Chamber decided to refer the case to theGrand Chamber. Father applied to the Wiesbaden District Court for a decision granting him a right of access to his daughter on every Sunday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., as well as on Boxing Day and Easter Monday. The court found as follows: “The Court is convinced that the petitioner's wish for [G.] to visit him is motivated by attachment to his child and genuine affection for her. It nonetheless takes the view that personal contact with her father is not in the child's best interests, since her mother dislikes her father so deeply and opposes all contact so fiercely.” The father's request was dismissed on 5 September 1991. On 12 March 1992 the applicant appealed to the Wiesbaden Regional Court. The Regional Court ordered a psychological expert opinion on the question whether contact with the applicant was in G.'s interests. On 8 July 1992, following a first conversation with the expert, the applicant challenged her for bias. He also requested that another expert be appointed on the ground that the scientific approach adopted did not reflect the latest state of research. On 9 September 1992 the Regional Court refused the applicant's request, finding that, taking into account the expert's explanations of 8 August 1992, there were no reasons to doubt her impartiality or her capabilities. On 17 December 1992, he also applied for a provisional order granting him a right of access to G. during one afternoon every week. The father and the child's mother entered into an agreement in 1993. Under the terms of this agreement, the father would refrain from making any enquiries about the mother's personal circumstances. The proceedings were suspended until the termination of this therapy. After the Federal Constitutional Court's decisions of 1971 and 1981, the constitutionality of Article 1711 can no longer be seriously doubted. The main reason for the weaker legal position of the father of a child born out of wedlock is his different social position. The law leaves it up to the person having custody, as a rule the mother, to determine whether and to what extent the father should be able to spend time with his child. Court ruled that a father's access to a child born out of wedlock is beneficial for the child's welfare. A reform of the law on children born out  is even more urgently necessary. The Regional Court is convinced that the father in this case is motivated by attachment to [G.] and genuine affection for her. It is in fact important for children not simply to have a fantasy picture of their fathers, but to be able to form a personal, realistic picture. The court is not necessarily obliged to grant him access if there are serious tensions between the parents, and there is reason to fear that every meeting with the father will interfere. The Regional Court finally considered that exceptionally it had not been required to hear the child, since questioning her about her relationship with her father would have placed a psychological strain on her. The decisive factor is always the child's point of view. of all this, the report finds that she does not suffer as a result of the present situation. The Court can rely fully on the report, which has no apparent defects and is not invalidated by the fact that the father sees the situation differently.” The Federal Constitutional Court, sitting as a panel of three judges, refused to entertain the applicant's constitutional complaint on 1 December 1998. The applicant complained that the refusal of access to his daughter infringed his parental rights and amounted to discrimination.

However, the guardianship court may decide that the father is entitled to access if this is in theChild's best interests. The courts are bound by Article 1711. It is in fact important for children not simply to have a fantasy picture of their fathers, but to be able to form a personal, realistic picture. If the father were granted access to [G.] in present circumstances, she would have to shuttle between hostile camps, which should not be asked of her. In view of the findings in the [psychological expert] report referred to above, it must be assumed this would happen in the instant case. The Regional Court finally considered that exceptionally it had not been required to hear the child, since questioning her about her relationship with her father would have placed a psychological strain on her. The decisive factor is always the child's point of view. The Court can rely fully on the report, which has no apparent defects and is not invalidated by the fact that the father sees the situation differently.” The Federal Constitutional Court, sitting as a panel of three judges, refused to entertain the applicant's constitutional complaint on 1 December 1998. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29287/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Three Turkish nationals, Mr Mehmet Ali Ayhan, Mr Ali Akkurt and Mr Şükrü Töre (‘the applicants’) were represented by lawyers practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) was represented by their Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government on 11 December 2006. The two men were accused of involvement in activities which undermined the constitutional order of the State. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 of the Criminal Code. At a hearing held on 5 August 1998, the applicants requested to be released for the first time. The court ordered the continuation of their detention, having regard to the nature of the offence and the length of the detention. On 24 February 2004 the Istanbul State Security Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to life imprisonment. This judgment was upheld by the Court of Cassation on 4 October 2004. The applicants, at their request, were released pending trial on 4 November 2002. However, the court continued of its own motion to examine the applicant’s detention. The applicants were convicted as charged and sentenced to life imprisonment in 2006. Their appeal against this decision is apparently pending before the Court of Cassation. It is unclear how long they have already spent in detention and the state of the evidence. of the length of time the applicants had already spend in detention. The appeal against the decision is also apparently pending in the Supreme Court of Justice. The applicants' case was heard in the Istanbul Assize Court on 27 December 2006. It was decided the applicants were guilty of the charge of attempted murder and sentenced them to life in prison. They were also convicted of the attempted murder of their co-conspirators.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35141/06) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged a breach of Article 8 of the convention in relation to the contact restrictions following the taking into public care of her three children. On 20 January 2009 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) On 1 February 2011 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1 of the Rules of Court) and the above application was assigned to the newly composed Fifth Section. The applicant contacted BUP in a state of despair and, in response, a social emergency unit (social beredskap) went to the applicant’s home. The authorities found the interior of the home completely destitute; there was hardly any furniture and there was no electricity or running water. On the following day, the applicant was committed to compulsory psychiatric care in accordance with the Act on Compulsory Psychiatric Care (Lagen om psykiatrisk tvångsvård, 1991:1128). The applicant claimed that she was not ill but agreed to the placement of the children in the temporary family home. A week later, she was released from psychiatric care and returned to her home. The Social Council applied to the County Administrative Court for a permanent care order in respect of all three children, in accordance with section 2 of the 1990 Act. The council maintained that the applicant had shown a serious lack of ability to care for her children. The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten) in Sundsvall. The Social Council contested the appeal. In its view, the children’s behaviour showed that their development had already been harmed and, moreover, the. applicant had no insight into her problems and had difficulties in interacting with her. children. Since the applicant did not agree to voluntary care, it was necessary to take the children into public care on a permanent basis. The children were placed in three different family homes, all within approximately 50 km of Skellefteå, as one family was not able to provide the care and support that each child needed. In November 2006 the applicant, through her legal counsel, requested the Social Council to allow her more time with her children as she felt that the children were being deprived of contact with her. The Social Council decided to restrict the applicant’s contact rights to all three children. According to the decision, each parent should meet with the children once every three months in a neutral environment where the family home parents and the social worker responsible for the file should be present. The decision was based on an investigation carried out by the Social Council, in consultation with BUP, into the children’s situation. The Social Council concluded in its investigation report that the children had a right to contact with their mother but that their best interests required that the contact be limited in order to ensure their secure and positive development. The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court and requested that she be granted contact rights to her children much more often than only twice a year. She could see no reason for such restricted contact and found it to be contrary to the best interests of the children as they would forget their mother. They had lived with her until May 2005 and they had had a close and warm relationship. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Administrative Court of Appeal. She wanted to see her children at least once a month in order to ensure that they would not forget her. She felt that the family home parents had a negative attitude towards her and that this influenced the children. The Social Council contested the appeal. It submitted that the children were currently in the process of developing and learning things that they had not had the opportunity to learn before. It noted that the last meeting between the applicant and her children, on 23 January 2007, had passed without incident, partly because eight adults had been present to ensure the children’s well-being. Social Council noted that despite the applicant’s visits having been planned and very structured, the children had still had negative reactions before and after each meeting. The court found that with the support of the Social Council and the family homes during the meetings, these could be increased to four times per year for the applicant. It noted that the limited contact had been in place for roughly two years and had contributed to the children developing positively during this time. The applicant appealed to the Administrative Court of Appeal, maintaining that she wanted contact rights with her children during one weekend per month, without the presence of others, in order to ensure that she and the children would establish a good contact. The applicant voluntarily underwent a neuropsychological examination during two days at Stavanger University Hospital, upon request by the Social Council. The council wanted to know if the applicant suffered from a disorder or mental illness and, if so, what support she would need. The examination concluded that the applicant fulfilled the criteria for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) that was mainly inattentive in nature. It recommended supplementary examinations and made a number of proposals for supportive measures, including establishing fixed structures and routines in her daily life. It was also stressed that this specific impairment of her capabilities could hardly be sufficient to “disqualify her as a parent” S. before, during and after the meetings.
