The judge found that, on the basis of all the material in the case, it had been shown that the. applicant lacked the ability to cared for her kids, which had already somewhat impaired their. health and development. The children were placed in three different family homes, all within approximately 50 km of Skellefteå, as one family was not able to provide the care and support that each child needed. In November 2006 the applicant, through her legal counsel, requested the Social Council to allow her more time with her children as she felt that the children were being deprived of contact with her. The Social Council decided to restrict the applicant’s contact rights to all three children. This meant that each parent should meet with the children once every three months in a neutral environment where the family home parents and the social worker responsible for the file should be present. The decision was based on an investigation carried out by the Social Council, in consultation with BUP, into the children’s situation. The Social Council concluded in its investigation report that the children had a right to contact with their mother but that their best interests required that the contact be limited in order to ensure their secure and positive development. The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court and requested that she be granted contact rights to her children much more often than only twice a year. She could see no reason for such restricted contact and found it to be contrary to the best interests of the children as they would forget their mother. name: Tommy Evaldsson
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 75252/01) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicants alleged that the levying of monitoring fees on the individual applicants’ wages involved violations of Articles 9, 10, 11 and 14. The Court declared the application admissible with respect to the five individual applicants and inadmissible insofar it concerned the Swedish Construction Industries (Sveriges Byggindustrier) (hereinafter ‘the Industries’) The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 June 2006. The case involves the Swedish Building Workers’ Union (Svenska Byggnadsarbetareförbundet, hereinafter ‘the Union’) and the Industries. The relevant local branch of the Union in the instant case was the Stockholm branch, Byggettan. The Union had the right to inspect on a continuous basis wage conditions by measuring piecework (ackordsarbete) and result work (resultatarbete), as well as monitoring time-based work (tidlönearbete). If inspections were carried out in accordance with the collective agreement, the local branch had the. right to reimbursement of the costs involved on the basis of a fee of 1.5%. Industries eventually brought the case before the Labour Court (Arbetsdomstolen), seeking a declaratory judgment to the effect that the company was not obliged to levy the monitoring fees in question. Byggettan insisted on payment and initiated formal local negotiations. No solution was reached, either in the local negotiations or in the subsequent central negotiations between the Industries and the Union. The conduct thus violated their negative freedom of association under Article 11 of the Convention as well as under domestic law. Furthermore, since the applicants did not share the political values of the Union, the levy on their wages also violated their rights under Article 10 of the convention. Industry claimed that a ban on the levying of monitoring fees on unorganised workers’ wages would violate the positive rights of its members. The Labour Court rejected the Industries’ claims. It referred to several of its previous judgments concerning various types of measurement and monitoring fees. The monitoring of time-based wages was wholly different from the measuring of piecework, as no special action had to be taken to establish the amount and type of work performed. Instead, the inspection aimed at securing the observance of the collective labour agreement and also served as a basis for the statistics used by the Union in wage negotiations with the employers. The court concluded that the monitoring fee deductions did not entail membership of the Union and that no pressure had been exerted to compel the applicants to join the Union against their will. It found that the fact that the applicants indirectly supported the activities of the. Union did not in itself amount to forced membership, since being a member. entailed certain other duties, such as loyalty to its objectives and payment of a membership fee. The Labour Court noted that, theoretically, the applicants could be inclined to join a trade union other than the Union in order to avoid the wage deduction for the monitoring. fee. But it found that it was not very realistic that an employee would regard the. wage deduction as a particular incentive to do so. The company had been obliged to make a deduction from their wages in accordance with the collective labour agreement. Union and had not influenced or forced the applicants to join the Union, the company had said in a letter to the union. The union said that while it had not forced them to join, it had influenced them to do so. The company had then deducted the money from the applicants' wages, the union said in the letter. It said the deduction was in line with the Collective Labour Agreement (CLA) and was not a form of  injunction against the union, but rather a recognition of its right to strike.

Five Swedish nationals, Mr Tommy Evaldsson, Mr Johan Svahn, Mr Tonnie Hodell, Mr Jonny Lindqvist and Mr Conny Brandt (“the applicants”), and the Swedish Construction Industries (Sveriges Byggindustrier) (hereinafter “the Industries”) on 4 September 2001. The applicants alleged that the levying of monitoring fees on the individual applicants’ wages involved violations of Articles 9, 10, 11 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. By a decision of 28 March 2006, the Court declared the application admissible with respect to the five individual applicants and inadmissible insofar it concerned the Industries. The case involved the Swedish Building Workers’ Union (Svenska Byggnadsarbetareförbundet, hereinafter “the Union’) and the Industries. The relevant local branch of the Union in the instant case was the Stockholm branch, Byggettan. The Union had the right to inspect on a continuous basis wage conditions by measuring piecework (ackordsarbete) and result work (resultatarbete), as well as monitoring time-based work (tidlönearbete). If inspections were carried out in accordance with the collective agreement, the local branch had the. right to reimbursement of the costs involved on the basis of a fee of 1.5%. Two of the applicants, Mr Evaldsson and Mr Hodell, were heard by the Labour Court. They submitted that they opposed the deductions because they did not think that the monitoring work was of any use to them and considered the deductions an unnecessary expense. The conduct thus violated their negative freedom of association under Article 11 of the Convention as well as under domestic law. Furthermore, since the applicants did not share the political values of the Union, the levy on their wages also violated their rights under Article 10 of the convention. Company complied with their requests, stopped paying the fees to Byggettan and did not provide it with the above-mentioned wage information concerning the applicants. Industry claimed that a ban on the levying of monitoring fees on unorganised workers’ wages would violate the positive rights of its members. Byggettan claimed that the positive aspect of the freedom of association under Article 11 of the Convention was stronger than its negative counterpart. The Labour Court stated that there was no reason to come to a different conclusion in the instant case as to the nature of the monitoring work. The court concluded that the levies of fees on the wages of members of the Syndicalist Union for monitoring work carried out by another trade union involved a violation of those worker’s positive freedom of Association. The court concluded that the monitoring fee deductions did not entail membership of the Union. It found that the fact that the applicants indirectly supported the activities of the. Union did not in itself amount to forced membership. Being a member of. the Union also entailed certain other duties, such as loyalty to its objectives and. payment of a membership fee. The court found that there was no indication that they opposed the deduction of the fees because they took exception to union activities in general or to the ideology of the union. The Labour Court concluded that all the above considerations indicated that the deduction did not breach the applicants’ rights under the Convention. The company had been obliged to make a deduction from their wages in accordance with the collective labour agreement. The company had not influenced or forced the applicants to join the Union, the company said. The union said that the company had made the deduction from the applicants' wages in line with its collective labour agreement and that it was not against the law. The case was settled at the High Court in London on Tuesday. The decision was returned to the Court of Arbitration for Sport in London at 3pm on Tuesday, with the judge making the final decision on the case at 5pm. The Labour Court rejected the Industries’ claims. It referred to several of its previous judgments concerning various types of measurement and monitoring fees. The company had made the deduction from the applicants' wages and had not coerced them into joining the Union. The deduction had been made as part of the collective Labour Agreement. name: Jarosław Kąkol
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 3994/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant's detention to the Government. The applicant was charged with several dozen counts of armed robbery which had acted in an organised group. The application relied on the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged and the severity of the anticipated penalty. It also considered that the prolongation of detention was justified by the need to obtain DNA evidence in order to corroborate evidence. The trial began on 28 December 2001. The bill of indictment listed 120 charges brought against 19 defendants, who were all detained on remand. The case file comprised 114 volumes. The prosecution asked the court to hear evidence from 366 witnesses. The trial court ordered the removal of the applicant and two other defendants from the court room. They disrupted the trial by screaming when theProsecutor was reading the bill of. indictment, notwithstanding a warning from the presiding judge. On 27, 28 and 29 May 2002 the Gdańsk Regional Court dismissed the applicant's requests for the presiding. judge to withdraw. On 11 September 2002 the Court of Appeal ordered that the. applicant and his seven co-defendants be held in custody until 30 September 2002. The applicant and his 17 co-defendants were kept in custody until 30 June 2003. The Gdańsk Regional Court dismissed the applicant's request for the judges and lay members of the trial court to withdraw. The Court of Appeal held that Article 258 of the Code of Criminal Procedure established a presumption to the effect that the likelihood of a severe penalty being imposed on the applicant might induce him to obstruct the proceedings. It also noted that the prolongation of his detention was justified by the volume of evidence to be heard at the trial. In addition, it observed that the trial could not have been terminated due to obstructiveness on the part of the defendants who had filed numerous requests. The Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's detention on several occasions. The applicant filed numerous but unsuccessful applications for release and appealed, likewise unsuccessfully, against the decisions prolonging his detention. By March 2006 the trial court had held some 135 hearings of the 162 which had been scheduled. It heard more than 400 witnesses. The case was adjourned until the end of 2008. The charges against the applicant are still pending. The application for release was dismissed on health grounds, relying on the report prepared by the Gdańsk Medical Academy. However the experts determined that the applicant could remain and receive treatment in detention. The appeal was dismissed again on July 27, 2005. The applicant's case was adjourned until 31 January 2006. On 18 October 2005 a different panel of the Court of Appeal quashed the impugned decision and ordered the applicant's release under police supervision. The applicant was released on 19 October 2005. It appears that the proceedings are still pending before the first-instance court. The judge rapporteur is still alive and well. The case is currently being heard by a judge at the Gdańsk Regional Court. The trial had to commence de novo due to the judge's illness. The court made a severance order and divided the case into eleven separate cases on 24 November 2005. The first-institution court is yet to hear the case.

The case originated in an application (no. 3994/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant's detention to the Government. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was charged with several dozen counts of armed robbery which had taken place in Gdynia between 1999 and 2001. He was also charged with eight other people in connection with the same investigation. The trial began on 28 December 2001. The bill of indictment listed 120 charges brought against 19 defendants, who were all detained on remand. The case file comprised 114 volumes. The prosecution asked the court to hear evidence from 366 witnesses. The trial court ordered the removal of the applicant and two other defendants from the court room. They disrupted the trial by screaming when the prosecutor was reading the bill of indicted. The Court of Appeal found that the prolongation of detention was justified under Article 263 § 4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by the particular complexity of the case. It further observed that the delays in the trial were partly attributable to some of the defendants who had attempted to disrupt the proceedings. Gdańsk Regional Court dismissed the applicant's request for the judges and lay members of the trial court to withdraw. Court of Appeal held that Article 258 of the Code of Criminal Procedure established a presumption to the effect that the likelihood of a severe penalty being imposed on the applicant might induce him to obstruct the proceedings. In addition, it observed that the trial could not have been terminated due to obstructiveness on the part of the defendants who had filed numerous requests challenging the court. It added that the risk of absconding or tampering with witnesses in the present case did not have to be supported by any concrete facts, but resulted from the above presumption. New legal-aid counsel was appointed for the applicant on 1 September 2003. Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's detention on several occasions. Court of Appeal stated that the grounds previously given for his detention were still valid. Court also stressed the exceptionally complex nature of the case. By March 2006 the trial court had held some 135 hearings of the 162 which had been scheduled. It heard more than 400 witnesses. The applicant filed numerous but unsuccessful applications for release and appealed, likewise unsuccessfully, against the decisions prolonging his detention. He maintained that the length of his detention was excessive and that the charges against him lacked a charge against him. In his appeal against the decision of 22 June 2005 the Court of appeal referred, inter alia, to the presumption established under Article 258 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and held that that presumption alone justified his continued detention. The case was adjourned in March 2005 due to the illness of the judge rapporteur. The trial had to commence de novo after the judge's illness. The applicant appealed the decision to extend his detention until 31 January 2006. On 18 October 2005 a different panel of the Court of Appeal quashed the impugned decision and ordered the applicant's release under police supervision. The case is still pending before the first-instance court in Gdańsk, Poland. The application was dismissed on 19 October 2005 and the applicant was released on 19 November 2005. It is not clear if the case will ever be heard at the first court.

The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant's detention to the Government. The applicant was charged with several dozen counts of armed robbery which had been committed in the course of an organised crime investigation in Gdynia. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The case file comprised 114 volumes. The prosecution asked the court to hear evidence from 366 witnesses. The bill of indictment listed 120 charges brought against 19 defendants, who were all detained on remand. The trial began on 28 December 2001. As of 22 April 2002 the reading out of the bill of. indictment by the prosecution had still not been concluded. Initially, the trial court held three hearings per month. On 27, 28 and 29 May 2002 the Gdańsk Regional Court dismissed the applicant's requests for the presiding judge to withdraw the case against him. On 11 September 2002 the applicant was found guilty of being a member of a criminal group. The main reason for the delays during the trial was the obstructiveness of the defendants and the abuse of the rights of the defence. The applicant filed numerous but unsuccessful applications for release and appealed, likewise unsuccessfully, against the decisions prolonging his detention. The trial court had held some 135 hearings of the 162 which had been scheduled. It heard more than 400 witnesses. The court found the charges against him lacked a case to answer. The judge ruled that the trial could be concluded by the end of 2004 provided that the Regional Court endeavoured to organise the trial efficiently. The case was to be tried de novo, but no hearing was held due to the serious illness of the judge rapporteur. Four defendants, who had been released from detention, were to be tested separately. The Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's detention until 31 January 2006. The applicant appealed against that decision. On 18 October 2005 a different panel of the Court of. Appeal quashed the impugned decision and ordered the. applicant's release under police supervision. It also imposed on him a prohibition on leaving the country. name: Józef Polejowski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38399/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been deprived of his right of access to a court. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The application was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The case was heard by the President of the Fourth Section of the Court on 1 September 2006. The applicant was 63 years old and in poor health. He was not even able to buy the necessary medication as his monthly disability pension amounted to PLN 556.5. For these reasons he believed that he should be exempted from court fees. The court dismissed his appeal and ordered him to pay a total of PLN 11,305.5 [approx. EUR 2,826] for lodging his statement of claim on pain of having it returned. After the applicant failed to do so, his statement was returned to him on 3 February 2003. The case was decided by the Gdańsk Regional Court in 2001 and the Gdansk Court of Appeal.

name: Franck Ladent
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 11036/03) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The French Government were invited to intervene in the proceedings. However, by a letter of 10 October 2006, they informed the Registry that they did not wish to exercise their right to intervene. The applicant is an artist and runs a small business in France which provides the only support for the family. The court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The case was decided on the grounds that the Polish Government had failed to provide a fair and just hearing to the applicant. Franck Ladent is accused of evading justice in Poland. He was arrested at the Słubice Border Guard detention centre. The applicant and his family went on holiday to Kraków at the end of 2002. In his submissions to the European Court, he said that various requests he made through his wife, such as to be allowed to contact the French Embassy or his family and to be provided with an interpreter or a lawyer, were refused. The court ordered the police to execute that decision and to serve a copy of it on the applicant immediately after his arrest and to inform him that he could appeal. The information that a wanted notice had been issued in respect of the applicant was subsequently entered in a central criminal register. Franck Ladent was detained on remand on the basis of a detention order issued by this court. The applicant's wife engaged counsel to represent the applicant. Counsel argued that the evidence obtained in the case had not sufficiently justified the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed slander. On 10 January 2003 the Kraków–Śródmieście District Court resumed the private prosecution proceedings against the applicant, noting that his abode had been established. On the same date it quashed the detention order of 15 July 2002 and replaced it with a ban on leaving the country and ordered the applicant to surrender his passport. The applicant was released from detention in the morning of 13 January 2003 (a Monday) Upon his release he received copies of the three documents translated into French. The applicant submitted that it was only then that he learnt for the first time that he had been accused of slandering B.M. The court has found the arguments raised by counsel to be compelling. In these circumstances, in the court's view the detention on remand should be replaced with other measures, namely a ban on leaving the country together with seizure of his passport. That measure will adequately secure the proper conduct of the proceedings...”. It appears that the applicant and his family returned to France on 27 January 2003. The applicant's case was placed under the Vice-President of the Kraków Regional Court's administrative supervision. The President of the Court of Appeal informed the MP that the principal error committed by the District Court in respect of the applicant's detention order was the unfounded assumption that the applicant had been evading justice and maliciously failing to comply with the court summons. He advised the applicant and his wife that they could seek to institute disciplinary proceedings against the judge who had issued the detention order and criminal proceedings for abuse of power. The lessons to be drawn from the case would be used for training purposes. The applicant was acquitted on 5 October 2004.

The applicant was arrested at 8.15 p.m. on the basis of the detention order and the wanted notice issued on 15 July 2002. In his submissions to the European Court, he said that various requests he made through his wife, such as to be allowed to contact the French Embassy or his family, were refused. The applicant was released on 31 January 2003. The applicant ran his own business in France and supported his family exclusively from the income he received from it. The court found the arguments raised by counsel to be compelling. In these circumstances, in the court's view the detention on remand should be replaced with other measures, namely a ban on leaving the country together with seizure of his passport. That measure will adequately secure the proper conduct of the proceedings...”. The District Court also ordered that the private bill of indictment, the decision to release the applicant and the summons to appear before the court be translated into French and served on the applicant. The applicant submitted that it was only then that he learnt for the first time that he had been accused of slandering B.M. The President of the Court of Appeal informed the MP that the applicant's case had been thoroughly considered and had been placed under the Vice-President of the Kraków Regional Court's administrative supervision. The President stated that the principal error committed by the District Court in respect of the applicant’s detention order was the unfounded assumption that he had been evading justice and maliciously failing to comply with the court summons. He advised the applicant and his wife that they could seek to institute disciplinary proceedings against the judge who had issued the detention order and criminal proceedings for abuse of power. He further advised them that he could seek compensation in the civil courts. The lessons to be drawn from the case would be used for training purposes.

name: Jerzy Zawisza
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 37293/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. name: Janusz Krawczak
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the excessive length of proceedings. The Government submitted a unilateral declaration and invited the Court to strike out the application. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The application was dismissed on the basis that the Government had not complied with its obligations under the Convention. The case was decided on appeal by the Court of Appeal, and the decision was made to dismiss the application on the grounds that it was not supported by the evidence. The proceedings are still pending. The applicant lodged a complaint about the undue length of the criminal proceedings under section 5 of the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. On 23 March 2006 the Gdańsk Court of Appeal dismissed his complaint on the ground that since the date of entry into force of the 2004 Act no undue delays in the proceedings could be discerned. The proceedings had to be restarted as a new bench should be appointed, which meant that the proceedings were restarted again. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the Act had entered into force on 17 September 2004 and could not be applied to the proceedings.

train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 16651/05) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, that the length of administrative proceedings in their case exceeded a “reasonable time” They also alleged that the delay in payment of compensation amounted to a breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. On 11 September 2008 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) In 1961 Ms Wacława Korsak applied for compensation for the nationalised property. She was awarded in part and awarded compensation for 23,000 sq. m of the land. Her son applied for the remaining part of the property in 1978. Other applicants joined the proceedings and that between 1991 and 2007 they made repeated requests for compensation. The administrative proceedings, pending before the Warsaw District Office (Urząd Rejonowy), were stayed in 1992. In 1998 the second applicant lodged a complaint about the inactivity of the Mayor of Warsaw (Prezydent Miasta Warszawy), but this was dismissed by the Supreme Administrative Court. The applicants appealed. The Mazowiecki Governor (Wojewoda) quashed the impugned decision and remitted the case for fresh consideration. The total compensation paid (PLN 5,782,335) was divided among Ms Barbara Czajkowska, Mr Tadeusz Korsak, Mr Tomasz Świeczak and Ms Agata Wicherek according to their share in Ms Wacława Korsack's estate. The remaining applicants were not parties to the proceedings at that stage as they had either donated or sold their shares in the inheritance to the other applicants. Mayor agreed to pay the applicants compensation for a part of the property measuring 12,009 sq. m. The total compensation paid (PLN 6,376,779) was divided among Ms Barbara Czajkowska, Mr Tadeusz Korsak, Mr Tomasz Świeczak and Ms Agata Wicherek. The Mayor also decided that the application regarding compensation for the remaining (and last) part of. the property, measuring 1,103 sq.m, would be settled at a later stage by a separate decision. The proceedings regarding this part of applicants' claim are pending.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36144/09) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1974 and lives in Diyarbakır. He was among those who were arrested on the night of 30 March 2006. The medical report indicated large ecchymoses on the applicant’s back and on the outer part of his left femur. The application was communicated to the Government on 21 June 2011. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. On 2 May 2006 the applicant was charged with involvement in the activities of an illegal organisation. On 25 May 2007 the Diyarbakır Assize Court convicted the applicant under Article 314 of the Criminal Code and sentenced him to six years and three months’ imprisonment. On 30 May 2011 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. On 27 October 2008 the public prosecutor issued a decision not to prosecute on the ground that the complainant’s statement had not been taken by the police. On 18 September 2006, on the basis of the medical reports, the applicant filed a complaint against police officers, alleging ill-treatment by them.

The case originated in an application (no. 36144/09) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1974 and lives in Diyarbakır. In the course of a military operation, several terrorists were killed by the security forces in Bingöl. On 28 March 2006 a large group of people assembled at their funeral and protested against the security force. About 1,500 to 2,000 people resisted the police, attacking them with stones, blocking the traffic by burning tyres and damaging nearby shops and public buildings by throwing stones. Many demonstrators were arrested by the police. The Diyarbakır Assize Court convicted the applicant under Article 314 of the Criminal Code and sentenced him to six years and three months’ imprisonment. In convicting the applicant, the assize court relied on video recordings and witness statements. The court also had particular regard to the statement of a police officer, who had identified the applicant as the person who had wounded him by throwing stones. It was therefore concluded that the applicant had acted in support of an illegal organisation. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court on 30 May 2011. The applicant was sentenced to 6 years and 3 months in prison.

train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 33402/96) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The judge also ordered him to pay a customs fine of FRF 1,470,000. He made an urgent application to the President of the Mulhouse tribunal de grande instance, arguing that the order for his imprisonment in default was defective, as the Customs Office had failed to serve him with a demand for payment. The urgent-applications judge dismissed that application in an order of 27 September 1994. On 4 September 1994 the applicant completed his prison sentence. He relied in particular on the Court's judgment in Jamil v France (judgment of 8 June 1995, Series A no. 317-B), in which imprisonment in default was found to constitute a ‘penalty’ for the purposes of the European Convention. Ali Göktan was found guilty of an offence under the drug-trafficking and customs-offences legislation. The case was decided on the admissibility and merits of the applications at the same time (Article 29) The judge ruled that the applicants' application was not in breach of any law. The judge also decided that the application should be allowed to be heard by a jury. The jury was allowed to hear the case and the decision was made to dismiss the case. The decision was then appealed to the European Court of Human rights. The applicants were taken to the Bayrampaşa Health Clinic for a medical examination. The doctor who examined the applicants concluded that both of them were unfit to work for seven days. The applicants filed a petition with the Beyoğlu public prosecutor against the police officers who had carried out their arrest. In November 2004 the public prosecutor issued a decision of non-prosecution in respect of the police officer who had been on duty at the relevant time. In his decision, the prosecutor considered that the force used by the security forces had been in line with Article 16 of Law no. 2559 on the Duties and Powers of the Police and had not been excessive. In delivering its decision, the Criminal Court had regard to a video recording of the incident, to witness statements and to the submissions of the intervening parties. The applicant was born in 1953 and was serving a sentence in Nazilli prison at the time of lodging his application. On 23 May 2001 the applicant was arrested and taken into custody by police officers at the Diyarbakır Security Directorate. According to the arrest protocol, signed by a police officer and the applicant, the latter was arrested at 18.00 p.m. and told of his rights. Government submitted that the applicant was taken for a medical examination at Diyarbakır State Hospital on the day of his arrest and on 24 and 25 May 2001. The applicant was convicted of being a member of a terrorist organisation and sentenced to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment in May 2002. He was arrested in May 2001 and accused of involvement with the PKK. The application was rejected by the Turkish Court of Appeal in May 2000. The court ruled that the application was not guilty of the charge and the case was dismissed. The case was referred to the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in April 2002. The ICC ruled in March 2002 that the case should be re-examined to determine whether or not the applicant’s detention was justified.

The judge ruled in favour of the applicants, and the case was adjourned until 16 October 2010 for further proceedings to be heard. The children were apprehended with a view to being deported to Pakistan. The police considered that it would be inappropriate to expel them without their mother who had disappeared around the turn of the year 2000‑2001. The applicants had no contacts with their mother until she was hospitalised in Norway in 2004. During this period they lived with an uncle and aunt in Oslo. In September 2005 the mother was expelled to Pakistan, in compliance with the immigration authorities’ decision (see paragraph 8 above). She died in August 2007. The City Court observed that the applicants, respectively twenty-one and twenty-two years old, had lived in Norway for 16 and a half years during major parts of their childhood and the entirety of their adolescence. The applicants had gone to school in Norway, had friends and acquaintances there and were mastering the Norwegian language, both oral and written. The authorities’ omission to implement “the refusal of residence” (“oppholdsnektelsen”) ought to be seen in the light of the fact that the police had been unable to get hold of their mother. The applicants’ choice to stay in Norway had been something for which they ought to bear the risk and responsibility. It was difficult to ascribe any responsibility to the applicants for not having taken any steps to leave the country while the mother had gone into hiding from the police. The High Court, nonetheless, arrived at the conclusion that the refusal of residence had not been unlawful as being contrary to Article 8. The applicant alleged that his detention on remand exceeded a “reasonable time’ within the meaning of Article 5 § 3. The courts considered that the applicant had been charged with the commission of crimes for which he was liable to a sentence of imprisonment exceeding 8 years, and that the circumstances of the case indicated that there was a reasonable risk that he might obstruct the proceedings. The case was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicant served prison sentences imposed in other sets of criminal proceedings against him. During the investigation and trial the applicant filed several unsuccessful applications for release and appealed, likewise unsuccessfully, against the decisions prolonging his detention. The Gdańsk Regional Court found that the necessary pieces of evidence had been obtained and the case was at its final stage, so there was no need to prolong the applicant’s detention. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26808/08) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 9 February 2010 the application was declared partly inadmissible and the complaints concerning the length of pre-trial detention and of the criminal proceedings were communicated to the Government. On 19 December 2002 the Istanbul State Security Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The Government objected to the examination of the application by a Committee. Taking into account the issues raised in the application, the Court finds it appropriate to allocate the case to a Chamber. The applicant's continued pre-trial detention was reviewed every thirty days on the basis of the case file. The Istanbul Assize Court rejected those requests several times in view of the reasonable grounds of suspicion established against the applicant. On 3 November 2009, having regard to the period he had spent in detention, the Istanbul Assizes Court released the applicant on the condition that he did not leave the country. According to the information in the casefile, the proceedings are currently pending before the IstanbulAssize Court. The applicant’s case is being heard by the 14th Division of the Istanbul Assize Court, which is currently deciding whether to appeal the decision of the above-mentioned court.

name: Patrick Grattan Foley
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 39197/98) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that civil proceedings brought by him were not determined within a reasonable time. The application was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court, which, on 11 September 2001, declared the application partially admissible and decided to dispense with a hearing. This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. The parties were represented by their Agent, Mr C. Whomersley, Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal on 1 November 2001. The defendants applied for security for their costs, and the court granted the application on 26 September 1985. The proceedings were stayed until the security was paid. The appeal was dismissed on 31 January 1986 and the plaintiffs paid the security on 28 February 1986. The plaintiffs’ solicitors filed a Notice of Intention to Proceed on 5 January 1989 as required by the rules of court since no steps had been taken in the prosecution of the claim for more than a year. The Government state that it was due to the parties not having ensured that sufficient court time would be available. A further hearing was proposed for 1 September 1989 but was also adjourned. According to the applicant, this adjournment was due by the court registry properly to notify the defendants’ counsel of the hearing date. Ferranti Instrumentation Limited was a joint venture between Ferranti plc and a group of British companies. The firm failed to establish that the venture would have been a commercial success had it proceeded. The plaintiffs appealed in December 1992. The appeal was stood out of the list by consent until 31 March 1995. On 18 June 1996 the applicant informed the Civil Appeals Office that he would be proceeding in person. The application for security for costs for the appeal was dismissed. The case was settled out of court in October 1992. On 2 October 1992, judgment was given in the plaintiffs’ favour. However, the damages award was limited to GBP 5 to each plaintiff. His request for a hearing date was passed to the Court of Appeal’s Registrar on 14 November 1996. The CAO learnt that Ferranti Instrumentation Limited had been struck off the register of companies in August 1998. The applicant was offered an ex gratia payment to cover his wasted costs in connection with the Court Service's admitted failures. Even if the applicant had won he would not have benefited financially given the financial state of the one remaining defendant (Ferranti plc) The plaintiffs’ request for leave to appeal to the House of Lords was dismissed on 19 April 1999, and the case was dismissed in January 1999.

name: Eliza Söderman
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5786/08) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the Swedish State had failed to comply with its obligation to provide her with remedies against her stepfather’s violation of her personal integrity. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. On 21 June 2012 a Chamber composed of Dean Spielmann, President, Elisabet Fura, Karel Jungwiert, Mark Villiger, Ann Power-Forde, Ganna Yudkivska, André Potocki, delivered its judgment. It decided to examine the complaint under Article 8 alone and unanimously declared it admissible. The applicant, from Ludvika, Estonia, was sexually molested by her stepfather when she was 14 years old. She asked the Grand Chamber to lift the anonymity granted to her. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 3 April 2013. The Court heard addresses by Mr Crafoord, Mr Lewis, Mr Södergren and Mr Rönquist, as well as their replies to questions put by Judges Ziemele, Sicilianos, Pinto de Albuquerque and Zupančič. The applicant was also present. The matter was heard in Strasbourg by the Court of Human Rights. The applicant, her stepfather, her mother and her cousin gave evidence before the District Court of Falun (Falu Tingsrätt) The applicant’s stepfather explained that he had lived with her mother from 1997 until the autumn of 2003. They had separated on account of the incident in question, among other things. He had wanted to try to film with a hidden camera, but it had been an impulsive act. He was not sure whether the camera had been in recording mode or whether a film had been recorded. The applicant's mother had burned the film without her seeing it. She had not reported the incident to the police until 2004, when she had heard that her cousin had also experienced incidents with the accused. The applicant’s stepfather was given a suspended sentence combined with seventy-five hours’ compulsory community service. He was also ordered to pay the applicant damages in the amount of SEK 20,000. The Court of Appeal acquitted him on the counts of sexual molestation allegedly committed against the applicant. The court of Appeal found it established that the applicant's stepfather had put a camera in the bathroom and that he had started the recording before she was about to take a shower. Whether a recording had actually been made, however, was unclear. It was apparent, the court continued, that his motive had been to film the applicant covertly for a sexual purpose. A man was acquitted of sexual molestation because he had not intended his girlfriend to find out about the filming. The isolated act of filming was not a crime in itself, as in Swedish law there was no general prohibition against filming an individual without his or her consent. The Court of Appeal went on to point out that the act might, at least theoretically, have constituted the crime of attempted child pornography (försök till barnpornografibrott) considering the applicant’s age. In conclusion, despite finding his behaviour extremely reprehensible, he was acquitted and the applicant's claim for damages dismissed.

name: Arkadiusz Demski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 22695/03) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his rights under Article 6. 1 and 3 (d) were violated as he had no opportunity to examine the main. witness in the criminal proceedings against him. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The case was heard by the Jelenia Góra District Court, at the request of the prosecutor, pursuant to Article 316. 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to four years’ imprisonment. The court established the following facts. On 10 June 2000 M.H., who was at that time 17 years old, met the applicant, J.K. and another man in a bar called “DIK’. The men were aggressive and intimidating, particularly J. k. They told her to come to the same bar the next day at 5 p.m., which she did. On 11 June 2000 the applicant and J.k. again threatened M. H. in the bar. The applicant then led M.h. out of the bar and together with J. K. they went to the latter’s house and raped her. The following day she told her grandmother, who informed the police. Victim M.H. described in identical terms the course of events of 10 and 11 June 2000. It is no surprise that it was out of fear of the accused that she went [back] to the bar. Despite the fact that she had been close to a police station she did not try to call for help. The victim could not have counted on anybody’s help in such a place and she believed that putting up any resistance would have been pointless. As the explanations of both accused are contrary to the testimonies of M. H. [they have been considered untruthful], the court ruled. The Wrocław Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) upheld the first-instance judgment and dismissed the appeal. On 18 September 2001 the applicant’s lawyer lodged an appeal against the judgment. In particular, he complained that the applicant's right to defence had been breached and that the testimonies taken from the victim at the investigation stage had been used by the trial court. On 14 February 2002 the applicant and his lawyer lodged a cassation appeal on his behalf with the Supreme Court. The appeal was dismissed on 13 December 2001 and the appeal was withdrawn. The case was brought by a woman called M.Ł. - the victim's grandmother - who had been living in Germany. The Supreme Court dismissed the cassation appeal. The applicant concluded that he had been deprived of the right to put questions to the witness and to confront her with other evidence. He complained that the victim has only been summoned to the hearing of 21 May 2000 once and that the summons had been sent to an address in Poland even though the trial court had known her new address in Germany. The Supreme Court stated, in so far as relevant: “...[Article 391 § 1] does not mean that in every case when a witness is abroad an automatic application of an exception from the rule of principle of directness should apply” The victim was heard in the preparatory proceedings by a court according to the provision of Article 316 § 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. At the time when the court (in the presence of a psychologist) heard the victim, the applicant had been in hiding. The author of the cassation appeal ... failed to indicate what concrete, additional information he would have liked to obtain from M.H ...” said the judge. The judge added: “By his own choice he did not participate in this important evidentiary stage of the proceedings and consequently deprived himself of the opportunity to put questions to the witness’”

At the time when the court (in the presence of a psychologist) heard the victim, the applicant had been in hiding. The author of the cassation appeal ... failed to indicate what concrete, additional information he would have liked to obtain from M.H ...” said the judge in the case of a man accused of attacking his ex-wife with a knife in a hotel room. The man was convicted and sentenced to two years in prison in June 2013. The appeal was dismissed on appeal in August 2013 and the case was adjourned until April 14, 2014. name: Hasan Erkan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29840/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant was represented before the Court by Ms Arzu Becerik, a lawyer practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not appoint an agent for the purpose of the Proceedings. The applicant asked for the days he worked in 1992 to be taken into account when calculating the total period of his service. On 22 December 1994 the Ankara Administrative Court dismissed his request. The applicant appealed on 5 May 1995 but did not pay the necessary appeal fees until 3 August 1995. In the opinion of the Council of State, the applicant should have been considered as a civil servant on the day of the appointment and not on theday of his actually taking up his duties. The court ruled that the applicant did not have the right to advance to a higher grade. This decision was served on the applicant on 17 February 2003. The decision was upheld on 15 November 2002.

name: Stephen Anthony Saccoccia
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that in proceedings before the Austrian courts concerning the execution of a forfeiture order issued by the United States courts he had not had a hearing. The parties disagree as to whether or not the applicant was the owner of the assets. By a decision of 5 July 2007 the Court declared the application partly admissible and dismissed the applicant's request for a list of the values of all his Austrian assets at the time of their seizure and when they were forfeited to enable him to calculate his just satisfaction claims. The applicant claims that the assets stemmed from lawful business activities carried out until 1988. The Government claim that they stemmed from the money laundering in 1990 and 1991 of which he was convicted (see below) and that he was holding them as a trustee for the drug cartel for which he had worked. The case had been heard on 26 March 1993 in the presence of the applicant’s counsel. The applicant had not been present since he had to appear before another court. The U.S. Supreme Court rejected an appeal on points of law by the applicant. On 7 November 1997 the Rhode Island District Court issued a final forfeiture order relating to a total amount of USD 136 million, including some USD 9 million. On 9 December 1997 the Rhode Island District Court issued letters rogatory which, so far as relevant, read as follows: “... the United States District Court for the District of Rhode Island requests enforcement in Austria of the enclosed Final Forfeiture Order against said cash, bonds and other financial instruments” The U.S. Department of Justice transmitted this request to the Austrian authorities on 18 December 1997. On 23 January 1998 the Austrian Ministry of Justice requested the Vienna Senior Public Prosecutor’s Office to open “exequatur” proceedings to enforce the foreign court's decision. The proceedings before the Austrian courts are still pending. The applicant claimed that the final forfeiture order also included “substitute assets’, i.e. assets not connected to or derived from criminal activity. In any event these penalties could not be applied in his case, as the relevant provisions had not been in force at the time he committed the offences. Furthermore, he had been convicted of money laundering in the United States, an offence which was not punishable under Austrian law. The Court of Appeal found that the Regional Court’s decision was based on Article 144a of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Strafprozeßordnung). In this connection, the court noted that pursuant to section 9(1) of the ELAA, the provisions of the code had to be enforced. The court notes that the letters rogatory requested first and foremost that any measures required under Austrian law for the execution of the final forfeiture order be taken. The court observes that it followed from the judgment concerning the applicant’s conviction that he had led an organisation which had laundered large sums of money. Between 1 January 1990 and 2 April 1991 he had transferred more than USD 136 million of drug-related money from the account of a sham company to various foreign bank accounts. Even if one applied the law in force at the time of the commission of the offences, the requirements for withdrawal of enrichment were met. The fact that they had not been in force when the offences were committed was therefore not material. Vienna Court of Appeal finds no indication that the proceedings before the United States courts had failed to comply with Article 6 of the Convention. In the forfeiture proceedings he waived his right to a public hearing before a jury since they only concerned questions of law. Under Article 20(3) of the 1998 Treaty, it applied irrespective of whether the underlying offences were committed before or after its entry into force. Article 17 provided for mutual legal assistance in forfeiture proceedings. The enforcement of the final forfeiture order of 7 November 1997. The United States central authority, relying on the 1998 treaty, made a new request for enforcement of a forfeiture order. According to the ELAA, only the provisions of theELAA had to be applied. Vienna Regional Criminal Court decided to take over the enforcement of the final forfeiture order of 7 November 1997. It ordered the forfeiture of the applicant’s Austrian assets for the benefit of the United States. The applicant appealed on 7 July 2000. He asserted that the 1998 Treaty provided for legal assistance in pending criminal proceedings, but did not contain a legal basis for mutual execution of final decisions. He also claimed that the five-year limitation period for enforcement had started running on 30 August 1993, when the preliminary forfeiture order was issued. He further claimed that, at the time of the commission of the offences, such assets had not been subject to forfeiture or withdrawal of enrichment under Austrian law. The applicant alleged that the criminal proceedings and the forfeiture proceedings before the United States courts had not complied with the requirements of Article 6 of the Convention. He also complained that the Regional Court had failed to hold a public oral hearing and requested that such a hearing be held by the appellate court. On 7 October 2000 the Vienna Court of Appeal, sitting in camera, dismissed the applicant’s appeal and ordered the forfeiture to the benefit of the Republic of Austria. The court noted at the outset that, pursuant to its Article 20(3), the 1998 Treaty applied irrespective of whether the underlying offences were committed before or after its entry into force. It was therefore not necessary to examine questions of United States constitutional law. The court ruled that the enforcement of the order was time-barred. The five-year limitation period pursuant to section 59 of the Criminal Code had not expired. The court found that the forfeiture to the benefit of the United States under Article 17(3) of the 1998 Treaty was not admissible. The decision was made by the court of appeals, which is the highest court in the country. The appeal was rejected by the Supreme Court, which ruled that it was not the right court to make such a decision. The Court of Appeal's decision was appealed to the European Court of Justice, which upheld the forfeiture, and the decision was quashed. The Supreme Court's ruling was overturned.

The case originated in an application (no. 69917/01) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of the United States of America. The applicant alleged, in particular, that in proceedings before the Austrian courts concerning the execution of a forfeiture order issued by the U.S. courts he had not had a hearing. He claimed Austrian courts’ decisions had violated his right to property. The parties disagree as to whether or not the applicant was the owner of the assets. In February 1993 the Rhode Island District Court convicted the applicant of money laundering and related charges, finding that he had headed an organisation which had laundered more than a hundred million United States dollars (USD) in 1990 and 1991. The applicant claims that the assets stemmed from lawful business activities carried out until 1988, while the Government claim that they stemmed from the money laundering in 1990/91 of which he was convicted (see below) and that he was holding them as a trustee for the drug cartel for which he had worked. U.S. Supreme Court rejected an appeal on points of law by the applicant in 1996. In November 1997 the Rhode Rhode Island D.C. District Court issued a final forfeiture order relating to a total amount of USD 136 million, including some USD 9 million in respect of the applicant. The applicant appealed against the confiscation of his assets. The proceedings before the Austrian courts are still ongoing. The U.S. Department of Justice transmitted this request to the Austrian authorities on 18 December 1997. On 23 January 1998 the Austrian Ministry of Justice requested the Vienna Senior Public Prosecutor’s Office to open “exequatur’ proceedings to enforce the foreign court's decision. The applicant appealed on 26 March 1998, submitting in particular that the Regional Court's decision amounted to an unlawful interference with his right to property, as it lacked a legal basis. An enforcement of the forfeiture order for the benefit of the United States was not admissible in Austria. Any fines or forfeited assets obtained by executing a foreign decision fell to the Republic of Austria. The applicant claimed that the final forfeiture order also included “substitute assets’, i.e. assets not connected to or derived from criminal activity. The measure requested did not correspond in any way to forfeiture (Verfall) or withdrawal of enrichment (Abschöpfung der Bereicherung) within the meaning of the Austrian Criminal Code (Strafgesetzbuch) In any event these penalties could not be applied in his case, as the relevant provisions had not been in force at the time he committed the offences. The Court of Appeal found that the Regional Court’s decision was based on Article 144a of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The court found that the applicant had led an organisation which had laundered large sums of money derived from drug dealing and had usually received a 10% commission for each amount laundered. Between 1 January 1990 and 2 April 1991 he had transferred more than USD 136 million of drug-related money from the account of a sham company to various foreign bank accounts. The final forfeiture order made a clear link between the offence of money laundering of which the applicant was convicted and the forfeiture of all monies obtained thereby. A forfeiture for the benefit of the United States would be contrary to section 64(7) of the ELAA, the court observed. The applicant claimed that both the criminal proceedings against him and the proceedings resulting in the final forfeiture order had failed to comply with Article 6 of the Convention. Vienna Court of Appeal found no indication that the proceedings before the United States courts had failed. The court noted that it was the applicant who had insisted on being represented by counsel H. although the latter had voiced concerns, albeit without substantiating them, that he might himself be charged. In any case, the applicant had been represented by a second counsel, who was free from any potential conflict of interests. In the forfeiture proceedings he waived his right to a public hearing before a jury since they only concerned questions of law. The Vienna Regional Criminal Court decided to take over the enforcement of the final forfeiture order of 7 November 1997 and ordered the forfeiture of the applicant’s Austrian assets for the benefit of the United States. The applicant made submissions on 22 December 1998, on 11 March 1999 and on 11 May 2000. He asserted that the 1998 Treaty provided for legal assistance in pending criminal proceedings, but did not contain a legal basis for mutual execution of final decisions. He also claimed that, at the time of the commission of the offences, such assets had not been subject to forfeiture or withdrawal of enrichment under Austrian law. He further submitted that the five-year limitation period for enforcement had started running on 30 August 1993. The applicant alleged that the criminal proceedings and the forfeiture proceedings before the United States courts had not complied with the requirements of Article 6 of the Convention. The Public Prosecutor’s Office also appealed. Its appeal was served on the applicant for comments, which he submitted on 21 September 2000. On 7 October 2000 the Vienna Court of Appeal, sitting in camera, dismissed the applicant's appeal. Upon the public prosecutor’S appeal, it amended the Regional Court's decision and ordered the forfeiture to the benefit of the Republic of Austria. The court noted at the outset that, pursuant to its Article 20(3), the 1998 Treaty applied irrespective of whether the underlying offences were committed before or after its entry into force. The court noted that the five-year limitation period had not expired. The court ruled that the forfeiture to the benefit of the U.S. under Article 17(3) of the 1998 Treaty was not admissible. The decision was handed down on 30 October 2000. The hearing was adjourned until 11 November 2000 at 2pm. The case was described as ‘a case of misconduct in public office’ by the judge. The judge’s decision was made on the basis that the allegations were ‘unsubstantiated’ and ‘not supported by the evidence’. The appeal was dismissed and the case was returned to the court.

name: Helmut Bönisch
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 8658/79) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission on 18 June 1979 by Mr. Helmut Bönisch. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43) and Mr. G. Wiarda, President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)). On 2 August 1984, the President drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of the five other members of the Chamber, namely Mrs. D. Bindschedler-Robert, Mr, D. Evrigenis, Mr F. Gölcüklü, Mr E. García de Enterría and Mr B. Walsh. President Wiarda requested that the Austrian authorities consider the possibility of suspending execution of fines imposed on him in Austria. Mr. Evrigenis and Mr. García de Enterría, who were prevented from taking part in the consideration of the case, were replaced by Mr. J. Cremona and Mr R. Bernhardt, substitute judges (Rule 24 para. 1). name: Yunus Atalay
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1249/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that a number of police officers had subjected him to ill-treatment and that the national authorities had not only failed to carry out an effective investigation into the circumstances, but had also failed to punish those responsible. On 10 May 2007 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the convention). The applicant was taken to the First Aid Hospital in Istanbul’s Taksim district where a medical report was prepared. The applicant was then brought to the office of the public prosecutor in Beyoğlu district where he told the prosecutor that the police officers had tortured him. The same day the prosecutor rendered a decision of non-jurisdiction, under the Law on the Trial of Civil Servants. On 10 October 1995 the applicant lodged a formal complaint against the three police officers responsible for the ill-treatment of the applicant. The prosecutor ordered the applicant's release the same day. The report concluded that the applicant would be unable to work for a period of ten days. The three police officers were convicted of the offence of ill-treatment contrary to Article 245 of the Criminal Code. The trial court reduced the prison sentences by a quarter and sentenced each officer to two months and seven days’ imprisonment. In 2002 the trial court suspended the proceedings against the two police officers in accordance with Law no. 4616, which provides for the suspension of criminal cases in respect of certain offences committed before 23 April 1999. The applicant lodged an objection with the Beyoğlu Assize Court against the trialCourt’s decision, pointing out that the Court of Cassation had waited two years before rendering its judgment. The ill-treatment to which he had been subjected constituted ‘torture’ within the meaning of the United Nations Convention Against Torture and Other Cruel Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment. The trial court had no choice but to apply Article 245 of the Criminal Code in the present case. On 28 May 2002 the Beyoğlu Assize Court rejected the applicant’s objection. Nevertheless, the fact remained that the ill- treatment had constituted “tortures” within the meanings of the Convention. The court ruled that the applicant had been treated in a manner that violated the terms of the UN Convention against Torture.

Three Turkish police officers were convicted of ill-treatment in 2000. The trial court suspended their sentences under Turkish law. The three officers who did not appeal were acquitted of the charges. The case is still pending in the Beyoğlu Assize Court. The trial court had no choice but to apply Article 245 of the Criminal Code in the present case. The ill-treatment to which he had been subjected constituted “torture’ within the meaning of the United Nations Convention Against Torture. On 28 May 2002 the Beyoğlu Assize Court rejected the applicant’s objection. The case was heard in a Turkish court and the verdict was returned in favour of the defendant. The defendant was sentenced to five years in prison. The sentence was suspended for one year and one month. He was also sentenced to a fine of 10,000 Turkish liras (about $300,000)

name: Eric Oldham
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36273/97) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant, a discretionary life prisoner who had been released on licence and recalled to prison, made two complaints. He complained, firstly, that he had been denied a fair hearing before the Parole Board on 8 November 1996 and, secondly, he had not had his detention reviewed until just over two years later. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). On 7 March 2000 the Court declared the complaint concerning the fairness of the Parle Board hearing inadmissible. It declared admissible the complaint about the delay between reviews. The Court's decision is obtainable from the Registry. In July 1996 the Secretary of State revoked the applicant's licence and recalled him to prison. He had been recalled to prison twice previously and had since been transferred to open prison conditions in 1989. The case was referred to the Parole Board which confirmed the revocation of the applicant’s licence on 12 July 1996. The applicant and M. married in prison on 6 February 1997. In November 1997 the applicant applied for legal advice on his case. The application was rejected on the grounds that the applicant had been responsible for M.'s injuries after drinking at least eight cans of lager. In its written decision of 12 November 1996 the DLP stated, in its reasons for rejecting the applicant, that it had accepted the evidence which indicated that the person responsible for the injuries was the applicant. It expressed the opinion that, in order to minimise the risk posed to members of the public, the applicant needed to carry out further work in respect of alcohol, anger and relationships. The DPP has decided not to extend the length of the legal aid. The decision was made on 17 December 1998. The judge ruled that it was not in the public interest for the DPP to extend it. The DPP is now seeking legal aid to continue its work on the case. The case has been adjourned for a further two years until the case can be re-examined. The appeal is expected to be successful in the near future and the judge will make a decision on the appeal in May 2009. The legal aid case is still pending, but the judge has decided that it is not necessary to continue the case as there is no evidence of a breach of law.

The case originated in an application (no. 36273/97) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant, a discretionary life prisoner who had been released on licence and recalled to prison, made two complaints under Article 5 § 4 of the Convention. On 7 March 2000 the Court declared the complaint concerning the fairness of the Parole Board hearing inadmissible. It declared admissible the complaint about the delay between reviews. The Court's decision is obtainable from the Registry. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). The Government submitted their observations on 19 March 1999, after an extension of the time-limit fixed for that purpose. The applicant's licence was revoked on the grounds that he had caused his partner's injuries after drinking at least eight cans of lager. The case was referred to the Parole Board which confirmed the revocation of the licence on 12 July 1996. The applicant and M. married in prison on 6 February 1997. The parole board's Discretionary Lifer Panel (“the DLP”) rejected the applicant's representations against recall. It expressed the opinion that, in order to minimise the risk posed by the applicant to members of the public, the applicant needed to carry out further work in respect of alcohol, anger and relationships. The D.C. Court of Appeal ruled that the case was a miscarriage of justice. The case was dismissed and the judge refused to extend the appeal. The judge ruled that there was no evidence that the claim was made out of malice. He said that it was unlikely that the judge would ever be able to make such a decision again. The appeal was dismissed on 15 March 1998. The court of appeal's decision was overturned and the appeal was thrown out on 14 March 1999. The next day, the judge ordered the appeal to be re-evaluated and the case to be returned to the Court of Appeals. The Appeal was denied on 17 March 1998, and the matter was dismissed.

name: Krystian Żywicki
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 27992/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his pre-trial detention had exceeded a “reasonable time’ within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the. Convention. He also alleged that the domestic courts had failed to examine “speedily” one of his appeals against the extension of the detention. It was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The applicant was born in 1976 and lives in Szczecin. He was arrested on suspicion of having committed several offences of drug trafficking. The applicant's detention was extended by the Szczecin District Court on several occasions. His applications for release were likewise unsuccessful. He was released on bail on payment of a security of 30,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) (approx. 7,500 euros (EUR) The applicant did not pay the security and his detention was then extended beyond the statutory two-year time-limit. The applicant was charged with two offences and in one of them he was found guilty of acting in an organised criminal group. The application for bail was rejected on 6 December 2005 and again on 18 January 2006. The court did not however indicate which of the accused had been involved in the criminal group and did not mention the charge. In this. case the anticipated penalty exceeded eight years’ imprisonment. In such a situation there is ipso iure a presumption that the applicant would obstruct the. proceedings because of the fear of a severe sentence’ (ze względu na obawę przed grożąca oskarżonemu surową karą). On 23 January 2006 the applicant lodged an appeal against the decision of 18 January 2006 and on 3 April 2006 he applied for release. On 26 April 2006 the Szczecin Court of Appeal extended the applicant’s detention until 30 December 2006.

name: Antonius Adrianus van der Tang
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 18 July 1994 by the Government of the Kingdom of Spain. It originated in an application (no. 19382/92) lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Netherlands national, Mr Antonius Adrianus van der Tang, on 2 December 1991. The Commission's request referred to Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby Spain recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The President gave the lawyer leave to use the Dutch language (Rule 27 para. 3). The Netherlands Government, who had been notified by the Registrar of their right to intervene, indicated that they did not intend to do so. Antonius Adrianus van der Tang was born in 1959 and lives in Haarlem in the Netherlands. He was found driving a lorry which contained 1,300 kg of hashish. The lorry belonged to the applicant, who was also found in possession of a pistol with its serial number chiselled off and of a radio pre-tuned to a station which coincided with that of another set found. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg on 20 February 1995. The Court heard addresses by the Government, the applicant's lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission as well as replies to its questions. The applicant had been offered 20,000 Netherlands guilders to transport 1,300 kg of “dope’ (droga) from Bayona to the Netherlands. Late in the evening of 25 May 1989, following the unknown person's instructions, he had taken his truck to Bayona, where another man had loaded the drugs and then gone away. The applicant had only been driving for about ten minutes when he was arrested. On 12 June 1989 Mr van der Tang made a written statement to Vigo investigating judge no. 1 in which he explained that he had not known that he was transporting drugs at the time of his arrest. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 39958/02) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. He filed a claim for payment against his former employer on 22 May 1991. On 2 December 1991 the court gave judgment. On 9 June 1998 the applicant lodged a cassation appeal. The applicant appealed to the Olsztyn District Court against a decision to dismiss him from work. He sought compensation for the alleged mistakes in the examination of his claims and for the protracted length of the proceedings. The Government maintained that such an appeal was pending before the Supreme court. The appeal was dismissed as it was inadmissible in law. The application was dismissed on 27 February 2002 for failure to comply with procedural requirements.
