train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 46034/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged on 30 January 1998 with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that their right to a “hearing within a reasonable time” had not been respected. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Court declared the application admissible by a decision of 10 January 2002. The case was transferred to the newly composed Fourth Section on 1 November 2001. The Polish Government was represented by their Agent, Mr Krzysztof Drzewicki, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The case was brought by a man and his wife. The couple made a claim in respect of 728,000 old Polish zlotys. In July 1984 the plaintiff died. The wife and daughter joined the proceedings as his legal successors. The case was eventually settled out of court in 1996. The court decided to obtain fresh expert evidence in order to determine the value of certain construction works made by the second applicant. In the meantime, the case had been assigned to a new judge. The judge ruled in favour of the plaintiffs and awarded them the money they had sued for. The decision was appealed by the applicant. The appeal was upheld by the Supreme Court. The applicants requested that the court index the repayment of their bank loan and the payment made to the original plaintiff in 1984. The applicants also requested to obtain documentary evidence from the land register. The court did not obtain any expert report even though the applicants had secured money for such a report. The case had been assigned to a new judge. None of the parties submitted a notice of appeal. The plaintiffs withdrew their claims against the first applicant and the court gave judgment on 26 March 1998. It partly granted the claim of the original plaintiffs’ daughter against the second applicant and dismissed the claims of the first plaintiff’s wife and daughter.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 9154/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr H. Meyer-Mews, a lawyer practising in Bremen. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs K. Behr, Regierungsdirektorin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The Court advised the parties on 14 January 2014 that it would continue processing the application under the name Schatschaschwili v Germany. The crimes were committed in Kassel on 14 October 2006 and in Göttingen on 3 February 2007 respectively. The applicant was sentenced to nine years and six months in prison. The Regional Court found it established that the applicant, acting jointly with an unidentified. accomplice and according to a previously agreed plan, entered by force into an apartment in. Kassel and robbed its occupants. The men were aware that the apartment was used for. prostitution and expected its two female occupants to keep valuables and cash in there. They had passed by the apartment in the. early evening in order to make sure that no clients were present. Two men entered the Göttingen apartment of O. and P. pretending to be potential clients. Once inside the apartment B. produced a knife that he had carried along in his jacket. Fearing for her life O. opened the safe from which B. removed EUR 300 and also handed over the contents of her wallet in the amount of EUR 250. P. jumped from the apartment’s balcony located approximately two meters off the ground and ran away. The applicant jumped after her but abandoned the chase after some minutes when passers-by appeared nearby on the street. He then called the co-accused waiting in front of the apartment on his mobile phone and gave him an account of the events. The women called their friend L. in Kassel and gave her a brief account of the events. The next day they also told their neighbour E. about the crime. Later that day the women, afraid of remaining alone in the Göttingen apartment, drove to Kassel where they stayed a few days with their friend. Following short subsequent stays in Frankfurt am Main and back in Götteden they returned to Latvia in February 2007. The Regional Court found L. and I.’s testimonies to be consistent and credible and noted that they were supported by the statements of the police officers who had attended the crime scene. Witnesses O. and P. had been summoned to appear before the Regional Court on 24 August 2007, the third day of the trial. Both had refused to attend the hearing relying on medical certificates dated 9 August 2007 that indicated their unstable post‑traumatic emotional and psychological condition. The Regional Court asked for the witnesses to be heard by a court in Latvia and the hearing to be transmitted by voice and image (audiovisuelle Vernehmung) However, a witness hearing scheduled by the competent Latvian court for 13 February 2008 was cancelled shortly before on the ground that the witnesses had demonstrated that they were still suffering from post-traumatic disorders as a consequence of the crime. The Regional Court concluded that it was impossible to have the witnesses examined in the foreseeable future. A further objection against the introduction of the witnesses’ pre-trial statements by counsel of one of the co-accused was rejected. The trial as a whole had been fair and had complied with the requirements of Article 6 § 3 (d) of the Convention. The court was thus not prevented from admitting O. and P.’s pre- trial statements as evidence in the proceedings. It also held that notwithstanding the resulting restrictions for the defence, the trial had beenfair. The applicant had not been informed about the preliminary criminal proceedings initiated against him with a view to not putting the investigations at risk. The Regional Court noted that O. and P. had given detailed and coherent descriptions of the circumstances of the crime. Minor contradictions in their statements could be explained by their concern not to disclose their illegal residence status and activities to the authorities. The witnesses had feared problems with the police and acts of revenge by the perpetrators. Their inability to identify the applicant also showed that the witnesses, as opposed to the defence’s allegations, had not testified with a view to incriminating him. The court had taken several items of evidence as corroborating the pre-trial testimonies into account when assessing their evidentiary value. O. had made considerable efforts to enable a direct examination of the accused and counsel for the defence at trial. The Regional Court had ensured that a maximum of further witnesses who had been in contact with O. in relation to the events at issue could be heard. The Regional Court noted that neither the defence nor the court itself had had an opportunity to observe the main witnesses’ demeanour at trial or by means of an audio-visual examination. The court further emphasised that when. taking into account the testimonies given by the witnesses' neighbour E. and their friend L. it had paid special attention to the fact that. their statements constituted hearsay evidence and had to be assessed particularly carefully. The link between the evidence obtained in the course of such separate investigations and the crime at issue could only be made after O. and P. had reported the incident of 3 February 2007 to the police. The applicant and the co-accused had denied any participation in the robbery as such or any premeditated criminal activity in this respect. Their own statements at trial had at least confirmed that one of them had visited the apartment at Göttingen on the evening before the crime. The applicant had testified that he and B. had come to the apartment with a view to making use of the women’s services as prostitutes. He further had conceded that he had followed P. when she escaped over the balcony in order to prevent her from calling the neighbours or the police since he had been afraid of getting problems in view of his criminal record and the problems he had previously had with prostitutes. The Prosecutor General argued that while it was true that the proceedings had been characterised by a “complete loss’ of the applicant’s right to examine O. and P. (“Totalausfall des Fragerechts”), they had as a whole been fair and there had been no reason to exclude the witness statements as evidence. The Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant's constitutional complaint against the decisions of the Federal Court of Justice dated 30 October and 9 December 2008 for examination without providing reasons. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18404/91) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the Turkish occupation of the northern part of Cyprus had deprived him of his home and properties. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 8 June 1999 the Court declared the application admissible. On 27 July 1999 his son, Mr Andreas Luca Nicolaides, who had become the administrator of his estate, informed the Court that he wished to pursue the application on behalf of the deceased. The applicant had been forced to leave Famagusta and flee to the area still controlled by the Cypriot Government in 1974. On 9 December 1990 he took part in a car convoy organised by persons from three villages in Kyrenia and from Trypimeni wishing to return to their homes in the north. The participants in the convoy had informed the commander of the United Nations (UN) forces in Cyprus of their intention to return home. They drove to the ‘buffer zone’ checkpoint on the main road linking Nicosia and FamagUSTa and asked the UN officer on duty to be allowed to return. They requested him to transmit their demand to the Turkish military authorities.

name: Grzegorz Drabek
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5270/04) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant and 13 co-accused had committed the offences with which he had been charged and the severity of the sentence that could be imposed. The court further submitted that only detention would secure the applicant’s appearance at the trial. Wroclaw Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) asked that the applicant’s detention be prolonged beyond the statutory time-limit of two years. The Court justified its decision with reference to the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offences and the complexity of the case. The court also considered that, given the severity of the penalty that might be expected, the applicant might obstruct the proceedings. In total, the trial court held the applicant in custody for more than a year. The applicant's numerous applications for release and his appeals against the decisions prolonging detention were to no avail. The application for release was dismissed on 22 October 2003. The applicant was indicted before the Lublin Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) on 13 February 2003. The bill of indictment comprised numerous charges brought against 8 co-accused. 43 hearings during which it heard 86 witnesses and the depositions of 130 other witnesses were read at the hearings. On 21 July 2004 the Opole Regional Court gave judgment. The applicant was convicted and sentenced to 3 ½ years’ imprisonment. The court found that, given his low sentence, there were no grounds for prolonging the applicant’s detention. On the same date the court decided to place the applicant under police supervision.

name: Eliane van Glabeke
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38287/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Ms Eliane van Glabeke (‘the applicant’) was compulsorily admitted to Lommelet de Saint-André Psychiatric Hospital in 2002. The Government submitted that the applicant had been “picked up” on the public highway by a police officer who had asked for her to be admitted to hospital. The applicant disputed that account and stated that she had been arrested while cycling to the shops and taken to the police station. The parties have been unable to establish the date on which the letter was received. The application was made to the President of the Lille State Counsel on 8 April 2002. The State Counsel's Office decided to take no further action on that application as it was devoid of purpose. The letter was sent back to the Secretary of State for Legal Affairs on 28 March 2002, but no action was taken at the time. It was not until 22 April 2002 that the application was finally made and the letter sent to the Attorney General's Office was returned to the Court of Appeal for legal advice on the matter. The appeal was dismissed and the case was dismissed on 24 April 2002, the day the letter arrived.

name: Ahmet Güven
train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 68694/01) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) 12 Turkish nationals, Mr Ahmet Güven, Mr Ramazan Akdağ, Mr Kadri Sönmez, Mr Metin Göktepe, Ms Neslihan Gök tepe, Mr İzzettin Koç, Mr Kadri Issı, Mr Mehmet Kışanak, Mr Rıdvan Karatay, Mr Ali Kemal Yıldız and Ms Emsihan Karaty were represented by Mr T. Fırat, a lawyer practising in Izmir. The applicants were born in 1968, 1972, 1964, 1966, 1973, 1962, 1976, 1962,. 1963, 1971, 1970 and 1969 respectively. A preliminary investigation was instigated by the İzmir public prosecutor's office into the allegations of the applicants. The applicants reiterated that they were beaten by the gendarmes and the prison wardens. A forensic expert examined Ahmet Güven, Kadri Sönmez, Metin Göktepe, Neslihan Gök tepe, İzzettin Koç, Kadir Issı, Mehmet Kışanak, Rıdvan Karatay, Ali Kemal Yıldız and Ms Emsihan Karaty in prison. The doctor considered that the injuries rendered the applicant unfit for work for fifteen days. As regards Mehmet Kışanak, the doctor observed swellings and erythemas on the upper part of the back, underneath the chin and around the nose and mouth as a result of blows. The doctor concluded that the injuries rendered  İzzettin Koç unfit for work for ten days and that he would recover within twenty days following a medical treatment. As regards Rıdvan Karatay, the medical report referred to an erythema and a swelling on the right eye orbit,  and to an ecchymosis behind his ear. The  doctor decided that R Turkey should be referred to the ophthalmologist at the Izmir State Hospital. Yaşar Avcı was hospitalised on 20 July 1995 with the diagnosis of ‘general body trauma’ He sustained the following injuries at the time of the hospitalisation: ecchymoses on the back and on both shoulders, a graze of 2 x 2 cm on the right zygoma, erythemas in the forehead, sensitivity on the left tibia. The prosecutor decided not to prosecute the Director of Buca Prison and his staff for alleged ill-treatment of the applicants. The applicants objected to this decision. On 25 June 1996 the Karşıyaka Assize Court dismissed the applicants' objection. On 1 May 2000 the İzmir Administrative Council decided to open an investigation against three gendarme. Ahmet Güven was convicted of carrying out activities for the purpose of bringing about the secession of a part of the national territory under Article 125 of the Criminal Code. He was sentenced to death on 2 December 1998. His sentence was commuted to life imprisonment by the İzmir Assize Court on 6 September 2002. In July 2003 the applicant requested the suspension of his sentence. The Bitlis public prosecutor, relying on the reports of the Bitlis State Hospital, dismissed the applicant's request. The Government decided not to bring proceedings against the gendarmes responsible for the transfer of the applicants to court on 20 July 1995. The applicants claimed that they were never informed of the outcome of the proceedings. The applicant was diagnosed in 2003 as suffering from hypertension and amnesia. They noted that he was receiving drug treatment and that he could physically continue to take care of himself within a prison facility. The Government submitted a number of documents as regards the applicant's transfer to various medical centres for check-up and the results of his analyses. On 1 November 2005, the applicant was transferred to a different prison facility for treatment. He was released from the other prison facility on 2 November 2005. The applicant was sentenced to a year in prison, but was released on 1 November 2009. He is currently serving a sentence of five years for a drug offence.

name: Teresa Jerzak
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29360/06) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Ms Teresa Jerzak (‘the applicant’) was born in 1940 and lives in Sulejówek. The Polish Government was represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. It was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The case was heard by the President of the Fourth Section on 25 September 2007. The case is still pending before the District Court in Warsaw, Poland. The case was brought under the 2004 Act, which entered into force on 17 September 2004. The applicant sued for breach of her right to a hearing within a reasonable time. The court awarded the applicant 200 Polish zlotys (PLN – approximately 50 euros (EUR) by way of just satisfaction. The application was dismissed by the Supreme Court of Poland in January 2005, which ruled that the delays had taken place before the date of the Act's entry into force and had not been remedied afterwards. The Supreme Court ruled that its provisions applied retroactively to all proceedings in which delays had occurred before that date.

name: Rifat Bayam
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26896/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was represented by Mr M. Vefa, a lawyer practising in Diyarbakır. The case was heard by the Supreme Court of Justice and the Court of Appeal. The applicant was sentenced to 12 years and six months' imprisonment for membership of the PKK and to five years, six months and twenty days' for having thrown explosives. The Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant's appeal, holding that it had not been submitted within the statutory time-limit. The Diyarbakır State Security Court convicted the applicant under Article 168 § 2 of the Criminal Code. However, it acquitted the applicant of the charge under Article 264 of the criminal Code. The applicant was acquitted of the charges under articles 168 and 264 under the Turkish penal code. The application was dismissed on 22 February 2001, and the applicant was released on bail.

name: Graham Jason Piper
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) Mr Graham Jason Piper (“the applicant”) was charged with the attempted importation of 163 kilograms (compressed weight) of cocaine with a potential street value of GBP 11 million. The applicant was represented by Mr C. Convey, a barrister practising in London, instructed by Lound Mulrenan Jefferies Solicitors. The United Kingdom Government were represented by their Agent, Ms Y. Ahmed, Foreign and Commonwealth Office. On 5 June 2001 the applicant was found guilty of the offences charged. On 6 June 2001 he was sentenced to 14 years' imprisonment. He lodged an appeal against sentence, which was unsuccessful. In 2004 he lodged an out-of-time appeal against conviction. He was released from prison in February 2006 and, on 17 November 2006, he abandoned his appeal (see further paragraph 29 below). The confiscation proceedings against the applicant were adjourned until the end of November 2001. The judge granted a short adjournment of 28 days to resolve the matter of transferring representation. The court granted a defence application for the transfer of legal aid. Defence counsel was unable to address the judge on the point of ‘exceptional circumstances’ owing to his lack of familiarity with the case. The judge set a timetable for the service of skeleton arguments on the jurisdiction point and fixed 14 March 2002 for legal argument on the matter. In early March, as a result of informal discussions between junior counsel for both sides regarding a case pending before the Court of Appeal, the 14 March 2001 date was vacated. On 22 March 2002, the prosecution indicated its intention to proceed with the confiscation hearing on 20 May 2002, as planned. The defence requested that legal. argument on jurisdiction and abuse of process be postponed to suit the diary of leading counsel. On 22, 23 and 27 May 2002 two defence applications submitted by newly instructed leading counsel were heard. The first was to stay the confiscation proceedings on grounds of abuse of process; the second was for an order declaring that there was no jurisdiction to continue the proceedings. The judge indicated his preference for retention of the May date for the substantive hearing with any legal argument to take place beforehand, suggesting that alternative leading counsel could be found. Defence counsel proposed instead that theMay date be set down for legal argument and after that, unless the confiscations had fallen away, the defence would serve their response by the end of May. On 27 June 2002 a confiscation order was quashed following a Court of Appeal judgment. Crown Court judge had not complied with the requirements of section 3 of the 1994 Act. The applicant asked the judge to reconsider his ruling of 27 May 2002. The judge considered the applicant’s case to be distinguishable on the facts. For unknown reasons, matters proceeded more slowly than the parties had expected and the September confiscation hearing did not go ahead. A further judgment in a similar appeal was handed down by the Court of Appeal on 16 December 2002 (R v Knights (Richard Michael) and others [2002] EWCA Crim 2954). An appeal against that judgment was lodged with the House of Lords.Further hearings took place in June and July 2004. The House of Lords handed down its judgments in two jurisdiction appeals on 21 July 2005. It upheld the confiscation orders, stating that any prejudice caused to the defendants by delay was outweighed by the public interest in not allowing convicted offenders to escape confiscation. On 1 February 2006, the applicant was released from prison, having served half of his sentence. On 17 November 2006, apparently following adverse outcomes on various issues relating to his appeal, he abandoned his appeal against conviction. The matter was listed for a hearing in late January 2007. The applicant’s counsel gave notice of a potential abuse argument arising from the deaths of two of his witnesses. At the hearing on 25 January 2007 it was agreed to seek suitable dates in April 2007. A procedural hearing was agreed for 6 July 2007. On 1 November 2007 the parties appeared before the judge. The substantive hearing was listed for 20 July 2008, with a time estimate of two weeks. The judge delivered his ruling on the confiscation on 19 December 2008. He identified the total amount of the applicant’s benefit from criminal conduct as GBP 1,840,563. He found the principal realisable asset to be a farm, which was valued at GBP 690,000. A confiscation order was made with a three-year term of imprisonment to be served consecutive to the main sentence in default of payment. The Court of Appeal granted the applicant leave to appeal but dismissed the appeal itself. The court found that the period from the applicant’s arrest in January 1999 to the conclusion of his first trial on 31 August 2000 was wholly unexceptional and reasonable. It accepted that the abandonment of the first trial was the fault of the prosecution, noting: “11. ... The trial had to start all over again. It was not concluded by conviction at the end of the second trial until 5th June 2001. That period is therefore potentially available to be considered as the responsibility of the State.” The court then examined the delay from the end. of second trial in June 2001 until July 2005, and found no violation of Article 6 § 1. Court considered that there would have been a hearing of the confiscation question in about the spring or early summer of 2002. Court observed that the applicant had engaged a third counsel for the appeal, and pursued it on grounds that had never been supported by those who had conducted his trial. Court concluded: “The simple fact is that the appeal on this ground, as on the others, had always been without any proper basis or merit.” The Court of Appeal considered that it was in the applicant’s interests to await the eventual authoritative ruling of the House of Lords. It therefore concluded that the delay that arose in this respect could not be criticised. The Court of Appeal noted that the parties had returned promptly to the Crown Court for the resumption of the confiscation issue within a fortnight of the abandonment of the appeal against conviction. The court made it clear that any additional passage of time as a result of that conduct was not attributable to any act of the State. The applicant’s representatives, on the other hand, wanted a longer timetable and were seeking additional time on the grounds that they had an enormous volume of work and would be calling a large number of witnesses, and might even be mounting an abuse argument that some potential witnesses had died. Hearings were adjourned owing to the applicant's applications. The court concluded that there had not been in the applicant’s case unreasonable delay attributable to the acts of the State. It concluded: “This was a defendant of resourceful approach who deployed every possible legal stratagem to delay the confiscation process.’ The appropriate remedy would, hypothetically, as it seems to us, have been a declaration. But that does not in the end arise. It follows that the substantive ground ... in relation to Article 6 fails.” The court also considered the impact of the passage of time upon the applicant, and acknowledged that he and his wife lived throughout this time with the uncertainty of whether they would lose his family home.

That period is therefore potentially available to be considered as the responsibility of the State” The Court of Appeal considered that there would have been a hearing of the confiscation question in about the spring or early summer of 2002. The court observed that the applicant had engaged a third counsel for the appeal, and pursued it on grounds that had never been supported by those who had conducted his trial. It noted that the various grounds advanced by the applicant fell away one by one over that period, but one of them remained and was not finally laid to rest until November 2006. The Court concluded: “The simple fact is that the appeal on this ground, as on the others, had always been without any proper basis or merit” The Court of Appeal noted that the parties had returned promptly to the Crown Court for the resumption of the confiscation issue within a fortnight of the abandonment of the appeal against conviction. It was apparent at the hearing of 8 December 2006 that the prosecution was pressing for a short timetable. The applicant’s representatives, on the other hand, wanted a longer timetable and were seeking additional time on the grounds that they had an enormous volume of work and would be calling a large number of witnesses. In the end, the defendant called five (not 49) witnesses and one of those was himself. The court made it clear that any additional passage of time as a result of that conduct was not attributable to any act of the State. The court concluded that there had not been in the applicant’s case unreasonable delay attributable to the acts of the State. It concluded: ‘The reality of this case is that this was a defendant of resourceful approach who deployed every possible legal stratagem to delay the confiscation process.’ The appropriate remedy would, hypothetically, as it seems to us, have been a declaration, but that does not in the end arise. On 6 June 2001 he was sentenced to fourteen years’ imprisonment. He lodged an appeal against sentence, which was unsuccessful. In 2004 he lodged an out-of-time appeal against conviction. He was released from prison in February 2006 and, on 17 November 2006, he abandoned his appeal (see further paragraph 29 below) The confiscation proceedings were adjourned until 9 October 2001. The judge ordered the defence to serve a written response to the prosecution’s statement within six weeks. The defence failed to serve its response within the six-week period. The court granted a defence application for the transfer of legal aid on 6 November 2001. Defence counsel was unable to address the judge on the point of ‘exceptional circumstances’ owing to his lack of familiarity with the case. Defence gave notice that it wished to challenge the validity of the postponement of the confiscation hearing on the basis that the Crown Court had no jurisdiction. The judge set a timetable for the service of skeleton arguments on the jurisdiction point and fixed 14 March 2002 for legal argument on the matter. In early March, as a result of informal discussions between junior counsel for both sides regarding a case pending before the Court of Appeal, the 14March 2002 date was vacated. On 22 March 2002, the prosecution indicated its intention to proceed with the confiscating hearing on 20 May 2002, as planned. Judge ruled that no prejudice had been caused to the applicant as a result of the postponement. He concluded that the court had jurisdiction to deal with the confiscation proceedings. The judge indicated his preference for retention of the May date for the substantive hearing with any legal argument to take place beforehand, suggesting that alternative leading counsel could be found. Defence counsel proposed instead that theMay date be set down for legal argument and after that, unless the confiscative proceedings had fallen away, the defence would serve their response by the end of May. TheJudge reluctantly put back the substantive confiscation hearings until 13 June 2002, noting that he was “very loath to have further slippage than is absolutely necessary” Crown Court judge had not complied with the requirements of section 3 of the 1994 Act. The applicant asked the judge to reconsider his ruling of 27 May 2002. For unknown reasons, matters proceeded more slowly than the parties had expected and the September confiscation hearing did not go ahead. An appeal against that judgment was lodged with the House of Lords. The judge allowed a one-week adjournment to obtain an update from the judicial office of the Lords. He was reminded by the applicant that he would again need to formally postpone the confiscation Hearings. The House of Lords upheld the confiscation orders on 21 July 2005. The applicant was released from prison on 1 February 2006, having served half of his sentence. On 17 November 2006, apparently following adverse outcomes on various issues relating to his appeal, the applicant abandoned his appeal against conviction. The matter was listed for a hearing in late January 2007. At the hearing on 25 January 2007 it was agreed to seek suitable dates in April 2007. The prosecution served the amended statement in January 2007 and the applicant’s counsel asked until the end of May to respond to the prosecution. The application was returned to the Crown Court for confiscation. A procedural hearing was agreed for 6 July 2007. On 1 November 2007 the parties appeared before the judge. The substantive hearing was listed for 20 July 2008, with a time estimate of two weeks, but in fact lasted four days from 22 to 24 July 2008. The judge delivered his ruling on the confiscation on 19 December 2008. He identified the total amount of the applicant’s benefit from criminal conduct as GBP 1,840,563. He found the principal realisable asset to be a farm, which was valued at GBP 690,000. A confiscation order was made with a three-year term of imprisonment to be served consecutive to the main sentence. Court of Appeal granted leave to appeal but dismissed the appeal itself. Decision upholds the confiscation order and finds no violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. Now for the applicant to seek other remedies. C.I.C. proceedings before the Court of Appeal in March 2010. The full court heard the case on 17 March 2010, and the decision was handed down on 17 April 2010, at a hearing held at the High Court in London. The decision was made on the basis of the evidence given in the oral hearing. The judge ruled that the delay in disposing of the proceedings was “well beyond acceptable”. Court of Appeal considered that there would have been a hearing of the confiscation question in about the spring or early summer of 2002, if that probable timetable had not been overtaken by the applicant's challenge to the court’s jurisdiction. Court observed that the applicant had engaged a third counsel for the appeal, and pursued it on grounds that had never been supported by those who had conducted his trial. Court concluded: “The simple fact is that the appeal on this ground, as on the others, had always been without any proper basis or merit” It concluded that nothing in that period can be called unreasonable delay attributable to the act or omission of the applicant. Court of Appeal noted that the parties had returned promptly to the Crown Court for the resumption of the confiscation issue within a fortnight of the abandonment of the appeal against conviction. The Court of Appeal did not blame the applicant for his conduct, but the court made it clear that any additional passage of time as a result of that conduct was not attributable to any act of the State. The court commented on the time taken by the judge to deliver his ruling as follows: “We do not doubt that that will be attributable to the demands made on the judges at the Central Criminal Court, but it is too long and that period, or at least part of it, is no doubt the responsibility of the state.” The court concluded that there had not been in the applicant’s case unreasonable delay attributable to the acts of the State. It concluded: “This was a defendant of resourceful approach who deployed every possible legal stratagem to delay the confiscation process.’ The appropriate remedy would, hypothetically, as it seems to us, have been a declaration. But that does not in the end arise. It follows that the substantive ground ... in relation to Article 6 fails.” The High Court has since reduced the amount of assets payable under the confiscated order by £1.2million. The confiscation order has also been halved to £2.5million.

name: Nadine Mladoschovitz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38663/06) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicants alleged a violation of Article 6 of the convention in proceedings concerning the enforcement of their claims for maintenance against their father. On 23 October 2008 the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 1). The application was dismissed on the grounds that it was not a valid claim. In support of his application to postpone enforcement regarding the sale of movable property, the debtor claimed he would risk losing his property rights over the objects seized for enforcement. He also argued that if a lien against outstanding claims from his own debtors was enforced, the recovery of the money from the applicants, who did not have any funds, would be nearly impossible if the enforcement order was, in fact, set aside. The Steyr Regional Court quashed the decision, ordering both kinds of enforcement to be postponed until the decision on the action under Section 35 of the Enforcement Act was rendered. It held that an appeal on points of law to the Supreme Court was not admissible.

train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 9 September 1994 by the European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 19178/91) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a British citizen. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 May 1995. The Court heard addresses by Mrs Liddy, Mr Owen and Mr Pannick as well as replies to its questions. The applicant appealed to the Secretary of State for the Environment under section 174 (2) (a), (b), (g) and (h) TCPA (see paragraph 19 below). An inspector was appointed to conduct an inquiry and determine the appeal. He was a Principal Housing and Planning Inspector, a civil servant and a member of the salaried staff of the Department of the Environment. The Commission produced to the Court the documents in the proceedings before it, as requested by the Registrar. The inspector rejected the appeal under grounds (a), (b), and (g) but allowed it under ground (h) to the extent that the compliance period should be extended from three to six months. He held, inter alia, as follows: “The appeal on ground (b) ... (12) What I need to decide in respect of this ground of appeal is whether, as a matter of fact and degree, the buildings could, from their appearance and layout, be considered to have been designed for the purposes of agriculture. The size, layout, and original external appearance of the buildings and their detailing did little to change that view.” The appeal on ground (a) fails. The appeal onGround (b) and (g) fail. Both appeal buildings lie in part of the green belt ... They also lie within the Higher Whitley Conservation Area. The use of domestic-style eaves and gable barge boarding. to that view. The residential look of the ‘porch’ to No. 1 building. And the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food’s view about the uneconomic layout of both buildings as originally built all add to the impression that these buildings were not designed for agricultural purposes, albeit they have since been modified and adapted for such a use. The appeal was dismissed by the High Court on 8 March 1991, the judge, Mr Lionel Read, QC, finding inter alia as follows: “A principal argument on behalf of the applicant at the inquiry under [ground] (b) was that the erection of the two buildings was permitted development under the General Development Order’. The appeal on ground (h) (21) ... Mr Bryan wanted more time in order to erect a replacement or replacements before demolition. I see no need to insist on a period which would make undue difficulty for him. I will increase the period to 6 months ... (22) I have taken account of all the other matters raised, including the possibility of your client putting up a large steel-clad building under permitted development rights, but find they do not affect my decision. Inspector extended the applicant’s time for complying with the enforcement notice under ground (h) The question whether the alterations proposed to a building were, as he evidently thought, a ‘matter of cosmetics’ and would not meet the main objections was entirely a matter of planning judgment for him. In the result, I find no error of law and I dismiss the application.“At the hearing held before the European Commission of Human Rights on 14 October 1993, the applicant's representatives stated that, although they had not represented the applicant before the High Court, they surmised that the challenge had been raised in the Notice of Motion and then abandoned at the hearing.”

name: Nigel Eastaway
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 74976/01) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that there had been a violation of his right to a hearing within a reasonable time. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 18 November 2003, the Court declared the application admissible. The Chamber having decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required, the parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. The Secretary of State’s evidence was completed and served on the applicant on 14 December 1992. On 13 May 1993 the applicant applied to strike out the proceedings. The applicant and one other defendant were acquitted, and two defendants were convicted. On appeal, the two convictions were quashed in February 1995. In November 1995 Mr Davies was granted leave to appeal out of time to the Court of Appeal, and his substantive appeal was dismissed by that court on 24 May 1996. The appeal to the High Court brought by the first defendant to the disqualification proceeding, Mr Davies, against the Registrar's decision of 27 January 1994, was dismissed on 2 May 1995. The defendants were required to serve their evidence to the court by 17 January 1997. The case was adjourned until 9 February 1998 after the defendants failed to comply with the deadline. The Court of Appeal ruled that the defendants could continue to give evidence until 9 March 1998. The hearing was continued until 10 July 1997 when the defendants concluded their evidence. The trial was ordered to be adjourned again on 6 February 1998, but was later adjourned to 9 March. The court ruled that it was not in the public interest to continue the case and ordered the defendants to provide more evidence in the form of a written reply to the secretary of state. The defendants were ordered to provide further evidence in response to this request. The applicant and the Secretary of State attempted to negotiate a ‘Carecraft’ settlement. In March 1998 the time-limit for the applicant’s further evidence was extended indefinitely. On 4 October 1998 the applicant broke off the settlement negotiations. The matter was set down for trial on 4 October 1999. The application for leave to apply for judicial review was refused in September 1999. On 2 February 2000, the applicant renewed his judicial review application before the Court of Appeal. On 23 March 2000 Buxton LJ refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords. On 27 January 2000, following an oral hearing, leave was again refused. In the course of a considered judgment, Lord Justice Buxton described the application as ‘misconceived’ The applicant appealed to the House of Lords, which granted leave on 11 July 2000. The House heard the applicant’s appeal on 18 October 2000, and on 2 November 2000 delivered judgment dismissing it. The application was heard by the Vice-Chancellor on 7 February 2001, and judgment was delivered dismissing it on 15 February 2001. The case was heard at the High Court, where it was dismissed on the grounds that the House had no jurisdiction to hear an appeal from the decision of the Court of Appeal refusing leave to apply for judicial review (R v. Secretary of State for Trade and Industry, ex parte Eastaway [2000] 1 WLR 2222). A large proportion of the undoubtedly long time which has elapsed since these proceedings were commenced is due to the various actions taken by Mr Eastaway. Those actions were taken not to obtain but to avoid a fair and public hearing by an independent or impartial tribunal either within a reasonable time or at all. In my view there has been no breach of MrEastaway’s Convention rights under Article 6 and for the Secretary of State now to proceed with these proceedings would not be incompatible with them.” The application was dismissed by the Vice-Chancellor, so the applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal, which also refused leave. On 31 May 2001 the applicant signed an undertaking which provided for an agreed period of disqualification of four and a half years, commencing on 25 June 2001.

The case was decided in favour of the applicant in November 2004. The applicant and three other defendants had applied to stay the disqualification proceedings pending the conclusion of the criminal proceedings. The Secretary of State’s evidence was completed and served on the applicant on 14 December 1992. On 13 May 1993 the applicant applied to strike out the proceedings. On appeal, the two convictions were quashed in February 1995. Two of the applicant's co-defendants appealed to the High Court. The applicant also lodged an appeal against his conviction on 12 April 1995. The case was adjourned after the defendants failed to provide evidence by the end of 1996. The Secretary of State issued an order requiring the defendants to provide further evidence by 17 January 1997. On 6 February 1998 the defendants were asked to provide additional evidence by 9 March 1998. On that day the court granted the defendants an extension to give them time to provide their evidence. The defendants were allowed to give their evidence until 1 July 1998, when they were ordered to give it to the court again. The case was finally settled on 6 August 1998, with the defendants agreeing to the terms of a settlement of the case. The judge ruled that the defendants had not provided sufficient evidence to prevent the case from going to trial. The applicant met the Secretary of State in March 1998. to negotiate a ‘Carecraft’ settlement. At a directions hearing on 23 March 1998, the time-limit for the applicant’s further evidence was extended indefinitely. On 4 October 1998 the applicant broke off the settlement negotiations. On 29 July 1999 there was a pre-trial review in the disqualification proceedings, at which the court gave detailed trial directions. The trial was set down to begin on 4 October 1999. On 23 March 2000 Buxton LJ refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords. The applicant appealed to the House of Lords, which granted leave on 11 July 2000. The House heard the applicant’s appeal on 18 October 2000, and on 2 November 2000 delivered judgment dismissing it. The application was heard by the Vice-Chancellor on 7 February 2001, and judgment was delivered dismissing it on 15 February 2001. In the judgments of the Court of Appeal given in November 1997, Mr Eastaway was granted leave to appeal against the decision of the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry to continue the proceedings. In his judgment, Mr Davies held that there had been no violation of Article 6 of the Human Rights Act 1998. A large proportion of the undoubtedly long time which has elapsed since these proceedings were commenced is due to the various actions taken by Mr Eastaway. Those actions were taken not to obtain but to avoid a fair and public hearing by an independent or impartial tribunal either within a reasonable time or at all. In my view there has been no breach of MrEastaway’s Convention rights under Article 6 and for the Secretary of State now to proceed with these proceedings would not be incompatible with them.” The application was upheld by the Court of Appeal on 13 September 2001. The applicant signed an undertaking which provided for an agreed period of disqualification of four and a half years commencing on 25 June 2001.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that there had been a violation of his right to a hearing within a reasonable time. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. The Court declared the application admissible on 18 November 2003. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine), and the parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. The case was decided by the Court of Appeal and the jury returned a verdict of not guilty. The Blackspur proceedings were brought against the applicant and three other defendants in July 1992. The Secretary of State’s evidence was completed and served on the applicant on 14 December 1992. On 13 May 1993 the applicant applied to strike out the proceedings. The applicant and one other defendant were acquitted, and two defendants were convicted. On appeal, the two convictions were quashed in February 1995. The appeal to the High Court brought by the first defendant to the disqualification proceeding, Mr Davies, was dismissed on 2 May 1995. In November 1995 Mr Davies was granted leave to appeal out of time to the Court of Appeal. His substantive appeal was dismissed by that court on 24 May 1996. The case went to court in December 1996. The defendants were ordered to serve their evidence by 17 January 1997. The hearing was adjourned until 9 February 1998. The judge ruled that the case should continue as it was in the public interest. The case was settled out of court in July 1998. This was the last opportunity for the defendants to give their evidence. They failed to do so and the case was returned to the court. The jury returned a verdict of not guilty on 9 January 1998. They had been given a deadline of 17 February 1997 to serve the evidence. The court denied the defendants the right to serve evidence until 17 February 1998, when the case went back to the Court of Appeal. The applicant tried to negotiate a ‘Carecraft’ settlement with the Secretary of State. The secretary of state said he would accept a settlement based on a disqualification period of five years. The matter was set down for trial on 4 October 1999. The application for leave to apply for judicial review was refused. On 2 February 2000, the applicant renewed his judicial review application before the Court of Appeal. Lord Justice Buxton described the application as ‘misconceived’, because the arguments on delay could, and should, have been made in the course of the disqualification proceedings and not in separate proceedings. On 23 March 2000 Buxton LJ refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords. The applicant appealed to the House of Lords, which granted leave on 11 July 2000. The House heard the applicant’s appeal on 18 October 2000, and on 2 November 2000 delivered judgment dismissing it on the grounds that the House had no jurisdiction to hear an appeal. The application was heard by the Vice-Chancellor on 7 February 2001, and judgment was delivered dismissal it on 15 February 2001. The case was decided in favour of Mr Eastaway, who was awarded a restraining order against Blackspur plc and others. The High Court rejected the application, and ordered the company to pay a fine of £1.5 million. In Re Blackspur Group [1998] 1 WLR 422, 427H and 433B it was recorded that Mr Davies did not suggest then that a fair trial was impossible. A very large proportion of the undoubtedly long time which has elapsed since these proceedings were commenced is due to the various actions taken by Mr Eastaway. Those actions were taken not to obtain but to avoid a fair and public hearing by an independent or impartial tribunal either within a reasonable time or at all. In my view there has been no breach of Mr Eastaways’s Convention rights under Article 6 and for the Secretary of State now to proceed with these proceedings would not be incompatible with them.

name: Jadwiga Hulewicz
train_texts: The case was brought by Mrs Jadwiga Hulewicz (‘the applicant’) against the Republic of Poland. The application was lodged under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant alleged, in particular, that her case had not been heard within a reasonable time in breach of Article 6 of the treaty. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court. By a decision of 12 November 2002 the Court declared the application admissible. The Court of Appeal found that the application was admissible and allowed the application to be heard. The applicant twice requested the Minister of Justice to grant her leave to file an extraordinary appeal with the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) Her first request was rejected on 10 October 1994. On 31 January 1997, upon the applicant’s second request, the Minister. of Justice filed a cassation appeal on the applicant's behalf, contesting the judgment of the. Słupsk Regional Court of 19 January 1994. The Lębork District Court joined the. applicant's case with similar proceedings against seven other members of the co‑operative. On 1 March 2002 the District Court gave judgment. On 8 April 2002 the applicant appealed against this judgment.

Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 12 November 2002 the Court declared the application admissible. The case was heard by the European Court of Human rights (‘the Court’) in October and November 2002. The applicant appealed against the Słupsk Regional Court of 19 January 1994. On 31 January 1997 the Minister of Justice filed a cassation appeal on the applicant’s behalf, contesting the judgment. The Supreme Court quashed both judgments given in the applicant's case and remitted the case to the court of first instance. On 1 March 2002 the District Court gave judgment. On 4 October 2000 the applicant challenged the expert's opinion of 19 May 2000. On 8 April 2002 the applicant appeal against this judgment. It appears that the proceedings are pending. name: Falter Zeitschriften GmbH
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 3084/07) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant company alleged that a court judgment under the Media Act ordering it to pay damages had infringed its right to freedom of expression. The application was communicated to the Government on 29 January 2009. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The judge ruled in favour of the applicant company. The case was adjourned until 9 February 2009, when it was decided that the application should be dismissed. Elaine B. (name changed, ed.) had been ill-treated by police officers in Cameroon. She was kicked by them in the abdomen and placed with 18 other women in ‘stinking, damp cells’ for having demonstrated on behalf of her son, abducted by the authorities. Her case was so well documented that Austria, in the form of the normally very strict Federal Refugee Office, granted her asylum quickly and without red tape. But then this country revealed its other side. Elaine B. became the first asylum seeker to lodge a complaint against a blind-drunk security officer who she claims abused his authority in the Traiskirchen centre. Security officers at the centre later state in court that female asylum seekers could be paid for quick sex. They also tell of pimps rolling up to the centre in their cars. ‘Please help us!’ pleaded the women. The Interior Ministry stated at the time that the police were confronted with a ‘wall of silence’ Elaine B. from Cameroon demanded an interview with the head of the Traiskirchen [branch of the] Gendarmerie. She described ‘through her tears’ how a drunken security officer had pursued her for days, pointing to his uniform and threatening to have her thrown out of the centre and to slit her throat. Elaine B. describes with precision how the man locked the door and removed the key. She tells of the pains in her lower abdomen afterwards and how she washed herself with warm water for weeks. She immediately identifies the security officer in a photo. For the first interview in the interview room no trained interpreter can be found. In their minutes the police officers at times refer to Elaine B. not by her name but as ‘the nigger woman’ She is repeatedly linked to prostitution. The investigation into the alleged rape took place over a year and a half. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights in 2007. Elaine B. denies this version of events. She says that she had other things on her mind at the time. She felt repelled by this fat man with a moustache who smelled of alcohol, she was afraid of him. If she had really been hoping to be granted asylum, why would she then have defamed the security officer? Next to take the witness stand are the employees of the bakery. Saleswoman R.Z.: ‘She gave him a kiss. She was fairly young, I’d say between 20 and 25. The two of them were talking quietly. I couldn’t describe the woman’ No evidence is taken either from other asylum seekers or from the female staff in the women’s quarters. Judge I.K. acquits the security officer. According to the court, the bakery employees could not have identified Elaine. ‘It cannot be established that the accused performed sexual intercourse against the will of Elaine B. be made out beyond doubt’, states the judgment. The ‘black African’ on the other hand, appeared ‘very confident’ and ‘it is hard to imagine that she could have felt so intimidated by the accused, who appears somewhat unsure of himself, that she left her quarters against her will' Elaine B. must appear before the investigating judge ‘or be brought by force’ She could face up to five years in prison. ‘That’s just routine, nothing unusual’ says a Justice Ministry spokesman. Justice Minister K.M. has promised to do more to protect the victims of crime. She is the highest-ranking public prosecutor. She has the right to give instructions. She bears the political responsibility if this woman, in addition to everything else, faces charges.” The compensation proceedings under the Media Act are under way. Judge I.K. brought an action for defamation against the applicant company. The judge ignored relevant evidence and delivered a scandalous judgment. In October 2005 the applicant company sought the disqualification of Judge N.F., the judge assigned to the media proceedings, for bias. It considered that by publishing the impugned statements it had merely expressed criticism, protected by the freedom of speech. On the same date the Vienna Regional Court found against the. applicant company. It held that the impugsned statements had constituted defamation under the. Freedom of Speech Act. The applicant company appealed to the Vienna High Court for review. The appeal was rejected on the grounds that the. transcript of K.’s examination had been included in the case file and. therefore no additional witness was required. The Regional Court found that the contents of the article had given a biased account of the taking of evidence at the trial of H.P. It said the judge had acted arbitrarily and out of racist motives and had disregarded evidence produced. I.K. was therefore entitled to compensation, which it set at 7,000 euros (EUR). It also ordered the applicant company to publish a summary of the judgment. The article claimed that the rape asserted by K. had been described as proven and the assessment of evidence by the Regional Court as absurd. Such an account was not an objective critique of the court's judgment, according to the court. The Regional Court found that the applicant company had not succeeded in proving the truth of the impugned statements. The accusation that a judge, who was under the duty to act objectively and impartially, had deliberately disregarded evidence in order to acquit an accused from the same country had to be qualified as defamation. There was hardly a more severe accusation which could be levied against a judge. The term scandal of justice was a value judgement, which, however, was based on assertions of fact which had been disproven in the proceedings. An error in the translation of that statement could not be excluded, but that did not allow the conclusion that there had been no basis in the file for the above finding of Judge I.K. The applicant company appealed on 8 March 2006 against the Regional Court’s judgment. On 19 June 2006 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the judgment. This judgment was served on the applicant's company lawyer on 29 June 2006. The amount of EUR 7,000 in compensation was appropriate. The judge said that the sharp critique of Judge I.K. in the impugned article had lacked any sufficient factual basis and had been excessive. The court ordered the company to pay the claimant an undisclosed amount of compensation. The decision was made in light of the gravity of the attacks on the claimant's professional reputation, the broad public attention the article had received and the consequences for the claimant.

The application was communicated to the Government on 29 January 2009. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The judge concluded that the case was not inadmissible. The case was decided in favour of the applicant company. Elaine B. (name changed, ed.) had been ill-treated by police officers in Cameroon. Now she faces trial for defamation. The Traiskirchen centre is home to 1,000 asylum seekers and another 100 arrive every day. The centre director later commented on the attacks in the washrooms of the women’s quarters by telling the court: ‘According to our information such incidents are very common and no one thinks anything of them' Elaine B. describes with precision how the man locked the door and removed the key. For the first interview in the interview room no trained interpreter can be found. A year later in court, a year after the incident, the court heard the case against the man was dismissed. His statement, like that of the victim, is disregarded. Elaine B. denies this version of events. She says that she had other things on her mind at the time. She felt repelled by this fat man with a moustache who smelled of alcohol, she was afraid of him. If she had really been hoping to be granted asylum, why would she then have defamed the security officer? Next to take the witness stand are the employees of the bakery. According to the court, the bakery employees could not have identified Elaine. They have unfinished business with the African woman and attribute the basest intentions to her – without furnishing any proof. The reasoning is diametrically opposed to that of the Court of Appeal. ‘It cannot be established that the accused performed sexual intercourse against the will of Elaine B. be made out beyond doubt’, states the judgment. Not a single line about the predicament in which female asylum seekers found themselves at the time. Elaine B. must appear before the investigating judge ‘or be brought by force’ She could face up to five years in prison. ‘That’s just routine, nothing unusual’ says a Justice Ministry spokesman. Justice Minister K.M. has promised to do more to protect the victims of crime. She should study this case. The judge ignored relevant evidence and delivered a scandalous judgment (“The judgment fails to give rise to a scandal”) Judge I.K. alleges in the judgment – without giving any reasons – that the asylum seeker was driven by the basest motives. “This judge and her lay assessors are in no doubt as to the woman's guilt.” Vienna Regional Court ruled that the impugned statements had constituted defamation under freedom of speech laws. The applicant company argued that the statements were true and sought to prove the truth of those statements. Vienna Regional Court refused to hear other witnesses proposed by the applicant company, as it considered that those persons could not make any statements relevant to the proceedings. The hearing was adjourned in order to hear three witnesses. On 12 December 2005 the Regional Court held another hearing in the defamation proceedings in which it examined two of the witnesses proposed. The third witness proposed did not appear. The Regional Court found against the. applicant company on the same date. The Regional Court found that the contents of the article had given a biased account of the taking of evidence at the trial of H.P. According to the article, the judge had acted arbitrarily and out of racist motives and had disregarded evidence produced. The rape asserted by K. had been described as proven and the assessment of evidence by the Regional Court as absurd. I.K. was therefore entitled to compensation, which it set at 7,000 euros (EUR). It also ordered the applicant company to publish a summary of the judgment. The judge ruled that the article was not an objective critique of the Judgment. It was based on the principle of in dubio pro reo. The Regional Court found that the applicant company had not succeeded in proving the truth of the impugned statements. The accusation that a judge, who was under the duty to act objectively and impartially, had deliberately disregarded evidence in order to acquit an accused from the same country had to be qualified as defamation. The term scandal of justice was a value judgement, which, however, was based on assertions of fact which had been disproven in the proceedings. The judgment had clearly indicated the court’s reluctance to accept the version of events given by K. also. In addition, the indication of K. having been a prostitute in the past had been based on a statement from the questioning of that witness. Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the judgment. Appeal was served on the applicant’s company lawyer on 29 June 2006. Judge I.K. in the impugned article had lacked any sufficient factual basis. The amount of EUR 7,000 in compensation was appropriate. It was necessary to protect public confidence in the judiciary against destructive attacks that were essentially unfounded. The applicant company appealed on 8 March 2006 against the Regional Court’S judgment. On 19 June 2006 the Court of Appeal dismisses the appeal. The application is dismissed and the case is dismissed. It is decided that the application should be thrown out of court. We are happy to make this clear.

name: Krystyna Seweryn
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 33582/08) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3) The application was filed by a Polish national, Ms Krystyna Seweryn (‘the applicant’), on 4 July 2008. The case is still pending before the first-instance court. The applicant sought a ruling that the length of the proceedings before the Warsaw District Court had been excessive and an award of just satisfaction in the amount of 10,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) (approx. 2,500 euros (EUR) The court did not analyse the conduct of the trial court. It limited its consideration to the applicant's conduct, namely to the fact that she had made use of her procedural rights, which, in the court's view, had led to delays in the proceedings. Hearings scheduled for 19 February and 2 April 2009 were adjourned.

name: Ali Gülmez
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant was accused of murder, armed robbery and membership of an illegal organisation, namely the TKP-ML (Türkiye Komünist Partisi / Marksist Leninist, Turkish Communist Party / Marxist Leninist) The court delivered its decision on the basis of the case file and referred to the applicant’s statement in which he had admitted committing these acts in protest against the general situation in F‑type prisons. The court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. On 15 February 2001, following a meeting with his lawyer, the applicant had refused to be searched by prison officers and had shouted slogans. On 17 May 2001 the Board found the applicant guilty of having damaged prison property, possessing a sharp cutting instrument made from a prison bed, and having an excessive amount of money in his possession. Board once again imposed a disciplinary sanction on the applicant and prohibited him from receiving visits for two months. The applicant filed an objection with the public prosecutor against this decision under Article 162 of the Regulations. The penalty was enforced between 27 April and 27 June 2001. On 21 June 2001 the decision was reviewed and upheld by the Enforcement Judge. The applicant was caught by prison guards as he was climbing onto the window bars of his cell. In his statement dated 14 June 2001, the applicant maintained that he had climbed up to reach a newspaper which was allegedly on the roof. On 18 June 2001 the applicant was once again prohibited from receiving visitors for three months by the Board. On 2 July 2001 the penalty was reviewed and upheld by the Enforcement Judge. That decision was served on the applicant on 1 November 2001. The applicant was convicted and sentenced to three months in prison. The sentence was later suspended and the applicant released from prison on 1 December 2001. It originated in an application (no. 20605/92) lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Ms Alison Halford, a British citizen, on 22 April 1992. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8, 10, 13 and 14 of the Convention. In May 1983 Ms Halford was appointed to the rank of Assistant Chief Constable with the Merseyside police. As such she became the most senior-ranking female police officer in the United Kingdom. She applied unsuccessfully on eight occasions during the following seven years to be appointed as Deputy Chief Constable. She then applied unsuccessfully to be promoted to Deputy Chief constable eight times. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 17 March 1997. The Court heard addresses by Mrs Liddy, Mr Makin, Mr Duffy and Mr Eadie and also the answer to a question put by one of its members. Ms Halford alleges that certain members of the Merseyside Police Authority launched a “campaign’ against her in response to her complaint to the Industrial Tribunal. This took the form, inter alia, of leaks to the press, interception of her telephone calls and the decision to bring disciplinary proceedings against her. Ms Halford was given an ex gratia payment of 10,000 pounds sterling (GBP) by the Chief Constable (the statutory maximum which the Industrial tribunal could have awarded), despite the fact that she had challenged the above decisions in the High Court. Mr Justice MacPherson found that the Chairman and Vice-Chairman of the Police Authority had acted ultra vires and quashed the relevant decisions. Ms Halford was provided with her own office and two telephones, one of which was for private use. No restrictions were placed on the use of these telephones and no guidance was given to her. She alleges that calls made from her home and her office telephones were intercepted for the purposes of obtaining information to use against her in the discrimination proceedings. It was agreed that she would retire from the police force on medical grounds (arising out of an injury to her knee in 1989). In addition, the Home Office agreed to implement various proposals put by the Equal Opportunities Commission, inter alia to update and review selection procedures for senior posts. Ms Halford applied to the Interception of Communications Tribunal (“the Tribunal’) for an investigation under section 7 of the 1985 Act. In a letter dated 21 February 1992, the Tribunal informed her that its investigation had satisfied it that there had been no contravention of sections 2 to 5 of the1985 Act in her case. The Home Secretary explained that Ms Halford’s complaint regarding the interception of calls made from her office telephones “[did] not fall within [his] responsibilities as Home Secretary nor within the terms of the [ 1985] Act“. The Tribunal confirmed that it could not specify whether any interception had in fact taken place (see paragraph 32 below).

name: Peter Brannigan
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 21 February 1992. It originated in two applications against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (nos. 14553-14554/89) both lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 19 January 1989 by Irish citizens, Mr Peter Brannigan and Mr Patrick McBride. For reasons of convenience Mr McBride will continue to be referred to in this judgment as the applicant. The Irish Government, having been informed by the Registrar of its right to intervene in the proceedings (Article 48, sub-paragraph (b), of the Convention), did not indicate any intention of so doing. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 November 1992. There appeared before the Court: Mrs A. Glover, Legal Counsellor, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr N. Bratza, Q.C., Mr R. Weatherup, Counsel, and Mr H. Danelius, Delegate. The applicants’ memorial was filed out-of-time on 31 August 1992. However, on 28 October 1992, the Chamber decided that it should be regarded as part of the case file (Rule 37 para. 1 in fine). The Court heard addresses by Mr Bratzia for the Government, by Mr Danelious for the Commission and by Mr Weatherup for the applicants. Government’s observations on the applicants’ Article 50 (art. 50) claims were submitted on 17 January 1993. Mr B. Repik, who had attended the hearing and taken part in the deliberations of 26 November 1992, was unable to sit in the present case after 31 December 1992. The first applicant, Mr Peter Brannigan, was born in 1964. He is a labourer and lives in Downpatrick, Northern Ireland. He was arrested at his home by police officers on 9 January 1989 at 6.30 a.m. pursuant to section 12 (1) (b) of the Prevention of Terrorism (Temporary Provisions) Act 1984 (“the 1984 Act’) Patrick McBride was arrested at his home by police officers on 5 January 1989. He was detained for a total period of four days, six hours and twenty-five minutes. During his detention he was interrogated on twenty-two occasions and was subject to the same regime as Mr Brannigan (see paragraph 10 above) He received two visits from his solicitor on 5 and 7 January 1989 and was seen by a medical practitioner on eight occasions during police custody. Mr Mc Bride was shot dead on 4 February 1992 by a policeman who had run amok and attacked Sinn Fein Headquarters in Belfast. The jury returned a verdict of not guilty.

name: Hans Peter Löffler
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court, by Mr Hans Peter Löffler (“the applicant”), an Austrian national, on 3 November 1998. It originated in an application (no. 30546/96) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The object of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention as regards the length of the criminal proceedings against the applicant. On 14 January 1999 the Panel of the Grand Chamber decided, pursuant to Article 5 § 4 of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention, that the application would be examined by one of the Sections. The applicant was charged with murder in 1991 and 1992. The applicant was acquitted on 29 August 1996 after the Assize Court acquitted him in August 1996. The DNA test results were transmitted to the court on 30 October 1995. The case was referred to the Court of Appeal of Linz. The High Court of Vienna refused to transfer jurisdiction of the case to the Linz Regional Court in February 1995. A DNA test of hair and skin parts which had been found on the victim and the applicant’s clothes was carried out on the applicant and the victim's clothes. The victim's DNA was found in the applicant's clothes and was found to be the same as those of the victim.

Winkler, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 14 January 1999 the Panel of the Grand Chamber decided that the application would be examined by one of the Sections. It was, thereupon, assigned to the Third Section. The applicant was charged with murder in 1991. On 15 June 1992 the Linz Court of Appeal granted the applicant's appeal and reopened the criminal proceedings against him. On 3 April 1995 the applicant filed a request under Section 91 of the Courts Organisation Act (Gerichtsorganisationsgesetz) with theLinz Court. of Appeal. The applicant's trial commenced on 19 August 1996 and finished on 29 August 1996. The Assize Court acquitted the applicant in August 1996, at the same time the applicant was released from prison. The DNA test of hair and skin parts which had been found on the victim and the applicant’s clothes was transmitted to the court on 30 October 1995.
