name: Selim Ünay
train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Mr Selim Ünay (‘the applicant’) was born in 1958 and lives in Kandıra. He was arrested in Istanbul during a bank robbery in July 1996. The public prosecutor at the Istanbul State Security Court filed an indictment against the applicant. In the subsequent hearings, the court refused to release the applicant on account of the nature of the alleged offence and the state of the evidence. The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to life imprisonment. In May 2004 the State Security Courts were abolished following a constitutional amendment, and the case’s case was dropped. The proceedings are still pending and the applicant is still remanded in custody. The case was transferred to the Istanbul Assize Court, where it is still pending. The applicant has not yet been formally charged with any crime. The trial is expected to last at least two weeks, if not longer. name: Guy Couez
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the French Government (‘the Government’) on 19 September 1997. It originated in an application (no. 24271/94) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under Article 25 by a French national, Mr Guy Couez, on 8 July 1993. On 25 September 1997 the President of the Court, Mr R. Ryssdal, decided that a single Chamber should be constituted to consider both the instant case and the case of Benkessiouer v France. The Chamber to be constituted for that purpose included ex officio Mr L.-E. Pettiti, the elected judge of French nationality. Couez had a heart attack during the annual cross-country race held by the company of CRS (Compagnies républicaines de sécurité – mobile security police units) on 20 January 1989. On 8 February 1991 he applied for extended sick-leave and asked that his heart attack and the subsequent periods of sick- leave should be recognised as work-related. On 14 May 1991 Mr Couez was notified of his authorities’ refusal to grant him the leave. On 24 February 1998 the Chamber decided to dispense with a hearing in the case, having satisfied itself that the conditions for this derogation from its usual procedure had been met. On 20 January 1992 the applicant brought proceedings in the Amiens Administrative Court to challenge the Prefect’s decision of 27 December 1991 to inform him that the medical board had refused to regard sick-leave on 8 April 1990 as having been due to a work-related accident. On 5 February 1992 he also applied for a stay of execution of that decision. In the meantime, on 25 January 1992, Mr Couez had refused transfer to the administrative staff and on 3 February 1992 the Ministry of the Interior had declared him unfit for active police duties. On 4 September 1992, in a fresh decision, he was maintained in the same position. According to the Government, the applicant submitted twenty-seven pleadings between 20 January 1992 (the date of the application to the Amiens Administrative Court) and 28 June 1996. On 25 July 1995 Mr Couez had appealed against the interlocutory order of 31 May 1995, and that appeal was still pending in the Nancy Administrative Court of Appeal on the date of delivery of the present judgment. The proceedings to challenge the decision requiring unpaid leave of absence to be taken were also brought in 1992 and 1995. On 18 March 1992 he brought proceedings in the Amien Administrative Court to challenge a decision of 10 July 1992 whereby he had been sent on compulsory unpaid leave. He subsequently withdrew these proceedings.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. Convention to be decided later. A Tunisian man was deported from France for not complying with a deportation order. The applicant and his wife were represented by Mr Chemama and Mrs d’Urso, respectively. He initially obtained acknowledgment forms for applications for provisional residence permits (not work permits) for renewable three-month periods. On 4 September 1995, however, he was given a new 3-month residence permit incorporating the right to seek employment. The applicant received notice of a decision dated 2 April 1996 refusing him a residence permit. to live and work in France for a prolonged period, as he was married to a French citizen. name: Metin Gültekin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 17081/06) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that their close relative, Toğay Gültekin, had died while doing his compulsory military service owing to the authorities’ failure to ensure prompt access to medical treatment for his serious health problems. The application was communicated to the Government on 2 April 2014. The case was brought by four Turkish nationals and the Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. Toğay Gültekin died on 27 March 2004 at the GATA Hospital. No autopsy was performed. A military investigation was carried out at the military unit where he had been doing his military service. The applicants initiated compensation proceedings against the Ministry of Defence. They argued he had not received prompt or adequate medical care in his regiment. The military officers who carried out the investigation concluded that the military authorities had acted in accordance with their duties when providing medical assistance to Toğay. GüLtekin's family are still waiting for the results of the compensation proceedings to be heard by the Supreme Military Administrative Court (‘the Military Administrative court’) Toğay Gültekin had been performing his military service and had thus not had the opportunity to leave his military unit and seek medical assistance of his own volition. The authorities had been under an obligation to protect his well-being and to ensure timely medical treatment for him. The applicants argued that it had been these inordinate delays that had caused Toğay Gülterkin’s death. The Ministry of Defence maintained that the military authorities had not acted in a negligent fashion when dealing with his medical problems. It argued that on 16 February 2004 toğay  told his superior that his friend had contracted hepatitis and that he suspected that he himself might have been infected as well. Military Administrative Court appointed three medical experts to clarify whether the military authorities had acted negligently. Medical experts reached the following conclusion in their report of 20 September 2005: “... An examination of the documents and other information in the file shows that Toğay Gültekin started his military service on 22 August 2003. On 2 January 2004 he was treated for a retractile testicle at Çorlu Military Hospital’s infirmary for an upper respiratory tract infection. On 17 March 2004 the regimentalinfirmary doctor decided to refer him to an infectious diseases clinic, but that was not done. On 20 March 2004 he. was diagnosed with and treated for an infection of the upper respiratory. tract and he was sent to the University Hospital with suspected. hepatitis and he died on 27 March 2004 as a result of fulminant hepatitis. Gültekin was contaminated with both hepatitis A and hepatitis B viruses. His liver was infected with both viruses at the same time. This is a condition which worsens the damage to the liver and increases the risk of fulminant hepatitis (fast-deteriorating acute liver failure) A liver transplant is the sole method of ensuring patient survival. The Military Administrative Court dismissed the applicants’ claim. In its decision the court relied on the medical expert report summarised above (see paragraph 18) and concluded that no fault could be attributed to the authorities for Toğay Gül Tekin’s death. name: İlhami Erseven
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 27225/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were members of the executive and auditors boards of the Pir Sultan Abdal Cultural Association (“the Association”), a non‑governmental organisation with its headquarters in Ankara. The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 13 June 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the alleged breach of the applicants' right to a fair hearing to the Government. The members of the executive and auditors boards of the Association were fined TRL 136,890,0000. Liras (TRL) per person. The applicants did not pay the fine within the statutory ten-day time-limit. On 11 September 2001 the Ankara Magistrates' Court found the applicants and the other co-accused guilty as charged. In their petitions, the applicants maintained that they had been deprived of the opportunity to make defence submissions and that, therefore, they did not receive a fair trial. The Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance dismissed the applicants' objections on the following dates: 11 October 2001 in respect of İlhami Erseven, Bekir Aslan, Süleyman Çetinkaya and İsmail Kaya.

name: Martin Schummer
train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) by a German national, Mr Martin Schummer. The applicant alleged in both applications, in particular, that the. retrospective extension of his preventive detention from a maximum period of ten years to an unlimited period of time breached the prohibition of retrospective punishment under Article 7. The applications were adjourned until the judgment in the case of M. v. Germany, no. 19359/04, has become final. The President decided on 20 May 2010 that the proceedings in the two applications at issue be resumed and granted priority to the applications (Rule 41 of the Rules of Court) The applicant was convicted of two counts of rape and abduction and of one count of attempted rape and deprivation of liberty committed in 1984. He served his full prison sentence in Freiburg Prison. He was then placed in preventive detention, executed in that same prison, for the first time on 27 June 1989. He had thus served ten years in preventive Detention by 26 June 1999. On 11 December 2001, in judicial review proceedings under Article 67e of the Criminal Code, the Freiburger Regional Court refused to suspend the applicant's preventive detention and grant probation. The first set of proceedings (application no. 27360/04) was heard in October 2001. The applicant's release could only be taken into consideration after his conditions of detention had been relaxed, combined with a successful social-therapeutic treatment. The Federal Constitutional Court rejected the applicant's appeal. The decision of the Karlsruhe Court of Appeal was also upheld by the Regional Court of Appeals. The application was dismissed by the Federal Court of Justice on 29 April 2002. The applicant was sentenced to a ten-year preventive detention term. The judge ruled that the sentence was not disproportionate because the detention did not constitute a penalty, but a measure of correction and prevention. The appeal was dismissed on 2 April 2002, and the applicant was allowed to leave prison. The applicant's constitutional complaint was dismissed as ill-founded on 22 March 2004. On 12 July 2006 the Freiburg Regional Court refused to suspend the applicant's preventive detention and grant probation under Article 67d § 3 of the Criminal Code. On 11 December 2006 the Karlsruhe Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal. It endorsed the Regional Court's view that there was still a risk that the applicant, if released, might commit serious offences resulting in considerable psychological or physical harm to the victims. It was for the prison authorities and the regional courts to extend the basis for a prognosis by therapeutic measures and by granting relaxations in the conditions of detention. The case was brought by an ex-convict who was being held in preventive detention. He argued that his continued preventive detention violated his right to liberty. The Federal Constitutional Court found that his complaint was inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies. The Freiburg Regional Court remanded the case to the Karlsruhe Court of Appeal. The appeal court ruled in favour of the detention of the ex-convicted sex offender. The case was later quashed and the case was remitted back to the Federal Court of Appeals. The Appeals court ruled that the applicant is still liable to commit serious sexual offences if released. The applicant was released on 10 September 2010 and has been submitted to constant surveillance by five police officers since then. The application of a new statutory provision retrospectively to the detriment of the person concerned was prohibited and the law in force at the time of the offence had to be applied. The applicant had no claim for damages under the Act on Compensation for Measures of Criminal Prosecution (Gesetz über die Entschädigung für Strafverfolgungs-maßnahmen) The applicant has been under constant surveillance since he was released. The Court of Appeal, referring to a leading decision of the Federal Court of Justice of 12 May 2010, ordered his supervision of conduct. German Criminal Code distinguishes between penalties (Strafen) and measures of correction and prevention (Maßregeln der Besserung und Sicherung) Measures are designed to rehabilitate dangerous offenders or to protect the public from them. They must be proportionate to the gravity of the offences committed by, or to be expected from, the defendants as well as to their dangerousness. The Court's judgment in the case of M. v. Germany (no. 19359/04, § 45-78, 17 December 2009) explains how preventive detention can be ordered in addition to a prison sentence for an intentional offence. The order for execution of the placement in preventive detention must reveal that, owing to his propensity to commit serious offences, the perpetrator presents a danger to the general public. The court responsible for the execution of sentences must review, before completion of the prison term, whether the person's preventive detention is still necessary in view of its objective. If that is not the case, it suspends on probation the execution. of the preventive detention order; supervision of the person’s conduct (Führungsaufsicht) commences with suspension. If the maximum duration of preventive detention has expired, the detainee shall be released. The former maximum duration of a first period of preventive detention was abolished. The application of the Court's findings in the M. v. Germany case by the domestic courts was also terminated. The abolition of the maximum period of ten years laid down in Article 67d § 1 of the Criminal Code in its version in force before 31 January 1998 could not be effected retrospectively and therefore still applied to preventive detention ordered in relation to offences committed prior to that date. The Federal Court of Justice, in a decision concerning a retrospective order of preventive. detention (nachträgliche Sicherungsverwahrung), found that the Criminal. Code was to be and could be interpreted so as to comply with Article 7. of the Convention. Several Courts of Appeal considered that the Court's findings in the case of M. v. Germany could not be applied at present by the domestic courts responsible for the execution of sentences. The Criminal Code as it stood did not permit its interpretation in compliance with Articles 5 and 7 of the Convention. It was therefore for the legislator to execute the court's judgment in the M. case. These Courts of appeal accordingly did not terminate the preventive detention of the persons concerned. Several of these cases subsequently submitted such cases to the Federal Court of Justice for a preliminary ruling under a new provision of the Court Organisation Act (section 121 § 2 no. 3) in force since July 2010.

The case originated in two applications (nos. 27360/04 and 42225/07) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr R. Kirpes, a lawyer practising in Offenburg. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The application alleged that the retrospective extension of his preventive detention from a maximum period of ten years to an unlimited period of time breached the prohibition of retrospective punishment. The applicant was convicted of two counts of rape and abduction and one count of attempted rape and deprivation of liberty committed in 1984. The court found that the applicant, acting with full criminal responsibility, had raped two young women and had attempted to rape another woman all of whom he had taken with him in his car. The applicant served his full prison sentence in Freiburg Prison. He was then placed in preventive detention, executed in that same prison, for the first time on 27 June 1989. He had thus served ten years in preventive Detention by 26 June 1999. In 2001 the Freiburger Regional Court refused to suspend the applicant's preventive detention and grant probation. The Karlsruhe Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal. The decision of the Federal Constitutional Court upheld the decision. The judge ruled that Article 67d of the Criminal Code, read in conjunction with section 1a of the Introductory Act to the Criminal code, which entered into force on 31 January 1998, were constitutional. The prohibition on retrospective punishment did not apply to orders of preventive detention, which did not constitute a penalty, but a measure of correction and prevention. In view of the fact that there was a risk that the applicant, if released, might commit sexual offences similar to those he had previously committed, his continued detention was not yet disproportionate. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint (file no. 2 BvR 664/02) as it was ill-founded. The Freiburg Regional Court refused to suspend the. applicant's preventive detention and grant probation under Article 67d. § 3 of the Criminal Code. The applicant's appeal was dismissed by the Karlsruhe Court of Appeal in 2006. The second set of proceedings are to be heard by the Federal Court of Justice in September 2013. The case is likely to take a long time to reach the final stage of the legal process. The decision is not likely to be made until at least the end of 2015. The case was brought by the man who was in preventive detention for sexual offences. The Freiburg Regional Court ruled that the man was still liable to commit serious offences due to his criminal tendencies. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint (file no. 2 BvR 157/07/07). It found that the complaint was inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies in so far as he had complained about the Regional Court's failure to decide on his continued preventive detention already in 2003. In August 2009 the Karlsruhe Court of Appeal quashed that decision and remitted the case to the Freiburger Regional Court. On 11 June 2010 the Federal Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant's request of 15 May 2010 that the Constitutional Court order his immediate release. On 8 July 2010 the Freiburg Regional Court again decided not to suspend the. applicant's preventive detention and grant probation. On 10 September 2010 the Karlsruhe Court of Appeal declared the applicant’s preventive detention terminated and ordered his supervision of conduct. A claim for damages under Article 5 § 5 of the Convention or official liability proceedings had to be brought in the civil courts. The applicant was released in September 2010 and has been submitted to constant surveillance by five police officers since then. The application of a new statutory provision retrospectively to the detriment of the person concerned was prohibited and the law in force at the time of the offence was applied. The German Criminal Code distinguishes between penalties (Strafen) and so‑called measures of correction and prevention (Maßregeln der Besserung und Sicherung) The purpose of such measures is to rehabilitate dangerous offenders or to protect the public from them. They may be ordered for offenders in addition to their punishment. The Court's judgment in the case of M. v. Germany (no. 19359/04, §§ 45-78, 17 December 2009) is contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure. The provisions relevant to the present case can be summarised as follows: The order of preventive detention by the sentencing court must be proportionate to the gravity of the offences committed by the defendants. The perpetrator must present a danger to the general public. The duration of preventive detention must be at least two years. Judicial review and duration of detention can be reviewed at any time. The perpetrator must be assessed for his propensity to commit serious offences. The detainee must not harm his victims physically or mentally or cause serious economic damage. The prison term must be completed before the placement in preventive detention is executed. The preventive detention order must be suspended on probation within a fixed time-limit. The detention should be terminated if there is no danger that the detainee will, owing to his criminal tendencies, commit serious offence. The sentence must be concluded before the detention order is placed in place. The former maximum duration of a first period of preventive detention was abolished. Pursuant to section 1a § 3 of the Introductory Act to the Criminal Code, the amended version of Article 67d § 3 was to be applied without any restriction ratione temporis. The application of the Court's findings in the M. v. Germany case by the domestic courts was upheld by the Federal Court of Justice in a decision of 12 May 2010 (file no. 4 StR 577/09) The Court had considered preventive detention to be qualified as a penalty for the purposes of Article 7 to which the prohibition of retrospective punishment applied. As a consequence, these courts declared terminated the preventive detention of the detainees concerned. Several Courts of Appeal considered that the Court's findings in the case of M. v. Germany could not be applied at present by the domestic courts responsible for the execution of sentences as the Criminal Code as it stood did not permit its interpretation in compliance with Articles 5 and 7 of the Convention. The legislator was therefore for the legislator to execute the court's judgment in the M. case. Several of these courts subsequently submitted such cases to the Federal Court of Justice for a preliminary ruling under a new provision of the Court Organisation Act in force since 30 July 2010, which is aimed at securing a uniform case-law of the German courts on that issue.

If the perpetrator has been sentenced twice already, to at least one year's imprisonment in each case, for intentional offences committed prior to the new offence, preventive detention may be ordered. The court responsible for the execution of sentences must review, before completion of the prison term, whether the person's preventive detention is still necessary in view of its objective. A comprehensive assessment of the perpetrator and his acts must reveal that, owing to his propensity to commit serious offences, the perpetrator presents a danger to the general public. The court may review at any time whether the further execution of the preventive detention order should be suspended on probation. For persons in preventive detention, this time‑limit is two years. The first period of preventive detention may not exceed ten years. If the maximum duration has expired, the detainee shall be released. The former maximum duration of a first period of preventive detention was abolished. The application of the Court's findings in the M. v. Germany case by the domestic courts has been terminated. The former maximum period of ten years could not be effected retrospectively and therefore still applied to preventive detention ordered in relation to offences committed prior to that date. Court decisions on measures of correction and prevention were to be based on the law in force at the time of the court's decision unless the law provided otherwise. The Court had considered preventive detention to be qualified as a penalty for the purposes of Article 7 to which the prohibition of retrospective punishment applied. Several Courts of Appeal found in cases comparable, as regards the temporal course of events, to the M-v-Germany case that the preventive detention of the detainees concerned was terminated. Several Courts of Appeal considered that the Court's findings in the case of M. v. Germany could not be applied at present by the domestic courts responsible for the execution of sentences. This was because the Criminal Code as it stood did not permit its interpretation in compliance with Articles 5 and 7 of the Convention. Section 1a § 3 of the Introductory Act to the Criminal code had expressly stipulated that the abolition of the maximum duration of ten years for a first period of preventive detention also applied to persons who had committed the offences in question prior to the entry into force of that abolition. It was therefore for the legislator to execute the court's judgment in the M. case.

The German Criminal Code distinguishes between penalties (Strafen) and so‑called measures of correction and prevention (Maßregeln der Besserung und Sicherung) to deal with unlawful acts. name: Pilar Moreno Gómez
train_texts: The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Ms Pilar Moreno Gómez alleged a breach of her right to respect for her home. The applicant has lived in a flat in a residential quarter of Valencia since 1970. Since 1974 the Valencia City Council has allowed licensed premises such as bars, pubs and discotheques to open in the vicinity of her home, making it impossible for people living in the area to sleep. In 1993 the City Council commissioned a report by an expert. The expert found that the noise levels were unacceptable and exceeded permitted levels. At 3.35 a.m. on Saturdays they were in excess of 100 dBA. The applicant lives in Valencia, Spain. In 1995 the police informed the Valencia City Council that nightclubs and discotheques in the sector in which she lived did not systematically close on time. In 1997 the City Council granted a licence for a discotheque to be opened in the building she lived in. The licence was subsequently declared invalid by a judgment of the Supreme Court of 17 October 2001. The applicant was exasperated by the situation, which prevented her from sleeping and resting and caused her insomnia and serious health problems. On 21 August 1997 she lodged a preliminary claim with the Valencia city council. The application was successful in 2000. The applicant lodged an application for judicial review with the Valencia High Court of Justice on 25 November 1997. She sought 3,907 euros (650,000 pesetas) for the damage she had sustained and the cost of installing double glazing. In a judgment of 21 July 1998, delivered after an adversarial hearing in public, the High Court dismissed the application. Relying on Articles 14 (equality) and 24 (right to a fair hearing) of the Constitution, the applicant appealed to the Constitutional Court. The Constitutional Court declared the amparo appeal admissible and invited the applicant, the representative of state council’s office and the Valencia City Council to submit their observations. The Valencia City Council raised a number of preliminary objections to the appeal. It argued that there was no evidence of noise levels inside the applicant’s home and that the authority concerned should not bear sole responsibility for the noise to which the applicant had allegedly been exposed. In a judgment of 29 May 2001, the Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal after also dismissing the Valencia city council's preliminary objections. It ruled that the amparo appeal was hybrid in nature, that is to say that it alleged a violation of Articles 15 and 18 § 2 of the Constitution by the City Council and a breach of Articles 14 and 24 by the Valencia High Court of Justice. The applicant had not established a direct link between the noise and the damage she had sustained, the court said. The Constitutional Court found that there was no evidence of any violation of Articles 14 and 24 of the Constitution. The only evidence she has adduced is a certificate stating that she was admitted to hospital and saw a doctor, without any indication of the period for which she had been suffering from lack of sleep or the cause thereof. The court also found that the applicant's entire case is based on a few sound-level readings taken inside her home which gave disparate results and do not establish that there has been a violation of the constitutional provision.  Constitutional Court dismissed the amparo appeal on the following ground: “Consequently, as regards the alleged violation of the rights relied on, the appeal must be dismissed, as the appellant has failed to prove the existence of a genuine effective breach of fundamental rights attributable to the Valencia City Council’” That judgment was delivered by the Constitutional Court sitting as a full court. However, two judges expressed concurring opinions. The first said that the judgment restricted the free development of the personality at home. The second judge pointed out in his concurring opinion that there was a preliminary problem that had not been adequately dealt with, namely the degree to which the relevant authority was required to provide the requested protection.

The applicant sought 3,907 euros (650,000 pesetas) for the damage she had sustained and the cost of installing double glazing. In a judgment of 29 May 2001, the Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal after also dismissing the City Council’'s preliminary objections. Council and a breach of Articles 14 and 24 of the. Constitution by Valencia High Court of Justice. The authorities were obliged to exercise their power when the breach of the fundamental rights attained a certain level of gravity, the second judge said. The case will be heard at a later date, the third judge said in an email to the MailOnline. The decision will be delivered by the Constitutional Court sitting as a full court.

name: Özgür Keskin
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was paid 16,985 Turkish liras in respect of severance pay and he signed a release (ibraname) discharging the City Council from all liability. The Labour Court held that the applicant’s discharge from the military shortly after he had been enlisted fell under the provision of the collective agreement, which called for the suspension of the employment contract when an employee was conscripted for reasons other than compulsory military service. Therefore the applicant was entitled to be reinstated in accordance with the terms of thecollective agreement. The City Council appealed against the decision and reserved its right to submit additional observations once the reasoned judgment of the first-instance court had been served on it. That appeal was not communicated to the applicant. On 21 July 2008, following an examination based on the case file and without holding a hearing, the Court of Cassation quashed the first‑instance court’s judgment and found in favour of the City Council. The City Council argued, inter alia, that the court's interpretation of the collective agreement had been erroneous. It held that a rejection of the applicant's request for reinstatement could not be regarded as the termination of his employment contract; therefore, the applicant could not technically ask to be reinstated.

The applicant relied on clause 19 of the collective bargaining agreement in force at the company (‘the collective agreement’), which provided for the reinstatement of employees who had quit their jobs to perform their military service, provided that they applied within three months. The City Council appealed against the decision and reserved its right to submit additional observations once the reasoned judgment of the first-instance court had been served on it. No appeal was possible against this decision. It was served on the applicant on 22 September 2008. The applicant could not technically ask to be reinstated. The Court ofCassation further held that clause 19 of the collective agreement was not directly applicable in the case before it. It found it established that the applicant had resigned from his job to perform his military service.

name: Andrej Furman
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 16608/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been unable to enjoy family life with his daughter on account of the lack of diligence on the part of the Slovenian and Austrian authorities in regulating and enforcing contact between them. The Slovenian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs B. Jovin Hrastnik, State Attorney. The Austrian Government were represented in the case by Ambassador H. Tichy, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for European and International Affairs. M.P. sent a letter to the Centre informing them that she would be living abroad in the period between 1 July 1998 and 31 August 1999 for the purposes of her doctoral studies. She requested that the contact proceedings be suspended during that period. The Centre sent a request to M.P’s employer, Maribor University, to provide the address of her foreign residence. On 26 August 1998 the applicant sought an interim order granting him contact with P once a month and for a week during both the winter and summer holidays. The applicant was supposed to pick up his daughter at his permanent address and bring her back to the same address. M.P. temporarily living in Graz, Austria. Appealed to the Ministry of Labour, Family and Social Affairs (hereinafter “the Ministry’s”). Centre sent the. decision, along with a request to appoint a representative authorised to receive her. official mail, to the Slovenian Embassy in Austria. Embassy requested M.P to collect the decision and the letter; however, she refused to do so. On 1 March 2000, M.M. was served with the documents at her workplace. Case was remitted to the Maribor Administrative Unit and the enforcement proceedings were subsequently stayed as a result of the quashing of the interim order. M.P. sent a reply to the Centre, without, however, providing the requested information on P. On 5 October 2000 the Centre issued an order granting the applicant contact with P. every Tuesday afternoon, every first weekend of the month and a few weeks during the winter and summer holiday periods. According to the order, an appeal against the contact schedule would not have a suspensive effect. M.P., however, did not attend a hearing in the applicant’s presence on 29 September 2000. On 27 February 2003 the Centre contacted the Ministry for Foreign Affairs with a view to finding the address of M.p. and P. The Centre attempted to obtain the information on M.P. and P.’s address to the Ministry of the Interior in 2003 and 2004, but was unable to do so. The applicant instituted proceedings before the Maribor District Court in June 2004. He complained that he had not seen his daughter P. for six years and that she had evaded proceedings conducted by the Centre and the District Court. He also sent a letter to the Graz Youth and Family Office asking them for help in re-establishing contact with P. in July 2005. The court also attempted to serve the document on M.-P. through the Slovenian Embassy in Austria. on 2 November 2005. Maribor District Court tried to serve a summons on M.P. in Austria. Two unsuccessful attempts were made to serve the summons at her home address. Court requested report on P’s situation from the Graz Youth and Family Office. Court ruled that the applicant could visit P. every two weeks by picking her up at M.p.'s home. Court found that there were no contact schedules for the applicant and P. M. did not attend the hearing; however, she informed the court that she did not wish to have contact with the applicant. A further request for a report was submitted on 28 September 2006. On 15 November 2006 the latter court sent a reply to the Maribor Court. On 5 July 2007, on the applicant’s proposal, the Maribor District Court issued an enforceable interim order allowing him contact with P. every two weeks. On 1 September 2007 the applicant saw P. for the first time in more than nine years. They had contact again on 6 October 2007. On the latter occasion, P. left after less than an hour, after which she refused to see the applicant again, although he attempted to see her on at least two more occasions. M.P. was ordered to comply with the terms of the order, subject to a fine of 200 euros (EUR) for each breach. P. lodged a request with the Graz-West District Court seeking suspension of the applicant’s contact rights. P. said that throughout the period in which she had been living in Austria the applicant had not wished to have any contact with her and had made no attempts to see her. She also said that she had no relationship with her father and that she was afraid that he would take her to Slovenia. M.P. appealed against the impugned order. On 23 April 2010 the Maribor Local Court invited the applicant to supplement his request for enforcement. On the basis of that request, a new enforcement order was issued on 2 November 2010, ordering M.p. to allow contact between the applicant and P., subject to a fine in the amount of EUR 500. M.P. asked the Graz-West District Court to increase the monthly child maintenance from EUR 137 to EUR 250 in June 2008. The court, taking into account the financial situation of both parents, allowed M.P’s request on 12 February 2009. An appeal lodged by the applicant was dismissed on 7 August 2009. P. had consistently expressed her wish not to have contact with the applicant and concluded that contact against her wishes would not be in her interest. The Graz Regional Civil Court dismissed the appeal on 31 August 2009, finding that there was no indication that P. was not expressing her wishes freely or was being manipulated.

The case originated in an application (no. 16608/09) against the Republic of Slovenia lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Slovenian national, Mr Andrej Furman. A hearing was scheduled for 22 October 1998, but the university was unable to reach the applicant and the hearing was adjourned. The Ministry of Labour, Family and Social Affairs quashed the order and remitted the issue of the provisional contact schedule for a fresh examination by the Centre. On 30 June 2000, the Centre invited M.p. to provide certain information. M.P. did not provide the requested information on P. on 19 July 2000. M.P.'s appeal against the order was upheld in July 2002. The case was remitted to the Centre with the instruction to acquire information about P.’s residence, living conditions and education. On 27 February 2003 the Centre contacted the Ministry for Foreign Affairs with a view to finding the address of P. and her mother. The court also attempted to serve the document on M. P. through the Slovenia Embassy in Austria. M.P. did not appear to be living at the indicated address. Attempts to serve a summons at her home address were unsuccessful. Court ruled that the applicant could visit P. every two weeks by picking her up at M.P’s home. Court found that there were no contact dates between the applicant and P. The case was adjourned until the end of February 2007, at which time a new contact schedule was set out for the applicant to pick up and drop off P. at the applicant's home. The application is still pending in the Maribor District Court for Civil Matters, but a hearing was held on 7 February 2007 to set a contact schedule. M.P. appealed against the contact order. On 1 September 2007 the applicant saw P. for the first time in more than nine years. On the latter occasion, P. left after less than an hour, after which she refused to see the applicant again, although he attempted to see her on at least two more occasions. On 11 September 2008, the Maribor District Court explained to the parties that the contact proceedings had been concluded by a final decision. She also said that she had no relationship with her father and that she was afraid that he would take her to Slovenia. M.P. appealed against the order, but the Maribor Higher Court set aside the impugned order on 28 July 2009. name: Ludwig Weh
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38544/97) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged, inter alia, that the first applicant's right to remain silent and not to incriminate himself had been breached in criminal proceedings against him. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) This case was assigned to the newly composed First Section. By a decision of 4 July 2002 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The applicant, Mr W. Weh, was born in 1952 and lives in Bregenz. He was fined 800 Austrian schillings for exceeding the speed limit by 21 km/h. The applicant did not comply with the anonymous order. The order became invalid (see paragraph 31, below) The applicant appealed to the Vorarlberg Independent Administrative Panel (Unabhängiger Verwaltungssenat). The panel dismissed the case on 15 April 1996. The case has been referred to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) for further proceedings. The decision to dismiss the case was made by the ECHR. The applicant was not prosecuted for exceeding the speed limit. He raised various issues regarding the tribunal quality of the Independent Administrative Panel and the fairness of the proceedings. He did not raise the issue of his right to remain silent and not to incriminate himself. The Administrative Court refused to deal with the applicant's complaint pursuant to section 33a of the Administrative Court Act (Verwaltungsgerichtshofgesetz) since the amount of the penalty did not exceed ATS 10,000, and no important legal problem was at stake. The applicant was ordered to pay ATS 180 by way of contribution to the costs of the appeal proceedings.

The other parties will be only too pleased, when it becomes so flagrantly evident how powerless the Austrian people's party is vis-a-vis one of their officials. Dr. Graff ist eine der folgreichsten Rechtsanwälte Europas. Er verwaltete zum Beispiel das gigantische Erbe Picassos, vertrat Kreisky and einen österreichischen Außenminister. Ein Anwalt darf nicht an der Entstehung von Gesetzen beteiligt sein, die seinen Mandanten Vorteile bringen. In solchen Fällen nicht ein bestimmter Verdacht entstehen kann, der keineswegs begründet sein. Mr Graff brought injunction proceedings under Section 1330 of the Austrian Civil Code (Allgemeines Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch) against the three applicants before the Vienna Commercial Court (Handelsgericht) He requested that the applicants be prohibited from stating or repeating that he “does not intend to comply with moral concepts existing in democracies all over the world, namely that one has to give up one’s law firm if one becomes a member of the government” He also requested the statement be retracted and that this retraction be published in the “Neue Kronen-Zeitung” The court found that the statement contained in the first paragraph of the newspaper article was an insult. The court concluded that the applicants could not successfully rely on Article 10 of the Convention. The interference with the applicants’ rights under this provision was justified in order to protect Mr Graff’s good reputation, which could be prejudiced by such untruthful statements. The applicants were the owners of several monthly magazines. Unlike daily newspapers, these magazines were usually on the market longer. If one of the applicants' magazines, for instance, had violated the Unfair Competition Act (Bundesgesetz gegen den unl unl), the magazine would have to pay a fine. The Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) dismissed the applicants’ appeal. It found that the Commercial Court had correctly taken the necessary evidence and assessed the relevant facts. The applicants also submitted that the impugned article constituted a criticism of Mr Graff’s behaviour as a politician and was therefore protected by the freedom of expression guaranteed by Article 10 of the Convention. The evidence proposed by the applicants was insufficient to prove such allegations. The contested statements were not value judgments, but (political) criticism based on alleged facts. Such criticism was only acceptable if the underlying facts were true. Since the applicants had failed to prove the truth of these facts, they could not rely on these facts. Supreme Court rejected as inadmissible the applicants’ extraordinary appeal on points of law (außerordentliche Revision) The court pointed out that disparagement by means of untrue statements, even if made in the course of political debate, went beyond acceptable (political) criticism and could not be justified by a weighing of interests or by invoking the right to freedom of expression. This decision was served on the applicants on 10 April 1995. Article 10 of the Convention was amended to read: ‘Disparagement by Means of Untruthful Statements’. The Court ruled that this was a ‘disparaging statement’, not a claim for freedom of speech.

On 16 February 2005 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. As the defendant’s costs order only arises when a prosecution is unsuccessful, it cannot be a sentence and cannot be appealed at the Court of Appeal Criminal Division’’

name: Turhan Yalçın Bürkev
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26480/95) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints (applications nos. 28291/95, 29280/95 and 26699/95). The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) On 27 January 1981 the Ankara Martial Law Court ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. On 27 December 1995 the Court of Cassation quashed the applicant's conviction on the ground that he should have been convicted of the offence. The criminal proceedings are still pending before the Ankara Assize Court (ağır ceza mahkemesi). The application was declared admissible after the applicant and the Government filed observations on the merits.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 17711/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant claimed he had been convicted on the basis of unlawful evidence provided by undercover police officers. He argued that the domestic court had failed to evaluate substantive evidence, namely, records of the telephone conversations he had had prior to his arrest. The application was communicated to the Government on 17 March 2010. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicant was born in 1965 and lives in Ҫanakkale. The Istanbul Criminal Police Laboratory established that the light brown substance, which had a net weight of 2.1 grams, was indeed heroin. On the same day the applicant was questioned by the Küçükçekmece Criminal Magistrates’ Court. He submitted that he had been using drugs for more than twenty years and that he purchased a certain amount of heroin from A. for TRY 120 every four days for his own consumption. The investigating judge held that he should be placed in detention pending the outcome of the proceedings. At a subsequent hearing on 14 October 2005 two police officers made statements. One of them submitted that after being informed that the applicant had been selling drugs, another police officer, C.D., had called the applicant on the telephone and arranged a meeting. The Bakırköy Assize Court found the applicant guilty of trafficking drugs and sentenced him to six years and three months’ imprisonment. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. On 21 April 2010 the applicant was granted conditional release. The court took into account the statements of the police officers, the testimony of M.T. and the evidence resulting from the police operation. The judge ruled that the evidence relied on by the public prosecutor had been obtained unlawfully. The applicant was sentenced to 6 years and 3 months' imprisonment. He was also sentenced to 3 years and 4 months' probation.

The crucial issue in the present case was the assessment of the [applicant's] condition and, consequently, it cannot be regarded as so complex as to warrant legal assistance.

name: Timothy Walker
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the obligation imposed on him as a man in employment over age 60 to pay national insurance contributions, which did not apply to a woman in work of over that age, was in violation of Article 14 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. By a decision of 16 March 2004, the Court declared the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. The applicant paid 10% of his earnings (between the primary threshold of GBP 385 and the upper earnings limit of 2,535) in NICs (Class 1), amounting to GBP 215 per month and GBP 2,580 per annum. A woman of 60 years or more who continued to work would not be required to pay any NICs on her earnings. The applicant wrote to his Member of Parliament and the Paymaster General complaining about the difference in treatment for men and women. Both replied stating that since liability to pay national insurance contributions is linked to the state pension age, the treatment of men and woman would equalise in 2020.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 80442/12) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a French national, Ms Cécile Lecomte. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the conditions of her detention for preventive purposes in two police stations had violated Article 3 of the convention. The Government of the French Republic, having been informed of their right to intervene in the proceedings, indicated that they did not wish to exercise that right. The application was communicated to the Government on 12 May 2014. The applicant and three others had let themselves down on a rope on a railway bridge. They had unrolled banners protesting against the castor transport. A commuter train had to be stopped because its passage would have put them at risk. The District Court considered that the applicant’s detention was indispensable in order to prevent the imminent commission of a regulatory offence of considerable importance to the general public. The Lüneburg District Court quashed the order of 6 November 2008 for the applicant's detention for preventive purposes and ordered her immediate release. On 7 November 2008 at 9.15 p.m. the Lünesburg Regional Court, having heard the applicant in person at 2.10p.m., dismissed the applicants appeal against the District Court's decision. The applicant was detained in a cell in the Lüneburg Police Station from 7 p.m. onwards. She was found not to suffer from any health problems. Her detention in Braunschweig Police Station had already led to her joints having stiffened. The applicant’s small cell, equipped with a mattress and a chair, was lighted at least via a ventilation slot and by electric light. She went outside for a walk on the banks of the Ilmenau river with the police officers three times during that period. The places and conditions of the applicant's detention were reviewed and the applicant was released on the same day at 6.32 p.M. The applicant was taken out for a walk on the premises of the Braunschweig Police Station, which did not dispose of a closed courtyard, on 8 November 2008. The applicant had climbed on the cupboard in her cell and passed the night thereon, failing to comply with the police’s order to descend. On 9 November 2008 the applicant was allowed to stay outside on those premises from 12.22 p.m. until 12.35 p.M., without being shackled. She was further allowed to receive three visits from a friend and two from her doctor C. The Lüneburg District Court dismissed the applicant’S action of 8 November 2009 under section 19 § 2 of the Lower Saxony Public Security and Order Act (see paragraph 43 below) The District Court noted that the detention order was executed in the detention wing of the Lüneburg Police Station until 7 November 2008. The photographs of shackled persons exposed in the Braunschweig Police Station may have been tasteless, but did not render the applicant’s detention unlawful as a result of intimidation. The recommendations of the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (CPT) were irrelevant here. The District Court considered that the manner in which the detention had been enforced had been lawful and had complied with the provisions of the Police Custody Regulations (Polizeigewahrsamsordnung) The applicant had to be shackled as, being an excellent climber, there had been a risk that she would climb on trees or buildings and abscond. The applicant had not, therefore, been “taken for a walk like an animal’ on the parking. On 9 November 2008 the applicant had been outside and had not been shackled and had been allowed to climb on a tree. She had not objected to returning to the detention wing afterwards. In that police station there were no detention cells suitable for a deprivation. The conditions of the applicant’s detention, albeit onerous for the applicant, had complied with the applicable legal provisions. The doctor who had visited the applicant in detention and persuaded the then competent District Court judge to order her release had probably been a sympathiser. The court considered that it had been lawful for the police to leave the light switched on during the night. It noted that the applicant had climbed on a cupboard measuring 1.90 metres and had failed to descend on the police’s request. Shackling the applicant to a female police officer on 8 November 2008 had been necessary in order to prevent the applicant from being shackled. The Regional Court found that the right provided by no. 10 of the Police Custody Regulations (see paragraph 46 below) to be allowed to stay outside for 45 minutes per day in so far as the staffing and infrastructural situation permitted had not been breached. The applicant, an excellent climber, had previously shown that she was not ready to comply with the police’s orders. On 9 November 2008 the applicant had not been shackled during her time outside and had been allowed to climb on a tree. She had also been able to move within her cell in order to alleviate ailments resulting from her rheumatism. The Regional Court noted that the Braunschweig Police had received some 200 telephone calls of sympathisers of the applicant, some of whom had insulted the police, which had considerably disturbed the execution of her detention. The applicant had been visited by three persons while in detention, in addition to two visits by her doctor, C., who had prescribed her necessary medication and had brought a couple of magazines. Her right to receive visits had not be unlawfully restricted in these circumstances. The case was heard by the Federal Constitutional Court of Germany on 1 December 2009. The decision was confirmed on 24 August 2010. The court declined to give a reason why the case was not dismissed. The case was eventually dismissed on 30 May 2012. The appeal can be appealed to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) which will decide whether the case should be dismissed or not. The ECHR will make a decision on the case on 1 November 2013. The ECHR's decision is expected to be made within the next few weeks. The next hearing will be held on 8 November 2013, when the ECHR’s decision is likely to be delivered.

The applicant alleged, in particular, that the prison authorities had interfered with a letter from him to the Scottish Minister of State. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998. It was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court, which declared it partly admissible on 18 September 2001. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) and the application was allocated to a new Second Section. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required.

name: Wim Capeau
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42914/98) against the Kingdom of Belgium lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Mr Wim Capeau complained of a violation of Articles 5, 6 and 14 of the Convention. He argued that the statutory requirement to establish his innocence by adducing factual evidence or submitting legal argument to that effect was incompatible with the presumption of innocence. By a decision of 6 April 2004, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Government filed observations on the merits of the case (Rule 59 § 1). The applicant did not submit any observations within the time allowed. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The applicant claimed compensation for unwarranted pre-trial detention, relying on the Law of 13 March 1973. The Minister of Justice refused the applicant's claim on the ground that he had not “established his innocence by adducing factual evidence or submitting legal argument to that effect” The Appeals Board upheld the refusal of his claim by a decision taken on the same day and served on the applicant on 29 March 1998. It noted that the grounds for presuming the guilt of the applicant, who had always denied committing the offence he stood accused of, had been held to be insufficient to justify committing him for trial. It observed that the applicant had announced his intention of submitting a pleading setting out the evidence in the file which “amply” proved his innocence, but had not done so and had not replied to the Government's submissions.

name: Ali Bülent Sarıtaç
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29702/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court ruled that the application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaint (Rule 43): No. 28291/95, 29280/96, 26699/ 95, 29700/96 and 43362/96. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation. The applicant was sentenced to the death penalty under Article 146 of the Criminal Code. The case was referred to the Military Court of Cassation (Askeri Yargıtay) The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits. The Court declared the application admissible. This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1) The case is still pending when it is heard in court in January 2015. The judge is expected to deliver his verdict in September 2015. Click here to read the transcript of the case in its entirety. The case was transferred to the Court of Cassation (Yargıtay) on 4 January 1994. On 18 April 1995 the Court upheld the applicant’s conviction. The applicant appealed the conviction to the İstanbul Martial Law Court. On 17 August 1990 the court convicted the applicant under Article 146 § 1 of the Criminal Code and sentenced him to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment. The Law of 27 December 1993 abolished the jurisdiction of the Martial Law Courts, which acquired jurisdiction over the case. The case file was transmitted to the Court of Cassation in January 1994 and the case was heard in April 1995.

The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. Mr Rıza Türmen, the judge elected in respect of Turkey, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The Government accordingly appointed Mr Feyyaz Gölcüklü to sit as an ad hoc judge, in his place. The application was joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaint (applications nos. 28291/95, 29280/95 and 26699/95) The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation, the THKP-C (Turkish People’s Liberation Party/Front). On 11 July 1979 the applicant was detained on remand. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 of the Criminal Code. The applicant was convicted in 1984 and sentenced to death. The case was referred to the Military Court of Cassation in 1988. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1) The Court declared the application admissible and the applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits. The applicant was convicted under Article 146 of the Criminal Code. He was sentenced to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment, permanently debarred from employment in the civil service and placed under judicial guardianship. The applicant appealed. to the İstanbul Martial Law Court. The Court of Cassation (Yargıtay) acquired jurisdiction over the case and on 4 January 1994 the case file was transmitted to it. On 18 April 1995 the Court ofCassation upheld the applicant’s conviction. The case is still pending. It is believed that the case will be heard again in January or February 2015. It has been decided that the applicant will be allowed to appeal again.

name: Ayhan Çakmak
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 53672/00) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Two Turkish nationals, Mr Ayhan Çakmak and Mrs Süreyya ÇKmak (“the applicants”), complained about the length of compensation proceedings. The applicants were represented by Mr O.K. Cengiz, a lawyer practising in Izmir. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicants filed an action with the Izmir Administrative Court against the Ege University Medical Department (hereinafter “the defendant”) and claimed compensation for medical malpractice. The applicants appealed against the judgment of the first-instance court. The Supreme Administrative Court, without holding a hearing, dismissed the applicants' appeal. The case was settled in 1999 when the applicants were awarded compensation for the treatment given to their daughter, C.Ç. The court found that the Medical Department was not competent to examine the acts of civil servants carried out in the exercise of their duties. The decision was published in the book ‘The Case of C. Ç. – A Case of Medical Malpractice’.

name: Bengt Pudas
train_texts: The case was brought before the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’s) on 13 March 1986. It originated in an application (no. 10426/83) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission on 30 March 1983 under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Swedish citizen, Mr. Bengt Pudas. The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 § 1 and 13 (Art. 6-1, art. 13). The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, the elected judge of Swedish nationality. The hearing was held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr. Corell for the Government, by Mr Gaukur Jörundsson for the Commission and by Mr Ravnsborg for the applicant. The applicant, Mr. Bengt Pudas, is a Swedish citizen born in 1959. He lives at Hedenäset, which is situated in the Municipality of Övertorneå and the County of Norrbotten, in the North of Sweden. On 1 February 1980, the County Administrative Board granted him a taxi traffic licence, and, on 20 May, a licence to carry passengers and their goods on specified interurban routes (linjetrafik) The applicant commenced his combined taxi and interurban traffic business on 20 May 1980. The applicant offered a service of two journeys a week at scheduled times. This service was available on request and had to be ordered one day in advance. On 17 August 1981, the County Administrative Board granted the County Traffic Company a licence, valid as from 1 September 1981, to provide interurban transport of passengers and goods. In another decision on the same day, the Board revoked the applicant’s and Mr. Wälimaa's licences forinterurban traffic, inter alia on the following grounds: “The plans for the future transport service offered by the County Company include a regular bus service which is to be created between the places in question”. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Board of Transport (transportrådet), in which he alleged, inter alia, the following. The County Traffic Company’s application for a licence for the routes covered by his licence had been motivated not by any public interest in improving the transport service, but by an arrangement between the Company and Mr. Wälimaa (see paragraphs 11 and 12 above). Only very serious reasons, such as misconduct of the licence-holder, could justify revocation. When revoking his licence, the County Administrative Board had failed to take due account of his interests. The transport service on the routes concerned was not likely to be improved simply by being carried out by Mr. Pudas and others instead of by himself.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36619/03) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the administrative proceedings to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the convention, the Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant was born in 1947 and lives in Orsa. The Government was represented by their Agent, Mr M. Falk, Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicant claimed that he had made transactions to obtain tax advantages. He appealed against the decision, disputing the Tax Authority’s findings. He sought SEK 6,850,000 (approximately EUR 736,000) in damages from the Swedish State. The application was rejected in 2002 and the Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal on 11 September 2003. The case was not decided in full until November 2003, when the applicant was awarded the full amount he had sought. The decision was not made public until after the appeal had been decided in November 2003 by the County Administrative Court of the County of Dalarna. The appeal was settled in November 2004 by the District Court (tingsrätten) in Stockholm. The applicant claimed damages for not being given a fair procedure. The State contested the suit, claiming that it had not caused the applicant any injury, either by fault or neglect, for which he could claim damages. The case is still pending in the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) where the case is awaiting a decision on leave to appeal. The Court of Appeal upheld the lower court’s judgment in full on 2 November 2005, without giving any reasons for the decision. The applicant appealed to the Supreme court on 12 October 2005, where the cases is still awaiting a Decision on Leave to Appeal. The Supreme Court is yet to rule on the appeal.

In the latter decision the court examined the course of the trial and found that there were no delays. The applicant submits that he was not informed about the majority of the scheduled court sessions at which his detention on remand was prolonged, therefore he could not attend them. The court reiterated the reasons invoked on the previous occasions. The applicant was convicted and sentenced to fourteen years’ imprisonment. It appears that he lodged an appeal against the judgment and that the appellate proceedings are pending. The appeal is expected to be heard in the next few weeks. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 3429/07) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. It was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3) The case dates back to 3 March 2005. At the present stage of the proceedings, counsel for the defence could not, however, claim to be entitled to unlimited access to the complete case files. The Düsseldorf Court of Appeal quashed the detention order issued by the District Court on 25 July 2002. Pursuant to section 114 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the facts leading to a strong suspicion that the accused had committed a particular offence and the reasons for detention had to be given. The applicant’s detention order was quashed on 14 October 2002 and the case remitted to the District court. The District Court ruled that the original detention order did not comply with the legal requirements, and that the applicant had a right to access the facts and evidence on which the order was based. name: Clifford George McKeown
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his trial for terrorism related offences was unfair because of the way the courts in Northern Ireland had approached the question of non-disclosure of prosecution papers to the defence on grounds of public interest immunity. He is currently detained at HMP Maghaberry, Northern Ireland. The case was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The applicant's case was that he had simply given M. a lift and that he knew nothing about the articles that he brought into the car. The applicant was arraigned on 8 June 2001 and pleaded not guilty to one count of possession of firearms and ammunition with intent. He claimed that he had been entrapped by a person known to him working with the police either for the purpose of incriminating him or his co-defendant. The application for an order preventing disclosure was made to a judge other than the trial judge. That judge is designated by the Lord Chief Justice of Northern Ireland and is referred to as the “disclosure judge” (see domestic law and practice below) The applicant opposed the ex parte hearing of the prosecution's application by the disclosure judge. The disclosure judge, in an ex tempore judgment, found that it was proper to hear the application. On 18 February 2002, the disclosure judge allowed the prosecution's application for non-disclosure. He outlined this Court's judgments in Rowe and Davis v. the United Kingdom [GC], no. 28901/95, §§6 60-62, ECHR 2000‑II. There was considerable debate in [Rowe and Davis] about the best way to deal procedurally with this situation. The majority took the view that it was important for the trial judge to see the material personally. That is certainly true if the material is not prejudicial to the accused and where the trial is before a judge and jury. However, in the case [of] a non-jury trial it is obviously undesirable that prejudicial material which is not going to be part of the evidence should be seen by the judge. The trial judge ruled that it was not in the public interest to disclose the material. He concluded that none of the material which is the subject of the application before me is such that it might reasonably be expected to undermine the case for the prosecution or to assist the accused's defence. The trial judge then suggested that one way of proceeding would be to appoint special counsel who would be shown the material and remain throughout the trial. A hearing took place on 1 August 2002 to allow the parties and counsel appearing for the Attorney-General to make submissions as to whether it was appropriate either for special counsel to be appointed or for the trial judge himself to consider the undisclosed material. Trial judge heard submissions from the defence, prosecution and counsel for the Attorney-General. The latter argued that the question of disclosure should be referred back to the disclosure judge for his decision. Counsel for the applicant's co-accused also suggested that the trial judge recuse himself since he had seen the statement of reasons which had not been made available to the defence. The trial judge ruled that it was not appropriate for him to Recuse himself. He added: “The fact that a judge had seen a document in a non-jury trial which has not been seen by the defence does not of necessity mean the trial is made unfair or becomes unfair” Disclosure judge said there were two types of material involved in the case. The first could not assist the applicant because it was adverse to him. The second related to police procedures, was general in nature and content, and did not relate directly to the applicant. I would not regard the case as requiring the appointment of special counsel... The present reality is that I cannot foresee any circumstance in which the undisclosed material, that is the material undisclosed to the trial judge, would be of assistance to the defence. But it may be that the defence may advance a proposition or raise an issue that might by remote possibility make that so, and I think if the Crown concedes that that's the position then the Crown should make the matter known. The trial judge rejected both applications. the defence of entrapment, further disclosure was required. The trial judge found that taking the circumstantial evidence and the inferences to be drawn from it, he was satisfied of the applicant's guilt of the two offences beyond reasonable doubt. On 12 November 2002 the applicant was convicted by the trial judge, without a jury, of two offences: possession of firearms and ammunition with intent, contrary to Article 17 of the Firearms (NI) Order 1981; and possession of articles for a purpose connected with terrorism. The applicant was sentenced to concurrent terms of imprisonment of twelve years and two years respectively. The applicant appealed against his conviction on both charges. On 28 October 2004, the Court of Appeal in Northern Ireland unanimously dismissed the appeal. The non-disclosed material was not considered by the Court before it gave judgment. Instead, it considered the House of Lords ruling in R. v. H and C [2004] A.C. 134 (see paragraph 32 below) and reviewed this Court's judgments in Rowe and Davis and Jasper, both cited above. The judge dealing with an application fornon-disclosure must have a full understanding and appreciation on an ongoing basis of all the issues in the trial and in particular the nature of the defence. Court of Appeal finds that the applicant's defence of entrapment was well known to the trial judge, the prosecution, and the disclosure judge. No other issue had been identified that might sound on the question of disclosure. There was nothing to indicate that the material characterised as wholly irrelevant to the applicant’s defence might have suddenly become relevant. The trial judge did not read the statement of reasons given by the disclosure Judge before the first hearing. In general, it will be inappropriate for the trialJudge in a non-jury case to see it. In the present case the trial Judge made clear that he had not seen any material that was adverse to the [applicant] and [counsel for the applicant] did not dispute this statement. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 19 November 2004. It also refused to certify a point of law of general importance or grant leave to appeal to the House of Lords. It had the opportunity to assess the circumstances in which they came to be involved with the applicant. matters and had the chance to assess them as they gave their explanations as to the circumstances. of which they were involved. The appeal was dismissed and the case was dismissed from the Supreme Court of England and Wales. The decision was made after a hearing by the High Court of Justice in London in October 2004. The case was heard by the Supreme Court ofEngland and Wales in October and November 2004, and the Appeal was dismissed on November 19, 2004.
