The case originated in an application (no. 6684/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his trial for terrorism related offences was unfair because of the way the courts in Northern Ireland had approached the question of non-disclosure of prosecution papers to the defence on grounds of public interest immunity. He is currently detained at HMP Maghaberry, Northern Ireland. The Government were represented by their Agent, Ms E. Willmott of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The President of the Chamber to which the case had been allocated decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the case at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was arraigned on 8 June 2001 and pleaded not guilty to one count of possession of firearms and ammunition with intent. A defence statement was served on his behalf on 12 June 2001. He claimed that he may have been entrapped by a person known to him working with the police either for the purpose of incriminating him or his co-defendant. On 21 September 2001, the prosecution informed the applicant that it would apply ex parte for an order preventing disclosure. In non-jury trials in Northern Ireland, such an application is made to a judge other than the trial judge. That judge is designated by the Lord Chief Justice of Northern Ireland and is referred to as the ‘disclosure judge’ The disclosure judge allowed the prosecution's application for non-disclosure. He outlined this Court's judgments in Rowe and Davis v. the United Kingdom [GC], no. 28901/95, §§6 60-62, ECHR 2000‑II. The majority took the view that it was important for the trial judge to see the material personally. In the case of a non-jury trial it is obviously undesirable that prejudicial material which is not going to be part of the evidence in the case should be seen by the judge who will be tribunal of fact, especially if it is not disclosed to the defence. There was considerable debate in [Rowe and Davis] about the best way to deal procedurally with this situation. The judge ruled that none of the material was likely to undermine the case for the prosecution or to assist the accused's defence. The trial judge then suggested that one way of proceeding would be to appoint special counsel who would be shown the material and remain throughout the trial. The judge then ruled that it was not in the public interest to disclose the material. The decision will remain confidential to the prosecutor and the trial judge. The disclosure judge had said that there were items which were capable of having a prejudicial effect on the trial if seen by the trial judge. The trial judge found that the disclosure judge was best equipped to know what procedural safeguards could be put in place as to the non-disclosed material. In an ex tempore judgment he ruled: “There is no further safeguard that I am aware of that would be of any assistance, that one could conceive would be any assistance at this stage, and that is why I refer the matter back to the disclosureJudge’s decision.” The disclosure judge said there were two types of material involved. I would not regard the case as requiring the appointment of special counsel. I cannot foresee any circumstance in which the undisclosed material would be of assistance to the defence. But it may be that the defence may advance a proposition or raise an issue that might by remote possibility make that so, and I think if the Crown concedes that that is the position then the Crown should make the matter known to the trial judge and consideration could be given then to referring back to me. H and C [2004] A.C. 134 (see paragraph 32 below) and reviewed this Court's judgments in Rowe and Davis and Jasper, both cited above; Fitt v the United Kingdom [GC], no. 29777/96, ECHR 2000‑II; Edwards and Lewis v. the United UK, nos. 39647/98 and 40461/98, 22 July 2003 and Dowsett v the. United Kingdom, no. 39482/98,. ECHR 2003‑VII. Court of Appeal found that the applicant's defence of entrapment was well known to the trial judge, the prosecution, and the disclosure judge. The disclosure judge had been unable to envisage any circumstances in which the non-disclosed material could assist the defence. No new line of defence ever emerged that might have prompted a reconsideration of the decision that the material did not assist the applicant. The judge did not read the statement of reasons given by the disclosureJudge before the first hearing on the question of disclosure. The trial judge made clear that he had not seen any material that was adverse to the [applicant] and [counsel for the applicant] did not dispute this statement. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and refused to certify a point of law of general importance. It also refused to grant leave to appeal to the House of Lords. The appeal was dismissed on 19 November 2004. The court had the opportunity to assess the circumstances in which the case was brought to light. The arguments were heard in front of a panel of judges, who then gave their reasons for the decision. The case was dismissed and the appeal was thrown out by the court of appeal on 18 November 2004, with the decision to be appealed to the Court of Lords on 25 November. name: Hüsamettin Keskin
train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) by a Turkish national. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) and joined to other applications against the same respondent State. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’. consent, the Court ruled that the application should be joined to the other applications raising the same complaints (applications nos. 26480/95, 28291/95 and 29280/95) The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The Court of Cassation quashed the applicant’s conviction on the ground that he should have been convicted of the offence. The Ankara Assize Court decided in 1997 that the criminal proceedings against the applicant should be discontinued since the prosecution was time-barred. The case was heard at the Turkish Court of Human Rights, the highest court in the country. The applicant was granted bail until the end of the trial in October 2014. The application for bail has now been returned to the applicant.

The case originated in an application (no. 32987/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ documents, the Court ruled in favor of the applicant. The case was heard by the European Court of Justice. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way). The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. In a judgment of 24 August 1988 the Martial Law Court convicted the applicant on account of his involvement in the Dev Yol. It sentenced the applicant to fifteen years’ imprisonment, permanently debarred him from employment in the civil service. In July 1995 the Court of Cassation quashed the applicant’s conviction on the ground that he should have been convicted of the offence. The Ankara Assize Court decided that the criminal proceedings against the applicant should be discontinued since the prosecution was time‑barred.

name: Orhan Akgül
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 65897/01) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was taken into custody by police officers from the Anti-Terror branch of the Izmir Security Directorate on suspicion of aiding and abetting an illegal organisation, namely the PKK (the Kurdistan Workers’ Party) The applicant denied the veracity of his signed statements taken in detention, alleging that they had been obtained under duress. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate a specific Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 4 October 2005 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. The applicant was charged with making statements under duress. He asked the court to dismiss the charges and release him. The court dismissed his request and ordered his continued detention on remand. On 13 October 1999 the State Security Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment under Article 169 of the Criminal Code. On 9 October 2000 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment. Two days later, this decision was pronounced in the absence of the applicant’s representative. As required by law, the decision was deposited with the registry of the Izmir State Security court for the applicant to review. The decision was returned to the applicant in November 2000.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) The applicant was taken into custody by police officers from the Anti-Terror branch of the Izmir Security Directorate. He was charged with aiding and abetting an illegal organisation, namely the PKK (the Kurdistan Workers’ Party), contrary to Article 169 of the Criminal Code. The applicant denied the veracity of his signed statements taken in detention, alleging that they had been obtained under duress. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Grand National Assembly amended Article 143 of the Constitution and excluded military members from State Security Courts. The military judge hearing the applicant’s case was replaced by a civilian judge. On 13 October 1999 the State Security Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment under Article 169 of the Criminal Code. On 9 October 2000 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment. Two days later, this decision was pronounced in the absence of the applicant's representative. The decision was deposited with the registry of the Izmir State security Court for the applicant to review. The applicant was found guilty and sentenced to 3 years in prison.

name: Władysław Krzych
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35615/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) by two Polish nationals, Mr Władysław Krzych and Mr Tadeusz Gurbierz. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Agent Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicants appealed against the judgment. The court quashed the impugned judgment and remitted the case. The applicants were convicted in 2002 and sentenced to suspended prison terms. The trial court held hearings in May, July and November 2001. Subsequently, hearings were held at year-long intervals: in October 2002 and September 2003. The applicants appealed. On 14 December 2004 the Katowice Court of Appeal dismissed the complaints. On 21 February 2005 the Gliwice Regional Court dismissed their appeal against the judgment of 28 September 2004. The judgment is final. The court examined the course of the impugned proceedings only as regards the period between 2002 and 2004 when the case had been pending before the District Court. It further held that the trial courts could not be held responsible for delays caused by the absence of witnesses or illness of the parties.

name: Nazif Töre
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 48095/99) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the applicant's right to a fair trial by an independent and impartial tribunal to the Government. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) and the case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section. The applicant was born in 1964 and lives in Istanbul. In 1988 the applicant was convicted of membership in an illegal organisation, namely the Marxist-Leninist Communist Party. The applicant was imprisoned, in total, for about six years and six months. On 10 October 2002 the applicant's representative informed the Court that the applicant was released from prison due to ill-health pursuant to Article 399 of the Criminal Procedure Code. On 30 November 1998 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the Malatya State Security Court without conducting a hearing. The applicant's lawyer was absent without justification. He was sentenced to life imprisonment and was released in October 2002 because of ill- health. He has since returned to prison and is serving his sentence in a prison in Yekaterinburg. He is currently serving his life sentence.

name: Wendy Costello-Roberts
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 7 December 1991. It originated in an application (no. 13134/87) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 17 January 1986. On 24 January 1992 the President of the Court decided that, pursuant to Rule 21 para. 6 and in the interests of the proper administration of justice, this case and the case of Y v. the UK should be heard by the same Chamber. Following a friendly settlement, the case was struck out of the list by a judgment dated 29 October 1992 (Series A no. 247-A) In September 1985 Mrs Costello-Roberts sent the applicant, who was then aged seven, to an independent boarding preparatory school in Barnstaple, Devon. The school had approximately 180 pupils, none of whose fees were paid out of public funds, and received no direct financial support from the Government. In September 1992, the applicant was allowed to attend the school. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 September 1992. The Court heard addresses by Mr Bratza for the Government, by Sir Basil Hall for the Commission, and by Ms Beale for the applicant. The Government’s representative was given the opportunity to make a statement to the Court. The headmaster of a school in Strasbourg gave the pupil three ‘whacks’ on the bottom through his shorts with a rubber-soled shoe. The pupil had received five demerit marks for talking in the corridor and for being a little late for bed on one occasion. The headmistress of the school wrote to the Governors of the School to express her ‘grave concern’ over the use of corporal punishment. The school had initially denied that the pupil had been punished, but later admitted that he had been ‘slippered’ by the headmaster. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights, which ruled in favour of the pupil’s right to be punished. The applicant’s mother complained to the police some time between 4 and 16 November 1985, but was told that there was no action they could take without any visible bruising. A complaint by her to the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children received a similar response. It was argued in Strasbourg, on behalf of the applicant, that he had been extremely disturbed by the slippering, which turned him from a confident, outgoing seven-year-old into a nervous and unsociable child. The Government contended that, according to their information, any change in the child's character during his time at the school was more likely to be caused by his inability to adjust to the constraints of boarding-school life.

name: Sidney Elmer Golder
train_texts: The Golder case was referred to the Court by the Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. The application was first submitted in 1969; it was supplemented in April 1970 and registered under no. 4451/70. The Government’s application, which was made under Article 48 (art. 48) of the Convention, was lodged with the registry of the Court on 27 September 1973. The purpose of the application is to submit the case for judgment by the Court. The five judges chosen were MM. R. Cassin, R. Rodenbourg, A. Favre, T. Vilhjálmsson and W. Ganshof van der Meersch. The Government should file a memorial within a time-limit expiring on 3l January 1974. The Delegates should be entitled to file a. memorial in reply within two months of the receipt of the Government’s memorial. The public hearings took place on 11 and 12 October 1974 in the Human Rights Building at Strasbourg. Sir Gerald Fitzmaurice, who had been elected a member of the Court in January 1974 in place of Sir Humphrey Waldock, took his seat in the Court as the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the Convention and Rule 2 para. 3) (art. 43) The Chamber decided under Rule 48 to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. Mr. Balladore Pallieri, assumed the office of President. Sidney Elmer Golder was convicted in 1965 of robbery with violence. In 1969 he was serving a sentence in Parkhurst Prison on the Isle of Wight. A serious disturbance occurred in a recreation area of the prison where Golder happened to be. On 26 October Golder, together with other prisoners suspected of having participated in the disturbance, was segregated from the main body of prisoners. On 28 and 30 October he was interviewed by police officers. At the second of these interviews he was informed that it had been alleged that he had assaulted a prison officer. He was warned that “the facts would be reported in order that consideration could be given whether or not he would be prosecuted’. Officer Laird made two statements about Golder during the riot. Golder was returned to his ordinary cell the same day. On 20 March 1970, Golder addressed a petition to the Secretary of State for the Home Department, that is, the Home Secretary. He requested a transfer to some other prison and added: “I understand that a statement wrongly accusing me of participation in the events of 24th October last, made by Officer Laird, is lodged in my prison record.“ Those entries were expunged from the prison record in 1971 during the examination of the applicant’s case by the Commission. "I would respectfully request permission to consult a solicitor with a view to taking civil action for libel in respect of this statement," he said. "I would accept her assurance that this statement is not part of my record and be willing to accept then that the libel against me has not materially harmed me except for the two weeks I spent in the separate cells" The Prison Rules 1964 are laid before Parliament and have the status of a Statutory Instrument. The relevant provisions concerning communications between prisoners and persons outside prison are contained in Rules 33, 34 and 37 as follows: “Letters and visits generally Rule 33 (1) The Secretary of State may ... impose restrictions, either generally or in a particular case, upon the communications to be permitted between a prisoner and other persons.” Golder was released from prison on parole on 12 July 1972. The Government made objection to this opinion of the Commission but stated in their memorial that they no longer wished to argue the issue. The Commission expressed the opinion that the restrictions imposed by the present practice of the United Kingdom authorities are inconsistent with Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention. The right of access to the courts is not qualified by the requirement “within a reasonable time’. Golder was sentenced to 15 years in prison, suspended for five years, and sentenced to 12 years in jail, suspended indefinitely, and fined £1,000. The Government submit that in consequence the refusal of the United Kingdom Government to allow the applicant in this case to consult a lawyer was not a violation of Article 6 (art. 6) of the Convention. The right of access to the courts is not unlimited in the case of persons under detention, and that accordingly the imposing of a reasonable restraint was permissible in the interest of prison order and discipline. The Government also submit that control over the applicant’s correspondence while he was in prison was a necessary consequence of the deprivation of his liberty. The questions to which the Court is requested to reply are the following: (1) Does Article 6 para. 6-1 secure to persons desiring to institute civil proceedings a right ofaccess to courts? (2) If Article. 6 is found to confer on the applicant a right to access to courts, does the Court find that the rights conferred by Article 6 include in general a right-of-access to Courts? Can a convicted prisoner who wishes to write to his lawyer in order to institute civil proceedings rely on the protection given in Article 8 (art. 8) of the Convention to respect for correspondence? If so, do the facts of the present case disclose the existence of a violation of Article 6 and of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights? If the answers given to the foregoing questions are correct, does this constitute a violation, as set out in the answers to the questions above? If not, what is the basis for such a violation and how does this relate to the case at hand? If it is found to be the case, does the answer to the above questions indicate a breach of the rights of the prisoner in question, and if so, how so?

The application was first submitted in 1969; it was supplemented in April 1970 and registered under no. 4451/70. On 9 October 1973, the then President of the Court drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of five of the seven judges called upon to sit as members of the Chamber. The five judges chosen were MM. R. Cassin, R. Rodenbourg, A. Favre, T. Vilhjálmsson and W. Ganshof van der Meersch. The case was heard in Strasbourg on 11 and 12 October 1974. Sir Gerald Fitzmaurice was elected a member of the Court in January 1974 in place of Sir Humphrey Waldock. G. Balladore Pallieri assumed the office of President of the Chamber in accordance with Rule 21 para. 5. The Chamber decided under Rule 48 to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. The Government's memorial was received at the registry on 6 March 1974 and that of the Commission - with observations by the applicant’s counsel annexed - on 26 July. The public hearings took place in the Human Rights Building at Strasbourg. There appeared before the Court: Mr P. Fifoot, Legal Counsellor, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Barrister-at-Law, Agent and Counsel, Sir Francis Vallat, K.C.M.G., Q.C., Professor of International Law. Sidney Elmer Golder was convicted in 1965 of robbery with violence. He was sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. In 1969 he was serving his sentence in Parkhurst Prison on the Isle of Wight. On the evening of 24 October 1969, a serious disturbance occurred in a recreation area of the prison where Golder happened to be. On 26 October Golder, together with other prisoners suspected of having participated in the disturbance, was segregated from the main body of prisoners. On 28 and 30 October he was interviewed by police officers. At the second of these interviews he was informed that it had been alleged that he had assaulted a prison officer; he was warned that ‘the facts would be reported in order that consideration could be given’ Officer Laird made two statements about Golder after the riot. He said Golder was present with Frazer, Frape and Noonan, when the three latter were attacking me. But he added: "I am not certain that he made an attack on me" On 7 November, another prison officer reported that: “... during the riot of that night I spent the majority of the time in the T.V. room with the prisoners who were not participating in the disturbance. 740007“ No such charge was eventually preferred against him and the entries in his prison record were marked “charges not proceeded with’ “I would respectfully request permission to consult a solicitor with a view to taking civil action for libel in respect of this statement .... name: Anthony Wakeling
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 61395/00) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court decided to adjourn the applicant’s complaint in relation to his claims for Widow's Benefits and Widows’ Bereavement Allowance and to declare the remainder of the application inadmissible. The applicant was represented by Ms P. Glynn, a lawyer practising in London. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr C. Whomersley of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London. The applicant received incapacity benefit in the sum of GBP 240.80 per month. On 3 January 2001 the applicant wrote to the Inland Revenue asking for his appeal claim to be left open pending a domestic decision on the matter. On 30 November 2000 the applicant made a further claim for WBA which was rejected on 25 December 2000. On 25 January 2001, the applicant asked that the appeal claim should be closed pending a decision on his appeal. The appeal claim was rejected. The applicant appealed the decision and received GBP240.80 in incapacity benefits. He was awarded a total of £8,000 in benefits.

name: Aziz Aydın Arslan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28353/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Mr Aziz Aydın Arslan (‘the applicant’) was born in 1957 and lives in Istanbul. In 1988 the applicant was recruited by Türkiye Emlak Bankası A.Ş., a state-owned bank (hereinafter ‘the Bank’). In 1991 he was appointed to the post of deputy director in charge of credit cards. An investigation was carried out as a result of fraudulent acts in the Topkapı branch of the Bank. Criminal proceedings were brought against the director of the Topkapı branch of the Bank and three other persons for having committed a fraud. The applicant and the Bank intervened in these proceedings as a third party. On 9 July 1999 the Bakırköy Assize Court in Istanbul convicted the director and sentenced him to one year’s imprisonment for having abused his duty. It however acquitted the other accused. On 29 May 2001 the Court of Cassation quashed the above judgment. On 31 December 2004 the Bak Turkey Assize court terminated the criminal proceedings against the. director since they were time-barred. The. applicant appealed against this judgment arguing that the punishment imposed on the director was lenient.

The prosecution offered no evidence in respect of the burglary charge and a not guilty verdict was recorded. The trial judge’s summing up to the jury contained the following direction: “We all know this is a horrific, a disgusting episode. We all know that, and we all know – there has not been any argument about this, has there? – where moral responsibility lies. ... We are not here to dish out admonitions for immoral conduct, disgusting behaviour. We are here to judge whether a crime has been committed, whether the criminal law of the land has been broken" The jury acquitted the applicant of the three remaining charges. The first applicant applied for his costs (which exceeded GBP 100,000 and had been met by his family) The trial judge said: ‘With regard to a defendant’s costs you [Counsel] are right, the costs should and almost invariably would follow the event. I cannot think of another case in my 35 years’ experience in the criminal courts in which it is more apparent that a defendant's conduct, albeit that it had led to him being acquitted, had led him to be brought before the court. It is one of those cases where I feel it is right for the court to exceptionally say a defendants’ costs order will be refused’ The tape was made in 2005 when the police began investigating a suspected theft. The second woman in the recording was charged with conspiring to steal. She denied the allegations and said the tape had been taken out of context. The case was settled out of court in 2007 and the case is still ongoing. The jury is still deciding whether or not to order the tape to be made public. It is believed to have been made in response to allegations of theft by the second woman. The first woman was the victim of an alleged theft from her mother-in-law. She was also the target of a criminal investigation into the alleged theft of £1.5 million. The second applicant was acquitted unanimously of the two counts facing her. Three defendants, including A.R. and C.R., were convicted of the majority of the charges against them. The trial judge refused the application for a defendant’s costs order, pursuant to section 16(2) of the Prosecution of Offences Act 1985 (see relevant domestic law and practice below) He stated: ‘The relevant features, in my judgment, in this case are these: that [the second applicant], acting very much on the advice of her then solicitor [name omitted], exercised her right to silence when answering ‘no comment’ in her police interview’ On 30 July 2007, the second applicant renewed her application in writing, relying inter alia on the fact the she had been unable to recall the conversation on the tape recording until the trial had started. The trial judge declined to hold an oral hearing on the renewed application and stated that he was unable to make the order for the reasons he had already given. In no way is that decision meant to indicate that she is in any way guilty of this offence, she is not, she has rightly been acquitted by this jury.“I have come to the conclusion that to that extent she brought this prosecution upon herself and in my judgment that is a proper reason for refusing a defendant’s costs order.”

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 76299/01) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, firstly Mr K. The court decided to admit evidence from experts in sexology and from experts attached to the Family Diagnostic and Consultation Centre (Rodzinny Ośrodek Diagnostyczno-Konsultacyjny) The court also requested the applicant's doctor A.S.K. for the medical records on his past treatment for sexual problems be admitted as evidence. The Warsaw Regional Court delivered its judgment on 26 May 1999, finding both parties at fault for the breakdown of the marriage. It further awarded the custody of their daughter to both parties and established her place of residence at her mother’s address. It also fixed a new amount of child maintenance to be paid by the applicant. Both parties appealed against the judgment. The applicant's further appeal was dismissed by the Warsaw Court of Appeal on 8 August 2000. The respondent for the first time consented to the divorce but demanded that the applicant be declared responsible for the break-up of their marriage. The court found that no appeal lay against this decision. Warsaw Court of Appeal dismissed the parties’ appeals against the judgment of 26 May 1999 and quashed ex-officio rulings in respect of the child who had in the meantime reached the age of majority. Case originated in an application (no. 76299/01) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Mr Sławomir Wróblewski (‘the applicant’) was born in 1955 and lives in Warszawa. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The Polish Government were represented by their Agents, firstly Mr K. Drzewicki and subsequently by Mr J. Wołąsiewicz. A hearing was held on 22 August 1994. The Warsaw Regional Court prohibited the applicant from introducing third persons into his house and registering them there as residents. The court refused the applicant’s request for a reduction of child maintenance. On 29 December 1994 the Warsaw Court of Appeal amended the decision of 30 August 1994 finding that the applicant could not be prevented from registering as residents his own children and their mother. The applicant's attorney renewed his request to appoint a court expert in sexology. The respondent requested an increase of the child maintenance award. Both parties appealed and the appeals were dismissed. The case was settled out of court in 1997. The Warsaw Regional Court delivered its judgment on 26 May 1999, finding both parties at fault for the breakdown of the marriage. It further awarded the custody of their daughter to both parties and established her place of residence at her mother’s address. Both parties appealed against the judgment. The applicant's further appeal was dismissed by the Warsaw Court of Appeal on 8 August 2000. On 17 January 2000 the presiding judge refused to entertain the applicant's appeal. The court also fixed a new amount of child maintenance to be paid by the applicant. The judge ruled that no appeal lay against this decision, the court finding that no case could lay against it. Warsaw Court of Appeal dismissed the parties’ appeals against the judgment of 26 May 1999 and quashed ex-officio rulings in respect of the child. The judgment became final on 8 December 2000. The child who had in the meantime reached the age of majority became a fully-fledged member of the family. The court ruled in favour of the parents and the child was given a new name. The case was settled out of court, and the case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) in Strasbourg, France, in 1999. The ECHR ruled that the child should be awarded the right to live in Poland for the rest of his life, and that he should be allowed to leave the country for good.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 12253/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant’s testators owned a piece of real property in Warsaw. By virtue of the 1945 Decree on the Ownership and Use of Land in Warsaw (Dekret o własności i użytkowaniu gruntów na obszarze m. st. Warszawy) all land in Warsaw was nationalised. The applicant's testators filed an application for the grant of a right of perpetual use of the real property. The applicant lodged a complaint about inactivity on the part of the Mayor of the Warsaw District with the Supreme Administrative Court. The legal regime governing compensation for the expropriation of detached houses had not changed since 1957. If a valid decision had been taken in 1972, a re‑examination of the case between the same parties and about the same claim was inadmissible. The applicant appealed against this decision. On 21 December 2004 the applicant instituted administrative proceedings in order to have a plot of land on which the real property was situated restored to her. The case file shows that the relevant proceedings are still pending before the Minister of Infrastructure.
